Most of these characters are each a token, and you can insert any amount of space between these tokens without changing the meaning of the program. However, there are a few combination characters that only retain their meaning if they are written together—and thus count as a token. Pay particular attention to <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> as well as <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp>, which were originally used to perform arithmetic operations, but which have been given additional meanings in C++.

When it comes to truth values, you will encounter <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> as well as <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>. In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp> are also important for navigating in nested data structures. All other (special) characters are each a separate token. These include, for example, the following: <samp class="listingcharacter">+ - * / = % , . ( ) [ ] { } < > : ;</samp>.

The main reason that you should know where the tokens are in your source code is that you can omit and insert spaces without changing the meaning of the program. This is because you can insert any spaces, tabs, and line breaks between tokens.

Exceptions are the literals: with these, you write a fixed value directly into the source code. This can be an integer such as <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp>, a floating-point number such as <samp class="listingcharacter">99.95</samp>, or a text such as <samp class="listingcharacter">"Donald E. Knuth"</samp>—and for all of these there are also variants in the notation. I will go into more detail in the discussion of the respective data types in [Section 4.4](#04_004.html_h4.4), where I discuss their literals in detail. Literals can sometimes look as if they consist of several tokens but count as a single one.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/33cc3xfo6
#         include <iostream>       // # must be at the beginning of the line
int            main(
    ){
    std::cout
<<"This is "
        "text with <brackets>\n"   // string literal interrupted by new line
        ;
        /*type:*/ int
        /*Variable:*/ a_Value
        /*Init:*/ = 100;              // inner comments
std::cout<<a_Value<<"\n";}         // no spaces 
```

**Listing 4.3**     A very unusually formatted piece of source code.

It becomes tricky when a construct is composed of several identifiers. For example, in <samp class="listingcharacter">std::sin()</samp> there is the scope resolution operator <samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp>. With templates, you will encounter pairs of angle brackets <samp class="listingcharacter"><...></samp>—for example, in <samp class="listingcharacter">numeric_limits<int>::max()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">map<int,string></samp>. All elements are individual valid identifiers, but only together do they form a unit.

### 4.2.2    Comments

You have already seen comments with <samp class="listingcharacter">//</samp>. If there is not enough space to the end of the line, you can also have a comment extend over several lines by starting it with <samp class="listingcharacter">/*</samp> and ending it with <samp class="listingcharacter">*/</samp>. For example, like you see in the next example.

```
int main() {
    /* My first program. It was
        written by Max Muster.*/
    return /* The zero of success */ 0;
} 
```

**Listing 4.4**     Comments with <samp class="listingcharacter">/*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*/</samp> can extend over several lines or interrupt a program line.

And because such a comment is delimited by <samp class="listingcharacter">*/</samp>, the program code can then continue on the same line, as you can see in the line with <samp class="listingcharacter">return 0;</samp>.

Within the comment, <samp class="listingcharacter">//</samp> may also occur. If you mainly use <samp class="listingcharacter">//</samp> for comments in your program, you can easily disable entire blocks of code in this way by enclosing the range with <samp class="listingcharacter">/*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*/</samp>—and reenabling it by removing it. The compiler would also swallow combinations such as <samp class="listingcharacter">/* /*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">// */</samp>, but it is better to avoid all such embeddings; they confuse the reader and yourself.

In the examples in this book, I prefer to use <samp class="listingcharacter">/*...*/</samp> comments when I want to add text to the program code itself—without reference to this book. For example, in [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2), I introduce program sections as follows:

```
/* Output divider */
... 
```

and

```
/* Determine number */
... 
```

### 4.2.3    Functions and Arguments

Don't be confused by the fact that the variable is named <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> when the function is called but is then called <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> inside the <samp class="listingcharacter">calculate</samp> function. As in mathematics, functions are defined in such a way that they provide their parameters with names under which you then use them—but what they are called with is a completely different matter. In mathematics, you can also have functions such as f(x) = x² + 2, sin(x), or compound interest.

![inline image](bilder/formula-04_01.png)

These functions all assign their own names to be used in the formula. You do not have to use these names when using them:

*   g(z) = z³ – 2 · f(z): For a nice curve, <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">f(x)</samp>.

*   sin(π): Here <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is the number π.

*   CompoundInterest(1000, 12, 3): Dollar gets the value 1000 in the function, Years gets 12, and Interest 3.

Back to the C++ function from [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2). As a reminder, it looks like the following example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/E4W9KhbnK
void calculate(int n) {                            // a separate function
    using namespace std;                           // for std::cout and std::endl
    /* output divisors */
    cout << " divisors of " << n << " are:\n";
    for(int divider=1; divider <= n; ++divider) {  // instead of divider=divider+1
        if(n % divider == 0)
            cout << divider << ", ";
    }
    cout << endl;
} 
```

**Listing 4.5**     A custom C++ function.

In the function itself, compared to [Listing 4.1](#04_001.html_l4.1), from <samp class="listingcharacter">/* Output divisors */</samp> everything is almost identical. You will actually only find an alternative notation to <samp class="listingcharacter">divider = divider + 1</samp> in the increment part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">for loop</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">++divider</samp>. So far, you have used the assignment. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">++divider</samp> is used as a side effect operator to change the value of <samp class="listingcharacter">divider</samp>.

### 4.2.4    Side Effect Operators

In [Listing 4.5](#04_002.html_l4.5), I used <samp class="listingcharacter">++divider</samp> to increase the variable by one.

This is the prefix operator <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp>, which normally increases a variable by one (“increments”). This results in an expression whose value is the value of the variable increased by one. The result of the expression is unimportant in the update part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, but you can use the value within a more complex expression, as in the next example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/4Mr6fnaEr
#include <iostream> // cout
int main() {
    int basis = 2;
    int index = 10;
    int number = 3 * (basis + ++index) - 1;  // index is incremented first
    std::cout << number << '\n';             // Output: 38
} 
```

**Listing 4.6**     Prefix operators are executed before the calculation.

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> is first increased by one and the new value <samp class="listingcharacter">11</samp> is used in the further calculation.

If you change the value of a variable within an expression, this is a side effect. Never change the same variable twice within a statement with side effects!

```
int value = 0;
std::cout << ++value << ++value << ++value;  // no more than one ++value 
```

The compiler will allow it, but the program may have different results on different systems. On a Mac I got “123” once here, on a Linux system “321”—and both are correct.

As you will see in [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), you cannot always rely on the order in which expressions are evaluated. Therefore, you must not use such constructs. In C++, this minor inconvenience is accepted because it allows the compiler flexibility, which leads to better performance.

In [Table 4.1](#04_002.html_t4.1), I have listed the side effect operators.

I recommend that if you have the choice, you prefer the first two variants (prefix operators). This is because the last two variants (postfix operators) are generally more complex because the computer has to remember the old value in a temporary variable.

| Operator | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">++var</samp> | As seen, <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> increases by one and returns the new value. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">--var</samp> | Decreases <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> by one and returns the new value. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">var++</samp> | Increases <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> by one and returns the old value. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">var--</samp> | Decreases <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> by one and returns the old value. |

**Table 4.1**     Prefix and postfix side effect operators.

There is also the family of side effect assignments. All arithmetic operations are available in these variants; all are expressions and therefore have a value that you can use as part of a larger expression. However, they are not usually used as expressions, but as instructions like a simple assignment:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/r5hjrqqK9
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    int var = 10;
    var += 2;
    var *= 3;
    var /= 4;
    var -= 5;
    std::cout << var << "\n"; // results in 4
} 
```

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>, there are a few others that I will refer to in [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3) in more detail.

### 4.2.5    The “main” Function

Let me briefly simplify the smaller example program even further so that almost only <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> remain.

```
int main() {
    if(2 < 1) return 1;    // one return
    return 0;              // other return
}                          // end of main 
```

**Listing 4.7**     A program that consists only of main and return.

Now you can see that <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> is also just a function—but a special function: every executable C++ program must have exactly one <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> function, because this is where the execution of the main part of what your program is supposed to do begins.

Without <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, the compiler and computer do not know where to enter the program. Only if you write a module or a library will you not have a <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> function. If you then combine all the modules into a finished program, one of the modules—exactly one—will contain <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>.

Put simply, the execution of your program begins with the first line of the <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> function, directly after the opening curly brace <samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp>. However, there are all kinds of tasks that have already been done for you beforehand. The initialization of global variables is one of them.

If your program runs without errors, it runs until it encounters one of the <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statements in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>. The number after the <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> is the return value of the function. Because <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> is a special function that is ultimately called by the surrounding operating system, this value has a special meaning. On Unix systems, a <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> means <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> that the program has run successfully and other programs can check this. And even on Windows, certain programs can signal success to other programs through the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>. While the convention is that <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> means success, all values other than <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> mean failure. Beyond that, there are no general rules, except that the most commonly used value for failure is <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>. There are also major differences in the possible value range between the systems, so you are on the safe side with values between <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">127.</samp>

A special feature of <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> is that you can omit the <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">return 0</samp>. You can even omit the whole line, in which case the program ends when the closing curly brace of <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> is reached. Both are possible in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>—but only here and nowhere else.

Speaking of the special features of <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, there is one more. As you can see in [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2) and [Listing 4.7](#04_002.html_l4.7), you can declare <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> in a short and a long form:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int main()</samp> or

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int main(int argc, const char* argv[])</samp>

If you are not interested in the call parameters of the executable program, opt for the first one. The second variant allows you to determine if users have invoked your program with arguments and to assess them accordingly.

Let's assume your program is called <samp class="listingcharacter">divisors.exe</samp>. In that case, (Windows) users can call up the program like this, for example:

```
$ divisors.exe 1001 
```

Here <samp class="listingcharacter">argc</samp> will have the value <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp>, and with <samp class="listingcharacter">argv[1]</samp> you can access <samp class="listingcharacter">1001</samp>.

There are only these two ways to define <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>. The form <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> is a shortcut in case you are not interested in the call parameters of the program.

### 4.2.6    Statements

Let's take a closer look at what's between the <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp> of our two functions: the statements. You already know that these are executed one after the other. This distinguishes them from expressions, for which the compiler can work its magic. Modern compilers and computers running your program do the craziest things to your program in the background, mainly to make it run faster. The only restriction on these transformations is that they must not change the meaning of the program. And this meaning is that the statements of your program are executed one after the other. This is exactly the difference from expressions, which are not executed in a certain order in this way. It is better to think that the expression takes on a value or that the computer evaluates it, but it does not execute it literally.

As a rule of thumb, a statement ends at its semicolon <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>. The most common exception to this rule is the statement block: the sequence of statements enclosed in curly braces.

In the next example, you can see an excerpt from the sample program as a reminder.

```
for(int divider=1; divider <= n; ++divider)  // for loop
{                                            // start of the loop block
    if(n % divider == 0)
        std::cout << divider << ", ";
}                                            // end of the loop block 
```

**Listing 4.8**     Here you only set the outer curly braces.

To make it clear once again: the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> is a single statement that goes from <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>. The same applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> branch. In the following listing, the condition part <samp class="listingcharacter">if(argc<=1)</samp> and the branching part up to the last <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp> belong integrally together and together form a single statement.

```
if(argc<=1) {                                // start of the if statement
    std::cout << "Enter a number: ";
    std::cin >> number;
    if(!std::cin) {
        return 1;
    }
} else {
    value = std::stoi(argv[1]);
}                                            // end of the if statement 
```

**Listing 4.9**     This is what it looks like if you set all curly brackets.

Why is this important? Because this makes it clear where the loop can be used and how far it extends. Formally, a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> always has the following format:

<samp class="listingcharacter">for(</samp> loop-variable-definition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> statement

And one of the formal possibilities for an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> branch is this:

<samp class="listingcharacter">if(</samp> condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> statement

As both of these are themselves statements, it is clear that I could have omitted some of the brackets in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> example. This is because statements can in turn contain statements. For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> statement block contains a single statement—namely, the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement.

```
for(int divider=1; divider <= value; ++divider)
    if(value % divider == 0)
        std::cout << divider << ", "; 
```

**Listing 4.10**     The “if” is a statement and does not actually require curly brackets.

This has the same meaning as the following:

```
for(int divider=1; divider <= value; ++divider) {
    if(n % divider == 0)
        std::cout << divider << ", ";
} 
```

However, it is good style not to omit the curly braces for <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>. It would have been really good style and also equivalent to use the <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp> of the statement block for <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> as well.

```
for(int divider=1; divider <= value; ++divider) {
    if(value % divider == 0) {
        std::cout << divider << ", ";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 4.11**     It is better to put individual statements in curly brackets.

And a little more clearly: there are different ways of writing where the brackets are placed. Some prefer them as the last character in the line with the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>; others put them on a separate line. As you have already read in the discussion of spaces, it does not matter whether you insert additional line breaks. It doesn't matter which of the options you choose, but it is certainly advantageous to follow one style consistently.

Although a semicolon belongs at the end of a statement, it should not be placed after the curly braces of a statement block. You have to be careful here, because unnecessary semicolons create an empty statement. This is harmless in most cases; for example, there are three empty statements between the semicolons in <samp class="listingcharacter">;;;;</samp> without any effect. But a semicolon after an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> means that the empty statement belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and ends it. In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << "smaller";</samp> no longer belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and is now always executed:

```
if(value<10) ;    //  a critical empty statement
    std::cout << "smaller"; 
```

It is therefore better not to enter any additional semicolons. Also make sure that you do not place a semicolon after the curly brackets of a statement block <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp>. Even if it has no direct effect, it is better to avoid the following superfluous semicolon:

```
if(value<10) {
    std::cout << "smaller";
} ;               //  also avoid harmless empty statements
std::cout << "next"; 
```

Somewhat annoyingly, I will tell you in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12) about <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> that you must end their definitions with a semicolon. So by way of anticipation, you will be writing <samp class="listingcharacter">struct type {...};</samp>, and omitting the semicolon here would be a mistake. The reason is that this is a definition that always ends with a semicolon: it is not a statement.

### 4.2.7    Expressions

The statements are joined by the expressions. Expressions occur in quite a few places in C++ programs—not least as part of statements, but also in many other places that are not statements.

An expression is “a sequence of operators and operands that perform a calculation.” This is so dry that it can only come from the text of the C++ language standard. But what does it mean?

It means that something like <samp class="listingcharacter">3+4</samp> is an expression in which <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">4</samp> are the operands and <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> is the operator. It can also get more complicated, such as in <samp class="listingcharacter">(3+4)*PI/sin(x)</samp>, where there are multiple operators and operands. Each operand must itself be a valid expression, and an expression is only valid if  it is complete. Therefore, 1+2+3+ is not an expression, because the last <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> is missing an operand. Similarly, 3+4) is not an expression because it is missing a parenthesis.

This example shows that expressions can be made up of smaller expressions. If you break <samp class="listingcharacter">(3+4)*PI/sin(x)</samp> apart, it contains the following expressions:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">(3+4) * PI / sin(x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">(3+4) * PI</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">sin(x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">(3+4)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">PI</samp> on the one hand, <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and even <samp class="listingcharacter">sin</samp> on the other

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">3+4</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">4</samp>

[![All subexpressions in one expression.](bilderklein/klein04_001.png)](img-f4.1.html)

**Figure 4.1**     All subexpressions in one expression.

In [Listing 4.1](#04_001.html_l4.1) and [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2), you will find all kinds of expressions, of which I can only list a few here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp> is a number literal—a number that is written directly into the source code.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">"Divisors of "</samp> is a text literal—a text directly in the source code.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << "Divisors of "</samp> is an expression that outputs to the screen (or writes to a file).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">value % divider</samp> calculates the remainder of the division <samp class="listingcharacter">value / divider</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">value % divider == 0</samp> checks whether this remainder was <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, and therefore <samp class="listingcharacter">divider</samp> is a divisor of <samp class="listingcharacter">value.</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> as part of <samp class="listingcharacter">return 0;</samp> is an expression that “calculates” the return of <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>.

In a few places, we have something other than an expression, and I will briefly discuss this here. <samp class="listingcharacter">int value = 100</samp> is not an  expression, but a declaration (<samp class="listingcharacter">int value</samp>) with an initialization (<samp class="listingcharacter">= 100</samp>). However, the initialization to the right of <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> must be an expression. <samp class="listingcharacter">Return 0</samp> is also not an expression, but a statement. It consists of the special word (keyword) <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> and, in this case, the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>.

One of the main characteristics of expressions is that each one has a well-defined type, and  this also applies to each subexpression. Because types are very important in C++, understanding the types of expressions is also an important step toward success with C++.

#### More about Statements and Expressions

Because statements and expressions are such elementary language elements, we dedicate a later chapter to them ([Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8)). Here you have been given an initial introduction and an overview.

### 4.2.8    Allocations

One of the most important expressions in C++ is the assignment. I did not mention assignment in the list of statements. That was not an oversight.

There are only a few assignments in [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2) apart from the initializations—namely, the following example.

```
value = std::stoi(argv[1]); 
```

**Listing 4.12**     Assigning the result of a function call.

And before I wrote <samp class="listingcharacter">++divider</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, it said what you see in the following example.

```
divider = divider + 1 
```

**Listing 4.13**     Assigning the result of a calculation.

In [Listing 4.12](#04_002.html_l4.12), <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> is assigned to the result of a function call. [Listing 4.13](#04_002.html_l4.13) contains a calculation whose result is assigned to the <samp class="listingcharacter">divider</samp> variable. The decisive factor is that the variable of the assignment already existed before and now receives a new value. This is done using the equals sign: the target of the assignment is on the left-hand side and an expression for the new value of the variable is on the right-hand side.

But an assignment falls into the category of expressions,  and you can therefore use it wherever expressions are permitted. The fact that an assignment is used like a statement without being further embedded in a larger expression is actually a special case—but quite common in the case of assignments, as you can see in [Listing 4.12](#04_002.html_l4.12) and [Listing 4.13](#04_002.html_l4.13).

In the following example, the use of an assignment as an expression becomes clearer.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/bh1MsPhje
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    int a = 3;
    int b = 7 + (a = 12) + 6;   // contains an assignment
    std::cout << a << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 4.14**     An assignment is an expression with the type of the assigned variable.

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">a = 12</samp> is the assignment. When executed, this expression has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp> and for the compiler the type of <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The variable <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> is therefore initialized with the calculation <samp class="listingcharacter">7 + 12 + 6</samp>.

You should not take this as an example and use assignments as expressions everywhere. The assignment then becomes an expression with a side effect if,  in addition to the main effect—changing <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>—another variable changes its value. We will later show you the few places where this is common in C++ and therefore there will be no surprises when reading and understanding.

#### Value versus Reference

In some programming languages, each variable is only a reference to an object. In Smalltalk, for example, this applies to all variables and in Java to everything that is derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. There, an assignment does not change the object itself, but only assigns another reference. For example, if you have <samp class="listingcharacter">string s = "a"; string t = "b";</samp> in Java, then <samp class="listingcharacter">s = t;</samp> is an assignment. Now <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> “point” to the same <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> object.

This is different in C++: an assignment is always made to the value of a variable. If you have <samp class="listingcharacter">string s = "a"; string t = "b";</samp> in C++, then the assignment <samp class="listingcharacter">s = t;</samp> copies the values of the variables. Without further precautions, you always work with values in C++, not with references. Yes, you can also work with references in C++, but you must make this clear. As you’ll learn later, you then use <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> for references and <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> for pointers and addresses.

### 4.2.9    Types

In C++, almost everything has a type. Variables and constants have a type, as do parameters and also functions, data, classes, and expressions. Types are everywhere.

The type determines how much memory the computer must provide for a variable or the intermediate result of an expression, what kind of values it can hold, how these values are to be interpreted in memory, and what operations are permitted on them.

The latter is a strength of C++. This is because the main work of the compiler consists of processing the type information. First, it determines the type and finds out which things are permitted for this type. These can be function calls, operations, or conversions. What is meant by this program code? When the compiler finds this out, it applies its selection and thus determines the type for the expression.

This is why type and value always belong together: they complement each other. Conceptually, the type only exists at translation time, as a tool for the compiler. When you start the translated program (runtime), the types have disappeared and only the values exist.[[ 4 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_01) So your program manipulates the values, and the compiler manipulates the types. Through its calculations, the compiler ensures that the desired operations on the values end up in the program.

You can determine the exact type of each (partial) expression. This depends on the operator and its operands. Sometimes it is easy to determine the type, sometimes not, but it is always possible. If it is difficult, you can get help from the computer. The right program for this is the C++ compiler! This is because it “calculates” the types of the expressions according to the rules specified by the C++ standard and your program.

If you already know other programming languages, then you may be familiar with less stringent type concepts than those of C++. Some languages (such as Python, PHP, or JavaScript) ignore them almost completely and work well with them in their respective domains. Other languages (such as Java or C) have types but see their use somewhat differently. In C++, you are much more likely to use types to let the compiler help you write a correct program.

For example, if the program says <samp class="listingcharacter">100+99</samp> somewhere, then for the compiler this is an operator <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> with two operands <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">99</samp>, each of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. According to the rules that the compiler has built in, a <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> with two <samp class="listingcharacter">int operands</samp> again results in a value of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and therefore the overall expression also has the type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. At this point, the compiler does not calculate with the concrete numbers <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">99</samp> and does not yet know anything about the meaning of <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, but it only applies knowledge “about” operands and operators—their types.

If you had the right teacher in physics lessons at school, this may sound familiar to you. To check whether your result was probably correct when dealing with long formulas, you could only calculate with the units of measurement and quantities instead of the concrete numbers (“dimensional analysis”). If you came up with the wrong unit of measurement, you had made a mistake (in the calculation or when checking).[[ 5 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_02)

For example:

![inline image](bilder/formula-04_02.png)

If you now want to know how much force is acting for a given mass of 8 kg, length of 12 m, and time of 4 s, then calculate 8 · 12/4 = 24 and kg × m/s at the same time and realize: “Oops, something's wrong with the seconds!” The correct calculation would have been 8 · 12/4² = 6, with the check kg × m/s²; that fits.

The compiler does something similar. You specify the rules of the calculation on types through the classes, functions, and templates of your program. These are supplemented by the standard library and other libraries that you use, as well as by the built-in rules. And just as dimensional analysis helped you in the physics exam, the compiler can help you to write a correct program by checking the type calculation rules, as in the next example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/9943MfExc
#include <vector>
class Image {
    std::vector<char> data_;
public:
    void load(const char* filename); // loads image data
};
class Screen {
public:
    void show(Image& image);         //  image should be const
};
void paint(Screen &screen, const Image& image) {
    screen.show(image);
}
int main() {
    Image image {};
    image.load("peter.png");
    Screen screen {};
    paint(screen, image);
} 
```

**Listing 4.15**     The compiler helps to write correct programs by checking the types.

The omission of “to the power of 2” in C++ corresponds perhaps to a missing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>: The screen <samp class="listingcharacter">Screen</samp> has a method <samp class="listingcharacter">show</samp> with which it paints an image. You would think that the image <samp class="listingcharacter">image</samp> would not be changed when painting. It is therefore likely that the type of the <samp class="listingcharacter">show</samp> parameter should have been <samp class="listingcharacter">const Image&</samp> rather than <samp class="listingcharacter">Image&</samp>.

A forgotten <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> alone is not yet critical, mind you. But what would happen if someone “accidentally” placed the call <samp class="listingcharacter">image.load("paul.png");</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">show</samp> method? That would change the image. This cannot happen with the <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> parameter: the compiler reports an error.

You should use type safety wherever you can. It represents one of the most powerful advantages of C++ over good old C. There, the transformations possible on types were (and are) much more restricted—and the checks much more succinct.

#### [Übung]  First Simple Types

Without perhaps realizing it, you have already dealt with all kinds of types in the small examples we have discussed. We will now cover the most important ones.

#### The “int” Type

In this chapter, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is a representative of all the types that you can use in C++ to represent integers—that is, negative integers, zero, and positive integers. However, a computer has limitations when it comes to its number range. With <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, you have a different number of bits available depending on the system. If you are working on a current system, it is probably 32 bits, but it could also be 16, 64, or a completely different number. With 32 bits, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> can store integers from about -2 billion to +2 billion. You can find out exactly with [Listing 23.29](#23_005.html_l23.29). If you want to cover other number ranges, you should take a closer look at the relatives <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> as well as <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> in [Section 4.4](#04_004.html_h4.4).

#### The “bool” Type

While an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> variable <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> can assume many states, a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> variable <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> is fixed to one of two states: <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>.

Comparisons are expressions whose result is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>, and you can store their result in a variable of this type instead of using it directly.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zK9Ke9n48
#include <iostream>                      // cout
int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    bool withParameters = argc > 1;      // comparison result stored
    if(withParameters) {                 // ... and used
        std::cout << "You have called the program with parameters.\n";
    }
    return 0;
} 
```

**Listing 4.16**     Variables of type <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> can store the result of a comparison.

#### The Types “const char*” and “std::string”

These two very different types have the same purpose: their variables represent strings—that is, text strings, like texts, messages, notes, names, and so on. Depending on the task, sometimes the “pointer variant” <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>, which cannot deny its origin in C, is suitable, and sometimes the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> “class“ <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> from the C++ standard library is suitable.

##### Pointers, Addresses, and Memory Areas

Note the asterisk <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>. This tells you: “I am only storing the address of something.” This means that there is a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> where the variable points to. There is also <samp class="listingcharacter">int*</samp> as a pointer to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and so on.

When it comes to character strings, however, another piece of information is missing because the pointer only contains the address of the first character; others may follow. In C, it is common for a text to extend to the next <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> with the value <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, also written <samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp>; this is then a C string. The C function <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(const char* fmt, ...)</samp> works in this way, for example.

Other functions prefer to take pointers and a length, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">memcpy(void* dest, const void* src, size_t n)</samp>. Here, starting from <samp class="listingcharacter">src</samp>, the next <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> bytes are copied to <samp class="listingcharacter">dest</samp>.

The third variant, using pointers to define a range, is often used in C++ for containers and algorithms. For example, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::find(const char* beg, const char* end, char c)</samp> to find the character <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> between <samp class="listingcharacter">beg</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp>.

If you only want to output a fixed character string, you usually work with <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> because in this form many program parts exchange character strings with each other. You have already seen the parameter for <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, which I described in [Listing 4.16](#04_002.html_l4.16) for the example <samp class="listingcharacter">argv</samp>. There, the system may bring several program arguments into the program in the form of <samp class="listingcharacter">const char* strings</samp>. And even if you write a string with <samp class="listingcharacter">"..."</samp> directly into the program text, the compiler stores this “string literal” as a <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> computer's memory. (More precisely, it is a <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp>, but this is very similar and should suffice at this point.) As long as you only want to output this text, as in

```
std::cout << "You have called the program with parameters.\n"; 
```

then you do not need to worry about this.

For most cases beyond that, I recommend that you use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> instead. If you want to save, copy, or manipulate strings, this is the best choice. Especially with regard to memory management—the dynamic creation of new strings—it is much easier to use the C++ class <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string.</samp>

For the sake of simplicity, a <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> literal is also used when initializing <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, but since C++14 you can also append an <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">"..."</samp> literal and thus turn it into a real <samp class="listingcharacter">string literal</samp>. To do this, however, the block must contain <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std::literals</samp> or one of the alternatives somewhere, as in the next example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/chTTqPjrM
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::cout << "string_literals\n";
    // using std::literals::string_literals::operator""s;
    // using namespace std::string_literals;
    // using namespace std::literals::string_literals;
    using namespace std::literals;
    std::cout << "Real string\n "s;
} 
```

**Listing 4.17**     This is how you can write a <samp class="listingcharacter">C++</samp> string as a literal in the source code.

This rarely makes a big difference but can sometimes be important.

Because you will be using <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> a lot (at least in this book), allow me to abbreviate it to <samp class="listingcharacter">string.</samp>

#### Parameterized Types

Some types contain angle brackets <samp class="listingcharacter"><...></samp> in their name. You have seen

```
std::vector<char> 
```

in the example. Even if this looks different from <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, the whole construct is still  a single type. The part in the brackets is a parameter to form the overall type. Here <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is the surrounding or main type, and <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is the parameter. Together, the two are a “<samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>.”

You could also form a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> and thus obtain a different type. This is important, for example, if the compiler is to decide which functions are available for selection or what the result of an operation is. As I have already mentioned, the compiler calculates with types in the translation phase; the program only calculates on the values at runtime.

One thing is particularly important here: with parameterized types, what is inside the angle brackets must always be known at compile time. This is only logical as the compiler calculates with types at compile time and the entire construct, consisting of the main type, brackets, and parameters, makes up the type. If you remember this, you will not be surprised when experimenting. For example, there is also the parameterized type <samp class="listingcharacter">std::array<...></samp>, which receives a number as the second template parameter. The number must be a constant or something that the compiler can already calculate, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">3+4</samp>. For example, you can write <samp class="listingcharacter">std::array<int,5></samp> but not <samp class="listingcharacter">int n=5; std:: array<int,n></samp>, because <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is a variable and as such cannot be part of the type.

##### Note

A type must be fixed at compile time.

#### Class Template Argument Deduction

You do not always have to specify the arguments of a parameterized type. If you call a constructor, the compiler can infer the types themselves, as in the next example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/GbbcnYbqv
std::vector vec { 1, 2, 3 };        // instead of vector<int>
std::tuple tpl { 5, 'x' };          // instead of tuple<int,char>
std::shared_ptr<int> ptr { new int(5) };
std::shared_ptr ptr2 { ptr };       // instead of shared_ptr<int> 
```

**Listing 4.18**     Since C++17, the compiler determines the type parameters of class templates based on the constructor arguments.

This allows you to keep your code concise and clear in some cases. However, this is not always possible; you will be naming the type parameters often enough yourself.

The class template argument deduction (CTAD) feature has been available since C++17\. You can read more about this in Listing 23.33\. If you are using an older compiler, write out the parameters of the types.

### 4.2.10    Variables: Declaration, Definition, and Initialization

It makes a difference whether you write

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int value;</samp>, a declaration;

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">value = 0;</samp>, one assignment; or

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int value = 0;</samp> a definition with initialization.

There are also variables that you can no longer change once they have been introduced. They are constant—and are then actually called constants. Apart from this fact, constants are also variables for the compiler—that is, a subset of them in terms of “set theory.” You can never reassign anything to them, so you only have the option of initializing them with a value when you declare them. I will go into more detail about <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> later, but you can probably guess the main purpose of this addition.

```
int main() {
    const int fest = 33;  // Initialization as constant
    fest = 80;            // an assignment is impossible
} 
```

**Listing 4.19**     You cannot assign anything to some variables; you can only initialize them.

There is another way in which you can distinguish between assignment and initialization or make them distinguishable yourself. With C++11, unified initialization was introduced. Wherever you initialize variables, you can now use curly brackets instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>.

```
int index = 1;        // old style, looks like an assignment
int zaehler { 1 };    // C++11 style, clearly an initialization
int counter = { 1 };  // in the C++11 style, the "=" is optional and is ignored 
```

**Listing 4.20**     Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp> for initialization.

There was previously a risk of confusion not only with the assignment, but also with a handful of other C++ constructs.

#### [Übung]  Risk of confusion()

This is a preview for things to come, but I'll give you an example. You can pass a temporary <samp class="listingcharacter">Thing</samp> to a function <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> that you initialize with the value <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp>—that is, call its constructor:

```
f(Thing(12)); 
```

If it is not intended to be temporary, for example, this works:

```
Thing d = Thing(12); 
```

For a constructor without arguments, this can be done in one of these ways:

```
f(Thing());
Thing d = Thing(); 
```

The following is also fine:

```
Thing d(12); 
```

You now have <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> that has been initialized with <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp>. Now you could conclude that you initialize such a <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> without constructor arguments like this:

```
Thing d();   //  Error: Declaration of d as a function 
```

And you would be wrong! You have now declared a function <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> that takes no arguments and returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Thing</samp>. Please note: You have declared it and not defined it. This is similar to <samp class="listingcharacter">int mydata();</samp> as a function declaration in a header file. As soon as you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> in any way, such as with <samp class="listingcharacter">d.print()</samp>, the compiler complains with the most obscure error messages, such as that “d has not yet been defined” or “a function call was expected.”

If you want to try it out, you don’t need a <samp class="listingcharacter">Thing</samp>. Try it with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/3G5Po9zEj
int main() {
    int d1(12);    // defines an int and initializes it with 12
    int b1 = d1+1;
    int d2();      //  declares a function d2 without parameters, return int
    int b2 = d2+1;
    int d3{};      // defines an int and initializes it with 0
    int b3 = d3+1;
} 
```

My error message today:

```
arithmetic on a pointer to the function type 'int ()' 
```

The solution is to consistently utilize <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp>, as <samp class="listingcharacter">Thing d{};</samp> does what you expect.

#### Old Equal Sign or Standardized Initialization?

The new initialization with <samp class="listingcharacter">{...}</samp> is supported by all current compilers. So you have a choice. The “old style” cannot be eradicated (and it is debatable whether this would make sense), but you should use the new style wherever you are not just initializing a native data type such as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. This will equip you for the tricky cases.

### 4.2.11    Initialize with “auto”

A word about initialization. It always consists of

*   the type of variable you are initializing,

*   the name of the variable, and

*   an expression for the first value of the variable.

The type of the expression is often the same as the type of the variable. Sometimes you let the compiler perform an implicit conversion. However, you can often save yourself the work of specifying the type of the expression again. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> instead. The compiler then takes the type of the expression to determine the variable type. This is called type inference:

```
auto number = 10;
auto value = 3.1415 * sin(alpha);
for(auto it = container.begin(); ... ) ... 
```

The variable <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> here becomes an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, while <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> becomes a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">it</samp> is of the type that <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> returns, probably an <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator</samp> of the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">container</samp>.

Since C++20, however, you can further restrict the type with a concept. This allows you to specify that the type of variable must fulfill certain criteria. Many concepts are available in the standard library for this purpose, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">integral</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">floating_point</samp>:

```
auto integral number = get_number();
auto floating_point pointy_number = get_ampere(); 
```

If there was only <samp class="listingcharacter">auto number</samp> here, then <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> could also be a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>—which would perhaps lead to problems with <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> in the further course of the calculation. On the other hand, if you were to completely define the type with <samp class="listingcharacter">int number</samp>, you would lose the option of extending the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">get_number()</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>. In addition, the line of code in question could also be in generic code, where the return type of <samp class="listingcharacter">get_number()</samp> can be <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, but you want to prevent <samp class="listingcharacter">get_number()</samp> from returning a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>.

The advantages of a concept together with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> are documentation and security against surprises.

In addition to the built-in concepts in the standard library, you can also define your own concepts.

Whether with a concept or without—<samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> defines the type of the variable as if you had explicitly written the type. It is by no means the case that <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> is its own mutable type. Once set, the variable retains its type.

The compiler determines the type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp>. A later assignment of a text literal is an error:

```
auto val = 12;
val = "Name";   // Error: Assignment of "const char*" to "int" 
```

You can find out exactly how <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> works in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12), [Section 12.12](#12_012.html_h12.12).

### 4.2.12    Details on the Include Directive

Includes always begin with a hash sign <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>. Such a character at the beginning of a line stands for an instruction to the preprocessor. If you remember [Chapter 2](#02_001.html_h2), [Figure 2.1](#02_001.html_f2.1), you are already familiar with this phase of the translation.

The file that is included here with <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> is inserted into your program by the preprocessor almost as if by copy and paste. The effect is that all declarations from that file are now part of your program.

There are other preprocessor directives, but <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> is the most important one for you. The others can be found in [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21).

Includes always belong at the top of your source files. In [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2), I have used two of them.

```
#include <iostream>  // cin, cout
#include <string>    // stoi 
```

Both <samp class="listingcharacter"><iostream></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><string></samp> are part of the C++ standard library. They therefore contain things that are not part of the core language. Something like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is always present on all systems without the need for an include. The standard library will usually be present—and we assume that it will be in this book—but not always.

As you introduce many identifiers into the current source code with <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp>, it is helpful to add a comment to indicate which of them you are using in this translation unit. This allows readers to find out where an unknown identifier comes from by simply searching the file. Some module names are self-explanatory. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">#include <vector></samp> imports <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>; there is no need to explain this.

You can recognize the includes of the standard library by the fact that the name does not have an extension such as <samp class="listingcharacter">.h</samp> or similar. The convention is that only header files of the standard library without an extension are used.[[ 6 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_03) If you create your own, then append an <samp class="listingcharacter">.h</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">.hpp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">.H</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">.hh</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">.hxx</samp>. In practice, <samp class="listingcharacter">.h</samp> is the most common, even if some programmers do not like this, as the header does not differ from C headers from the outside. The <samp class="listingcharacter">.hpp</samp> file extension is often chosen as an alternative. Regardless of which extension you use, you name it in the <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> directive:

```
#include <iostream>          // Module of the standard library
#include <asteroids.h>       // Module of a third-party provider
#include "myModule.hpp"      // Module of the current project
#include "algo/myModule.h"   // in a subdirectory 
```

Write the name of the header file in angle brackets if the file is installed on your system; the compiler should search for it. Use the quotation marks <samp class="listingcharacter">"..."</samp> if the header file is part of your current project and not installed somewhere. Some compilers then search for the file in the current project first.

#### Don'ts for Includes

Pay attention to upper- and lowercase when naming the file, as this is observed on some systems, dear Windows users! If the header file is located in a subdirectory, always use <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> to separate it:

```
#include "MY_MODULE.H"           //  not good if the file is called "myModule.h"
#include "algo\myModule.h"       //  also use "/" under Windows
#include "c:/project/myModule.h" //  no absolute paths
#include "../algo/myModule.h"    //  no relative paths with ".." 
```

Instead of using the absolute path or <samp class="listingcharacter">..</samp>, you should store the header files somewhere else in your project or/and must adjust the search paths for header files in the compiler options. This will make it easier for you to move your project and reorganize it if necessary.

One more note on brackets versus quotation marks: Originally, <samp class="listingcharacter"><...></samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter">"..."</samp> meant that the header may be part of the compiler and not a file at all. However, it has become accepted that the brackets are also used if it is simply a header file that you are expected to have installed on the system. Therefore, only use <samp class="listingcharacter">"..."</samp> for files that are part of your project and should have priority over other libraries. Whether the priority works depends on the compiler used.

### 4.2.13    Modules

Modules were introduced with C++20\. Instead of “copying” textual <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> directives into a translation unit, divide your code into interface and implementation areas. To do this, use the new keywords <samp class="listingcharacter">module</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">import</samp>. You can find the exact usage in the C++ reference and in tutorials such as [https://youtu.be/tjSuKOz5HK4](https://youtu.be/tjSuKOz5HK4) by Dos Reis. However, there is still no “best practice,” and the standard library is not yet divided into modules. With C++23, the two standard <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std.compat</samp> modules were introduced, which contain everything from the standard library. The <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp> module contains the symbols that can be accessed with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::vector</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">std.compat</samp> module contains the identifiers of the global namespace, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">::fclose</samp>.

But today, in 2024, not much of this has been implemented with the major g++ 13, clang++ 18, and msvc++ 19.37 compilers, and some implementations are incompatible with others. As long as it is not foreseeable that modules are within reach for you, I refer you to the highly topical media if you are interested.

However, I would like to briefly pass on some recommendations from Nico Josuttis on how you can best work with the emerging conventions and have as few problems as possible when porting to another platform:[[ 7 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_04)

*   Interface files should have the <samp class="listingcharacter">.cppm</samp> extension (do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">.ixx</samp>; use <samp class="listingcharacter">/interface</samp> for MSVC ).[[ 8 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_05)

*   Keep module implementation files as  <samp class="listingcharacter">.cpp</samp>.

*   Internal partition implementation files should have the <samp class="listingcharacter">.cppp</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">.cppm</samp> extension.

But if you use them, modules and includes are not mutually exclusive. As long as you adhere to certain schemas, you can use both in parallel—and will probably have to for a long time to come, because even if modules are the better alternative, includes will still be around for a very long time for historical reasons.

### 4.2.14    Input and Output

Now you know all the important elements of the program, except—some would say—the most important ones. After all, what is a program without an input and output?

You have already seen that <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> is used as an operator for the output. And <samp class="listingcharacter">#include <iostream></samp> was also included because of <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout.</samp> Here is an excerpt from [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2), which is mainly about the output:

```
std::cout << "Divisors of " << n << " are:\n";
for(int divider=1; divider <= n; ++divider) {
    if(n % divider == 0)
        std::cout << divider << ", ";
}
std::cout << std::endl; 
```

You can see that you can simply string several <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> together. More specifically, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << "divisors of "</samp> is an expression that does the output as a side effect and then returns <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> again. This effectively executes <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << n</samp>, again with the output and the result <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>. Last but not least, the third operator of the statement comes into play and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << " are:\n"</samp> is executed. What is special about this operator is that it contains a newline. In C++ strings, this is represented by <samp class="listingcharacter">\n.</samp> Exactly this newline was omitted within the loop in the output; therefore, the numbers appear on one line.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << std::endl</samp>, the program outputs the line break at the end of the list. But, oops, where is the <samp class="listingcharacter">\n</samp>? This time there is a special element of <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> in the listing, the manipulator <samp class="listingcharacter">std::endl</samp>. This ensures the line change and also guarantees that the system does not buffer the output. It forces everything you have output so far to actually appear on the screen. This is because (screen) output is time-consuming, and the system tries to summarize as many steps as possible and complete them all at once. With <samp class="listingcharacter">std::endl</samp>, you ensure that the system really outputs everything that has occurred.

### 4.2.15    The “std” Namespace

Now there is one more thing I need to explain to you before we dive deeper into the individual topics. In [Listing 4.2](#04_002.html_l4.2), you can see <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std</samp>. With this tool, you save yourself the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp> in front of identifiers that you would otherwise have needed.

```
#include <iostream>                            // for std::cin, std::cout, std::endl
#include <string>                              // for std::stoi
void calculate(int n) {
    using namespace std;                       // for std::cout and std::endl
    /* output divisors */
    cout << "divisors of " << n << " are:\n";  // cout instead of std::cout
    for(int divider=1; divider <= n; ++divider) {
        if(n % divider == 0)
            cout << divider << ", ";           // cout instead of std::cout
    }
    cout << endl;
} 
```

**Listing 4.21**     You can include a namespace to make program text shorter.

Normally, the compiler checks for each identifier whether its name exists locally or on the outer levels. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">divider</samp> is a local variable and <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is a parameter within the function. If you were to use <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> without <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>, the compiler would check whether there is a local variable or a parameter with this name, then whether a global variable <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> exists, and then inform you with an error that this is not the case—and that the identifier is therefore unknown.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>, for each identifier that could not be found, the system tries whether it works with a preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp>. This can save you a lot of typing, where you would otherwise type a lot of <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp>s.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace</samp> directive has an effect within the range in which it is defined—in the example, only within the <samp class="listingcharacter">calculate</samp> function. You can also write <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace</samp> globally, in which case the scope is larger.

```
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;            //  has a global effect; works, but is critical
void calculate(int n) {
    /* output divisors */
    cout << "divisors of " << n << " are:\n";
    // ...
}
// ... also in other functions ... 
```

**Listing 4.22**     You can also use “using namespace” globally, but you should rarely do so.

Does that sound so tempting that you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace ...</samp> all the time? Don't do that! With <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">...</samp>, you no longer know where the identifiers of your program come from. For example, if you are not yet familiar with the standard library and come across a free-standing <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>, how are you supposed to know that it is actually <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>?

#### Avoid Global “using namespace”

Do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace ...</samp> at a global level in a file. When reading each identifier, you ask yourself where it comes from, and you have no chance of finding out even by searching in the current file.

Within a block—for example, locally in a function, as I have shown in [Listing 4.21](#04_002.html_l4.21)—a <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace ...</samp> is not frowned upon, however. The range for wondering which namespace an identifier comes from is limited enough. And the probability that several <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace</samp>s are active at the same time is lower.

But there is a solution: do not get all the identifiers of a namespace, but only the identifiers that you need, as in the following example.

```
#include <iostream>                     // cin, cout, endl
using std::endl;                        // applies globally in this file
void calculate(int n) {
    using std::cout;                    // applies locally in this function
    /* output divider */
    cout << "divisors of " << n << " are:\n";
    for(int divider=1; divider <= n; ++divider) {
        if(n % divider == 0)
            cout << divider << ", ";
    }
    cout << endl;
} 
```

**Listing 4.23**     Get individual identifiers with “using.”

Including identifiers in this way causes few problems. If a standalone <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> appears <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> somewhere in the file, you can find the original namespace with a simple search within the file.

#### In This Book

As the listings in this book rarely become long and confusing, I will make an exception here. It saves space and repetition to write <samp class="listingcharacter">using ...</samp> at the beginning after the includes. Therefore, I will mainly abbreviate <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::endl</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> but will write out other identifiers with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp> so that you know where they come from.

## 4.3    Operators

One- and two-character operators are very often used in expressions. <samp class="listingcharacter">3+4</samp> is a simple example, but an expression such as <samp class="listingcharacter">!isBad && (x >= x0) &&(x <= x1)</samp> could also appear. You can achieve a lot in C++ with such sequences of operators and operands. Now that you know a lot about variables, types, and expressions, you should get to know the possible operators.

As an example, I will explain operators mainly using the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> types so that you get to know the repertoire first. However, many operators can also be applied to other types. These include built-in types, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, but also types from the standard library, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::stream</samp>.

In C++, you can define your own types that also support operators. It is up to you to ensure that these then also do something that applies to the built-in types. For example, we expect <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> to perform an addition—like with an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. However, the class <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> uses <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> for concatenation, which is still “addition-like.” But you can, if you want, write a class <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> that stores itself in a file with <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> followed by a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. (Please don't do this!) We will deal with this in a suitable place. Here you will first find out what operators there are.

### Operators for Built-In Types Cannot Be Overwritten

When I describe operators in this chapter, I therefore mean those for the built-in types. You cannot change these in C++. There is already a <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and you as a programmer cannot change its meaning. In some places, I refer to the types of the standard library, but for many things, the reference must serve.

### 4.3.1    Operators and Operands

An operator is something that behaves like a function, but without being one. What is different is that you would expect a function to have its name at the front and the arguments in brackets after it, i.e. <samp class="listingcharacter">func(arg1, arg2)</samp>. With a little creative freedom, you could write <samp class="listingcharacter">func</samp> in the middle and omit the brackets, and you would get <samp class="listingcharacter">arg1 func arg2</samp>. And if the function name were <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">func</samp>, you would have an operator <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> with its two operands <samp class="listingcharacter">arg1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">arg2</samp>.

Most operators are written with symbols, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>. Many have two arguments and are therefore called binary operators. In C++ it always looks like this:

*   Operand operator symbol operand

If they are unary operators, the operator is placed before the operand as in <samp class="listingcharacter">-4</samp> or, more rarely, after it as in <samp class="listingcharacter">idx++</samp>:

*   Operator symbol operand

*   Operand operator symbol

There are other forms of operators, which are explained next.

### 4.3.2    Overview of Operators

The operator symbols can be divided into several groups:

*   Arithmetic operators
    These are the four basic arithmetic operators <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>, plus <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> for the remainder of the division (modulo). You can influence the sign with the unary operators <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>.

*   Bitwise arithmetic
    You can combine numbers bit by bit with <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>.

*   Compound assignment
    In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>, there are also assignments that perform another operation at the same time. These are compound assignments: <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">/=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>>=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">&=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">^=</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">|=</samp>.

*   Increment and decrement
    The two single-character operators <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp> are each available in a prefixed and a postfixed variant (prefix and postfix). If possible, prefer the prefix variant, as it does not require a temporary variable.

*   Relational operators
    Relational operators perform a comparison and return a truth value <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>: <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>. If you are working with the standard library, <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> are the most important, as many algorithms only use these two to derive the others if necessary. This is important if you want to make your own data types fit with the standard library.

*   Logical operators
    <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> combine truth values to form more complex expressions.

*   Pointer operator and dereference operator
    You use the unary operators <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and the binary operators <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> to address and to dereference. This means that you retrieve an address, turn an address into data, or access a structure. You will see their use in detail later.

*   Special operators
    You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> together to write an either-or expression. The comma <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> can be used as a sequence operator in expressions. With C++20, the spaceship operator <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp> is added, which helps to implement the relational operators.

*   Function-like operators
    Strictly speaking, some special types also belong to the operators that have real names and are used like functions. These are type conversions such as <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)value</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof(a)</samp>, and some others. The fact that these are operators means, for example, that you cannot request the address from <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof</samp>. You can only give a function values and variables as parameters, but with <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof()</samp> you can also use a type, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof(int)</samp>. Strictly speaking, the brackets are also optional; you could write <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof a</samp>, for example, but that would be very unusual.

### 4.3.3    Arithmetic Operators

You can calculate with numbers as normal in C++. In addition to the basic arithmetic operations <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>, there is <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> also <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> for the division remainder. If you do not use brackets, then dot before dash calculation applies, as you can see in the next example:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/cEGGfoeT7
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::cout << "3+4*5+6=" << 3+4*5+6 << "\n";          // dot before dash; = 29
    std::cout << "(3+4)*(5+6)=" << (3+4)*(5+6) << "\n";  // Parentheses; = 77
    std::cout << "22/7=" << 22/7
        << " remainder " << 22%7 << "\n";                // 22/7 = 3 remainder 1
    for(int n=0; n < 10; ++n) {
        std::cout << -2*n*n + 13*n - 4 << " ";           // with unary minus
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
    // output: -4 7 14 17 16 11 2 -11 -28 -49
} 
```

**Listing 4.24**     Arithmetic operators in the application.

What was shown here for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> works with all integer types. And except for <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp>, it also works with all floating-point types (<samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and the like).
