In the standard library, you will find <samp class="listingcharacter">std::complex<></samp>, with which you can also use these operators.

Many types use the plus operator <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> for joining. For example, you can use

```
std::string before="Robert";
std::string after="Reynolds"; 
```

with <samp class="listingcharacter">before+" "+after</samp> to make a new string, <samp class="listingcharacter">"Robert Reynolds"</samp>.

### 4.3.4    Bit-by-Bit Arithmetic

Bit-by-bit arithmetic probably looks a bit strange at first:

```
int a = 41;      // decimal 41
int b = a & 15;  // results in 9 
```

The explanation is that numbers are represented in the computer as a sequence of <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>s <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>s—that is, as bits. The decimal 41 is <samp class="listingcharacter">101001</samp> in bit representation—that is, in binary.

#### Binary System

Because 10 is the base in the decimal system, we write “four hundred and twelve” as 412 as an abbreviation for 4 · 10² + 1 · 10¹ + 2 · 10⁰ = [10]412\. For a computer, with base 2, this is 1 · 2⁸ + 1 · 2⁷ + 0 · 2⁶ + 0 · 2⁵ + 1 · 2⁴ + 1 · 2³ + 1 · 2² + 0 · 2¹ + 0 · 2⁰, abbreviated to [2]1 1001 1100\. The subscript 10 or 2 indicates the number system in which the number is represented.

Any conversion from the decimal system to another is simply done by repeatedly dividing by the base and noting the remainder until the value reaches zero. For example, to convert <samp class="listingcharacter">10412</samp> to the binary system, divide repeatedly by 2:

```
412 / 2 = 206, remainder 0
206 / 2 = 103, remainder 0
103 / 2 =  51, remainder 1
 51 / 2 =  25, remainder 1
 25 / 2 =  12, remainder 1
 12 / 2 =   6, remainder 0
  6 / 2 =   3, remainder 0
  3 / 2 =   1, remainder 1
  1 / 2 =   0, remainder 1 
```

Read the remainders from bottom to top and write them down as a binary sequence. The lowest <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> therefore represents the highest digit: [2]<samp class="listingcharacter">110011100</samp>.

Of course, this is also possible in C++. [Listing 4.25](#04_003.html_l4.25) is partly a preview of things you will get to know, but I think it is still instructive.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/nMcsbxvvv
#include <iostream>
void printBin(int x) {
  while(x>0) {      // done?
    int a = x/2;    // division by 2
    int b = x%2;    // modulo, remainder of the division
    std::cout << x <<" / 2 = " << a << ", remainder " << b<<'\n'; // Output
    x = a;
  }
}
int main() {
  printBin(412);
} 
```

**Listing 4.25**     Programming example for the conversion of an integer into a bit sequence.

However, only a few people can do this in their heads. I myself calculate smaller numbers in my head the other way round: starting from the top, I subtract the powers of 2—32, 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1—until I reach zero. In [10]25[,] 16 fits, then 8, then 1, which results in binary [2]<samp class="listingcharacter">11001</samp>.

The computer often calculates with 32 bits for an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. It therefore fills the front with <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>s—that is, [2]<samp class="listingcharacter">00000000 00000000 00000001 10011100</samp> for [10]412.

#### Negative Integers and the Two's Complement

For signed integers, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, which is implicitly <samp class="listingcharacter">signed int</samp>, the most significant bit represents the sign; <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> stands for a positive number and <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> for a negative number.

If the sign is positive, the remaining bits contain the value of the number as usual. However, if it is negative, the interpretation of the value bits changes. The computer stores this in the two's complement. To convert the bit representation of a negative binary number into a decimal number, proceed as follows:

*   Invert all value bits.

*   Convert this to a decimal number as usual.

*   Add one.

*   Set the negative sign.

The value bits of [2]1100 are [2]100, inverted therefore as [2]011\. This corresponds to [10]3, which after the addition of one gives the value [10]4\. In total, [2]1100 therefore represents [10]-4 in two's complement.

The two's complement makes optimum use of the value range of the data types and has proven to be the most practical for computer calculations. Incidentally, a side effect of this representation is that the smallest negative number that can be represented always has an amount that is one greater than the largest positive number that can be represented. The range of 16 possible values for four bits goes from -8 to 7\. For eight bits, the range goes from -128 to 127, and so on.

The arithmetic is now the bit-by-bit combination of the numbers written in the two systems. If you think of the <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> as “true” and the <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> as “false,” then you can perform the bitwise operations for AND, OR,  and XOR yourself. For the sake of simplicity, I will limit myself in the example in [Table 4.2](#04_003.html_t4.2) to 4 bits for unsigned integers.

| Operation | Binary | Decimal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">1001</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">9</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0011</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> |
| And <samp class="listingcharacter">a & b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0001</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> |
| Or <samp class="listingcharacter">a &#124; b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">1011</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">11</samp> |
| Xor <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ c</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">1010</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">10</samp> |
| Not <samp class="listingcharacter">~b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">1100</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp> |

**Table 4.2**     Bitwise arithmetic with a (hypothetical) four-bit-wide unsigned int.

The <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> operators should no longer scare you: simply shift the bit representation of the first operand to the left or right by the number of bits of the second operand. In the computer, it is the same as if you were multiplying or dividing by two just as often:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">345 << 3</samp> is like <samp class="listingcharacter">345*2*2*2</samp> and results in <samp class="listingcharacter">2760</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">345 >> 3</samp> is like <samp class="listingcharacter">345/2/2/2</samp> and gives <samp class="listingcharacter">43</samp>.

As soon as you need such number magic, you will have to deal with the number representation in the computer again, for example in [Section 4.4.3](#04_004.html_h4.4.3). Until then, remember that C++ has these operations.

So the use of this in the real world is limited to the view of numbers as a series of bits; otherwise <samp class="listingcharacter">*2</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">/2</samp> make much more sense. So that you can see this use, the following code reverses the bits of an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned short</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/qdY41d5a9
#include <iostream>
#include <bitset>
constexpr unsigned n_bits = sizeof(unsigned short)*8; // 8 bits per char
auto reverse_bits(unsigned val) -> unsigned short {
  unsigned short ret = 0;
  for (unsigned i = 0; i < n_bits; ++i ) {
    ret = (ret << 1) | (val & 1);  // one to the side, set lowest bit
    val >>= 1;                     // one in the other direction
  }
  return ret;
}
void tell(unsigned short val) {
  std::bitset<n_bits> bits{val};
  std::cout << val << "=" << bits << " -> ";
  auto lav = reverse_bits(val);
  std::bitset<n_bits> stib{lav};
  std::cout << lav << "=" << stib << "\n";
}
int main() {
  tell(36u);  // Output: 36=0000000000100100 -> 9216=0010010000000000
  tell(199u); // Output: 199=0000000011000111 -> 58112=1110001100000000
  tell(255u); // Output: 255=0000000011111111 -> 65280=1111111100000000
  tell(256u); // Output: 256=0000000100000000 -> 128=0000000010000000
} 
```

#### Operators for Streams

The input and output data streams of the standard library streams use the <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> operators, which are actually intended for bitwise arithmetic, for writing and reading. You have already seen this for <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp> in many listings. In C++ today, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> are used far more frequently for streams than for real bitwise arithmetic.

### 4.3.5    Composite Assignment

If you use an arithmetic operator, a new value is created. If the expression requires intermediate results, these are usually briefly available in the computer memory. Within an expression, new temp-values are then constantly generated and discarded. To avoid this, all arithmetic operators are available in variants that change a variable directly instead.

Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">int a = 3; a = (a * 4 + 7 - 3)/4;</samp> you can also write the following:

```
int a = 3;
a *= 4;
a += 7;
a -= 3;
a /= 4; 
```

In both cases, <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> then contains the value <samp class="listingcharacter">4</samp>. However, you should avoid such long calculations as the code quickly becomes confusing. Saving the temp-values is only really a big gain in the rarest of cases.

You can also use the operators of bitwise arithmetic in this way:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5hqanTeYh
#include <iostream>
#include <bitset>  // helps with the output of numbers as a bit sequence
int main() {
    int a = 0;
    for(int idx=0; idx<8; idx++) {
        a <<= 2;                         // shift two bits to the left: "...100"
        a |= 1;                          // set the lowest bit: "...1"
    }
    std::cout << std::bitset<16>(a) << "\n"; // 0101010101010101
    std::cout << a << "\n";              // 21845
} 
```

The compound assignments available are therefore:

*   The standard arithmetic <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">/=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">%=</samp>

*   The binary arithmetic <samp class="listingcharacter">|=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">&=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">^=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>>=</samp>

### 4.3.6    Post- and Preincrement and Post- and Predecrement

I have already said the most important things about the unary operators <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp>. Let me summarize it once again:

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">++number</samp>, number is first increased by one; with <samp class="listingcharacter">--number</samp>, it is decreased by one. You can continue to use the result of this calculation in the surrounding expression. Because the operation is performed first here, this is the pre variant.

*   If you readjust the operator, use the post variant. The value of the expression (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">number++</samp>) is then the value of the variable before the change. It is only actually executed at the end of the entire statement. Until then, the computer has to remember the new value somewhere. This may consume memory and time. It is therefore generally better to get into the habit of using the pre variants.

*   More importantly, you should never use two of these operators on the same variable within a statement. The compiler allows this, but the result is not defined.

### 4.3.7    Relational Operators

You can also compare values with each other. Very often you need <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> for equality and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> for their opposite. Of course, you can also compare numbers for smaller and larger with <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> as well as in combinations with equal: <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>.

The result of such a comparison is a true or false outcome—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>—and therefore of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. These are particularly popular in loops and <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> conditions. However, you can also store the result in a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> variable <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> or return it from a function:

```
// as conditions:
if(x < 10) ...
for(int idx=0; idx < 12; ++idx) ...
while(it != end) ...
// store:
bool isLarge = value >= 100;
// return:
bool isPositive(int a) {
    return a > 0;
} 
```

With C++20, the three-way comparison <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp> is added. Because of its visual similarity to a spaceship, it is often called the spaceship operator. The return of such a comparison is a new (simple) object that can be compared with <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, for example:

```
if(a <=> b > 0) ... 
```

This corresponds roughly to what <samp class="listingcharacter">strcmp</samp> does for strings in C or <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo</samp> in Java.

This is there to make it easier to provide your own data types with an order. Previously, you had to implement <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> for a new data type if it was to be complete and ordered. As of C++20, it is sufficient to define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and the compiler derives the normal comparison operators. Implemented correctly, <samp class="listingcharacter">(a<=>b)>0</samp> is the same as <samp class="listingcharacter">a>b</samp>, and so on.

### 4.3.8    Logical Operators

If you want to know whether <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is between <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">200</samp>, you must check both relational expressions <samp class="listingcharacter">x>100</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">x<200</samp>, and both must be true. You could do this with two consecutive ifs. But to combine expressions of type <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> with each other, there are logical operators: they each have two operands and return <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> again. If the operands <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> are both <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> expressions, then

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">u && v</samp> is true if <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> are both <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>,

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">u || v</samp> is true if <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> are <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, and

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">! u</samp> is true if <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>.

If this is completely new to you, you will find the detailed information in [Table 4.10](#04_004.html_t4.10) helpful.

You can then combine the expression:

```
if( x > 100 && x < 200 ) ... 
```

#### Short-Circuit Evaluation

The preceding <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement is in fact equivalent to the following nested <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements:

```
if(x > 100)
    if(x < 200)
        ... 
```

Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">x < 200</samp> comparison <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> is only evaluated if <samp class="listingcharacter">x > 100</samp> was actually <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp>, for example, then <samp class="listingcharacter">x < 200</samp> is not reached.

This is important if the second comparison only makes sense (or may only be carried out) if the first was positive. For example:

```
if( y != 0 && x/y > 5 ) ... 
```

You certainly know that you can never divide by zero. So if the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">x/y</samp> has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, then you are doing something forbidden. However, if you check this beforehand, nothing can go wrong. In C++,

*   in <samp class="listingcharacter">u && v</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> is only evaluated if <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> is true; and

*   in <samp class="listingcharacter">u || v</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> is only evaluated if <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> is false.

This is called short-circuit evaluation.

##### “And” Is Always “And;” “Or” Is Always “Or”

If you define your own types later, you will learn that you can also define the operators on them yourself. This also includes the logical operators.

However, never redefine a logical operator in such a way that it does anything other than perform the intuitive calculation. This is because nasty surprises would be inevitable in combination with the short-circuit evaluation: parts of your expression are executed unexpectedly.

If you overload <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> for a custom type, then there is no short-circuit evaluation there. On types other than <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>, an expression is always evaluated in full.

#### Alternative Tokens

A small note on the <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> operator: I personally find it a little difficult to see in the source text. Despite its inconspicuousness, it completely reverses the meaning of the whole expression. It's a matter of taste, but I resort to a syntax trick from time to time. You can replace the <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> with the word <samp class="listingcharacter">not</samp>. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">while(!file.eof())...</samp> in Listing 10.1 becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">while(not file.eof())...</samp>

This is called an alternative token,  and there are a few of them; the one I find most useful is <samp class="listingcharacter">not</samp>. I don't want to name them all—not that you'll start using them everywhere. If you are curious, take a look in the language reference under “alternative tokens” or the related area of “di- and trigraphs” (trigraphs are no longer allowed since C++17).

As I said, <samp class="listingcharacter">not</samp> is not to everyone's taste and you should discuss this with your team. I would advise against the widespread use of these character combinations because they are really very rarely used. Your readers could become confused.

### 4.3.9    Pointer and Dereference Operators

You have already learned that we call methods with a dot <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp>—for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>:

```
void checkName(std::string& name) {
    if( name.length() ) ...
} 
```

You will see later, when we discuss pointers and C-arrays, that you can also use a pointer to this variable instead of the reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>:

```
void checkName(std::string* pname) {  // Pointer to a string
    if( (*pname).length() ) ...
} 
```

If the type of your variable is <samp class="listingcharacter">string*</samp> and not <samp class="listingcharacter">string&</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, then it is only “indirectly” linked to the value. To get to the value, use the unary <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> operator—<samp class="listingcharacter">*pname</samp> in this case. The method call is then <samp class="listingcharacter">(*pname).length()</samp>. However, as this is somewhat cumbersome, there is the binary <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> operator <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> as a shorter form:

```
void checkName(std::string* pname) {
    if( pname->length() ) ...
} 
```

In particular, this is all worth mentioning because both dereference operators (the unary <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and the binary <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp>) can be defined by you on your own types. Knowing them is therefore not only important for pointers and C-arrays.

In fact, pointers are just a very special form of indirection. The standard library is riddled with iterators, the generalization of the pointer concept. You will come across iterators in the containers and algorithms and use <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> there as a matter of course, without pointers being involved. (See Part IV and [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20).)

### 4.3.10    Special Operators

As we are discussing operators here, two oddballs must also be mentioned.

There is a single ternary (three-character) operator <samp class="listingcharacter">? :</samp> that allows an <samp class="listingcharacter">if-else</samp> query as an expression. It has the following form:

Condition-expression ? Then-expression : Else-expression

Depending on whether the condition is evaluated to true or false, either the then expression or the else expression is the overall result. Note that the two parts must therefore be of the same type so that the compiler can determine the type of the overall expression:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xrMYz93WP
int main() {
    for(int w1 = 1; w1 <= 6; ++w1) {     // 1..6
        for(int w2 = 0; w2 < 10; ++w2) { // 0..9
            int max = w1 > w2 ? w1 : w2; // ternary operator
        }
    }
} 
```

Here <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp> is assigned the larger of the two values <samp class="listingcharacter">w1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">w2</samp>.

The comma can be used as a sequence operator in expressions. If you write several expressions in parentheses <samp class="listingcharacter">(...)</samp> and separate them with commas, then the compiler evaluates the expressions from left to right, but only keeps the result of the last expression as the overall result. The construct therefore only makes sense if the leading expressions have side effects.

It looks like this for two expressions:

( Expression-1 , Expression-2 )

The compiler first calculates Expression-1 and then Expression-2. The result of the first expression is dissipated so that the total expression receives the value and type of the second expression.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/rq66cWr3d
int main() {
    int a = 0;
    int b = 0;
    for(int w1 = 1; w1 <= 6; ++w1) { // 1..6
        for(int w2 = 0; w2 < 10; ++w2) { // 0..9
            int max = w1 > w2 ? (a+=b , w1) :( b+=1 , w2); // sequence operator
        }
    }
} 
```

**Listing 4.26**     You can concatenate several expressions with commas in brackets.

If <samp class="listingcharacter">w1 > w2</samp>, then the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">(a+=b, w1)</samp> is evaluated. Although <samp class="listingcharacter">w1</samp> is returned as the result for <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp>, the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">a+=b</samp> is executed first. In the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">w <= w2</samp>, the term <samp class="listingcharacter">w2</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">(b+=1, w2)</samp> is assigned to the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp> after <samp class="listingcharacter">b+=1</samp> has been evaluated.

I have deliberately chosen a particularly bizarre example here for the sequence operator because, first, it is difficult to find a meaningful example; and, second, you should avoid this special construct like Darth Vader avoids magma. The sequence operator thrives on side effects, but within an expression, each variable must not be affected by more than one side effect, so its use is dangerous.

There are exceptions where it makes sense to use it—namely, where only a single expression is permitted and it would otherwise be more complicated.

This can be the case, for example, in the incrementation part of <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/vd85f7rMj
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    int arr[] = { 8,3,7,3,11,999,5,6,7 };
    int len = 9;
    for(int i=0, *p=arr; i<len && *p!=999; ++i, ++p) { // first ++i, then ++p
        std::cout << i << ":" << *p << " ";
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
    // output: 0:8 1:3 2:7 3:3 4:11
} 
```

**Listing 4.27**     The sequence comma can be useful in<samp class="listingcharacter">for loops.</samp>

Note that in a declaration <samp class="listingcharacter">int a, b, c;</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> the comma is not the sequence operator. This also applies to the declaration part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, <samp class="listingcharacter">int i=0, *p=arr</samp>, where the comma only separates the declarations.

The comma that separates function arguments in <samp class="listingcharacter">func(x,y,z)</samp> or list elements in <samp class="listingcharacter">{1,2,3}</samp> is not the sequence operator either.

### 4.3.11    Function-Like Operators

Even if they do not look like it, the following cases also belong to the operators:

*   kind<samp class="listingcharacter">..._cast<target_type>(value)</samp>
    All of these are type conversions. <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> is converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">target_type</samp> in the C++ notation. There are multiple different kinds: <samp class="listingcharacter">static_cast</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">const_cast</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">dynamic_cast</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">reinterpret_cast</samp>. They differ slightly in what they do and what conversions they can perform, but the type of the expression is always <samp class="listingcharacter">target_type</samp>. If a type conversion is not possible, the compiler reports an error. Otherwise, the <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> is made to fit, which harbors dangers. For example, when converting from <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, information can be lost without you realizing it. Forcing types is not desirable, but it does happen sometimes. In an optimal world, you can manage without explicit type conversions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">(type)value</samp> This is the type conversion notation adopted from C. In <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)value</samp>, the compiler attempts to convert <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> into an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, regardless of the type of <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp>. Depending on the context, this notation corresponds to one of the C++ notations, most commonly <samp class="listingcharacter">static_cast<></samp>. Simply because you are emphasizing the type of conversion, you should always choose the C++ notation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof</samp> You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">(type)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">(value)</samp> to find out the size of a type or a variable in <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> units. A <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof(char)</samp> always returns <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">class{}</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> are used to manage dynamic memory, as you will see in [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> With <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">ExceptionClass{};</samp> you trigger an exception, which is explained in [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10).

### 4.3.12    Operator Sequence

If you use several operators in an expression—possibly different ones—then these are evaluated in a specific order.

Just as you can demand that a proper pocket calculator observes the rule of point before dash calculation for <samp class="listingcharacter">3+4*5+6</samp> and produces the correct result of 29, C++ also masters this. Furthermore, all other operators also have a precedence: the higher an operator is in this ranking, the earlier it is evaluated compared to other operators.

Remember this simple sequence, which starts with the strongest bond:

*   Multiplicative
    <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp>

*   Additive
    <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>

*   Stream operators
    <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>

*   Compare
    <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>

*   Equality
    <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>

*   Logical
    In this order: <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> then <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp>

*   Assignments with <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>
    But also all compound assignments such as <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>

This allows you to write many a complex expression without having to correct the meaning with parentheses:

```
bool yesno = 3*4 > 2*6 && 10/2 < 13%8; 
```

This saves you the parentheses shown in the following:

```
bool yesno = (((3*4) > (2*6)) && ((10/2) < (13%8))); 
```

Note that the stream output operator <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> binds more loosely than normal arithmetic with <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>. However, if you have comparisons in the output, you need brackets around the comparison:

```
std::cout << 2*7 << x+1 << n/3-m << "\n"; // no () required between <<
std::cout << (x0 >= x1) << (a<b || b<c);  // (): << would bind more tightly 
```

But what happens if several operators of the same precedence are next to each other? In expressions such as <samp class="listingcharacter">10-5-2</samp>, the left <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> is evaluated first because <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> is left-associative—as if the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">((10-5)-3)</samp> were in parentheses. The result is therefore <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp>. All binary arithmetic, Boolean, and comparative operators are left-associative, so you can intuitively calculate with them. Sometimes this is also called left-to-right associative or LR-associative.

The group of assignment operators, in turn, is consistently right-associative, which is why the compiler for <samp class="listingcharacter">x += y += z += 1</samp> executes <samp class="listingcharacter">(x += (y += (z += 1)))</samp> as expected and first increments <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> by <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> in order to then deal with the other variables one after the other. If the expression were evaluated as <samp class="listingcharacter">(((x += y) += z) += 1)</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> would receive a new value several times because <samp class="listingcharacter">x += y</samp> also returns <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>, and then <samp class="listingcharacter">+= z</samp> would be executed; <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> would not be changed. And <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> would be returned once again, and <samp class="listingcharacter">+= 1</samp> would increment it by <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> instead of increasing <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp>.

Most of the time, precedence and associativity work intuitively and as expected. If in doubt, it is better to bracket as later readers will probably ask themselves the same questions as you.

## 4.4    Built-In Data Types

So far you have only learned about types in a flyover—and around them, just as much fundamental C++ as was necessary to understand them.

This section builds on these basics. You now know enough about the language to understand the comprehensive explanations of all the built-in types.

In this section, you will learn which data types are available to you in C++ if you do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> in your program or do not use the standard library. What are the built-in data types, and what can you do with them?

Pay attention to the types of variables and function parameters in the following example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/MPPsbdq9c
#include <iostream> // cin, cout for input and output

void input(unsigned &birthDay_,
           unsigned &birthMonth_,
           unsigned &birthYear_,
           unsigned long long &taxnumber_,
           double &bodyheight_)
{
    /* Inputs still without good error handling... */
    std::cout << "Date of birth: "; std::cin >> birthDay_;
    std::cout << "Month of birth: "; std::cin >> birthMonth_;
    std::cout << "Year of birth: "; std::cin >> birthYear_;
    std::cout << "Tax number: "; std::cin >> taxnumber_;
    std::cout << "Height: "; std::cin >> bodyheight_;
}

int main() {
    /* data */
    unsigned birthDay_ = 0;
    unsigned birthMonth_ = 0;
    unsigned birthYear_ = 0;
    unsigned long long taxnumber_ = 0;
    double bodyheight_ = 0.0;
    /* Input */
    input(birthDay_, birthMonth_, birthYear_, taxnumber_, bodyheight_);
    /* Calculations */
    // ...
} 
```

**Listing 4.28**     Some new data types are used here.

I have used the following data types:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long long</samp> as representatives of the integer data types

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> for saving a (floating-) point number

*   The variables <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>, whose types are not explicitly mentioned

The first important distinction between these data types is whether they are built-in or not.

### 4.4.1    Overview

If you do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp>, you have a very limited number of data types available. For example, you can define additional types with <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> or create aliases with <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef</samp>, but your selection is then very limited:

*   Integers—<samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>, each <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp>
    Integers store numbers without a decimal point—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-12</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">987654321</samp>. The different-sized variants store either signed or unsigned numbers. Consider which variant you need for each application. When in doubt, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is a good choice. Once you have chosen the type, you must ensure above all that you adhere to the number range of the type in order to avoid a dangerous overflow.

*   Floating-point numbers—<samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp>
    Integers are unsuitable for some things. Use <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> to store decimal numbers such as <samp class="listingcharacter">3.14</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-0.00001</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">6.281e+26</samp>. Their space is still limited, even if it is large, but the biggest problem is the accuracy; you cannot store even a value of 1/3 accurately. Always use floating-point numbers with caution.

*   Truth values—<samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> is a data type for storing truth values. A <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> is either <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. You have often used this type in <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements and the like. Although a single bit would actually suffice to store <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>, this data type is by no means more space-saving than <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>.

*   Character types—<samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp>
    In C++, there are only a few places where there is a real distinction between numbers and characters, so you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> character type as a number. This is the smallest unit, and if you ask for the actual size of a type or a variable with <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof(x)</samp>, then it is the number of <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> units that is returned to you. <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> becomes a character type because you store character strings in <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> sequences—either as an array in <samp class="listingcharacter">char[]</samp> or in a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> from the standard library. As <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is not designed for international characters (Unicode), there are <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and the somewhat outdated <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t</samp> with more space. Examples of characters are <samp class="listingcharacter">'a'</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">'Z'</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and international (Unicode) characters. In C++20, <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> added.

*   References—<samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>
    Indirect references with <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> refer to another variable. This allows you to address the same variable under a different name—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">int x = 7; int& ref = x;</samp>. Changes to the reference, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">ref=12</samp>, actually change the original—in this case, <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>. As long as it exists, a reference always refers to the same variable. A reference cannot refer to “nothing.”

*   Pointers and C-arrays—<samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp>
    Indirections with <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> point to a variable as a memory address, in the case of a C-array as <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp> with length information. A character string such as <samp class="listingcharacter">"Your name"</samp> is an example of <samp class="listingcharacter">char[9]</samp>[[ 9 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_06) and is passed to functions as <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp>. We will discuss this in [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20) on pointers. In contrast to references with <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> pointers can be changed so that they refer to another variable. If you refer to <samp class="listingcharacter">nullptr</samp>, this stands for the reference to “nothing.”

In the source code, data is represented by variables (or similar) or by literals. When the compiled program is running, however, things look quite different. Then the data needs a physical representation: in the processor, where it is calculated, and in the memory, where it is loaded, saved, and changed. Memory can mean many things here: from the fast register to the cache, the main memory and graphics card memory to the hard disk, and, in a broader sense, the network or cloud.

Each data type has a physical representation that the processor understands. In this section, we will briefly discuss this representation, because C++ is also a language that is close to this representation and can manipulate it directly.

### 4.4.2    Initialize Built-In Data Types

One of the most important differences between these data types and the majority of other—non-built-in—data types is that you have to initialize the variables of these types! For example, write <samp class="listingcharacter">int x = 7;</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">int x{7};</samp>. If you omit the initialization with <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is not initialized at all. Its initial value is then random, which can have consequences.

If you want to leave it not to chance but to the compiler to choose a “good” value for the initialization, then write a pair of empty curly braces <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> after the variable. The rule of thumb is that it is then initialized with zero or something equivalent:

```
int x{};           // initializes x with 0 - built-in type
double y{};        // y becomes 0.0 - built-in type
std::string s{};   // empty string - class
struct tm mytm{};  // all fields 0 - tm is aggregate from <time.h> 
```

#### Value Initialization Leaves Nothing to Chance

You can get into the habit of always initializing at least with <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> if you have no other more sensible initialization, because even the noninstalled types benefit from this. So you are not doing anything wrong if you include this in your repertoire. It is called value initialization, which means initialization with a meaningful type-specific value. For types that don't provide anything else with <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp>, you at least get something other than cosmic noise in the computer memory.

Among the noninstalled types, there are a few exceptions that do not tolerate initialization with <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp>. The compiler will point these out to you. These are usually classes where you have to specify arguments between the braces.

### 4.4.3    Integers

We have used the <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> type in several places in the examples. This is just an abbreviation of <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp>. In contrast to the normal <samp class="listingcharacter">signed int</samp>, abbreviated <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, this can store slightly larger positive numbers, but not negative ones.

Normally, you should use the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> type for integers. However, the number range is limited. If you need more length, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>. If you need to save space, there is <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>. All these variants are also available in the <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> variant, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long</samp>. It is not necessary to write <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> in front of the number type instead as this is the default. An <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> (whether <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp>) is what your system handles most naturally and can usually calculate the fastest.

You can perform arithmetic calculations with the integer types—that is, multiplication and the like. However, you are already reaching the limits of the data type with basic arithmetic operations, because logically an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp> cannot take on a negative value. And both the <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> variants have a limit for large numbers.

To understand what actually happens when calculating with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> types and relatives, you only need to know that the computer works in the binary system. This is nothing other than the decimal system that you are used to, except that each digit cannot be <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">9</samp>, but only <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>—one of two possible values (hence the bi in binary). In [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3), I discuss this in the “Binary System” box.

The individual positions that can be 0 or 1 are called bits. How many bits fit into a variable of an integer type depends on your system. The standard says that <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is the smallest and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> is the largest type, with <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> in between, in that order. On today's machines, <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is eight bits and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> is 64 bits. [Table 4.3](#04_004.html_t4.3) gives examples of two common systems today. The Windows column applies to both 32-bit and 64-bit Windows, as well as 32-bit Linux.

| Bits | Linux, 64-Bit | Windows | Minimum For… |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> |
| 16 | <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> |
| 32 | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> |
| 64 | <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> |

**Table 4.3**     Bit widths of two architectures and the minimums as examples.

If an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp> has 32 bits, then the largest number that this data type can represent is 1 · 2^(31) + 1 · 2^(30) + … + 1 · 2¹ + 1 · 2⁰ = 2^(32)–1, which corresponds to just over 4 billion. This is shown in [Table 4.4](#04_004.html_t4.4). You must use your program to ensure that an expression of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> never assumes a larger value.

#### [Übung]  Minimum Widths for Integer Types

Since C++20, the numbers listed under “Bits” apply as the minimum widths of the implementation for the data types specified in the “Minimum For…” column. However, you don't have to get used to this, as all implementations actually adhered to these widths even before standardization. However, you will probably still find people for a long time who believe that C++ does not specify minimum widths except for <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. Now you can shine with new knowledge.

A note on the names of the integer types: officially, the types are called <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long int</samp>. I myself usually abbreviate <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp>, but you will often see it written out in full. With <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>, the written-out version with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> behind it is rarely used.

| Bits | Unsigned | Signed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | 0 ... 255 | –128 ... 127 |
| 16 | 0 ... 65 535 | –32 768 ... 32 767 |
| 32 | 0 ... 4 294 967 295 | –2 147 483 648 ... 2 147 483 647 |
| 64 | 0 ... 18 446 744 073 709 551 615 | –9 223 372 036 854 775 808 ... 9 223 372 036 854 775 807 |

**Table 4.4**     Numerical ranges.

#### Physical Representation of Integers

Have you noticed that the number of bits that can be integers wide is divisible by eight? I'm probably not telling you anything new by saying that in most computer systems, eight bits make up one byte (there are exceptions). In C++, a byte is the smallest addressable data unit. A byte in memory has an address x; the byte next to it has address x+1.

On a typical system, an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp> has 32 bits—that is, four bytes, as you can see in [Table 4.3](#04_004.html_t4.3). The unit that is particularly advantageous on a given architecture is called a data word (or simply word). For the purposes of this book, let’s assume that four bytes make up a data word. However, this need not be the case in all architectures.

From this we derive the terms half word, double word,  and quadruple word, which comprise 16 bits, 64 bits (eight bytes), and 128 bits (16 bytes). If you assume a smaller word size, there is also the term eightfold or double quad word. Instead of half word or double word, short word or long word is often used, and here you can see the proximity of C and C++ to machine representation. However, particular caution is required, as Linux and Windows jargon diverge here; long word in particular can sometimes mean the same thing as word.

Last but not least, there is the term nibble, which refers to half a byte: the upper nibble denotes the four high-order bits, the lower nibble the four low-order bits. You can represent a nibble with a hexadecimal character (see [Table 4.7](#04_004.html_t4.7)).

As already mentioned, the terminology may be shifted on different architectures. However, it is important to know the terms because they are often used in documentation. Interface descriptions for specialized hardware such as graphics cards refer to them (and often have their own interpretation of the widths). Hardware-related tools also refer to these terms. For example, in assembly code (AT&T or GAS syntax) on an x86-64 Linux, <samp class="listingcharacter">imull</samp> means multiply long and is used when a <samp class="listingcharacter">C++-int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">-short</samp> is multiplied. An <samp class="listingcharacter">imulq</samp> for multiply quad multiplies <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>. The same code on a 64-bit MIPS uses <samp class="listingcharacter">mul</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">dmult</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>. What I mean by this is that you always have to be careful about what the tool you are using in your architecture means. In [Table 4.5](#04_004.html_t4.5), I have compiled the same code in assembler on two different 64-bit architectures. Note the suffixes of the commands that refer to the operand width.

| C++ | x86-64-Linux | MIPS64 |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  
```
long long sq(
  long long n)
{
  return n * n;
}
```

 |  
```
sq(long long):
  imulq %rdi, %di
  movl %rdi, %rax
  ret
```

 |  
```
sq(long long):
  dmult $4,$4
  j $31
  mflo $2
```

 |
|  
```
long sq(long n) {
  return n * n;
}
```

 |  
```
sq(long):
  imulq %rdi, %di
  movq %rdi, %rax
  ret
```

 |  
```
sq(long):
  dmult $4,$4
  j $31
  mflo $2
```

 |
|  
```
int sq(int n) {
  return n * n;
}
```

 |  
```
sq(int):
  imull %edi, %di
  movl %edi, %eax
  ret
```

 |  
```
sq(int):
  j $31
  mul $2,$4,$4
```

 |
|  
```
short sq(short n) {
  return n * n;
}
```

 |

```

  andi $4,$4,0xffff
  mul $2,$4,$4
```

**Table 4.5**     Even on two 64-bit architectures, different tools can select different terms for word sizes.

Whether words or bytes, they are stored next to each other in the memory. Assuming an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp> has 32 bits, the abstract integer 123456789 is stored in four bytes with the values 7, 91, 205, and 21\. You can recalculate the original value from this by interpreting the individual values as positions in a 256 number system—that is, 7 · 256³ + 91 · 256² + 205 · 256¹ + 21 · 256⁰.

The values of bytes are rarely written as decimal numbers. It is very common to write them as hexadecimal numbers—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">0x07</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">0x5b</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">0xcd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">0x15</samp>. This means that each byte has exactly two letters (plus the <samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp> prefix). If you add them together, you get an eight-character hexadecimal number: <samp class="listingcharacter">0x075bcd15</samp> or, without a leading zero, <samp class="listingcharacter">0x75bcd15</samp>.

With this notation, you can now beautifully represent a densely packed sequence of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values in memory (see [Figure 4.2](#04_004.html_f4.2)).

[![Data in memory (big-endian).](bilderklein/klein04_002.png)](img-f4.2.html)

**Figure 4.2**     Data in memory (big-endian).

The two decimal numbers 123456789 and 447888868 at the beginning are stored directly next to each other. The content of the memory cells is shown in hexadecimal numbers.

The figure contains further data for illustration purposes. The hexadecimal byte sequence <samp class="listingcharacter">0xe89a</samp> is interpreted as 59546 for a <samp class="listingcharacter">uint16_t</samp> (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned short</samp>). If the byte sequence is read with an <samp class="listingcharacter">int16_t</samp> (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>), this corresponds to -5990\. The C string <samp class="listingcharacter">"Manual"</samp> has a terminating <samp class="listingcharacter">\0</samp> byte. Which letters mean which hexadecimal byte is defined in the ASCII standard. Finally, I have stored the decimal floating-point number 45.45 as <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, for which you see the hexadecimal representations.

##### Memory Alignment

It is not entirely coincidental that the data elements in the figure are always stored such that their first byte is at an address divisible by four. This is called memory alignment. Four bytes correspond to a 32-bit alignment. Most modern machines work faster when this is the case. To achieve optimum speed, data is not packed close together if necessary, but shifted with “empty” bytes in between. In the example, this is the case at 59546 and -5990: the addresses <samp class="listingcharacter">0c</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">0d</samp> in between do not contain any meaningful data.

Some machines cannot even cope if the data of certain data types is not stored with the correct alignment. In this case, the data must first be copied in a time-consuming process when reading. In addition to 32-bit alignment, there is also 16-bit, 64-bit, and even 128-bit alignment. No alignment means that the start position does not matter; this corresponds to 8-bit alignment and occurs in practice as well.

You do not normally have to worry about memory alignment; the compiler does this for you.

#### Byte Sequence

For the rest of this section, I would like to omit the <samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp> prefix. If not mentioned otherwise, decimal numbers like 123 are set in normal font, hexadecimal numbers like <samp class="listingcharacter">a87f</samp> in listing font.

The number 447888596 is divided into bytes—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">1a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">3c</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">d4</samp>. At address x you store <samp class="listingcharacter">1a</samp>, at address x+1 <samp class="listingcharacter">b2</samp>, at x+2 <samp class="listingcharacter">3c</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and finally at x+3 <samp class="listingcharacter">d4</samp>—or written together, at addresses x..x+3 <samp class="listingcharacter">1a b2 3c d4</samp>. In [Figure 4.3](#04_004.html_f4.3), I have illustrated this. If you number the eight hex digits from their lowest significance so that the digit with the highest significance is given the number <samp class="listingcharacter">8</samp> and the one with the lowest the number <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>, the numbering is <samp class="listingcharacter">87 65 43 21</samp>.

This format seems natural to us because, like our number system, it names the most significant digit of the whole number first and the least significant last—just as we assign the highest significance to the digit 1 and the lowest to the digit 3 in 123\. This memory format is called big-endian. It stores the most significant byte (MSB)  first.

The other way to store the number 447888596 is the little-endian memory format—with the least significant element first. This then results in the values <samp class="listingcharacter">d4 3c b2 1a</samp> at the addresses x..x+3 in the memory—so, with the least significant byte (LSB) first. In my opinion, this looks confusing, especially because each individual two-digit hex number nevertheless names its larger component first and the lower component afterward. If you number the eight hex digits again as before, the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">21 43 65 87</samp>. It helps me to write down such a sequence the other way round.

[![Numbers can be stored with the highest or lowest byte first.](bilderklein/klein04_003.png)](img-f4.3.html)

**Figure 4.3**     Numbers can be stored with the highest or lowest byte first.

However, LSB also has advantages. If the computer starts reading at address x and interprets the byte there, the significance of <samp class="listingcharacter">d4</samp>, for example, which it reads, always remains the same, regardless of whether <samp class="listingcharacter">d4</samp> is part of an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> or a <samp class="listingcharacter">long.</samp> It is a small advantage that the early CPUs probably made use of.

Why am I asking these questions and not simply dismissing little-endian as an esoteric eccentric? Because it isn't one: Intel processors, including the Pentium inside your computer—I claim, without taking any great risk of being wrong—is one of these representatives. Of course, this also applies to the compatible AMD Opterons and accelerated processing units (APUs). By the way, another name for this memory format is Intel byte order convention. But other early acquaintances were also born as little-endian: the famous Zilog Z80 processor, as well as the honorable MOS Technology 6502 of the Commodore 64, Apple II, Atari, or NES.

What has historically competed against it? Big-endian is spoken of in the Motorola 68k family, PowerPCs, MIPS, and SPARC. Yes, a few of them are still around.

##### Cross-Platform Presentation

To prevent the data from being mixed up due to different interpretations of the byte order by the sender and receiver when exchanging data between machines, there is an agreement, particularly in the network area, on the byte order in which the data is to be transmitted. This is therefore called the network byte order. When you write a program, your program is the “host,” so you are always responsible for translating the data from the host order to the network order when saving or sending and vice versa when reading or receiving.

Most platforms have functions such as <samp class="listingcharacter">htons</samp> (host-to-network short) and <samp class="listingcharacter">ntohl</samp> (network-to-host long). You should always use these functions if you want to write a portable program. However, read the specification of your protocol carefully as there are exceptions.

Are you now asking whether the network sequence is little- or big-endian? Do you really want me to tell you? If you want to write portable programs, you shouldn't need to know; you should use the conversion functions even if the host and network order are identical. But if you really want to know: the network order corresponds to big-endian. So if you are on such a system, the functions will do nothing. Better call them anyway.

With the internet, the big-endian camp has gained a strong representative. And this is perhaps also the reason that the current conquerors—the mobile CPUs of cell phones, tablets, and other connected devices, in which an ARM computing unit usually performs its services—are bi-endian; that is, they can do both.

#### Integer Literals

In the source code, you can simply write down an integer in the decimal system. You can use a suffix to specify whether it is <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> and what width the literal represents. Without a suffix, it is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> In practice, however, this specification is only necessary in special cases as the compiler itself recognizes what type of integer the literal is during initialization and the like. In [Table 4.6](#04_004.html_t4.6), you can see the possible suffixes with examples.

| Type | Suffixes | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">42, -12</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">u, U</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">3u, 123U</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">l, L</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">-999l, 88'888L</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ul, UL,</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">77'777ul, 6'666UL</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ll, LL</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">43'214'321ll, -12'341'234LL</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ull, ULL</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">23'443'212ull, 1ULL</samp> |

**Table 4.6**     Integer suffixes and the corresponding types.

As of C++23, you can also use the suffix <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Z</samp> for a <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> literal, optionally combined with <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp>—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">42z</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">42zu</samp>. This is useful, for example, if you compare a literal with the return value of the <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp> function, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">(10z > size(v))</samp>.

Since C++14, you can place single quotation marks <samp class="listingcharacter">'</samp> between digits in any number literal. They do not affect the number. For decimal numbers, groups of three are useful to achieve the usual reading grouping.

C++ also allows you to write an integer in the base 8 system (octal) or 16-digit system (hexadecimal). These have the advantage that three or two digits always result in a byte (eight bits) and are sometimes easier to read than in the decimal system. Since C++14, you can even write a number in the base 2 system (binary) as a literal. To specify the number system (the base) of the literal, use a prefix. In [Table 4.7](#04_004.html_t4.7), you can see the possible prefixes. Both the prefixes and the letters of the 16-letter system are case-insensitive; for example, no distinction is made between <samp class="listingcharacter">0xFF</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">0Xff</samp>.

Here too, you can insert single quotation marks <samp class="listingcharacter">'</samp> between the digits to group them. Groups of three are common for decimal and octal literals. Groups of two, four, or eight are common for binary and hexadecimal literals.

It becomes more advanced if you combine the prefixes for the number system with the suffixes of the data type—but as I said, the suffixes are rarely necessary. With <samp class="listingcharacter">0xffULL</samp>, you define <samp class="listingcharacter">255</samp> as an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long long</samp>.

| Base | Prefix | Examples | Decimal as int |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">255</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-4</samp> | 255, -4 |
| 16 | <samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0xff</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">0xCAFE</samp> | 255, 51966 |
| 8 | <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0377</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">0777666</samp> | 255, 262070 |
| 2 | <samp class="listingcharacter">0b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0b1111'1111</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">0b0101</samp> | 255, 5 |

**Table 4.7**     Integer prefixes for the different number systems.

#### Operations on Integers

You can calculate arithmetically with all integer types, as you would expect: multiplication with <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, addition and subtraction with <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and division without remainder with <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>. The latter means that if you calculate <samp class="listingcharacter">20 / 7</samp>, the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp>; the decimal places are simply cut off. With <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> you get the remainder modulo operation).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ebPcdxzvj
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::cout << 3 + 4 * 5 + 6 << "\n";               // 29
    std::cout << 20/7 << " Rest " << 20%7 << "\n";    // 2 remainder 6
} 
```

**Listing 4.29**     Arithmetic with integers.

For more complex calculations, you must write your own functions or use floating-point numbers such as <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, for which there are a large number of calculating functions in the standard library in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp> header.

The bit operations have already been described in [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3). The following listing is another short example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jeTs5Exqx
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    unsigned a = 0b1111'0000;        // 240
    unsigned b = 0b0011'1100;        // 60
    std::cout << ( a | b ) << "\n";  // Bit-Or: 252, in bits 1111'1100
    std::cout << ( a & b ) << "\n";  // Bit-And: 48, in bits 0011'0000
    std::cout << ( a ^ b ) << "\n";  // Exclusive-Or: 204, in bits 1100'1100
    unsigned int c = 170;            // in bits 0..(24x0)..0'1010'1010
    std::cout << ( ~c ) << "\n";     // Inv.: 4294967125, Bits: 1...(24x1)..1'0101'0101
} 
```

**Listing 4.30**     Bit operations.

At this point, it is important to me that you understand the concepts of integers in C++ and learn how to use them. I will point out the typical pitfalls and give a few case studies:

*   There are the integer types <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>, each in <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> form.

*   These have different widths on the different systems; only the order of their sizes is fixed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is special because it is used not only for arithmetic but also for storing characters (hence the name).

*   Your general-purpose integer types should be <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp>.

*   You can calculate “normally” with all numbers in C++; simple arithmetic and bit operations are supported directly.

*   Within an expression with two operands of different types, one may be converted before the calculation is executed.

#### Integer Overflow

If you calculate <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int x = 5 - 10;</samp>, then strange things happen: for the computer, this becomes a huge number. The same thing happens at the other end of the spectrum: on many current computers, an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp> has 32 bits, and if these are not enough to store a number, the computer starts again from zero. Both are called an overflow. Be careful here if you are working with the <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> variants, as these do not specify what happens in the event of an overflow. In general, an overflow should be avoided unless you know exactly what you are doing with a <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> type.[[ 10 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_07)

#### Arithmetic Type Conversion

So far, we have made it easy for ourselves: we have always given an operator two operands of the same type. If you use two different types, the compiler performs an implicit type conversion for the smaller integer type: it is first copied into a temporary variable of the larger type. The result type of the expression is then the larger type.

For example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char c = 50; int n = 500;</samp> in the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">c+n</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> is converted into an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> with the value <samp class="listingcharacter">50</samp> before the calculation. This makes it possible for the result of <samp class="listingcharacter">550</samp> to be calculated at all (a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> would be too small for this). The result type of the expression is also <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, as this is the larger of the two types involved.

It gets tricky when you mix <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> types. Here are a couple of rules of thumb:

*   If the signed operand involved is larger than the unsigned operand, it will also be used for the result, and you can be reasonably sure that the conversion will not destroy anything.

*   If both are the same size, the result is given the unsigned type and any negative numbers are lost.

In practice, this has the following effect: <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> are both the same size—both <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. If you add a <samp class="listingcharacter">signed ss = -4;</samp> and an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned uu = 2</samp>, the compiler specifies <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> as the type for the result. This has the effect that <samp class="listingcharacter">-4</samp> is converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> before the addition—and thus becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">4294967292</samp> (for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> with 32 bits). The result is then somewhat surprisingly <samp class="listingcharacter">4294967294</samp>. And as these rules apply to comparisons as well as arithmetic, <samp class="listingcharacter">if(ss < uu)</samp> is also surprisingly evaluated to false—or even more explicitly, the value of the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">if(-4 < 2u)</samp> is determined as <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> by the compiler in C++ because the signed literal <samp class="listingcharacter">-4</samp> is compared with the <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> literal <samp class="listingcharacter">2u</samp>.

##### Avoid Mixing

If you are dealing with number ranges that are at risk during such a conversion—negative or large numbers—then you should not rely on the implicit conversion. In this case, convert the operands yourself beforehand. Do not write <samp class="listingcharacter">if(mySize > theLimit)...</samp> if the two types have different signs, but convert them yourself. This will make you aware that something is happening here that you need to keep an eye on:

```
if(mySize > (long)theLimit) ... 
```

Better still, both figures would have been the same type right from the start.

As of C++20, safer auxiliary functions such as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cmp_less()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cmp_equal()</samp>, and the like are available, but these are more complicated to use than simply writing <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>. To check whether a value can be safely stored in a specific type, use <samp class="listingcharacter">in_range<T>()</samp>. In generic template code, this is often the only safe way.

#### Alias Number Types

There are number types that are defined differently on systems. A prominent example is <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp>: sometimes this type is identical to <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned int</samp>, sometimes to <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long</samp> or even to <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long long</samp>. But if you only use variables of these types for the purpose for which they are intended, you are not interested in the exact underlying type.

For example, if you want to know the size of a data structure, use <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof(data)</samp>. The return is a <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp>—and you should store the result in this. Of course, this is actually one of the other <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> types, but you don't need to know exactly which one. It is an alias for the (unknown) real type.

There are several reasons to use an alias. The most important are these:

*   You save yourself typing work. An alias is shorter, especially with templates.

*   They say something about the usage; that is, they use the alias as a semantic label. <samp class="listingcharacter">ptr_diff_t</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> may be identical, but their names already tell you something about their usage.

*   They are more flexible for later changes, as different types may be useful for specific purposes in different systems. In this case, you only need to change the alias in one place.

Aliases such as <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> have been created with <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> and are usually available if you are already using the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> anyway. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> could have been defined like this:

```
using size_t = unsigned long long; 
```

##### “typedef” versus “using”

If you look now, you might not find any <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> in your headers at all, because the way to do this before C++11 was as follows:

```
typedef unsigned long long size_t; 
```

I recommend that you use the new style. It may be a matter of taste (or habit), but I personally like the style where the newly introduced name is to the left of an equals sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>. But I'm showing you the <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef</samp> style because we'll probably be seeing it for a very long time.

As you will see in Part IV, a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> can hold a large number of elements. You can access the individual elements by index using square brackets <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp>. This index must be a number—more precisely, a <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp>. So if you define a count variable for a vector index, you can very well let it be a <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zGso3xGcj
#include <vector>
#include <cstddef> // size_t
int main() 
{
    std::vector<int> data = { 100, -4, 6'699, 88, 0, } ;

    int sum = 0;

    for(size_t idx = 0; idx < data.size(); ++idx) 
    { // a specific int type
        sum += data[idx];
    }
 } 
```

**Listing 4.31**     Index variables can be of type “size_t”.

However, it should not be concealed from you that the sum in the preceding example could of course have been implemented much better using <samp class="listingcharacter">for(auto d: data) sum += d;</samp>. Or you could immediately use an algorithm from <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">auto sum = std::accumulate(data.begin(), data.end(), 0);</samp>. In both cases, you can see that with C++11 you can now often save yourself the trouble of knowing the exact type.

Other frequently used aliases with typical definitions for certain integer types are shown in [Table 4.8](#04_004.html_t4.8).

| Alias | On 64-Bit Linux | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long unsigned int</samp> | Sizes that cannot be negative, such as container sizes |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ptrdiff_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long int</samp> | Distance between two addresses as <samp class="listingcharacter">ptrdiff_t d = &x - &y;</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">time_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long int</samp> | From <samp class="listingcharacter"><ctime></samp> to store seconds since 1.1.1970 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int8_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">signed char</samp> | Integer with exactly eight bits from <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstdint></samp> |
