| <samp class="listingcharacter">int64_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long int</samp> | Integer with exactly 64 bits from <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstdint></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">uint8_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp> | Positive integer with exactly eight bits |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int_least64_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long int</samp> | Integer with at least 64 bits |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int_fast16_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long int</samp> | Fast integer with at least 16 bits |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">uint8_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp> | Positive integer with exactly eight bits |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> | special | Access and manipulate raw memory with <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstddef></samp> |

**Table 4.8**     Some frequently used aliases for certain integer types.

All types from <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstdint></samp> are available for 8, 16, 32, and 64 bits. The <samp class="listingcharacter">least</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">fast</samp> variants can be larger. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">int8_t</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int64_t</samp> variants <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> are only defined if they exist on the system in exactly this size—which should usually be the case.

##### std::byte as a Special Case

Traditionally, C and C++ programmers often prefer to use one of the integer types to manipulate raw memory. This is actually not ideal. Unless you want to do arithmetic like <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> with the values, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp> can actually do too much. In most cases, you only need to perform bit manipulation (<samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> etc.). And this is exactly what <samp class="listingcharacter">std::byte</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstddef></samp> header was added for in C++17.

This data type is intended for manipulating raw memory and has the width of an <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp>, which means eight bits on the most common platforms. If you have two variables, <samp class="listingcharacter">byte a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">byte b</samp>, then the following operations are available to you, where <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> stands for any integer value:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::byte b{n}</samp> creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">to_integer(b)</samp> returns the numerical value.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">b << n</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b >> n</samp> returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> with bits shifted to the left or right.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">b <<= n</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b >>= n</samp> shifts bits in <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> to the left or right.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">a | b</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">a & b</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ b</samp> links two bytes bit by bit using OR, AND, or exclusive-or (XOR).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">b |= a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b &= a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b ^= a</samp> saves the result of the link back to <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">~b</samp> returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> with all bits negated.

A typical use is <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<byte></samp>, in which you then read the content of a file, for example.

### 4.4.4    Floating-Point Numbers

In addition to the integer types, there are also <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> types for floating-point numbers. Instead of throwing away the remainder of <samp class="listingcharacter">5/2</samp> when dividing, you can store it in a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>; for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">double x = 5.0 / 2.0;</samp> stores <samp class="listingcharacter">2.5</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>. But beware, floating-point numbers also have their limits: they also only have a fixed number of bits available, but they use them differently than the integer types do. They use some of the bits for “scaling” the value. This means that you can use them to store extremely large and tiny numbers, but only up to a certain precision. You need to keep the following things in mind:

*   Overflow
    Although the number range is much larger than for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can also overflow. It cannot store numbers larger than 10^(300) and smaller than -10^(300).

*   Precision
    Precision is much more critical. The further you move away from zero as the center, the coarser the values that <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can store become. The distance between two “neighboring” <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> numbers increases. From around 10^(15), this is more than 1\. If you store them in <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, the numbers 10^(16)+1 and 10^(16)+2 are identical for the computer; see [Listing 4.33](#04_004.html_l4.33).

*   Rounding
    But <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> also has problems with numbers close to zero. Because where an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, for example, can store <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> exactly, a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> has problems with <samp class="listingcharacter">0.1</samp>—and even more so with 1/3, so 0.3, as you can see in [Figure 4.4](#04_004.html_f4.4).

The standard data type is <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. The bit widths of these types are not fixed, but usually <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> has 64 bits, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> 32 bits, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> 80 or 128 bits. As of C++23, there are also fixed-width types (see [Table 4.10](#04_004.html_t4.10)).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/8ae83nPYs
#include <iostream>     // cout
#include <iomanip>      // setprecision, etc.
#include <cmath>        // fabs
using std::cout;        // cout as abbreviation for std::cout
int main() {
    cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(25);     // for better readable output
    // 0.1 and 0.01 cannot store double exactly
    double x = 0.1 * 0.1;
    cout << "0.1*0.1: " << x << "\n";
    // Output: 0.1*0.1: 0.0100000000000000019428903
    if(x == 0.01) {     //  never compare double with ==
        cout << "Yes! x == 0.01" << "\n";
    } else {
        cout << "Uh-oh! x != 0.01" << "\n";           // you see this output
    }
    // Attention especially when comparing with 0.0
    double null = x - 0.01;
    cout << "null: " << null << "\n";
    // Output: null: 0.0000000000000000017347235
    if(std::fabs(null) < 0.00000001) {               // compare with an "epsilon"
        cout << "Yes! null is close to 0.0" << "\n";  // you see this output
    } else {
        cout << "Uh-oh! null not close to 0.0" << "\n";
    }
    // fractions of powers of 2 are less critical
    double y = 0.5 * 0.5;
    cout << "0.5*0.5: " << y << "\n";
    // Output: 0.5*0.5: 0.2500000000000000000000000
    if(y == 0.25) {     // here the dangerous comparison works exceptionally
        cout << "Yes! y == 0.25" << "\n";             // you see this output
    } else {
        cout << "Oh-oh! y != 0.25" << "\n";
    }
    //
    return 0;
} 
```

**Listing 4.32**     “double” cannot always store numbers exactly. Calculating and comparing with “==” is an error.

#### Do Not Compare Floating-Point Numbers with ==

Because none of the floating-point types, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> can store all numbers exactly, you should never test for equality by using <samp class="listingcharacter">==.</samp> Instead, calculate the difference and check whether the result is close to zero. For example, if you want to know whether the two <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> values <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are “almost equal,” you can check this in this way:

```
if( fabs(b-a)<0.0001 )... 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">fabs()</samp> function determines the absolute value (makes it positive) and is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp> header. For <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0001</samp>, use <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> an epsilon that suits your application.

#### Floating-Point Literals

Similar to integers, you can write floating-point numbers naturally in the source text. However, you must use the dot <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> as a decimal separator; the continental comma does not work here. In the literal <samp class="listingcharacter">124.258</samp>, the compiler recognizes from the dot <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> that it is not an integer.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/qx8h7a4j9
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>                                 // fixed, setprecision
using std::cout;                                   // abbreviated cout
int main() {
    cout << std::setprecision(2) << std::fixed;    // two decimal places
    cout << "1/4: " << 0.25 << "\n";               // comma notation for double
    // output: 1/4: 0.25

    cout << "2/4: " << 0.5 << "\n";
    // Output: 2/4: 0.50
    cout << "3/4: " << 0.75 << "\n";
    // Output: 3/4: 0.75
    cout << "4/4: " << 1 << " or " << 1.0 << "\n"; //  recognizes 1 as int
    // Output 4/4: 1 or 1.00
    cout << "1e0: " << 1e0 << "\n";                // scientific notation
    // output: 1e0: 1.00
    cout << "0x10.1p0: " << 0x10.1p0 << "\n";      // hexadecimal notation
    // output: 0x10.1p0: 16.06
} 
```

**Listing 4.33**     Several ways to mark “double” literals.

If, as with <samp class="listingcharacter"><< 1 <<</samp>, the floating-point number happens to have no decimal places, then write at least the dot to distinguish it from the integer literal—and zeros if you want: <samp class="listingcharacter">1.</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">1.0</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">1.00</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">1.000</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and so on. A <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> without a dot is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> for the compiler. This still works in many cases, because if the compiler knows that you actually mean a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, it converts the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> 1 <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> into a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> 1 without loss. However, in cases where both would be possible, you should (or must) indicate the floating-point number. The output operator for <samp class="listingcharacter"><< 1 <<</samp> does not know whether you mean an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, so it outputs the <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> as such. The compiler recognizes the <samp class="listingcharacter">1.0</samp> as a floating-point number and the output is correct.

Since C++17, you can also use hexadecimal notation for floating-point literals, as you can see in the example at <samp class="listingcharacter">0x10.1p0.</samp> This is close to the internal representation, which we will discuss a little later in this section. In short, these are the building blocks of the literal:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp>, the hexadecimal prefix

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">10.1</samp>, the signifier in hexadecimal notation (here, decimal 1.125)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp>, the separator

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, the exponent in hexadecimal notation

The significand or parts of it are optional, but <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp> and the exponent always occur.

The type of such a floating-point literal is <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. In most cases today, it makes sense to use this data type as the first choice when calculating with floating-point numbers. Today's hardware is designed for calculating with it. If you need to save space, want to use a third-party API, or have other reasons, make a floating-point literal a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> by appending an <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">F</samp> to it. Appending an <samp class="listingcharacter">l</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">L</samp> indicates a <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp>. As of C++23, there are extended floating-point types that have suffixes such as <samp class="listingcharacter">f128</samp> and the like (see [Table 4.9](#04_004.html_t4.9)).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6qfo4oYnr
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip> // fixed, setprecision
int main() {
    using std::cout;
    cout << std::setprecision(30) << std::fixed;    // always output 30 digits
    cout << 1.111222333444555666777888999f << "\n"; // float literal
    // Output: 1.111222386360168457031250000000
    cout << 1.111222333444555666777888999 << "\n";  // double is default
    // Output: 1.111222333444555676607023997349
    cout << 1.111222333444555666777888999d << "\n"; // double literal
    // Output: 1.111222333444555676607023997349
    cout << 1.111222333444555666777888999L << "\n"; // long double
    // Output: 1.111222333444555666740784227731
} 
```

**Listing 4.34**     Floating-point literals become imprecise at some point.

There are many ways to output floating-point numbers or prepare them for output:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format("{}", number)</samp> As of C++20, you can convert any arguments into a string. Format attributes for width, precision, and more are available for numbers. You can combine <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << format("{}", number)</samp> as well.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">to_chars(buffer, buffer + size, number)</samp> This function writes numbers to a buffer. There are optional arguments for formatting and an error check. You can use it from C++17 on.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">to_string(number)</samp> This is only possible with numbers. You have no control over the format and can do little to check for errors.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << number</samp> The direct output of almost any type to a stream. For numbers, there are manipulators such as <samp class="listingcharacter">setprecision</samp> that influence the format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">print(cout, "{}", number)</samp> As of C++23, you can output any arguments to a stream as with <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>. The implementations are not yet complete as of the end of 2023.

#### The Floating-Point Features

Unlike integers, the limits and accuracy of floating-point types are the same on almost all systems. You would have to have a venerable old system if there were to be any differences here.

The pitfalls in dealing with floating-point numbers actually lurk elsewhere—namely, as mentioned earlier, in the realms of precision and rounding decimals. There are also operations in the “dark areas” of mathematics. For example, a floating-point variable can not only store a valid number, but can also take on a few very special values:

*   If you divide by <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0</samp>, this does not trigger an exception for floating-point numbers. The result is then infinite. Check a variable <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> with the function <samp class="listingcharacter">std::isfinite(x)</samp> from the header <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp> to see whether it still represents a finite value.

*   Only <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0/0.0</samp> results not in infinity, but in “not a number” (NaN), just like <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt(-1.0)</samp>, the square root of -1\. All further calculations with NaN result in NaN again. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::isnan(x)</samp> function to check a value for this.

You can learn more about the even more technical details in the next sections.

#### Floating-Point Internals

If you really want to understand how floating-point numbers work in C++, you have to deal with their internal representation in C++. This is based on the IEEE 754 standard. Even if you don't manipulate the bits of the floating-point number individually, it helps to understand what the computer does, can do, and especially cannot do.

The floating-point types available by default are <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp>. For the sizes of these types, it is only specified that they are equal or ascending; the details depend on the compiler used and the target platform. In x86 in practice, a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> has 32 bits, a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> 64 bits, and a <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> 80 bits or, more rarely, 128 bits. This corresponds to the IEEE 754 standard sizes, which you can find in [Table 4.9](#04_004.html_t4.9).

With the 64 bits of a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, you can store numbers as large as 10^(300), and amounts as small as 1/10^(300) can be stored. The bits are divided internally into three groups: the sign, the exponent,  and the significand (also called the mantissa). The number is then stored scaled, in binary, according to this formula: V × 1.S× 2^E.

| Description | Simple | Double | Quadruple | Octuple |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sign V | 1 bit | 1 bit | 1 bit | 1 bit |
| Exponent E | 8 bit | 11 bit | 15 bit | 19 bit |
| Significand S | 23 bit | 52 bit | 112 bit | 236 bit |

**Table 4.9**     The components of the machine representation of floating-point numbers.

Because this is very abstract, [Figure 4.4](#04_004.html_f4.4) shows a few examples of <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>.

Optional support for extended floating-point numbers has been introduced in C++23\. New floating-point types with a defined layout can be used with the <samp class="listingcharacter"><stdfloat></samp> header. This means that, if available, the widths are the same on all platforms.

[![Some examples for the representation of floating-point numbers as “double.”](bilderklein/klein04_004.png)](img-f4.4.html)

**Figure 4.4**     Some examples for the representation of floating-point numbers as “double.”

I have provided you with a different perspective on comparing the numerous types in [Table 4.10](#04_004.html_t4.10). The classic types are shown as an example for the x86 platform with g++ 13.2\. The “suf” column shows the suffixes for literals. “d2/d10” contains the binary and decimal precision. In “max e2”, you will find the maximum binary exponent. “max()” contains the largest displayable number and “eps()” the smallest distance between two displayable numbers.

In the “Time” column, you can see a sample calculation on my 64-bit Linux. It will be completely different on other architectures, especially embedded systems and GPUs. I just want to illustrate here that “smaller” is not necessarily faster and that accuracy can cost a lot of time.

It is worth noting that <samp class="listingcharacter">bfloat16_t</samp> acts like a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">float32_t</samp> with reduced precision. However, it can store larger numbers due to the larger exponent. It is often used in AI. The <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> on the x86 Linux calculates with 80 bits, the traditional width of the x87 coprocessors.

##### [Übung]  Pitfalls: No Streams and No Aliases

You can format the new types with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::format("{}", val)</samp>, but types wider than <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> are not supported for streams.

For example, even if the type <samp class="listingcharacter">float64_t</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> on the 64-bit Linux, <samp class="listingcharacter">float64_t</samp> is not an alias of <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, but a separate type. This means that you can have overloads for both types:

```
void f(double);
void f(float64_t); // okay: other overload 
```

This is different from the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> types, where <samp class="listingcharacter">int32_t</samp> is an alias for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and such overloads are acknowledged by the compiler with an error. Note, however, that you should normally choose one of the two variants for your code, either the classic types or the types with a defined layout.

An implementation—that is, a compiler and standard library—can offer further types, but these must then be divisible by 32\. Whether a type is available can be checked with the <samp class="listingcharacter">__STDCPP_</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Typ</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">__</samp> macro—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">__STDCPP_FLOAT128__</samp>.

| Name | suf | bits | d2/d10 | max e2 | max() | eps() | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| float16_t | f16 | 16 | 11/3 | 16 | 6.55e+04 | 0.0009766 | 208ms |
| bfloat16_t | bf16 | 16 | 8/2 | 128 | 3.39e+38 | 0.007812 | 191ms |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> | f | 32 | 24/6 | 128 | 3.403e+38 | 1.192e-07 | 40ms |
| float32_t | f32 | 32 | 24/6 | 128 | 3.403e+38 | 1.192e-07 | 40ms |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |  | 64 | 53/15 | 1024 | 1.798e+308 | 2.22e-16 | 40ms |
| float64_t | f64 | 64 | 53/15 | 1024 | 1.798e+308 | 2.22e-16 | 40ms |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> | l | 128 | 64/18 | 16384 | 1.19e+4932 | 1.084e-19 | 81ms |
| float128_t | f128 | 128 | 113/33 | 16384 | 1.19e+4932 | 1.926e-34 | 514ms |

**Table 4.10**     The floating-point types added in C++23 in comparison to the classic ones (in bold) on a 64-bit Linux system.

Let's go into even more detail. I will use an example to explain the exact conversion of a floating-point number into the machine representation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>. When I use the term floating-point number, I mean the mathematically abstract notion of a number, but now specifically in the decimal system we are used to. By <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, I mean the IEEE 754 standardized binary representation of a floating-point number in single precision.

As an example, I take the number 45.45 and convert it into a 32-bit <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> representation with one sign bit, eight bits for the exponent, and 23 bits for the signifier.

The sign is quickly converted. The <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> for a positive number is saved as a <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> bit. A negative number would result in a <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> bit. There’s not much there yet, but in the machine it now looks as shown in [Figure 4.5](#04_004.html_f4.5).

[![The beginning of the conversion of a floating-point number.](bilderklein/klein04_005.png)](img-f4.5.html)

**Figure 4.5**     The beginning of the conversion of a floating-point number.

The next step is to convert the decimal notation into binary notation. Here we take care of the parts before and after the comma separately.

You can treat the part before the decimal point—in this case, 45—as an integer. You divide this number by 2 and write down the remainder (0 or 1) until there is nothing left, as described in [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3) (see also [Listing 4.25](#04_003.html_l4.25)).

For [10]45, you then get binary [2]101101.

Proceed slightly differently for the decimal part, .45\. Multiply the number repeatedly by 2 and note the 0 or 1 before the decimal point. Ignore the part before the decimal point for the next step. Continue until you have already carried out a multiplication operation once:

```
.45 x 2 = 0.9
.9  x 2 = 1.8
.8  x 2 = 1.6           <---+
.6  x 2 = 1.2               |
.2  x 2 = 0.4               |
.4  x 2 = 0.8               |
.8  x 2 ... we already had -+ 
```

You could continue endlessly, but it is more practical to note this period somehow—for example, with a line above the repeating part: ![inline image](bilder/formula-04_03.png). If the repeating part were a zero, the result would be exact and the number would have no period in binary notation.

The parts before the decimal point and after the decimal point now add up to the following in binary notation: ![inline image](bilder/formula-04_04.png).

You can now determine the exponent from this representation. To do this, move the decimal point after the first 1 and count how many positions you have moved—five positions in this case. In scientific notation in the decimal system, you could now write “e5” after the scaled number. In this case, you first convert the integer 5 into a binary number and obtain ![inline image](bilder/formula-04_05.png).

You now almost have the exponent for the machine representation. So that exponents smaller than zero can also be saved, you now only need to add 127 (for <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>) to the exponent—that is, 132 for 5, or binary ![inline image](bilder/formula-04_06.png).

There are eight bits, just as much space as in the exponent for a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>. If there were fewer, you would pad with zeros in front; if there were more, you would have an overflow and the number could only be stored as be stored as infinity. If the result for the exponent were negative, this would be an underflow—a number so close to zero that it can only be stored as zero.

Now I’ll write the bit sequence as an exponent in the machine representation (see [Figure 4.6](#04_004.html_f4.6)).

[![Here, 127 was added to save the exponent.](bilderklein/klein04_006.png)](img-f4.6.html)

**Figure 4.6**     Here, 127 was added to save the exponent.

In the significand, the computer only stores the digits after the decimal point. This procedure guarantees that there is always exactly 1 before the decimal point. Only in the case of subnormal numbers, if the exponent to be stored were exactly zero, there would be no 1\. The illustration deals with this case in particular.

##### Subnormal Numbers

If the exponent to be stored in bit representation is exactly zero, then the conversion of the significand is slightly different—“not normal.” The number is then denormalized or subnormal. In this case, the computer assumes that there is no 1 before the decimal point in binary notation. If it becomes necessary to store a number in denormalized form, it's a sign that you're on the verge of an underflow. I won't delve further into that here.

It is typical that calculations on denormalized numbers are much slower. You can check whether a number <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is denormalized by calling <samp class="listingcharacter">std::fpclassify(x)</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp>. If the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">FP_SUBNORMAL</samp>, then the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is close to an underflow.

As a final step, I transfer the decimal places from ![inline image](bilder/formula-04_07.png) into the significand. I roll out the period so long as I have space in the 23 bits. Without a period, I would fill it with zeros. The result is shown in [Figure 4.7](#04_004.html_f4.7).

[![The number 45.45 in IEEE 754 with single precision.](bilderklein/klein04_007.png)](img-f4.7.html)

**Figure 4.7**     The number 45.45 in IEEE 754 with single precision.

You cannot store a period in a finite bit sequence in this way. This is why some numbers that you can easily write down on paper in decimal notation do not have an exact representation for the computer. The preceding representation results in 45.449996 when recalculated. Some numbers can be stored exactly, such as 0.5, but even 0.1 gives you a period in binary notation.

#### Special Values

Some bit patterns have a special meaning and help the computer (and you) to detect and handle edge cases. If you have a floating-point number <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>, you can use the function <samp class="listingcharacter">std::fpclassify(x)</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp> to determine whether you have such a special number:

*   If the exponent stores zero as a bit sequence, it is a subnormal number very close to zero and therefore just before an underflow. <samp class="listingcharacter">fpclassify</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">FP_SUBNORMAL</samp> for such numbers.

*   For numbers that are too large, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">1.0/0.0</samp>, there is positive infinity, +∞. The function <samp class="listingcharacter">fpclassify</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">FP_INFINITE</samp>; <samp class="listingcharacter">signbit(x)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>.

*   For numbers in the negative range such as <samp class="listingcharacter">-1.0/0.0</samp>, there is negative infinity, -∞. <samp class="listingcharacter">fpclassify</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">FP_INFINITE</samp>; <samp class="listingcharacter">signbit(x)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>.

*   Invalid numbers such as <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0/0.0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt(-1.0)</samp> are called NaN. <samp class="listingcharacter">fpclassify</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">FP_NAN</samp>.

*   If a calculation is too close to zero in terms of precision, the computer saves <samp class="listingcharacter">+0.0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-0.0</samp> as separate values. <samp class="listingcharacter">x==0.0</samp> is true for both, and <samp class="listingcharacter">fpclassify</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">FP_ZERO</samp> for both. If you need to distinguish them, use <samp class="listingcharacter">signbit(x)</samp>, which returns <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">-0.0</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Tvx4qcrE6
#include <iostream>
#include <cmath>   // fpclassify
#include <limits>  // numeric_limits
#include <string>

std::string fpclass(double x) {
    switch(std::fpclassify(x)) {
        case FP_INFINITE:  return "infinite";
        case FP_NAN:       return "NaN";
        case FP_NORMAL:    return "normal";
        case FP_SUBNORMAL: return "subnormal";
        case FP_ZERO:      return "zero";
        default:           return "unknown";
    }
}

int main() {
    const auto dmin = std::numeric_limits<double>::min();
    std::cout
      <<"1.0/0.0 is "<<fpclass(1/0.0)<<'\n'   // Output: 1.0/0.0 is infinite
      <<"0.0/0.0 is "<<fpclass(0.0/0.0)<<'\n' // Output: 0.0/0.0 is NaN
      <<"dmin/2 is "<<fpclass(dmin/2)<<'\n'   // Output: dmin/2 is subnormal
      <<"-0.0 is "<<fpclass(-0.0)<<'\n'       // Output: -0.0 is zero
      <<"1.0 is "<<fpclass(1.0)<<'\n';        // Output: 1.0 is normal
} 
```

**Listing 4.35**     Among other things, you can discover special values with “fpclassify<samp class="listingcharacter">.”</samp>

The header defines macros or constants for the special values. <samp class="listingcharacter">HUGE_VAL</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">HUGE_VALF</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">HUGE_VALL</samp> contain very large values, <samp class="listingcharacter">INFINITY</samp> the positive infinity, and <samp class="listingcharacter">NAN</samp> not a number.

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">fpclassify</samp>, other functions are available in <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp> to determine the properties of floating-point numbers. <samp class="listingcharacter">isfinite</samp> (not <samp class="listingcharacter">NAN</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">INFINITY</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">isinf</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">INFINITY</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">isnan</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">NAN</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">isnormal</samp> (not <samp class="listingcharacter">INFINITY</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">NAN</samp>, zero, or subnormal), and <samp class="listingcharacter">signbit</samp> (sign) have the obvious meanings. <samp class="listingcharacter">isunorderd</samp> checks whether at least one of two numbers is <samp class="listingcharacter">NAN.</samp>

#### Tips for Almost Exact Calculation

When adding, it is better to add large numbers to large numbers and small numbers to small numbers rather than large numbers to small numbers.

Multiplication is a little trickier. Due to the scaling in the exponent, calculations between <samp class="listingcharacter">-1.0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">+1.0</samp> are more accurate than those further away from <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0</samp>. It is advisable to bring calculations as close to this range as possible. This means, if you can influence it, arrange the multiplications in such a way that you follow this rule: “Large to small, small to large.”

This means that <samp class="listingcharacter">(0.1 * 10.0) * (10.0 * 0.1)</samp> is better than <samp class="listingcharacter">(0.1 * 0.1) * (10.0 * 10.0)</samp>, but mainly for extreme values. This means that the intermediate results do not move further away from <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> than necessary.

I think a detailed example will help you to see what can happen if the calculation elements are arranged unfavorably. For example, there is Heron’s formula to calculate the area of a triangle given three side lengths (a, b, c):

Rewritten slightly, Heron’s formula in C++ looks like this:

```
float heron(float a, float b, float c) {
    auto s = (a+b+c) / 2;
    return sqrt(s*(s-a)*(s-b)*(s-c));
} 
```

For comparison, there is the Kahan method,[[ 11 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_08) which first sorts the side lengths of the triangles according to a ⩾ b ⩾ c and then looks for a better grouping.[[ 12 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn04_09) After sorting, the following formula results:

![inline image](bilder/formula-04_08.png)

However, only if c ⩽ a–b, because otherwise the sides do not form a triangle. In C++, it looks like this:

```
float kahan(float a, float b, float c) {
    auto x = max(a,max(b,c));
    auto y = max(min(a,b), min(max(a,b),c));
    auto z = min(a,min(b,c));
    return sqrt( (x+(y+z))*(z-(x-y))*(z+(x-y))*(x+(y-z)) )/4;
} 
```

For a right-angled triangle with the side lengths 3, 4, and 5, the area 6 can be calculated in the head using the Pythagorean theorem. The following program is the same for both methods. I have used the template variable <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> as the type in order to be able to execute the same code with <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23)):

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/We3oWrcWW
#include <iostream>
#include <cmath>     // sqrt
#include <concepts>  // floating_point
using std::min; using std::max; using std::floating_point;

template<floating_point T> T heron(T a, T b, T c) {
    auto s = (a+b+c) / 2;
    return sqrt(s*(s-a)*(s-b)*(s-c));
}

template<floating_point T> T kahan(T a, T b, T c) {
    auto x = max(a,max(b,c));
    auto y = max(min(a,b), min(max(a,b),c));
    auto z = min(a,min(b,c)); return
    sqrt( (x+(y+z))*(z-(x-y))*(z+(x-y))*(x+(y-z)) )/4 ;
}

template<floating_point T> void triangle(T a, T b, T c) {
    std::cout << "heron: " << heron(a,b,c) << '\n';
    std::cout << "kahan: " << kahan(a,b,c) << '\n';
}

int main() {
    triangle(3.0f, 4.0f, 5.0f);
} 
```

The output is then <samp class="listingcharacter">6</samp> for both procedures.

Funny things happen when you insert the side lengths (100000, 99999.99979, 0.00029) and let the computer calculate the area. I run both calculations for <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and output more digits:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/863b1z4GY
int main() {
    std::cout << std::setprecision(15) << std::fixed;
    triangle(100'000.0f, 99'999.999'79f, 0.000'29f);
    triangle(100'000.0,  99'999.999'79,  0.000'29);
} 
```

The exact result would be 10\. The example was carefully chosen so that <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> has difficulties in the calculation: while the classic Heron formula gives 0, the Kahan formula calculates 14.5\. And 14.5 would look like a nice result if you didn't know that 10 is correct. Even though both methods give a better result with <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>—because I told you that 10 should come out—such an example could also have been found for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. The actual outputs are as follows:

```
heron: 0.000000000000000
kahan: 14.500000000000000
heron: 9.999999809638329
kahan: 10.000000077021038 
```

However, it is even more important that you have to perform as few calculations as possible. Let's assume you work in video editing and want to calculate the length of a movie. Videos often have one frame per 1/25 of a second. Then you can calculate the current movie time in a loop in two ways. First, try it accumulated, and second, try it with closed multiplication, as the following two listings demonstrate.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/sEE94bh5K
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip> // setprecision, fixed
constexpr int framesPerSec = 25;
constexpr int runtimeInSecs = 3600;
constexpr int framesTotal = runtimeInSecs * framesPerSec;
constexpr float frametime = 1.0f / framesPerSec;

int main() {
    float filmtime = 0.f;
    for(int n=1; n <= framesTotal; ++n) { // 1 .. framesTotal
        filmtime += frametime;            // accumulate
        // ... here code for this frame ...
    }
    std::cout << std::setprecision(10) << std::fixed
        << filmtime << '\n';              // output: 3602.2695312500
} 
```

**Listing 4.36**     Accumulated time measurement.

You shouldn't be surprised that more than two seconds of errors have accumulated in one hour of film.

##### [Übung]  Labeling Constants

For <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> refer to [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13), [Section 13.10.6](#13_010.html_h13.10.6). It is advantageous for the compiler and for you if you mark unchangeable values (i.e., constants) as such. You can use (<samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>) <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> for this purpose. The latter ensures that the compiler can calculate the constant in advance. If it cannot do this, it will inform you accordingly.

I let the loop run from <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter"><= framesTotal</samp> to be able to compare it better with the next example.

However, you can also approach this differently. So long as the <samp class="listingcharacter">frametime</samp> remains constant over the course of the movie, you can calculate it in one step. So you are scaling as in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/dKPo7andE
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip> // setprecision, fixed
constexpr int framesPerSec = 25;
constexpr int runtimeInSecs = 3600;
constexpr int framesTotal = runtimeInSecs * framesPerSec;
constexpr float frametime = 1.0f / framesPerSec;
int main() {
    float filmtime = 0.f;
    for(int n=1; n <= framesTotal; ++n) { // 1 .. framesTotal, because of formula
        filmtime = frametime * n;         // scale
        // ... here code for this frame ...
    }
    std::cout << std::setprecision(10) << std::fixed
        << filmtime << '\n';              // output: 3600.0000000000
} 
```

**Listing 4.37**     Closed time calculation.

And there is no longer any deviation.

Here you can see why I preferred to run from <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter"><= tramesTotal</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop instead of from <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">< framesTotal</samp>: only then does <samp class="listingcharacter">filmtime = frametime * n</samp> actually correspond to <samp class="listingcharacter">filmtime = frametime *</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">framesTotal</samp> in the last loop pass.

##### Tips on the Calculation Sequence

*   When adding, keep the large numbers together with other large numbers and the small numbers together with the small ones.

*   Carry out multiplications as close to the interval from -1.0 to +1.0 as possible.

*   Perform as few calculations as possible so that errors are less likely to propagate. For example, prefer a single multiplication to a repeated addition.

These rules apply if you have decided to calculate with floating-point numbers. Before doing so, you should ask yourself whether integers are not better suited to your task. Integers are fast and precise with the right operations. However, they do not cover such a large calculation range.

When calculating amounts of money, you should never (never! never! never!) calculate with floating-point numbers. Calculate in hundredths of a cent or similar and do not continue to calculate with the rounded values that you need for the output.

##### From Zero and Less Than

Because indexes usually start at zero, it is common in C++ to also start loops at zero. This means that you normally run <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops up to <samp class="listingcharacter">< size</samp> when they run through a C‐array or <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, for example. If the loops exceptionally start at <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> or run up to <samp class="listingcharacter"><= size,</samp> you should mark this clearly. Otherwise, speedy readers might overlook it out of habit or wonder whether you have made a careless mistake.

### 4.4.5    Truth Values

The data type with which you can represent true or false is <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. You can declare <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> variables and cache truth values in them. Many functions return a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> or take one as an argument. Just as there are literals for integers, floating-point numbers, and so on, there are also literals for <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>: namely, <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>.

This data type is also essential in many C++ language elements, as conditions are always written as <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> expressions. <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> This means that an expression for the condition in an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> or the like is converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. For example, all comparisons have <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> as the result, like <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> as well as <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>:

```
if(a >= b) ...
for(int idx; idx < 100; ++idx) ...
while(!finished && linesRead < LIMIT) ... 
```

You can link two <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> expressions with each other. Write “Are a and b both true?” as <samp class="listingcharacter">a && b</samp>. Find out whether at least one of them is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">a || b</samp>. Turn <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> into <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> and vice versa with <samp class="listingcharacter">!a</samp>. Because there are only two possible values for <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> [Table 4.11](#04_004.html_t4.11) contains all possible combinations. The somewhat unusual exclusive OR operator <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> is also included there. And last but not least, you can of course put expressions in parentheses with <samp class="listingcharacter">(...)</samp>. You can find out more about these operators and expressions in [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3).

| <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | Operator | Expression | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a && b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;&#124;</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a &#124;&#124; b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">!a</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |  |  |  | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |

**Table 4.11**     Truth table for all Boolean expressions with two values.

It would actually be sufficient for the computer to output a bit to store a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. However, the computer actually uses at least one <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and more often an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> for this. This is because the computer always blocks an entire “memory word” when manipulating bits and would therefore slow down neighboring bits. So you spend a little more space on independence and speed.

If you want to save a large number of individual <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>s, you should take a look at the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::bitset</samp> data type in the standard library.

This relationship with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is one of the reasons that you can also simply use an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> in tests with <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and the like in C++:

```
int idx = 100;
while(idx) {   // an int as a test
    readLine(line);
    --idx;
} 
```

This loop reads in exactly 100 lines. As soon as <samp class="listingcharacter">idx</samp> reaches zero, the loop is terminated. The <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value of <samp class="listingcharacter">idx</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> implicitly converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. This is done according to the following rules, which take some getting used to:

*   A value of <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> is converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>.

*   All other values become <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>.

Because many C++ programmers originally come from C, where there was no pure <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> data type, you will encounter this pattern quite often.

You can also use other data types in tests. To do this, the data type only needs to have the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator bool()</samp> method. This is the case, for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::istream</samp> and therefore with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp>. You can see an application example in the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop in [Chapter 27](#27_001.html_h27), [Listing 27.6](#27_005.html_l27.6).

### 4.4.6    Character Types

What is a “character” in abstract terms? It is a building block of a text that is to be displayed or processed. In C++, many things are mixed up here, and some things are not intuitive.

The main data type for characters is <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. At the same time, however, you can also regard <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> as an integer data type, as you can calculate with it in the same way as with all other <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> relatives. And yet it is different here, because it is not specified whether <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> without further specifications. So if you want to calculate with a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and the range is important, then you should always write <samp class="listingcharacter">signed char</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp> instead of simply <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>; reserve the latter for texts.

#### “char” Is the Smallest “int”

It is even specified that <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is the smallest integer data type and something like a base unit for memory usage. If you apply <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof(...)</samp> to any type or value, you get its size in <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> units:

```
sizeof(char);   // 1
char x;
sizeof(x);      // 1
int value;
sizeof(value);  // 4 or something else on other systems 
```

On current systems, you can assume that a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> has eight bits. Because you cannot rely on the sign, you should only assume that the number range from 0 to 127 is available to you; calculating outside this range can lead to overflow (at the positive or negative end).

Now let's move on from number interpretation to text interpretation. If you want to combine <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> elements into text, then you normally do this as follows:

*   In <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> if you want to save, pass around, or manipulate the text

*   In <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp> if you are outputting a literal or using an old C API

A text literal such as <samp class="listingcharacter">"Hello"</samp> is made up of individual <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> elements. The first is an <samp class="listingcharacter">'H'</samp>, the second an <samp class="listingcharacter">'a'</samp>, and so on. Note the single quotation marks <samp class="listingcharacter">'…'</samp> around the respective character: these make the character a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. You cannot combine several characters in such a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> literal; for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">'botch'</samp> makes no sense.

If you initialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> variable with a literal or assign one to it, then you are free to do this with quotation marks <samp class="listingcharacter">'…'</samp> or numbers, depending on how it fits better in the context:

```
char lower_a = 'a';                        // as a character
char letters_in_the_alphabet = 'z'-'a'+1;  // do the math
char small = 5;                            // as a number
signed char less = -10;                    // negative only with explicit signed
unsigned char large = 200;                 // large only with explicit unsigned
char flags = 0x7f;                         // hexadecimal for bit pattern 0111'1111 
```

#### International Signs

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, there are other character types. As <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is only suitable for 256 different characters, it would not be suitable for storing Chinese characters, for example. There are character types with more space for this:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t</samp>
    With its 32 bits, this is sufficient for the most obscure international characters. Every possible Unicode character can be represented with a single <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> With the prefix <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> you write a literal such as <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t zed = U'Z';</samp> and character strings in <samp class="listingcharacter">std::u32string</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp> This character type, which is always 16 bits wide, is good for 65,536 different characters and is sufficient for most international texts. Use the prefix <samp class="listingcharacter">u</samp> before a character literal—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t zed = u'Z';</samp>. The character string type <samp class="listingcharacter">std::u16string</samp> is based on this. A single <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp> is sufficient for the vast majority of Unicode characters. Only very rarely do you need two consecutive ones, which are then encoded in UTF-16.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp> This type is added in C++20\. It accepts UTF-8 code units and is therefore at least eight bits wide, just like <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp>, but is different as a type. Only ASCII characters fit into a single <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp>. This means that even for a Unicode ä, you need two <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp>—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">0xC3</samp> followed by <samp class="listingcharacter">0xA4</samp> in UTF-8 encoding. You write literals of this type with a <samp class="listingcharacter">u8</samp> prefix—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">u8'a'</samp> for characters and <samp class="listingcharacter">u8"gr\uF6n"</samp> for character strings.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t</samp> Depending on the system, this character type has 16 bits (Windows) or 32 bits (many Linux variants). If you write an <samp class="listingcharacter">L</samp> in front of a character literal, it is of this type—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t zed = L'Z';</samp>. As it can be of different widths, you should not use this type in programs that have to run on several systems. The character string type <samp class="listingcharacter">std::wstring</samp> is based on this type; to output it, use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::wout</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">std::werr</samp> or as input <samp class="listingcharacter">std::win</samp>.

There are many ways to save a Z. To make the differences clearer to you, [Table 4.12](#04_004.html_t4.12) shows the representations for the computer.

| Character Type | Literal | Interpretation in Bits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">'Z'</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0101'1010</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">u8'Z'</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0101'1010</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">or</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">L'Z'</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0000'0000'0101'1010</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">0000'0000'0000'0000'0000'0000'0101'1010</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">u'Z'</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0000'0000'0101'1010</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">U'Z'</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0000'0000'0000'0000'0000'0000'0101'1010</samp> |

**Table 4.12**     The different ways to write a Z with the different character types.

With a Z, this is not very exciting. But you can't write a Θ (theta) in the source code. You have to use an escape sequence for this. The Unicode character theta has the number [16]0398, so you can write <samp class="listingcharacter">u'\u0398'</samp> in a <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp> character literal or <samp class="listingcharacter">U'\U0000398'</samp> in a <samp class="listingcharacter">char32_t</samp> character literal. The <samp class="listingcharacter">\u</samp> notation requires a character number with exactly four hexadecimal digits after <samp class="listingcharacter">\u</samp> or exactly eight after <samp class="listingcharacter">\U</samp>. Four digits should usually be sufficient. Only for something as exotic as the Gothic letter ahsa would you have to write <samp class="listingcharacter">U'\U00010330'</samp>.

[![The Gothic ahsa character with the hexadecimal Unicode number 10330 must be escaped with “U.”](bilderklein/klein04_008.png)](img-f4.8.html)

**Figure 4.8**     The Gothic ahsa character with the hexadecimal Unicode number 10330 must be escaped with “U.”

The correct character should then appear on the correct medium—for example, in dialog boxes or file streams that can accept characters or strings of these types.

#### Unicode in C++

Internationalization, Unicode, and encoding are very complex topics that we cannot go into further in this book. It is best to limit yourself to <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> first and then read up on the use of the other character types if you need to.

With the introduction of <samp class="listingcharacter">char8_t</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">u8string</samp> in C++20, we have come a big step closer to full Unicode support. The standardization of encodings will still take some time, but it is planned.

### 4.4.7    Complex Numbers

If you know what complex numbers are, you may also want to calculate with them. This is possible because the <samp class="listingcharacter">complex</samp> template data type from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><complex></samp> header is part of the standard library.

For those who do not know what this means, here is a brief explanation. You probably know that whole numbers are the numbers 0, +1, –1, +2, –2, +3, and so on. You can do anything in this number range until you discover multiplication and the division that goes with it. Then you need the rational numbers; these are any two whole numbers in a fraction—so, for example, –3/4\. You are happy with this number range until you get the idea of adding very long fractions that get smaller and smaller. This is practical if you want to give all points on a line a name. The sum of such sequences results in real numbers, which include π and √2, for example. Do we have everything now? Yes—so long as you don't want to calculate the square root of a negative number. Because every real number squared results in a positive number (or zero)—for example, -4² = 16—it is not easy to define what the square root of a negative number should be. For example, what is √–1?

Such a gap robs mathematicians of sleep, which is why they define it as follows: let √–1=i or i² = –1\. Phew, that helps mathematicians: now they can solve equations that have no solution in real number space. For example, (x + 1)² = -9 does not result in a true statement for any real number x. However, if we take the earlier definition, we see that x has the two solutions: -1 + 3i and -1 – 3i. It looks strange, but you get used to it. A complex number such as -1 + 3i always has two components: the real part without i, here –1, and the imaginary part, here +3i. If you look at the two parts as x and y coordinates on a plane, you can see the complex numbers as points in the plane—just as you can see the real numbers as points on a line.

Special rules apply when calculating with complex numbers. They’re not really anything special; you just have to keep in mind that every i² can be replaced with –1\. Otherwise, the normal arithmetic rules apply:

*   Addition: (3 + 5i) + (8 – 1i) = (3 + 8) + (5 – 1)i = (11 + 4i)

*   Multiplication: (-2 + 3i) · (4 + 2i) = -2 · 4 + 3 · 4i – 2 · 2i + 2 · 3 · i · i = -8 + 12i – 4i + 6i² = -8 + 8i – 6 = -14 + 8i

*   Exponent: ((-1 + 3i) + 1)² = (3i)² = (3²) · (i²) = 9 · (-1) = -9

No sooner had this number space been discovered than physicists and mathematicians found all kinds of “practical” applications for it. In fact, complex numbers can be used to solve problems that were previously unsolvable.

#### Complex Numbers in C++

What does this look like in C++? If you use the <samp class="listingcharacter"><complex></samp> header, the following things are available to you:

*   The template data type <samp class="listingcharacter">complex<></samp>
    You can choose whether the imaginary and real parts should be calculated in <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> by specifying this as a template argument.

*   Operator overloads
    You can perform arithmetic calculations with <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, and the like, and stream operations with <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> on <samp class="listingcharacter">complex</samp> variables.

*   Free auxiliary functions
    You get auxiliary functions for manipulation and calculation, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">sin</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">pow</samp>, and so on, as well as conversions, such as polar coordinates with <samp class="listingcharacter">polar</samp>.

*   User-defined literals
    Among other things, <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""i</samp> is defined in <samp class="listingcharacter">std::literals::complex_literals</samp> so that you can easily write complex literals in the source code.

If you output a complex number with <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>, the number appears in the form <samp class="listingcharacter">(real, imag)</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/43rYYeKx9
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip> // setprecision, fixed
#include <complex>
using std::cout; using std::complex;

int main() {
    using namespace std::complex_literals;   // for i-suffix
    cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(1);
    complex<double> z1 = 1i * 1i;            // i times i
    cout << z1 << '\n';                      // Output: (-1.0,0.0)
    complex<double> z2 = std::pow(1i, 2);    // i-square
    cout << z2 << '\n';                      // Output: (-1.0,0.0)
    double PI = std::acos(-1);               // Length of half a unit circle
    complex<double> z3 = std::exp(1i * PI);  // Euler formula
    cout << z3 << '\n';                      // Output: (-1.0,0.0)
    complex<double> a(3, 4);                 // usually as a constructor
    complex<double> b = 1\. - 2i;             // practically as a literal

    // Calculations:
    cout << "a + b = " << a + b << "\n";     // Output: a + b = (4.0,2.0)
    cout << "a * b = " << a * b << "\n";     // Output: a * b = (11.0,-2.0)
    cout << "a / b = " << a / b << "\n";     // Output: a / b = (-1.0,2.0)
    cout << "|a| = " << abs(a) << "\n";      // Output: |a| = 5.0
    cout << "conj(a) = " << conj(a) << "\n"; // Output: conj(a) = (3.0,-4.0)
    cout << "norm(a) = " << norm(a) << "\n"; // Output: norm(a) = 25.0
    cout << "abs(a) = " << abs(a) << "\n";   // Output: abs(a) = 5.0
    cout << "exp(a) = " << exp(a) << "\n";   // Output: exp(a) = (-13.1,-15.2)
} 
```

**Listing 4.38**     You can calculate arithmetically with complex numbers.
