Before we delve further into how to write functions yourself, let's first look at their usage.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TdrebYodx
#include <iostream>                     // cout
#include <cmath>                        // sin
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using std::sin;
int main() {
    std::cout << "sin(0.0): " << sin(0.0) << "\n";       // call sin() with literal
    double angle = 3.1415/2;
    std::cout << "sin("<<angle<<"): "<<sin(angle)<<"\n"; // call with variable
    std::string name = "Han Solo";
    std::cout << name.length() << "\n"; // call a method
                                        // ... conceptually like length(name)
    std::vector<int> data{};
    data.push_back(5);                  // further method call with parameter
    data.push_back(10);
    std::cout << data.back() << " ";
    data.pop_back();
    std::cout << data.back() << "\n";
    data.pop_back();
} 
```

**Listing 7.1**     Use functions.

The function <samp class="listingcharacter">sin()</samp>is called once with the literal <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0</samp>—as a literal also a constant value—and once with the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">angle</samp>. As you would expect from the mathematical function sin, the result of a calculation is returned here.

You can see that the variable with which I call <samp class="listingcharacter">sin()</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. That fits, because in the standard library the function is declared as <samp class="listingcharacter">double sin(double)</samp>: it takes a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and also returns one. Parameter types must match each other when called: you could not have called <samp class="listingcharacter">sin("Han Solo")</samp>, because <samp class="listingcharacter">sin()</samp> is not intended for character strings. There are exceptions where a conversion takes place; you will get to know them and write some of them yourself.

Note that I am also presenting method calls here, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">name.length()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">data.push_back(5)</samp>. The main difference is that a function like <samp class="listingcharacter">sin()</samp> is “free” (a free function), but <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> is firmly associated with the class <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp>. When you call a function using variable<samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp>functionname,  this is the special form of the method. This term comes from object orientation and is discussed in detail in the chapter on classes (see [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12)). Note here that <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">back()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_back()</samp> are also constructs that you use like functions (and define later) and that you constantly will make use of.

## 7.4    Defining a Function

In general, you define a function as follows:

ReturnType FunctionName <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> ParameterType ParameterName <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> ... <samp class="listingcharacter">) {</samp> FunctionBody <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>

Or you can use the newer syntax, where the return type is at the end or can be omitted altogether. I will go into this more detail in [Section 7.11](#07_011.html_h7.11). Sometimes it can be clearer:

<samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> FunctionName <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> ParameterType -name <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> ... <samp class="listingcharacter">) [ -></samp> ReturnType <samp class="listingcharacter">]</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp> FunctionBody <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>

You have already heard some of this in passing, but I would like to say something about all these elements once again:

*   Return type
    The return type is the type of a value that you return from the function with <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>. All expressions in the <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statements must be of this type or convertible to this type. If the return type is <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp>, you do not need to specify a <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>. If you do, then write <samp class="listingcharacter">return;</samp> without a value. At the point where you then use the function, you can use the return value in an expression of the appropriate type—for example, in a calculation or an assignment. You can see some examples of return types in [Listing 7.2](#07_004.html_l7.2).

*   Function name
    This is a regular identifier under which you will later use the function. It may be that your function belongs to a class (method), in which case the function name is made up of ClassName<samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp>MethodName. Also, when you get to know function templates later, the name may be followed by angle brackets <samp class="listingcharacter"><...></samp>. I will cover this in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23).

*   Parameters
    If your function does not take any parameters, the parentheses are empty <samp class="listingcharacter">()</samp>. Otherwise, the types and names of the function parameters are listed here, separated by commas.

*   Parameter type
    Each parameter must be specified with at least its type. The abundance of possible types ranges from simple ones (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp>) to complex ones with several angle brackets (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">map<string,vector<int>></samp>). It is particularly important to distinguish whether you want to specify a parameter as a reference or pointer; in the latter two cases, an <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> is part of the type. If the parameter cannot be modified within the function, <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> is part of the type.

*   Parameter name
    To be able to use the parameter in the function at all, refer to it by the name given here. You can omit it if you are only declaring the function here (and not defining it) or if you do not use the parameter in the function at all. However, I recommend using a clear, descriptive name so that the function header becomes meaningful.

*   Function body
    The function body (together with the surrounding curly brackets) consists of statements: none, one, or many of them, as you see fit. If the function has a return value, there must be at least one <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statement here.

```
int func();                        // returns an int
std::string func();                // a string from the standard library
void func();                       // no return value
std::pair<int,std::string> func(); // composite type from the stdlib
vector<int> func();                // returns a new container
vector<int>& func();               // reference to some container
const vector<int>& func();         // same, but you cannot change it 
```

**Listing 7.2**     Different return types of functions.

### [Übung]  C++20: Abbreviated Function Template

As of C++20, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> as the parameter type. You then define a function template without the cumbersome notation with <samp class="listingcharacter">template</samp> and angle brackets. The compiler turns

```
void func(auto a) { ... } 
```

into

```
template<type name A> void func(A a) { ... }. 
```

You can read more about templates in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23). I mention it here because on the one hand, this notation does not reveal the template; on the other hand, it offers great opportunities for versatile yet compact code.

## 7.5    More about Parameters

In C++, the declaration of the parameter in the function header determines how the parameter behaves when called. The most important distinction is whether the parameter is passed as a value or as a reference.

### 7.5.1    Call-by-Value

If you do not take any special precautions, the parameters of a function in C++ are passed as values (call-by-value). This means that if a variable <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> currently has the value <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> and you pass <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> to a function, then the <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> ends up in the function—not the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/8zcvMdM3b
#include <iostream>

void print_val8(int n) {           // parameter as value
    std::cout << n << " ";
    n = 8;                         // sets parameter to 8
    std::cout << n << "\n";
}

int main() {
    int x = 5;
    print_val8(x);                 // x as value: prints 5, then 8
    std::cout << x << "\n";        // x remains unchanged at 5
    print_val8(42);                // 42 as value: prints 42, then 8
} 
```

**Listing 7.3**     Parameters are initially passed as a value.

When <samp class="listingcharacter">print_val8</samp> is called, the compiler copies the value of the arguments to the position <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> for the function. Therefore, the change at <samp class="listingcharacter">n = 8;</samp> has no effect on the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> with which <samp class="listingcharacter">print_val8(x)</samp> was initially called.

#### Call-by-Value for Structures with Pointers

At this point I must warn you that when interacting (especially) with pointers, things get a little more complex. If a pointer <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> is part of a structure or class that you pass by value, only the pointer is copied in this structure, not what it points to. This means that if you change what the pointer points to, you also change the original.

### 7.5.2    Call-by-Reference

If you want the assignment to affect the outer variable, you need to declare the function in C++ in such a way that it receives the parameter as a reference (call-by-reference). To do this, use the ampersand <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>.

I will vary the previous example for comparison before showing you the meaningful use.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/63dTshz3Y
#include <iostream>
void print_ref8(int& n) {          // parameter as reference
    std::cout << n << " ";
    n = 8;                         // sets parameter to 8
    std::cout << n << "\n";
}
int main() {
    int x = 5;
    print_ref8(x);                 // x as reference: prints 5, then 8
    std::cout << x << "\n";        // x is now 8
} 
```

**Listing 7.4**     Add an ampersand to make it a reference parameter.

The function <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8</samp> corresponds exactly to <samp class="listingcharacter">print_val8</samp> from the previous listing, except that in this example the parameter of <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8</samp> is declared with the <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> as a reference—namely, <samp class="listingcharacter">int& n</samp>. Therefore, when calling <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8(x)</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, the compiler does not copy the value of <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> into the function, but passes the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> itself as a reference; within the function, it is then addressed with the parameter name <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>. This way, you can call <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8</samp> from completely different program locations and pass completely different variables; within <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> they are always called <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>.

There is another difference: you cannot use <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8(42)</samp>. Can you see why? Within <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> the <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> would be referred to by the name <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>—and later an assignment is made in <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">n = 8</samp>. This means it would be <samp class="listingcharacter">42 = 8</samp>, and that obviously is not possible. However, the compiler prevents this not only at the assignment <samp class="listingcharacter">n = 8</samp>, but at the call <samp class="listingcharacter">print_ref8(42)</samp>: the parameter type is <samp class="listingcharacter">int&</samp> (read: “reference to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>”) and not <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and the compiler cannot refer to <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> in this way; <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> is not compatible with <samp class="listingcharacter">int&</samp>, and the compiler will complain.

### 7.5.3    Constant References

To pass both <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> to a function that takes a reference as a parameter, you must “promise” the compiler that you will not assign anything to the reference. With <samp class="listingcharacter">const int& n</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> you tell it that <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is constant inside the function.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/dcKnx3Pno
#include <iostream>
void print_cref(const int& n) {  // parameter as constant reference
    std::cout << n << " ";
}

int main() {
    int x = 5;
    print_cref(x);               // call with a variable
    print_cref(42);              // call with a constant literal
} 
```

**Listing 7.5**     You can use constant references as parameters for any call.

Now, of course, the line with n = 8 is gone, because otherwise you would be breaking your promise. The compiler would now find fault with this line, because you cannot assign anything to a <samp class="listingcharacter">const int&</samp>, which <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> now is. However, you can use a variable when calling <samp class="listingcharacter">print_cref8(x)</samp> or a literal <samp class="listingcharacter">print_cref8(42)</samp>. This means that the following two function declarations can be used equally broadly as far as the arguments are concerned:

```
void print_val8(int n);         // Parameter as value
void print_cref(const int& n);  // Parameter as constant reference 
```

### 7.5.4    Call as Value, Reference, or Constant Reference?

All these variants of declaring a parameter have their justification, and you have to decide which one to use on a case-by-case basis:

*   When called as a value,  a copy is created. This can be a time- and memory-consuming process at program runtime. On the other hand, you can be sure that you will not accidentally change any external values.

*   When called as a reference,  no copy is created, but the compiler transfers the address of the parameter into the function. This is quick and saves space. But do you really want to change externally defined variables? Sometimes, yes, but not always.

*   Use a const reference if you decide for a reference but do not want the have the variable changed.

*   If you use a non-const reference, you simply cannot pass some parameters, just as the literal <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> cannot be passed to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int&</samp>, for example. There are also constant values and objects, all of which you exclude with an <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> only parameter.

A disadvantage when using references (and pointers) can arise due to aliasing. There are cases in which a reference in a function refers to a variable (via an alias) that no longer exists; it has already become invalid outside. Program crashes are the result. As the parameter is copied specifically for the function call when it is called as a value, this cannot happen here.

One way to avoid these program crashes is to forego references. Because a typical application is the output parameter, I recommend that you use a return value instead:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/oh91YvaqT
#include <iostream>
void twice(double &num) {      // output parameter as modifiable reference
    num *= 2.0;
}

int main() {
    double num = 7.25;
    twice(num);
    std::cout << num << "\n";  // now 14.5
} 
```

It may look silly in this simple example, but if you have larger objects, you'll be tempted to do this all the time. Write instead:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/q4ov41cnv
#include <iostream>
double twice(double num) {     // value parameter and return value
    return num * 2.0;
}
int main() {
    double num = 7.25;
    num = twice(num);          // change expressed by return value
    std::cout << num << "\n";  // also 14.5
} 
```

Here, the parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> is copied when <samp class="listingcharacter">twice</samp> is called, but this makes the program safer and also clearer. The good news is that copying has improved since C++11, especially for data types from the standard library: values are now often moved instead of copied, which is always beneficial for performance.

#### When in Doubt, Use Value

If in doubt, opt for a value parameter. This must be copied when called; for large objects, you can consider whether a constant reference is more suitable.

## 7.6    Functional Body

The really exciting thing about a function is, of course, what it does—because that's what a program is all about. I'm not telling you anything new here. You've already become familiar with <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> as a function, and other functions are not much different.

Take a look at the functions in [Listing 7.6](#07_006.html_l7.6). We will need them later, so let's examine how their function bodies are structured now.

```
std::vector<int> primes = {2};        // global variable
bool isPrime(int n) { // own function
    for(int factor : primes) {        // access to global variable
        if(factor*factor > n)         // access to parameter
            return true;
        if(n%factor==0)
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}
void calculatePrimesUpTo(int limit) { // another custom function
    for(int n=3; n<limit; n=n+2) {
        if(isPrime (n)) {             // use custom function
            primes.push_back(n);
        }
    }
 } 
```

**Listing 7.6**     Various definitions of functions.

First comes the definition of the <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrim</samp> function. The function receives a parameter of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, which is used within the function under the name <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>. However, variables other than the <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> parameter are used in the function body.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">for(int factor :...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> I introduce a new <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> variable for the loop—a local variable. You already know that it is only visible within the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop. You cannot access <samp class="listingcharacter">factor</samp> from another function.

I also use <samp class="listingcharacter">primes</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>—a global variable: this was declared outside the function and is “visible” within the function. You can access all global variables that were previously declared within this module. This is the case with <samp class="listingcharacter">primes</samp>.

The same applies to other functions: you can use other functions if they have been declared beforehand. This happens, for example, in <samp class="listingcharacter">calculatePrimesUpTo</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>: I call <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrim</samp>, and the compiler already knows the function because I defined it earlier (higher up in this module)—and a definition is even better than a declaration in this regard.

If for some reason I had written the function <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrim</samp> later in the program code, the compiler would not yet know it and would complain. However, I could remedy this by at least declaring the required function beforehand.

```
// ... extract ...
bool isPrime(int n);                  // Declaration of function defined later
void calculatePrimesUpTo(int limit) {
    for(int n=3; n<limit; n=n+2) {
        if(isPrime(n)) {              // Use of function defined later
            primes.push_back(n);
        }
    }
}
bool isPrime(int n) {                 // Definition after useage
    // ... as before ...
} 
```

**Listing 7.7**     A forward declaration without a function body.

This is sometimes called a forward declaration.

When you combine a program from multiple modules (<samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> files), you can also use functions from another module. In principle, you use exactly the forward declaration mechanism just explained: if you have defined a function <samp class="listingcharacter">f()</samp> in module A that you want to use in module B, then simply declare <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> identically at the beginning of module B, and the parts will come together when the entire program is linked.

However, this is only the first step toward the correct procedure. For the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file of module A, you also maintain a corresponding header file <samp class="listingcharacter">*.h</samp> that contains all function declarations that are potentially to be used elsewhere. Then, in module B, use an <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> of this header file and effectively achieve the same result as with the manual forward declaration.

I will demonstrate this cleaner solution in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12).

## 7.7    Converting Parameters

When a function receives a parameter with a certain type, there are several possibilities for this parameter when it is called. Let's assume you have declared the <samp class="listingcharacter">func</samp> function as follows:

```
void func(double param); 
```

Then the following can happen when you call it up:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">func(5.3)</samp>—the type matches
    <samp class="listingcharacter">5.3</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">double literal</samp> and therefore exactly matches the parameter type <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. The call works.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">func("Text")</samp>—the type does not match
    Here, the call is attempted with a <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp>, which does not match <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. This is an error that the compiler will inform you about.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">func(7)</samp>—the type can be converted
    Although <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, it can be converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> by the compiler. The call works, but the compiler first converts <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">7.0</samp>.

For the built-in types, the compiler has some rules about which conversions it can perform. Here is a very brief overview:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is not a problem during conversion.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is also done by the compiler, but a dangerous overflow can occur here.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> can be converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, although large <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> numbers <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> can lose a few digits of precision when converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can be converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long.</samp> However, the fractional parts are lost here, and an overflow can occur again if the numbers are too large.

*   For a <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp>—such as the literal <samp class="listingcharacter">"Text"</samp>, for example—there is <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> a conversion to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> (this is not provided by the compiler, however, but by the standard library).

The next listing shows some transformations that are possible and the problems you might encounter. However, note that the types can vary in width depending on the system, and you might encounter different transformations. In addition, overflows should strictly be avoided as some behavior can become arbitrary (technical term: undefined). The example outputs were generated on a 64-bit Intel Linux system using GCC 4.9.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zb1T7Kr3G
#include <iostream>
#include <format>
void prints(short s, int i, float f, double d) {
  std::cout << std::format("short: {} int: {} float: {:.2f} double: {:.2f}\n",
    s, i, f, d);
}
int main() {
  int mill = 1000*1000;                // 1 Million
  prints(mill, mill, mill, mill);      // short overflows
  // Output: short: 16960 int: 1000000 float: 1000000.00 double: 1000000.00
  long bill = 1000L*1000L*1000L*1000L; // 1 Trillion
  prints(bill, bill, bill, bill);      // even int overflows, float becomes inaccurate
  // Output: short: 4096 int: –727379968
  // float:999999995904.00 double: 1000000000000.00
  float three = 3.75f;
  prints(three, three, three, three);  // decimal places are lost
  // Output: short: 3 int: 3 float: 3.75 double: 3.75
} 
```

**Listing 7.8**     Some conversions take place here. The conversions may look different on your system.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">prints(mill,…)</samp>, the parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">short s</samp> overflows during the transformation of the value <samp class="listingcharacter">1000000</samp> (1 million), and the content is meaningless. The transformation to a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> occurs without issues. <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> has been available since C++20; before that, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << s …</samp>.

The even larger value of 1 trillion also causes the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to overflow with <samp class="listingcharacter">prints(bill,...)</samp>. The conversion to a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> does avoid overflow, but the <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> does not have enough precision to store the exact value.

No integer type, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, can hold a decimal number like <samp class="listingcharacter">3.75f</samp>. When converting in <samp class="listingcharacter">prints(three,...)</samp>, the decimal places are simply truncated. However, a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> can be converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> without loss. The other way around, information could be lost.

### [Übung]  Outlook: Conversion of Own Types

If you later define your own types, you can decide for yourself which conversions to or from your type are permitted. You can convert a type <samp class="listingcharacter">A</samp> into your type <samp class="listingcharacter">MyType</samp> by defining a constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">MyType(A)</samp>. And <samp class="listingcharacter">MyType</samp> can be converted to type <samp class="listingcharacter">B</samp> if you define a method <samp class="listingcharacter">operator B()</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">MyType</samp>.

## 7.8    Overloading Functions

If you have defined the function

```
void print(int value) {
    std::cout << "int value: " << value;
} 
```

but do not want <samp class="listingcharacter">print(3.75)</samp> to output a nonsensical <samp class="listingcharacter">int value: 3</samp>, you can also define the <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> function for a parameter of type <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. If a function with the same name is defined multiple times, it is called overloading.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/9YcPraT15
#include <iostream>
void print(int value) { std::cout << "int value: " << value << " "; }
void print(double value) { std::cout << "double value: " << value << " "; }
void print(int v1, double v2) { std::cout << "Values: "<<v1<<", "<<v2<<" "; }
int add(int n, int m) { return n + m; }
double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }
int main() {
    print( add(3, 4) );         // add(int, int) and print(int)
    print( add(3.25f, 1.5f) );  // add(double, double) and print(double)
    print( 7, 3.25 );           // print(int, double)
} 
```

**Listing 7.9**     The “print” and “add” functions have been overloaded for multiple types.

You see that <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> has three overloads. If you call it with an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">print(int value)</samp> is called, with a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, of course: <samp class="listingcharacter">print(double value)</samp>. You can also define overloads with a different number of parameters, as you see in the third <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> variant. The call to <samp class="listingcharacter">print(7, 3.25)</samp> fits this.

When choosing the right overload, the compiler follows a few rules. If the parameters exactly match an overload, it's easy. But if a parameter doesn't match exactly, then the compiler has to choose. For example, I wrote:

```
add(3.25f, 1.5f) 
```

Now, <samp class="listingcharacter">3.25f</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">1.5f</samp> are <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> literals; if I had written <samp class="listingcharacter">3.25</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">1.5</samp>, they would have been <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> literals. However, it is clearly better for the compiler to choose the <samp class="listingcharacter">add(double, double)</samp> variant instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">add(int, int)</samp>, as nothing is lost when converting from <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, unlike a conversion from <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>.

If you try <samp class="listingcharacter">print(1.25, 2.75)</samp>, the compiler obviously cannot choose either <samp class="listingcharacter">print(int)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">print(double)</samp>; the number of parameters simply doesn't match. So, it will call <samp class="listingcharacter">print(int, double)</samp> and convert <samp class="listingcharacter">1.25</samp> to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. You will get the output <samp class="listingcharacter">Values: 1, 2.75</samp>.

If the compiler doesn't find a suitable overload with the conversions it can perform, it will complain to you with an error.

Sometimes, however, the compiler can find multiple overloads that all fit equally well or equally badly. In this case, the compiler will also respond with an error message, stating that the overload resolution was not unambiguous. If you call

```
add(4, 2.85);                 //  Overloading unclear 
```

the compiler cannot decide whether to use <samp class="listingcharacter">add(int, int)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">add(double, double)</samp>. It will then tell you that this call cannot be resolved unambiguously.

To protect you from surprises, it should be mentioned that while parameter types contribute to overload resolution, return types do not. The compiler will complain about overloads that differ only in return type:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/58cTfvYhe
int two() { return 2; }       //  once with int as return type…
double two() { return 2.0; }  //  … and once with double
int main() {
    int x = two();
    double y = two();
} 
```

However, together with distinguishable parameter types, return types can also be different:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/evGqG1oqa
int twice(int a) { return a * 2; }
double twice(double a) { return a * 2.0; }
int main() {
    int x = twice(7);
    double y = twice(7.0);
} 
```

This is widely used in the standard library. For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp> methods of containers sometimes return <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator</samp> and sometimes <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp>, depending on whether the (implicit) <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> parameter is marked as immutable with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> or not. In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> on the parameter type, modifiers like <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> are also involved in the resolution of overloads.

One more thing: before you write countless overloads for a function, consider using a function template instead (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23)). As of C++20, this is even easier with the abbreviated function templates of the form <samp class="listingcharacter">void func(auto a)</samp>.

### Overloading

I have only briefly touched on the topic of overloading here. I recommend that you experiment a bit and get a feel for it. Especially in conjunction with type conversion and default parameters, function overloading in C++ is a powerful and omnipresent feature. If you master it, you will have understood a lot.

## 7.9    Default Parameter

In the previous section, I defined a function that adds two values:

```
int add(int n, int m) { return n + m; } 
```

If you want to write a function that adds more than just two values, you can now overload it:

```
int add(int n, int m, int o) { return n+m+o; }
int add(int n, int m, int o, int p) { return n+m+o+p; }
int add(int n, int m, int o, int p, int q) { return n+m+o+p+q; } 
```

Here you have various versions of <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp>, which allow you to sum up to five numbers at once. They all share the same name <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp>. But wouldn't it be convenient to write just one function? This becomes even more practical if you need more than five variants.

You can achieve this with the help of default arguments. Simply write default values for the parameters, which will be used when you call them with fewer arguments.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/fjc37rvEr
int add(int n=0, int m=0, int o=0, int p=0, int q=0)  {
    return n+m+o+p+q;
}
int main() {
std::cout << add(1,2,3,4,5) << " ";
std::cout << add(1,2,3,4) << " "; // like add(1,2,3,4,0)
std::cout << add(1,2,3) << " ";   // like add(1,2,3,0,0)
std::cout << add(1,2) << " ";     // like add(1,2,0,0,0)
std::cout << add(1) << " ";       // like add(1,0,0,0,0)
std::cout << add() << " ";        // like add(0,0,0,0,0)
} 
```

**Listing 7.10**     Default parameters act like multiple overloads.

For example, if you omit the last parameter with <samp class="listingcharacter">add(1,2,3,4)</samp>, the compiler will automatically insert it for the call. The same applies to further calls: because I have provided all parameters with <samp class="listingcharacter">=0</samp> as a default value, you can even call <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> without any arguments, and the compiler will fill <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">q</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>.

There are a few simple rules for default parameters:

*   You can only omit parameters from the end toward the beginning of the parameter list when calling a function. For example, in the previous example, it would be impossible to omit <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> but provide a value for <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> or any other parameter when calling.

*   The default value must be a constant (a <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>). A numeric literal is therefore not a problem, and the compiler would also accept <samp class="listingcharacter">3*4+5</samp>.

*   You can also have multiple overloads, all of which take default parameters. In combination, you must ensure that there are no ambiguities.

For example, you can have two <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> overloads for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, each with a set of default parameters:

```
// up to three int parameters:
int add(int n=0, int m=0, int o=0) { return n+m+o; }

// 0 … 3 doubles:
double add(double a=0., double b=0., double c=0.) { return a+b+c; } 
```

If you call <samp class="listingcharacter">add(1,2)</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> variant will be selected, and for <samp class="listingcharacter">add(1.25, 3.75)</samp>, the overload for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>s will be chosen. In each case, the last parameter will be filled by the compiler with the specified default value.

To avoid conflicts, it should be briefly mentioned that when defining with three <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> arguments, you should not add another one like this:

```
int add(int x);  //  conflict with three-int overload 
```

Because if you then call <samp class="listingcharacter">add(4)</samp>, the compiler will always tell you that it cannot decide between the three-argument and the one-argument overload. In this case, the conflict is still easy to recognize. When you later deal with function templates, it can become more difficult.

## 7.10    Arbitrary Number of Arguments

The <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> function discussed previously can take up to five arguments, and it would certainly not be difficult for you to extend this to 20 or even 100 default arguments. I don't want to leave the example as is without giving you a glimpse that you can handle an arbitrary number of arguments. If you want an <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> function that takes an arbitrary number of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values, take a detour via <samp class="listingcharacter">std::initializer_list</samp>:

```
int add(std::initializer_list<int> ns)  {
    return std::accumulate(begin(ns), end(ns), 0); // or a for loop
} 
```

Now, when calling, you just need to add a few curly brackets around the arguments, but they can be any number. For example:

```
add({1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9}) 
```

## 7.11    Alternative Notation for Function Declaration

There is another way to write the function header with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp>, which is at least equivalent, if not better:

<samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> FunctionName<samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp>ParameterType ParameterName<samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp>…<samp class="listingcharacter">)-></samp> ReturnType

For [Listing 7.2](#07_004.html_l7.2), it would look like this:

```
auto  func() -> int;
auto  func() -> std::string;
auto  func() -> void;
auto  func() -> std::pair<int,std::string>;
auto  func() -> vector<int>;
auto  func() -> vector<int>&;
auto  func() -> const vector<int>&; 
```

**Listing 7.11**     Alternative syntax for function declarations with trailing return type.

The advantage is that you can recognize the function name better when the return type becomes more complex. This can happen with templates that have multiple type arguments. For programmers who are used to C, this notation looks very strange, but there is really no reason not to use it—except that it will probably take a long time to catch on, if at all.

From C++14 onward, you can omit the return type in function definitions and let the compiler deduce it instead. The compiler then deduces the type based on the first <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statement.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6d5fxn9ed
auto maxOf2(int a, int b) {
    return a<b ? b : a;   // one return: the compiler determines int
}

auto minOf3(int a, int b, int c) {
    if(a<b) return a<c ? a : c;
    else return b<c ? b : c;
}

auto medianOf3(int a, int b, int c) {
    // more complex, but no problem for the compiler
    return minOf3(maxOf2(a,b), maxOf2(b,c), maxOf2(a,c));
} 
```

**Listing 7.12**     Since C++14, you can let the compiler deduce the return type.

## 7.12    Specialties

There are still some special cases regarding function definitions that I will briefly mention here so that you can recognize them when you stumble upon them.

For example, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> to return more than one value. To do this, use the data type <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>. I will go into more detail in [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Section 28.1](#28_001.html_h28.1). There you will see how to easily bundle multiple values into a single return value using <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>—which feels like returning multiple values.

### 7.12.1    “noexcept”

If you find the <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> keyword after the function declaration, then the author of the function promises that this function will not throw an exception (see [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10)). Let's assume the hypothetical class <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp>, which has the following function:

```
File openFile(const char* filename) noexcept; // Function does not throw an exception
```

The function <samp class="listingcharacter">openFile</samp> returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> object. If anything goes wrong, there are many C++ libraries that throw an exception. This function promises with <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> not to do that; <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> probably has other mechanisms to detect errors.

This information might be useful for users, but it is mainly intended for the compiler. Normally, it has to generate a little bit of code in case an exception[[ 14 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn07_01) could be thrown. With this keyword after the function declaration, the compiler can skip that.

### 7.12.2    Inline Functions

At runtime, for a function call, a stack area is created where the function stores its data. You will also find the return address stored there so that the function knows where it was called from and can return there. In addition, the stack area is used to store local data, local parameters, and the return type. Modern CPUs can handle all of this easily. What hurts, however, is that caches and pipelines need to be cleared for a function call—things that make modern CPUs really fast. This is a considerable effort for a simple function call. If speed is crucial and such a function is called frequently in a loop, then unnecessary computation time is wasted.

For such purposes, you can mark a function with the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp>:

```
inline int simple_func(double a, double b, double c); 
```

With the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> before the function, you suggest to the compiler that it should not integrate the function code as a callable function but should insert it in place of the function call.

#### Suggestion for the Compiler

The term should is used here because it is merely a suggestion for the compiler. Whether the compiler integrates the function in place or not is ultimately decided by the compiler itself.

There are other scenarios where the compiler can inline:

*   The compiler can decide to inline a function definition from the same source file, even without the <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> keyword, especially if the function is used frequently.

*   If this function definition is also a function template, compilers are even more eager to inline it.

*   And at the maximum optimization level, newer compilers even inline arbitrary functions across source file boundaries.

What the compiler actually inlines depends on many factors and is hard to predict.

### 7.12.3    “constexpr”

A function whose return is not only marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> but also with <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> must have a quite simple function body that the compiler can compute during translation to insert the result. As a rule of thumb, if you only write a <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statement in the function body, then the chances are good that the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> is allowed:

```
constexpr int doubledUntil100(int value) {
    return value<=50 ? value*2 : 100;
} 
```

The chances are also good that this will lead to very fast program code. And unlike with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp>, the compiler will inform you if it can no longer compute the result at translation time but when the computation would cost runtime. However, whether the compiler actually precomputes the result in the described manner is still up to it.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, you can define your own literal data types, as you can see in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.7](#23_007.html_h23.7).

The highest form for the ultimate minimal time consumption when running the program is the <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp> modifier for immediate functions introduced in C++20\. This ensures that the compiler can compute an expression at translation time and insert it at the call site: as always, it doesn't have to, but it is likely. You can learn more about <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp> in [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13), [Section 13.10.8](#13_010.html_h13.10.8).

### 7.12.4    Deleted Functions

If you want to prohibit a specific use of a function, you can write <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp> instead of the function body:

```
double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }
double add(int, int) = delete;   // prohibit add(3,4) 
```

Without the second line with <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp>, the compiler would automatically convert <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">4</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. By making the declaration for <samp class="listingcharacter">add(int,int)</samp> known to it, it then chooses this one. However, by using <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp>, you tell the compiler that you explicitly do not want this behavior, and it will issue an error message.

### 7.12.5    Specialties in Class Methods

For functions that are part of a class, you will encounter a few more things that you should at least see here so that you recognize them when reading. Starting in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12), I will go into more detail on this:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/8Gdso36zf
class Widget : public Base {
    explicit Widget(int);      // no automatic conversion from int
    ~Widget();                 // Destructor with ~ before the name
    virtual void update();     // prefixed with virtual
    void calc1() override;     // suffixed with override
    void calc2() final;        // suffixed with final
    void draw() const;         // suffixed with const
    virtual void paint() = 0;  // abstract method
}; 
```

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">explicit</samp>, you prevent <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> from being automatically converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp>. This is used before constructors (the initializer) and conversion operators.

*   The symbol <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp>, a tilde, before the name of a function makes it a destructor. This is automatically called when the object is removed. The name of the destructor must match the name of the class.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp> keyword prepares the method to be overridden by another implementation in a derived class. This is often used for extensibility in logically related object hierarchies.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">override</samp> is a programming aid that protects against careless mistakes when overriding with <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp>. It guarantees that you are indeed overriding a method.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> is also intended for <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp> methods in a derived class and prevents this method from being overridden again in the future.

*   Methods marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> promise not to change the state of the object.

*   A virtual method that is set to <samp class="listingcharacter">= 0</samp> instead of an implementation is a pure virtual function. This method must be overridden in a derived class for the class to be instantiable at all. In Java and some other languages, this is called an abstract method.

# 8    Statements in Detail

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Empty statement
    The statement consisting of the semicolon <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>; does nothing.

*   Block statement
    A sequence of statements enclosed in curly braces <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp>.

*   Declaration statement
    The announcement of new variables, possibly with initialization.

*   Expression statement
    Any expression can also be used as a statement.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement
    The conditional execution of further statements.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop
    Repeated execution of statements, tied to a condition at the beginning.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop
    Like a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, but with the condition at the end.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop
    Like a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, but with an additional initialization and progress part.

*   Range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop
    A loop over all elements of a container.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement
    Multiple distinctions with <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> in a single statement.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> statement
    Exit the current loop or switch.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> statement
    Continue the current loop with the next iteration.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statement
    Exit the current function.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> statement
    Jump to another statement named with a label.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> block
    A block of statements where exceptions are handled (preview).

In this chapter, you will learn about the different types of statements in detail. I will demonstrate their use mainly through a practical example.

At the beginning, I will revisit some topics from previous chapters and discuss them in more detail. This way, you will encounter some repetition, but with deeper understanding, and you won't have to keep flipping back.

## Statement

A statement is a piece of code that does something; for example, it performs an assignment or a loop. Statements (of a thread) are executed sequentially.

This program calculates all prime numbers within a freely determinable range—quite efficiently for the brevity of the program.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Y33Tzcf5T
#include <iostream>                   // cout
#include <vector>                     // container vector
#include <string>                     // stoi
int inputUpTo(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    /* Determine number */
    int upTo = 0;                     // introduce new variable
    if(argc<=1) {                     // if statement with then and else block
        std::cout << "Up to what number do you want to calculate prime numbers? ";
        if(!(std::cin >> upTo)) {     // check return value
            return -1;                // error in user input
        }
    } else {                          // else part of the if statement
        upTo = std::stoi(argv[1]);
    }
    return upTo;                      // return input
}
std::vector primes{2};                // new vector<int> with initialization
bool isPrime(int n) {
    /* primes must be sorted in ascending order */
    for(int factor : primes) {        // range-based for loop
        if(factor*factor > n)         // too large to be a divisor at all?
            return true;              // … then terminate inner loop early
        if(n%factor==0)               // is divisor?
            return false;             // … then exit
    }
    return true;                      // no divisor found
}
void calculatePrimesUpTo(int upTo) {
    /* Primes calculation */
    /* vector must contain {2} at this point */
    for(int n=3; n<upTo; n=n+2) {     // standard for loop
        if(isPrime(n)) {
            primes.push_back(n);      // is prime – mark as divisor and result
        }
    }
}

void outputPrimes() {
    for(int prime : primes) {         // range based, over all elements
        std::cout << prime << " ";
    }
    std::cout << " ";
}

int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    int upTo = inputUpTo(argc, argv); // declares variable
    if(upTo < 2) { return 1; }        // exit main with nonokay value.
    calculatePrimesUpTo(upTo);
    outputPrimes();
    return 0;
} 
```

**Listing 8.1**     Calculates all prime numbers in a user-defined range.

First, look at the rough structure of this program. After that, I will go into detail about the different statements.

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, I define four helper functions: <samp class="listingcharacter">inputUpTo()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrime()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">calculateUpTo()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">outputPrimes()</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">inputUpTo()</samp> function receives the same parameters as <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, to either evaluate the command line or ask for a number on the console, as you saw in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Listing 4.10](#04_002.html_l4.10). <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrime()</samp> takes the potential prime number as an argument and returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> value, which indicates whether the argument is prime or not.

Between the functions, the <samp class="listingcharacter">primes</samp> global variable is defined. Because it is global and not within a function or even within a block, all functions can access it.

The variable is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp>: this is a container that is particularly suitable for sequentially adding new elements. I use <samp class="listingcharacter">primes.push_back(n)</samp> to accomplish this. In C++17, it is sufficient to write <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> as the compiler infers <samp class="listingcharacter"><int></samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp> during initialization.

## 8.1    The Statement Block

Anywhere you are allowed to write a single statement, you can also group multiple statements within curly braces <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp>. You can see the schematic flowchart in [Figure 8.1](#08_001.html_f8.1). This is also called a compound statement. You do not need to end this block with a semicolon; doing so would create an empty statement, which you should avoid (see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.2](#09_002.html_h9.2)).

[![Flowchart for the statement block.](bilderklein/klein08_001.png)](img-f8.1.html)

**Figure 8.1**     Flowchart for the statement block.

In [Listing 8.1](#08_001.html_l8.1), I have attached those blocks to most <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements and <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops. Using <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> consistently here prepares for future extensions and improves readability. In <samp class="listingcharacter">if(factor*factor > n)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">if(n%factor==0)</samp>, you see <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> without block braces. The same applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>.

```
for(int prime : primes)             // for followed by a single statement
    std::cout << prime << " ";
std::cout << " ";                   // not part of for anymore 
```

**Listing 8.2**     This “for” refers to only one statement.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> is only coupled with the first of the two outputs. The second line is output only once. If you wanted to do more things within the loop, then use <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp>. This way, you get a statement block that counts as a single statement for the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>.

```
for(int prime : primes) {         // Beginning of the block
    std::cout << prime;
    std::cout << " ";
}                                 // End of the block
std::cout << " "; 
```

**Listing 8.3**     A statement block is enclosed in <samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>.

Now the separated <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> outputs are both executed within the loop.

### 8.1.1    Standalone Blocks and Variable Scope

However, you don't have to bind blocks to a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> or similar; you can introduce them anywhere it makes sense to you instead of a single statement. The following listing is an example of this.

```
if(number > 50) {                // outer block
    {                            // 1st inner block
        int result  = number*number;
        std::cout << "Square: " << result << std::endl;
    }
    {                            // 2nd inner block
        int result  = number+number;
        std::cout << "Doubled: " << result << std::endl;
    }
} 
```

**Listing 8.4**     Where statements are allowed, you can also create a block.

The inner blocks are both executed linked to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>, as they are both within the outer block that belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>.

You can freely choose whether you want to group your statements in this way. This would be useful, for example, if you wanted to introduce the same variable names in both inner blocks. In [Listing 8.4](#08_001.html_l8.4), <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> is introduced as a new <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> variable in both inner blocks. Variables are only valid within the block in which they were defined. Without the division into two blocks, both <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> definitions would interfere with each other.

```
if(number > 50) {
    int result = number*number;        // Definition of result
    std::cout << "Square: " << result << std::endl;
    int result = number+number;        //  Error: result has already been defined
    std::cout << "Doubled: " << result << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 8.5**     Using “result” twice as a new variable in one block is not allowed.

Of course, you could have used the already existing <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> variable here without redeclaring it with <samp class="listingcharacter">int result = number+number</samp>. However, there are sometimes reasons that you don't want to or can't do that.

You could also have introduced a new variable with <samp class="listingcharacter">int result2 = …</samp>. But maybe you didn't want too many variables lying around that you don't actually need anymore. By introducing inner blocks, you made it clear, among other things, where <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> is needed from and to. Later readers then don't have to think about this anymore.

```
if(number > 50) {
    int result1 = number*number;           // a result
    std::cout << "Square: " << result << std::endl;
    int result2 = number+number;           // another result
    std::cout << "Doubled: " << result << std::endl;
    int result3 = number+number+number;    // and another result
    // … many lines of code in between …
    // and here?
    // … even more lines of code …
} 
```

**Listing 8.6**     Too many variables are also not good.

Someone who wonders at the <samp class="listingcharacter">// and here?</samp> point whether they can use any of the <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> N variables for their own purposes will only be able to find out with difficulty—and will probably introduce another variable out of despair.

Introducing a new block for each individual variable and indenting left each time fragments the code and unnecessarily lengthens it. Neither is conducive to understanding when reading.

Use common sense when it comes to introducing new standalone blocks.

## 8.2    The Empty Statement

When you write a semicolon where a statement is expected, that is an empty statement. This statement does nothing.

```
int main() {  ;;;                 // 3 empty statements
    int number = 12 ; ;           // 1 empty statement
    ; int q = number*number ;     // 1 empty statement
    if(q>50) {
        q = q - 50;
    } ;                           // 1 empty statement
    std::cout << q << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 8.7**     Empty statements everywhere.

Doing nothing is usually completely uncritical. However, there are cases where an inserted empty statement is dangerous. You already know from [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4) that an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> is followed by a statement that should be executed if a condition is met. Suppose you insert an empty statement after <samp class="listingcharacter">if(q>50)</samp> in the preceding example:

```
 if(q>50) ;  {               // empty statement with serious consequences
        q = q - 50;
    } 
```

Then it is the empty statement that gets executed in the case <samp class="listingcharacter">q>50</samp>. The subtraction <samp class="listingcharacter">q=q-50</samp> is no longer part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> but is now executed always.

### Avoid Empty Statements

Even though empty statements are mostly harmless, when they do cause issues, they're a right pain to track down. Develop the habit of not ending your statement block <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> with a semicolon.

Be especially vigilant with <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> constructs to avoid inadvertently slipping in empty statements.

## 8.3    Declaration Statement

We have seen in several places that a new variable was introduced. In [Listing 8.1](#08_001.html_l8.1), for example, it was this:

```
int upTo = 0; 
```

This introduces a new variable—it declares it. First, its type is specified—here, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>—and then the name under which the variable will be used—here, <samp class="listingcharacter">upTo</samp>. Done. But what about the equals sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> and what stands to its right? That is the initialization, and it is optional in this form of declaration. I have already discussed the various forms of initialization in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.2](#04_002.html_h4.2).

So, note the following. With

```
int upTo; 
```

is the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">bis</samp> declared. You must not use it as it is now (for calculations and the like) because it does not yet contain a value. More precisely, its value is undefined. This means that if you use the variable for calculations, it contains an arbitrary value—and in most cases, this will lead to unforeseen behavior in your program. There is more to say about this because many types are also initialized with this form of declaration, but not <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. Read more about this in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12).

It is also important that variables are only known within the block in which you declare them. Once the program passes the closing brace of the block, they are no longer available. Therefore, this declaration does not overlap with the previous one:

```
int upTo = inputUpTo(argc, argv); 
```

This declares a “different” <samp class="listingcharacter">upTo</samp>, which is only visible in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>.

You can also see here that initialization can occur not only with <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> or a constant. Here, a complex function call returns the value with which <samp class="listingcharacter">upTo</samp> is initialized.

You can also combine declarations separated by commas. You can declare multiple variables like this:

```
int from, to, result; 
```

Here, all variables will be of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. If you wanted to initialize all (or some) at the same time, you can do so:

```
int from, to = 0, result; 
```

Here you declare three variables, but only <samp class="listingcharacter">to</samp> is initialized with <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>.

### 8.3.1    Structured Binding

Since C++17, it is also possible to declare multiple elements at once and initialize them all with a single equals sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>. To do this, use <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> before square brackets <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp>, which then contain the variables to be declared.

Three variants are possible: binding a C-array, binding a tuple, and binding a structure.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xWbqeeq3n
#include <iostream>
#include <tuple>   // make_tuple
auto mkTpl() {
    return std::make_tuple(2, 'b', 3.14);  // tuple<int,char,double>
}
struct Point {
    int x, y;
};
int main() {
    // Structured binding of a C-array
    int odd[5] = { 1,3,7,9,11 };
    auto [ one, two, three, four, five ]  = odd;
    // Structured binding of a tuple
    auto [ zwei, be, pi ]  = mkTpl();
    // Structured binding of a struct
    Point p0{  10, 15 };
    auto [ the_x, the_y ]  = p0;
} 
```

**Listing 8.8**     With <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, you can also initialize multiple variables at once.

Here, the count must match exactly. So, if <samp class="listingcharacter">odd</samp> one day contains six elements, binding will fail. The same applies to a tuple that is too large or too small, or to an unsuitable structure.

You don't need to copy out the values; you can also let the declaration be references:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/3zo8GnbW3
int main() {
    int odd[5] = { 1,3,7,9,11 };
    auto &[ one, two, three, four, five ] = odd;
    auto &[ zwei, be, pi ] = mkTpl();           //  no & binding to temp-values
    Point p0{  10, 15 };
    auto &[ the_x, the_y ] = p0;
} 
```

Here, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">three</samp> is a reference to the <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> within <samp class="listingcharacter">odd</samp>.

This, of course, only works if there is an object that can be referenced. In the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">mkTpl()</samp>, this is not the case, as the function returns a temp-value that is not yet stored anywhere.

## 8.4    The Expression Statement

You can also use any expression as a statement. Although it makes little sense to use <samp class="listingcharacter">3+4;</samp> as a statement, for example, assignments are expressions and are used as statements very often.

Assuming you have previously declared <samp class="listingcharacter">int upTo;</samp>, the following listing gives examples of expressions used as statements.

```
upTo = 99;                    // an assignment is an expression
upTo = upTo * 2 + 1;          // combining an assignment with a calculation
calculatePrimesUpTo(upTo);    // a function call is an expression
std::cout << "Friedrich III"; // the output operator 
```

**Listing 8.9**     These are all expressions used as statements.

As I mentioned earlier, every expression has a value and a type. If an expression is used as a statement, the type disappears and is discarded by the compiler.

### Control Structures

The <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statements are control structures and allow you to program branches and loops. With <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp>, you influence the flow of control structures. <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> also belongs to this family in the broadest sense. I would prefer not to mention <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> (to find out why, see [Section 8.14](#08_014.html_h8.14)).

## 8.5    The “if” Statement

With the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement, you program the conditional execution of statements. The simplest form executes the statement assigned to it only if a specified condition is met:

<samp class="listingcharacter">if(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement

You already know a bit about the statement part: here you should use a block with <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> so that you can group multiple statements and link them to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>. This is called the then branch of the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement.

The condition, however, is still somewhat ominous. This must be an expression that evaluates to a truth value—that is, true or false. This applies to a specific group of expressions—namely, those that have the type <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>.

More correctly, it must be possible to convert the expression to <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. This is a subtle but important difference that I explained in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.4](#04_004.html_h4.4). This simply means that you can also use a number like <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> and many other things directly as a condition in <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>. If you know how to handle it, <samp class="listingcharacter">if(x-30)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">if(cin>>val)</samp> will come easily to you.

Here are a few conditions that can only be true or false:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">number > 100</samp>
    A simple arithmetic comparison that checks if <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> is greater than <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp>. You can also test for less than <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, greater than or equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>, less than or equal to <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, and not equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">number > 100 && number < 200</samp>
    With the Boolean AND <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp>, you check if both expressions are true.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">x < 0 || y < 0</samp>
    The Boolean OR <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> fits when at least one condition should be met.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">x == y+1</samp>
    You can perform arithmetic calculations before a comparison.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">(x > 0 || y > 0) && (maxx < 100 || maxy < 100)</samp>
    Parenthesize complex expressions if necessary.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">!(x < y)</samp>
    With the operator <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> for not, you negate a Boolean expression; true becomes false and vice versa.

With this repertoire, you are already well-equipped for the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> condition.

There is another useful form of the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement, which you can also see in [Figure 8.2](#08_005.html_f8.2):

<samp class="listingcharacter">if(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement1 <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> Statement2

This implements: “Execute either Statement1 or Statement2.” The Statement2 is called the else branch of the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement. Thus,

```
if(x > 1) {
    std::cout << "x is greater than 1" << std::endl;
}
if(!(x > 1)) {            // test alternative
    std::cout << "x is not greater than 1" << std::endl;
} 
```

is almost the same as

```
if(x > 1) {
    std::cout << "x is greater than 1" << std::endl;
} else {                  // with else you save a comparison
    std::cout << "x is not greater than 1" << std::endl;
} 
```

[![Flowchart of the “if” statement with and without the “else” branch.](bilderklein/klein08_002.png)](img-f8.2.html)

**Figure 8.2**     Flowchart of the “if” statement with and without the “else” branch.

Why only almost? Because you don't have to execute <samp class="listingcharacter">x > 1</samp> here twice—and above all, you don't have to write it twice. We have already used blocks <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> here instead of a single statement. You could also have written the following:

```
if(x > 1)
    std::cout << "x is greater than 1" << std::endl;
else                      // a block or a single statement follows else
    std::cout << "x is not greater than 1" << std::endl; 
```

But because <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branches make the code more complex, blocks are really recommended here.

Now you actually know everything about <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> that you can know. What remains is to combine the knowledge: An <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> is a statement; the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> condition, <samp class="listingcharacter">then</samp> branch, and optional <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branch all together is a statement. And both <samp class="listingcharacter">then</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> each get a statement associated. You can combine this into complex nestings. It is common to use another <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branch to sequentially query different possibilities:

```
if(number < 0) {
    std::cout << "The number is negative.\n";
} else if(number == 0)  {    // else and if follow directly one after another
    std::cout << "The number is zero.\n";
} else if(number > 1000)  {  // also possible multiple times
    std::cout << "The number is too large.\n";
} else {  /* x > 0 but x <= 1000 */
    std::cout << "The number is positive.\n";
} 
```

Here it is common to save yourself from wrapping every <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement in a block with only one statement. However, if you once make it clear to yourself where you would place all block braces, then you learn something about statements. Completely with all <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> around each single statement, the example would look like this:

```
if(number < 0) {
    std::cout << "The number is negative.\n";
} else {
    if(number == 0) {
        std::cout << "The number is zero.\n";
    } else {
        if(number > 1000) {
            std::cout << "The number is too large.\n";
        } else {  /* x > 0 but x <= 1000 */
            std::cout << "The number is positive.\n";
        }
    }
} 
```

Here it becomes clear which <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> exactly belongs to which <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>. But the ever-deeper indentation comes at the expense of readability. For standard <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> cascades, it is better not to wrap the <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branch in its own block.

### 8.5.1    “if” with Initializer

Since C++17, you can place an (initialization) expression before the actual condition:

<samp class="listingcharacter">if(</samp> Initialization <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement

Typically, you declare a variable in Initialization, but you can also write any expression here. A declared variable is valid within the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement, as this is equivalent to the following:

<samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp> Initialization <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">if(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>

In a program, it looks like the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/d6PscKx4M
#include <map>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm> // any_of
#include <iostream>  // cerr
std::map<int, std::string> m;
int main() {
    if(auto it = m.find(10); it != m.end()) { return it->second.size(); }
    if(char buf[10]={0}; std::fgets(buf, 10, stdin)) { m[0] += buf; }
    std::string s;
    if(auto keywords = {"if", "for", "while"};
        std::any_of(keywords.begin(), keywords.end(),
        [&s](const char* kw) { return s == kw; })) {
            std::cerr << "Error ";
   }
} 
```

**Listing 8.10**     These <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements contain initializers.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">it</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">buf</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">keywords</samp> variables are only valid within the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement. Of course, you can also use an <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branch. The initialization is also valid within it.

### 8.5.2    Compile-Time “if”

If you don't want a piece of code to be included in your compiled program under certain circumstances, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr if</samp> since C++17:

<samp class="listingcharacter">if constexpr(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement

The compiler then evaluates the condition at compile time and has the option to exclude an entire piece of code from the final program. This really makes sense for debug constants or generic functions.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Ycse4EWav
#include <iostream> // cout

template<typename T>
void memory(T x) {
    if constexpr(sizeof(T) > 4) {
       std::cout << "Requires a lot of memory: " << x << "  ";
    }
}

constexpr auto DEBUG = true;
int main() {
    if constexpr(DEBUG) {
        std::cout << "Debug is on. ";
    }
    memory<long long>(44LL);
} 
```

**Listing 8.11**     The compiler can evaluate the condition at compile time.

Such things were previously only possible with macros or clever template programming.
