You can certainly add an <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branch and use it together with an initialization expression.

Starting from C++23, there is also an <samp class="listingcharacter">if consteval</samp>, which determines if the calling context is <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>; see [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13), [Section 13.10.9](#13_010.html_h13.10.9).

## 8.6    The “while” Loop

The <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop executes a statement so long as a specified condition is met. The process is shown in [Figure 8.3](#08_006.html_f8.3). You write it like this:

<samp class="listingcharacter">while(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement

For Condition and Statement, everything I mentioned about <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> applies. Therefore, the following example should pose no difficulty for you.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/h466fYq4W
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    /* Sum up from 1 to 100 */
    int sum = 0;
    int number = 1;
    while(number <= 100)      // condition
    {                         // block that is repeatedly executed
        sum += number;        // for the result
        number += 1;          // next number
    }                         // end of the repeated block
    std::cout << sum << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 8.12**     The loop runs 100 times.

Before the loop block is executed, the condition is checked first. Therefore, this loop will run for every <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> between <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp> inclusive—exactly 100 times. And each individual number will be added to <samp class="listingcharacter">sum</samp>. At the end, <samp class="listingcharacter">sum</samp> contains the result of adding all numbers from 1 to 100—the task that the mathematician Gauss is said to have solved in his head within seconds in elementary school because he supposedly realized he only needed to calculate (100 · 101) / 2\. Well, with the help of the computer, you are even faster than Gauss.

[![Flowchart of the “while” loop.](bilderklein/klein08_003.png)](img-f8.3.html)

**Figure 8.3**     Flowchart of the “while” loop.

When you come up with such loops, it is very important to ensure that the condition eventually no longer holds true and the loop then terminates. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> is a simple counting variable and is incremented within the block. Common mistakes include forgetting to increment or setting the condition incorrectly. Can you see what happens if you forget <samp class="listingcharacter">number = number + 1</samp>?

```
while(number <= 100) {          // number is checked but never incremented
    sum += number;
}; 
```

This loop will run forever because <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> is never incremented, so the condition <samp class="listingcharacter">number <= 100</samp> will always be true. The program will never reach the line for the output, and you will have to terminate it from the outside. If you don't yet know how to do that, now is the time to find out. In an IDE, you will find a button or menu item for this. In the console, (Ctrl)+(C) usually saves you.

It may also be that the condition is not met right from the start. In that case, the block of statements is not executed at all.

### Loop Design

Have you noticed that <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">101</samp> when the loop ends, not <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp>? It has to be this way as otherwise the condition would still be met, and the loop would run one more time. Therefore, the postcondition of the loop is that after its complete run-through, <samp class="listingcharacter">number>100</samp> .

Loops are a challenging aspect of programming and a common source of errors. The mistake is not always as easy to find as forgetting to increment. To work safely, make it clear to yourself what roles the involved variables have in the loop: Is the variable the counter? Is it mutable? And what is its relationship to the condition?

## 8.7    The “do-while” Loop

This much rarer variant of the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop has the condition at the end:

<samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp> Statement <samp class="listingcharacter">while(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>

Here, the Statement is executed first and then the Condition is checked, as you can see in the flowchart in [Figure 8.4](#08_007.html_f8.4). The check occurs after each iteration. This means that the statement is executed at least once.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6hh5KhExM
#include <iostream>                  // cin
#include <string>
int main() {
    std::string line;
    do {                             // execute getline at least once
       std::getline(std::cin, line);
       if(!std::cin) break;          // error or end of file
    } while(line != "quit");         // end on specific input
} 
```

**Listing 8.13**     The body of a “do-while” loop is executed at least once.

You should not use this variant of the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop with <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp> very often as it is quite uncommon. In addition, the condition in a loop is so important that having it at the end can hinder understanding when reading.

[![Flowchart of the “do-while” loop.](bilderklein/klein08_004.png)](img-f8.4.html)

**Figure 8.4**     Flowchart of the “do-while” loop.

## 8.8    The “for” Loop

You have seen in the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop that you often initialize a counter variable for the loop and then increment it at the end of the loop. Because this is so common, it is packed together and thus simplified in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop:

<samp class="listingcharacter">for(</samp> Initialization <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> Update <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement

Statement and Initialization are statements, while Condition and Update are expressions.

It is common to define a loop variable in the initialization, modify it in the update, and check it in the condition.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop corresponds to this well-organized <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop:

<samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp> Initialization <samp class="listingcharacter">; while(</samp> Condition <samp class="listingcharacter">) {</samp> Statement <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> Update <samp class="listingcharacter">; } }</samp>

In [Figure 8.5](#08_008.html_f8.5), you can see the process schematically.

I will rewrite [Listing 8.12](#08_006.html_l8.12) into a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/7foYcMMaz
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    /* Sum up from 1 to 100 */
    int sum = 0;
    for(int number=1; number <= 100; number+=1)  {  // compact form
        sum += number;                              // for the result
    }
    std::cout << sum << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 8.14**     Sum with a “for” loop.

Here is the initialization <samp class="listingcharacter">int number=1</samp>. Before the statements in the loop are executed, the condition <samp class="listingcharacter">number <= 100</samp> is checked. Then follows the execution of the loop, here <samp class="listingcharacter">sum += number;</samp>. At the end of the block, the update is executed with <samp class="listingcharacter">number += 1</samp>.

Then the condition is checked again. If it is met, the next loop iteration follows; if not, the loop ends.

Even with <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> ends up at <samp class="listingcharacter">101</samp>. As I have written it, I cannot output it because the <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> variable only exists within the loop. However, you can declare it before the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> and leave the initialization part empty.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/185ha3q3f
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    /* Sum up from 1 to 100 */
    int sum = 0;
    int number = 1;                            // Initialization before the loop
    for(  ; number <= 100; number=number+1) {  // empty initialization
        sum = sum + number;
    }
    std::cout << number  << std::endl;         // number now also exists outside
} 
```

**Listing 8.15**     “for” loop with empty initialization part.

Here you can also access <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> outside the loop and thus see how <samp class="listingcharacter">101</samp> is printed.

It is also possible to leave the update part empty. Then you will have to take care of the update within the loop block. But this is rather rare, because then you almost have a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. In extreme—and particularly rare—cases, you can also omit the condition. Then you must be able to end the loop in some other way. How to do this without (Ctrl)+(C) is something you will learn when I explain <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> in this chapter.

A frequently used way to execute something “forever” is to omit all three parts.

```
int main() {
    for( ; ; )  {  // no init, no condition, no update – so forever
        /* ... User input */
        /* ... if user chooses Quit, end program */
        /* ... otherwise, perform calculation and output */
    }
} 
```

**Listing 8.16**     Loops without conditions must be terminated in some other way.

Of course, a lot of program code is missing here. But using a loop that runs forever as a last resort should make the use case clear to you.

[![Flowchart of a “for” loop.](bilderklein/klein08_005.png)](img-f8.5.html)

**Figure 8.5**     Flowchart of a “for” loop.

## 8.9    The Range-Based “for” Loop

When I explain the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, I must also cover its new variant, the range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop (or ranged <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>). Especially with standard containers, it is very useful.

To examine the contents of the <samp class="listingcharacter">prims</samp> container, I use the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop with the colon notation <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp>. I refer to the following excerpt from [Listing 8.1](#08_001.html_l8.1).

```
// Excerpt
std::vector<int> primes{2};    // vector is a container, ready for a ranged for
void isPrime(int n) {
    /* primes must be sorted in ascending order */
    for(int factor : prims) {  // range-based for loop
        if(factor*factor > n)
            return true;
        if(n%factor==0)
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}
void outputPrimes() {
    for(int i=1; int prime : prims) {  // range-based for loop
        std::cout << i++ << ". Prime number: " << prime << " ";
    }
    std::cout << " ";
} 
```

**Listing 8.17**     You can recognize the range-based “for” loop by the colon.

<samp class="listingcharacter">primes</samp> collects the overall result so that it appears on the screen in <samp class="listingcharacter">outputPrimes</samp>. On the other hand, it is used in <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrime</samp> to perform only the necessary divisibility tests for the previous prime numbers.

You can read <samp class="listingcharacter">for(int factor : primes)</samp> this way: Select an element from the <samp class="listingcharacter">primes</samp> container one by one, assign it to <samp class="listingcharacter">factor</samp>, execute the loop statement, and repeat this process for all elements of the container. That is:

<samp class="listingcharacter">for(</samp> Destination <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> Container <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> Statement

That already allows you quite a lot. You can even equip your own data types to be used in these <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops like a container. All you need to do is appropriately define <samp class="listingcharacter">begin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp> methods.

When outputting with <samp class="listingcharacter">int prime : primes</samp>, it is the same, but here we also have an initialization part with <samp class="listingcharacter">int i=1;</samp> before it. This has been possible since C++20\. Before that, you had to define such a counter variable before the loop.

Normally, you apply the range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> to containers, which you will get to know in [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24). If you write container-like classes yourself, you can make them fit the range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>.

## 8.10    The “switch” Statement

You have already seen that you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> cascades to check multiple cases in succession. The <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement is a specialized form of the case where you always test the same expression, and the expression has an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>-like type—or is an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp>, as you will see in [Chapter 16](#16_001.html_h16), [Section 16.12.2](#16_012.html_h16.12.2):

<samp class="listingcharacter">switch(</samp> Expression <samp class="listingcharacter">) {</samp> Cases <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>

Since C++17, it works analogously to <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> as well:

<samp class="listingcharacter">switch(</samp> Initialization <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> Expression <samp class="listingcharacter">) {</samp> Cases <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>

Where Cases consist of a sequence of cases of the following form:

<samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> Constant<samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> Statements

From the list of Cases, those Statements are executed whose Constant matches the result of the Expression. There are still some things to consider or that are worth knowing:

*   Cases must not contain duplicate Constants, but they also do not need to follow a specific order.

*   Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp>, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> once to catch everything else. Normally, this is the last or first <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp>, but it doesn't have to be.

*   You can also write multiple <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> instructions directly in a row without statements in between if you want to combine multiple cases.

*   Statements of a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> should always end with <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>. Exceptions to this rule are very rare and should be clearly highlighted with a comment. If you forget this <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, the statements of the next <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> will be executed, regardless of what its constant is. This is called fall-through.

[![Flowchart of a “switch” statement.](bilderklein/klein08_006.png)](img-f8.6.html)

**Figure 8.6**     Flowchart of a “switch” statement.

In [Figure 8.6](#08_010.html_f8.6), you can see the flowchart of the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> construct. Although the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> statements do not strictly belong to the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> flowchart, I have included them here as an option because they are so common and important.

The very simple calculator from [Listing 8.18](#08_010.html_l8.18) places digits in a stack. An arithmetic operation takes the top elements of the stack and places the result back on top.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Y4W11oW8b
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>       // cout

void calculator(std::ostream& out, std::string input) {
    std::vector<int> stack {};
    for(char c : input) {
        if(c>='0' && c<='9') {
            stack.push_back( c-'0' ); // numeric value of the character
            continue;      // next loop iteration
        }
        int top = 0;
        int second = 0;
        switch(c)  {       // condition on character
        case '+':
            top = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            second = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            stack.push_back(second + top);
            break;
        case '-':
            top = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            second = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            stack.push_back(second - top);
            break;
        case '*':
            top = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            second = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            stack.push_back(second * top);
            break;
        case '=':
            for(int elem : stack) { out << elem; }
            out << " ";
            break;
        case ' ':
            break;
        default:
            out << " '" << c << "' I don't understand. ";
        } /* switch */
    } /* for c */
}
int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    if(argc > 1) {
        calculator(std::cout, argv[1]);
    } else {
        // 3 + 4 * 5 + 6 with multiplication before addition results in 29
        calculator(std::cout, "345*+6+=");
    }
} 
```

**Listing 8.18**     Each “case” covers one scenario, and nowhere was the “break” forgotten.

Much more relevant, however, is <samp class="listingcharacter">switch(c)</samp>. As a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> here, just like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and its relatives. However, you must not write a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> here. It must be an “enumerable” type.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> cases follow one after another. Depending on the value of <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>, these jump labels are directly accessed, and the subsequent statements are executed. Each block is properly concluded with a <samp class="listingcharacter">break;</samp> to prevent accidentally executing another calculation.

A small comment on the calculation <samp class="listingcharacter">c-'0'</samp>: Here, I subtract the character value <samp class="listingcharacter">'0'</samp> from the entered <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> to get the numeric value of the character. Mind you, this is not the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> number <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, but the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> character <samp class="listingcharacter">'0'</samp>. The result is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> number between <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">9</samp>. This works partly because <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> behaves very much like an integer type and partly because the characters <samp class="listingcharacter">'0'</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">'9'</samp> have consecutive values as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">'0'</samp> usually has the number <samp class="listingcharacter">48</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">'4'</samp> (for example) the value <samp class="listingcharacter">52</samp>. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">'4'-'0'</samp> is the same as <samp class="listingcharacter">52-48</samp>, which is the <samp class="listingcharacter">int 4</samp>. I then put this numeric value onto the <samp class="listingcharacter">stack</samp>.

### [Übung]  It Can Be Better; It Can Be Dynamic

The <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>-based <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> is quite nice as a small example, but it is very static and can become unwieldy when you want to extend it. However, if you want to see a version that is better suited as a basis for an elaborate calculator, flip far ahead to [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Listing 28.43](#28_007.html_l28.43). There, it is a dynamic <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> that takes function objects for the operations.

If you're wondering why the <samp class="listingcharacter">calulator</samp> function has an <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> parameter: It's always good to never use the global variables <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cerr</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> inside of functions. This makes such functions more testable. You should only access these global variables in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> ends up here as a parameter of <samp class="listingcharacter">calculator()</samp> in the function. You can see such a test in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12), [Listing 12.8](#12_004.html_l12.8).

### Don't Forget “break”

Never forget the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> that concludes a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block. In 99.99% of cases, you need it to prevent falling through to the next <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block. Forgetting it is a common oversight.

If you ever intentionally program a fall-through, write an unmistakable comment at that point. Otherwise, anyone else will think at first glance that you made a mistake and forgot the <samp class="listingcharacter">break;</samp>.

Cases where a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block is not concluded with a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> are rare. Often, a series of separate <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements will suffice. [Listing 8.19](#08_010.html_l8.19) will help you understand the principle of fall-through.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jaMTcshEf
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

using std::string; using std::cout;

void guessMonth(unsigned whatDayIsItToday) {
    switch(whatDayIsItToday) {
    /* missing break statements: fall-through intended */
    default:
        if(whatDayIsItToday>31) {
            cout << "You are cheating";
            break;
        }
    case 28:
    case 29:
        cout << "Feb ";
    case 30:
        cout << "Apr Jun Sep Nov ";
    case 31:
        cout << "Jan Mar May Jul Aug Oct Dec ";
    }

    cout << ". ";
}
int main() {
    guessMonth(31);  // if today were the 31st?
    // Output: Jan Mar May Jul Aug Oct Dec .
    guessMonth(30);  // what if it were the 30th?
    // Output: Apr Jun Sep Nov Jan Mar May Jul Aug Oct Dec .
    guessMonth(4);
    // Output: Feb Apr Jun Sep Nov Jan Mar May Jul Aug Oct Dec .
    guessMonth(77);
    // Output: You are cheating.
} 
```

**Listing 8.19**     Very rarely are there “case” blocks without “break”—and even more rarely meaningful ones.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">guessMonth(30)</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> directly jumps to the label <samp class="listingcharacter">case 30:</samp> and skips the cases <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">28</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">29</samp>. For <samp class="listingcharacter">30</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">"Apr Jun Sep Nov "</samp> is then output. Because there is no <samp class="listingcharacter">break;</samp> at the end of the block for <samp class="listingcharacter">case 30</samp>, the statements of the next block are executed, so <samp class="listingcharacter">"Jan Mar May Jul Aug Oct Dec "</samp> is output.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">guessMonth(4)</samp>, no <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> matches, so the <samp class="listingcharacter">default:</samp> block is executed. For <samp class="listingcharacter">4</samp>, the test in the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> will result in <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. The end of the block is reached, but due to the missing <samp class="listingcharacter">break;</samp>, the following <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> blocks are executed.

Only in the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">guessMonth(77)</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> reached. Although the <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> block is also executed, the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> condition is true this time, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">break;</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">then</samp> branch is thus reached. With the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, the entire <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> is now exited, and it continues directly with <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << ". ";</samp>.

## 8.11    The “break” Statement

The <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> keyword allows you to exit the current loop—the innermost one, from the perspective of <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>. The program continues with the statement following the loop. You can use this in all <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loops, including the range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>. In this sense, <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> is considered a loop.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/75h9Y95vf
#include <iostream>                 // cout

int main() {
    for(int x=1; x<20; x+=1) {      // outer for-loop
        for(int y=1; y<20; y+=1) {  // inner for-loop
            int prod = x*y;
            if(prod>=100) {
                break;              // exit inner y-loop
            }
            std::cout << prod << " ";
        } /* end for y */
        // destination of break
    } /* end for x */               // first actual line after break
    std::cout << " ";
} 
```

**Listing 8.20**     With <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, you terminate a loop prematurely.

Let's assume the task is to output only the two-digit results of the products of <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> between 1 and 20\. Once <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> is large enough that the product is 100 or greater, then an even larger <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> will not yield a smaller product. In that case, we can terminate the <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> loop prematurely using <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>.

The rest of the <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> loop is skipped; in particular, the output of <samp class="listingcharacter">prod</samp> is not executed. Rather, execution continues with the first statement following the inner loop. Well, this is a special case: here, at <samp class="listingcharacter">/* end for x */</samp>, the end of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> loop is reached, where no more statements are present. Therefore, the next thing to be executed is the update expression of the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> loop—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">x+=1</samp>.

Note that only the current innermost loop will be exited by the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, meaning that the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> loop will not be exited. If you had placed a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> after <samp class="listingcharacter">/* end for y */</samp>, then the <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> loop would be exited and continued at <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << " "</samp>.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, you only exit loops like <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>, as well as the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> (which is not a loop). An <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> does not count as a loop when searching for the current “innermost” loop.

## 8.12    The “continue” Statement

The <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> statement has a similar role as <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>. However, the current loop is not aborted; only the rest of the current loop iteration is skipped, and the loop continues with the next iteration. In the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loops, the loop header is executed next. That means, in <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, that the update and condition are executed, and in <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> (and <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>), that the condition is checked. If the condition still holds, the loop body instructions are executed again.

You saw an example in [Listing 8.18](#08_010.html_l8.18). When the program execution hits <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp>, it immediately jumps back to <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> and fetches the next <samp class="listingcharacter">char c</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">input</samp>.

In a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> has no meaning like <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>. It thus affects an enclosing loop.

## 8.13    The “return” Statement

You have already seen <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> as a statement to exit the program from <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>. Besides <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, you can use it to exit any function you write.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5ddxa9v1j
#include <iostream>                      // cout
int min3(int x, int y, int z) {          // function returns an int
    if(x<y) {
        if(x<z) return x;
        else return z;
    } else if(y<z) {
        return y;
    }
    else return z;
}
void printMin(int x, int y, int z) {    // function returns nothing
    if(x<0 || y<0 || z<0) {
        std::cout << "Please only numbers greater than 0\n";
        return;
    }
    std::cout << min3(x,y,z) << "\n";
}                                        // no return here
int main() {
    printMin(3, -4, 8);
    printMin(6, 77, 4);
    return;                              // special return in main
} 
```

**Listing 8.21**     With “return”, the current function is exited. If necessary, provide a value for the return.

In this example, you see the two self-written functions <samp class="listingcharacter">min3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">printMin</samp> (as well as the familiar <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>). <samp class="listingcharacter">min3</samp> is supposed to return an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> as a result, while <samp class="listingcharacter">printMin</samp> is specified with <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp>, indicating that no return value is expected.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter">min3</samp> is supposed to return an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, every <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> in it must be followed by an expression of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> (or one that can be converted to it). This is the case for all <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> lines in the function, as the variables are of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">printMin</samp>, however, no return value is expected, so the <samp class="listingcharacter">return;</samp> must not receive an expression. Note that execution can “fall out” of the function without encountering a <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>; this is allowed in <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> functions.

You already know that <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> has a special role in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>: although <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> has the return type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> here—and only here—does not need to receive a return expression, as shown in the final <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>. It is then assumed to be <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>.

### [Übung]  C++20: Coroutine Statements

With C++20, coroutines introduce a new feature to the C++ language. They enable generators and simpler asynchronous programming. I won't go into detail here, but I would like to mention that you might encounter two new keywords where previously only return could be used:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">co_return</samp> Expression <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">co_yield</samp> Expression <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>

You need this and <samp class="listingcharacter">co_await</samp> to turn a function into a coroutine—a function that you can resume at the same point after leaving.

## 8.14    The “goto” Statement

The question of whether to use <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> is complicated. Let me summarize it this way: it is difficult to use <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> correctly, and it is easy for something bad to come out of it.

My tips for you when programming in C++: Avoid using <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>. Always check all alternatives first when you think about using it. Only when you are familiar with all other ways to structure your program, and <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> remains the best option, can it sometimes be used effectively.

If you have not yet mastered those alternatives and therefore use <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>, you will make your code unclear and unmaintainable in the long run.

When a <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> might be better, you can read, for example, a key work from Donald Knuth[[ 15 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn08_01) (an excellent paper, of which I suggest you read at least the introduction). Until then, the rule is to avoid using <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>. And so you know what to avoid, the syntax of a <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> statement looks like this:

<samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> Label

Where a label is defined somewhere else:

Label <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> Statement

When the program execution encounters the <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>, it immediately jumps to the statement labeled as such.

It is difficult to find a somewhat meaningful example for <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>. I apologize that the following example is even more contrived than usual.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ohd5Pr8fb
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    int idx = 4;
    goto more;                      // jump to label more
  print:                            // label for the next statement
    std::cout << idx << std::endl;
    idx = idx * 2;
  more:
    idx = idx + 3;
    if(idx < 20)
        goto print;                 // goto can also be used in an if statement
  end:                              // this is a label, but it is not used
    return 0;
} 
```

**Listing 8.22**     Avoid <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> statements.

The danger is that when using <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>, you jump wildly back and forth. Or can you quickly determine which numbers [Listing 8.22](#08_014.html_l8.22) outputs? The answer is <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">17</samp>, but figuring that out is tedious.

With the alternatives described in this chapter, you have enough tools at your disposal to manage without <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>.

In [Listing 8.1](#08_001.html_l8.1), I actually introduced the <samp class="listingcharacter">isPrime()</samp> function only because I couldn't jump behind the <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp>; I would have had to introduce and manage an extra <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> variable. Maybe such a case is a justifiable use of <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>? But please only use it in code that will never be extended and where there is no risk of the <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> moving far from the label.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/fnsWhn5T3
// #includes, inputUpTo(), outputPrimes() and main() as before
std::vector<int> primes{2};
void calculatePrimesUpTo(int upTo) {
    /* Primes calculation */
    /* vector must contain {2} at this point */
    for(int n=3; n<upTo; n=n+2) {
        for(int factor: primes) {
            if(factor*factor > n)
                goto prime;     // using goto, because a break ...
            if(n%factor==0)
                goto notPrime;  // ... doesn't work over two loops.
        }
      prime:  ;                 // Target of the jump before push_back
        primes.push_back(n);    // n is prime! Remember as divisor and result
      notPrime:  ;              // Target of the jump after push_back
    }
} 
```

**Listing 8.23**     One less function, but one label and two more “goto” statements.

## 8.15    The “try-catch” Block and “throw”

Exceptions are an important but advanced topic. Because the <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> with the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> is the only remaining statement, I will still give you a preview. I will go into detail in [Chapter 10](#10_001.html_h10).

With a <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> block, you enclose program code where you expect certain errors that you want to handle. You handle these errors in the subsequent <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jhPaEjh1r
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    try {                                        // beginning of the try block
        for(int n=1; ; n=n*2) {
            if (n > std::numeric_limits<int>::max()/2) { // check for coming overflow
                throw "There would be an overflow";
            }
        }
    }                                            // End of the try block
    catch(const char *error) {                   // if this error occurs, …
        std::cout << "Error: " << error << " ";  // … handle it this way
    }
} 
```

**Listing 8.24**     As a preview, here is your first exception handling with “try” and “catch”.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> is followed by a statement block <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp>. This is followed by the handling of errors that occur within the block. This error handling is initiated with <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>, followed by the type of error to be caught in parentheses. After the parentheses, there is a block <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> with the instructions for the case in which an error of this type occurs.

If an error of type <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> is triggered somewhere between <samp class="listingcharacter">try {</samp> and the corresponding brace <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>, it will be “caught” in <samp class="listingcharacter">catch(const char *error)</samp> and handled in the associated statements. After that, the program continues with the next statement after the entire <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> block, including all associated <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> blocks.

In this example, I trigger such an error with <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> because the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> checks if the next <samp class="listingcharacter">n=n*2</samp> would overflow. Immediately, the normal execution of statements is interrupted and instead continues with the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>. This is just a simplified explanation; it gets really exciting when you trigger such errors while deeply nested in function calls. That's when these exception-handling mechanisms show their strengths.

You can specify multiple <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> blocks for one <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp>. The first matching one will be executed when an error occurs.

A word about how the error was actually triggered in this program: Could we just check <samp class="listingcharacter">if(n<0)</samp> when the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> overflowed and wrapped around? Well, there is a small yes and a big no: while on most machines this indeed might happen and work, the C++ standard considers integer overflow undefined behavior and is therefore to be avoided (see [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.4.3](#04_004.html_h4.4.3)).

## 8.16    Summary

You have now learned all the types of statements that C++ offers. I will summarize them again in groups:

*   Simple statements
    Statement block <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp>, declaration, expression—and empty statement

*   Branches
    <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> with and without <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp>

*   Loops
    <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>

*   Jump statements
    <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>—and, if necessary, also <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp>

*   Exception handling
    <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> block with <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> statement

# 9    Expressions in Detail

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Result
    The result of an expression can be reused.

*   Side effect
    A side effect occurs when an expression not only provides a result but also makes further changes to the state of the computer.

*   Overloading
    Multiple functions with the same name, which the compiler distinguishes based on different types of parameters.

*   Literal
    A concrete value directly written in the source code.

*   Parentheses
    Use them to group sub-expressions within expressions.

*   Function call
    The function name is followed by parentheses containing the list of arguments.

*   Index access
    When accessing an index, you use square brackets <samp class="listingcharacter">[…]</samp> to access an element among several similar ones.

*   Assignment
    An expression with the left side as the target, the equals sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>, and the right side as the source.

*   Operator
    A function-like construct where the function name is often a symbol and sometimes stands between two arguments.

*   Type conversion (cast)
    Forcing the type of an expression to another type.

With our discussion of statements, you’ve deepened your knowledge of a very important basic element. Statements usually consist of expressions, which we have only briefly discussed so far and which I will now examine in detail. And last but not least are types, which form the most complex topic of these three.

Statements, expressions, and types are closely related. It is difficult to explain one without the other. That's why I chose the approach of confronting you with all three one after the other and going into more detail each time. With this chapter, you will reach the penultimate level of detail for expressions together with types. The final level is programming practice.

## 9.1    Calculations and Side Effects

According to the C++ standard, an expression is “a sequence of operators and operands that specifies a computation.” (The exact definition is, of course, also given in the form of formal computer science grammar, but that is of little use for learning, and more as a reference.)

This computation is what programming is really about. And there I have two larger areas to distinguish:

*   Result
    There is a direct result of a calculation, like <samp class="listingcharacter">sin(alpha)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">count*4</samp>. This can be assigned or further used, for example in <samp class="listingcharacter">x = sin(alpha)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">print(count*4)</samp>. For C++, the type of this result is also important, as it determines how to proceed; see [Listing 9.1](#09_001.html_l9.1).

*   Side effect
    Instead of or in addition to the result, more happens; the further “state” of the computer changes. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << x</samp> results in an output as a side effect. This expression does not directly perform a calculation.

I will go into more detail on these outcomes.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/M6en1GMrE
#include <iostream>            // cout
#include <string>
void print(int n)  {           // function print for type int
    std::cout << "Number:" << n << "\n";
}
void print(std::string s)  {   // same name, different type
    std::cout << "String:" << s << "\n";
}
int main() {
    int number = 10;
    std::string name = "Bilbo";
    print(number);             // calls print(int), number is int
    print(name);               // calls print(string), name is string
    print(11 + 22);            // expression is int
    print(name + " Baggins");  // expression is string
} 
```

**Listing 9.1**     Types of expressions are important because they determine what happens next.

For example, the result of <samp class="listingcharacter">11 + 22</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>—and it is this property that determines that <samp class="listingcharacter">print(int)</samp> is called and not <samp class="listingcharacter">print(string)</samp>. It's different with <samp class="listingcharacter">name + "Baggins"</samp>, whose result is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>—so <samp class="listingcharacter">print(string)</samp> is called.

You have surely noticed that in both examples <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> was used: once to add numbers and the other time to concatenate strings. The <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> operator is overloaded as our own <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp>. Applied to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, it returns an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>; applied to <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, it returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. How to use operators like <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> was discussed in detail in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3).

### Either Calculation or Side Effect

It is important to always keep these two aspects of an expression in mind. It is good if an expression either performs a calculation or has the side effect as its main purpose—and if this is clear from the code or the documentation.

## 9.2    Types of Expressions

For better clarity, I list here the most important kinds of expressions—not as strict definitions, but in a highly summarized list as an overview. This is good for learning, but not for writing a C++ compiler. I summarize many special cases here that formally do not belong together.

*   Literal
    A literal is a value written directly into the source code—for example, a number like <samp class="listingcharacter">42</samp> or a text like <samp class="listingcharacter">"Goofus"</samp>.

*   Identifiers
    There are identifiers for variables, functions, types, and so on, possibly accessed through a scope with <samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>.

*   Parenthesized expression
    For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">( 3 + 4 + 5 )</samp>.

*   Function call
    A function call is recognizable by the parentheses <samp class="listingcharacter">(…)</samp> that follow it—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">sin(x)</samp>.

*   Index access
    An index access uses square brackets <samp class="listingcharacter">[…]</samp> instead of the parentheses of a function call, as in <samp class="listingcharacter">data[3]</samp> .

*   Operators
    There are binary operators like <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">a+b/2</samp>, or dereferencing with <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">it-> second</samp>, as well as unary ones like the <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> postfix in <samp class="listingcharacter">idx++</samp>, but also the <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> prefix in <samp class="listingcharacter">-10</samp>.

*   Assignment
    An assignment is an expression with the equals sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> as an operator, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">x=4</samp>. The value of the right operand is assigned to the left operand.

*   Type casting
    Type casting comes in various forms. The C cast uses the target type in parentheses before the value to be cast—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)30.1</samp>. Alternatively, you can also use the function notation for this, like <samp class="listingcharacter">int(30.1)</samp>. A C++ cast also looks similar to a function call, with the target type written in angle brackets—for example, in the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">static_cast<int>(30.1)</samp>.

If you can master and apply these kinds of expressions, then you are already very well equipped. While the listed expressions appear in C programs, the following are typical of C++ and are therefore powerful tools:

*   Memory management
    Allocating with <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and deallocating with <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp>

*   Lambda expression
    An anonymous function that is (usually) defined at the place where it is used

*   Template usage
    When the name of a called function can also include angle brackets <samp class="listingcharacter"><…></samp>, like <samp class="listingcharacter">numeric_limits<int>::is_signed</samp>

*   Throw exception
    A <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> followed by an expression, as you have briefly seen in [Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8)

## 9.3    Literals

Literals are fixed, concrete values directly written in the source code. In C++, these can be integers, floating-point numbers, characters, or strings. The basics are the easily recognizable forms <samp class="listingcharacter">123</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">3.141592</samp> for numbers, <samp class="listingcharacter">'a'</samp> as a single character, and <samp class="listingcharacter">"Gugelhupf"</samp> as a string.

It only becomes a bit more complicated because there are prefix and suffix modifiers for these base literals. As you have already seen in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.4](#04_004.html_h4.4), there are the following forms for integers, floating-point numbers, Boolean values, and strings:

```
999       0xffff    0777      0b10101   1L        0u  // integer forms
72.75     1e+10     3.141592f                         // floating point
'a'       "Text"                                      // strings
true      false           // truth values, the two bool literals
nullptr                   // the only nullptr_t literal 
```

## 9.4    Identifiers

Many things have a name: variables, constants, functions, classes, macros, and many more. These names consist of letters, digits, and the underscore character <samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp>. By letters, we mean <samp class="listingcharacter">A</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">Z</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp>; you should not use umlauts and other international characters, although some compilers support them.

An identifier must not start with a digit—so you cannot use <samp class="listingcharacter">9eye</samp>, for example.

Regarding the underscore, you should not start anything with two underscores <samp class="listingcharacter">__</samp> and should avoid an underscore followed by an uppercase letter at the beginning, as these forms are reserved for the standard library internally: <samp class="listingcharacter">__number</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">_Text</samp> can cause problems, for example.

Here are a few valid identifiers—all of which are different, as C++ is case-sensitive:

```
number            number_with_0
Number            NUMBER_WITH_0
NUMBER            NumberWith0
_number           OneHundredEleven
number_           onehundred11
_number_          one100eleven 
```

### Compound Identifiers

When you use functions and similar constructs, C++ combines the complete identifier from multiple elements. Thus, the complete C++ identifier can contain the scope operator <samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>. You have also seen that <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> as an operator for C++ is actually called <samp class="listingcharacter">operator+</samp>, and that is its identifier. The angle brackets for function and class templates are also always written together later, resulting in the entire identifier, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">numeric_limits<int></samp>.

You don't need to memorize the exact language definition here. What is important is that you get a feel for what constitutes an identifier through practice.

## 9.5    Parentheses

With parentheses, you can influence the order of calculations within an expression, just like in mathematics. This achieves roughly the same effect as if you were to split the expression into multiple statements. Therefore,

```
int interest = 3 * (4 + 7) * 8; 
```

is the same as

```
int intermediateResult = 4 + 7;
int interest = 3 * intermediateResult * 8;. 
```

The order of other evaluations (here, <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>) is not affected.

## 9.6    Function Call and Index Access

A function call in C++ is made with parentheses. Within these, the arguments (or parameters) for the call are listed, separated by commas:

Function <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> Parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> Parameter<samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> … <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>

Each parameter is again an expression, with function calls without parameters also occurring, and the list is then empty with <samp class="listingcharacter">()</samp>. And if you look closely, Function is also an expression, which usually simply consists of the name of the function to be called:

```
sin(3.141592);
print(6*6+number, "text", name);
justDo();
numeric_limits<int>::max();
[](auto x, auto y) { cout << x+y; } (3, 4);  // lambda expression instead of function 
```

It looks similar with index access, but you use square brackets there. You cannot list multiple parameters (this will change soon though). However, it is common to apply index access multiple times in a row:

```
data[10];                     // index access with number
image[x][y];                  // multiple times in a row
addresses["John Doe"];        // access to associative container 
```

## 9.7    Assignment

The assignment is also “just” an expression, in which <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> is the operator:

Expression left side <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> Expression right side

Here, however, the change to the left operand can be referred to as a side effect. On the right and left, there are again expressions, where on the left side there must be something to which you can assign something—for example, a variable:

```
int number;
number = 26 * 12 + 3; 
```

It would make no sense to use a literal on the left side of the assignment, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">26 = number * 3</samp>. Constants are also out of the question. However, there are cases where a real expression stands there—one that actually computes something.

You have seen that a function can also return a reference. You got a more detailed insight into this in [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7). The result of the expression on the left must be a writable reference. If the return type of a function is something with <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>, then this function can also be on the left side.

For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">front()</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> is such a function. It returns a reference to the first element in the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. It looks like this in principle (though within the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> template class and thus simplified here):

```
int& front(); 
```

Therefore, you can write the following:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/EY5K6Wsr3
std::vector<int> data(10);     // 10 times 0 in a vector
data.front() = 666;            // writes 666 to the front position 
```

### [Übung]  Outlook: Pointers, Arrays, and Iterators

When you learn about pointers, C-arrays, and iterators in [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20), you will write something like this:

```
int numbers[10] = {0};        // 10 contigous int values initialized to 0
*(numbers+3) = 666;           // writes 666 to the fourth position in numbers
std::vector<int> data{10};    // also 10 values initialized to 0
*(data.begin()+3) = 777;      // writes 777 to the fourth position 
```

The first two lines operate on a C-array of 10 <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values. With <samp class="listingcharacter">*(numbers+3)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">numbers</samp> is used as a pointer: <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> simply moves three positions forward in the array, and <samp class="listingcharacter">*(…)</samp> turns the position into a memory location, which is then written to with the <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>. Except that the last two lines involve a class (or to be precise, a template class), it works the same way. Here, it's not called a pointer, but <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> returns an iterator. You can add three to this and use <samp class="listingcharacter">*(…)</samp> to access the actual variable.

And because the assignment is an expression, you can embed it almost anywhere. The result of an assignment is the assigned value. You will often see an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> condition where an assignment is also made (in this example, with an initialization separated by a <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>, as has been possible since C++17):

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/K9c913had
if(int result; (result = read(buffer, 100)) != 0) {
    std::cerr << "Error number "<< result << " occurred.\n";
} 
```

This is quite a tricky expression:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">(result = read(buffer, 100)) != 0</samp> calls the function <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> .

*   Its result is assigned to <samp class="listingcharacter">result =</samp>.

*   The result of this expression is then compared to <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>. With <samp class="listingcharacter">!=0</samp>, it checks if it is not equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>.

*   And this is true or false, so the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> can decide which way to go.

However, use such assignments within other expressions sparingly. Under no circumstances should you perform “magic” and change values in the middle of a calculation:

```
3 + ((number = 2) * 4)-- 6 * (value = (6/2)) //  not good style at all 
```

No one will be able to understand that anymore. It is downright wrong also to use the target of the assignment elsewhere in the expression:

```
3 + (number = 2) * (number = 4) + 6          //  modified and used 
```

This is faulty code of the sort that allows the program to do whatever it wants—not what you want (undefined behavior).

### Using an Assignment as Part of a Larger Expression Is Dangerous!

Do not reuse the target of an assignment in the same statement. The result is undefined; the compiler does not have to warn you. This applies to all operations with side effects that modify a variable.

## 9.8    Type Casting

It is easy to explain type conversion for the previously introduced <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and their relatives because there is not much to convert with these types yet. Later, however, this will become an extensive topic that I will return to multiple times. In the context of expressions, I will exemplify the conversion between <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> to illustrate the concept.

You can convert an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> by simply using the type name as a function:

```
int value = 10;
bool yesNo = bool(value);  // function notation for type conversion 
```

Coming from C, there is another notation for this. It is still very popular, and you will see it often:

```
bool yesNo = (bool)value;  // C notation for type conversion 
```

There is yet a third variant in C++ to perform the preceding type conversion:

```
bool yesNo = static_cast<bool>(value); // detailed C++ type conversion 
```

This is because the other two variants can perform different types of type conversions depending on the type. And in such cases, specifying exactly which conversion—or cast—to perform is sometimes indispensable.

In addition to the <samp class="listingcharacter">static_cast</samp> shown here, there are also <samp class="listingcharacter">reinterpret_cast</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">const_cast</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">dynamic_cast</samp>, which I will not cover further here as they are an advanced topic. These are all the built-in cast variants. The standard library adds some things with “cast” in their name, like <samp class="listingcharacter">any_cast</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">duration_cast</samp>, but I call these explicit type conversions to distinguish them from the built-in casts.

# 10    Error Handling

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Error
    An error is something abnormal or unexpected. An abnormal situation could be, for example, an attempt to open a nonexistent file, and the program will handle it; that is, it deals with an exceptional situation. But if something completely unexpected occurs, it could be a program error.

*   Exceptional situation
    Within the scope of this chapter, an exceptional situation is a more or less anticipated but unusual event to which the program responds. This can happen via an exception or through error codes.

*   Program error
    Reaching an undefined state of the program.

*   Programming error (software bug)
    An error in the program that leads to a poor or incorrect result.

*   Exception
    An exception is triggered using <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>. The current blocks upward of the call chain are exited until a matching <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> is reached, or the program is terminated if no <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> matches.

*   Error code
    Alternative to handling errors using exceptions through return value or output parameters (or in extreme cases, a global variable).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> The act of triggering (throwing) an exception

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> Start of a handling block for exceptions.

Often a program must respond to events that are not what you want them to be: a file is not found, a zero is entered for a calculation period, or so on. There are many ways to deal with such events:

*   You can ignore them and expect users to live with the resulting errors. Perhaps you are one of the users yourself.

*   You can proactively check the conditions and intermediate results of actions and respond to such behavior in the program: output a message, try again, or terminate the program in an orderly manner.

The latter can usually be done as elaborately as you like. Good handling of unexpected states and errors is a very difficult task.

In C++, you have several options to master this, of which I will discuss two here:

*   Error codes
    Use return values or output parameters as side information about a process. Check these regularly and handle the event on the spot.

*   Exceptions
    Instead of passing the error through a side channel, raise an exception at the point of occurrence and handle the error elsewhere, probably at a central location for such handling.

First, it must be clear that there are different types of “errors” that need to be handled differently:

*   Undesirable state
    An undesirable state is an error that you should respond to on the spot because you suspect that something might go wrong. Maybe the document loaded by a user is corrupted. You should be as prepared as possible for such things. In the strictest sense, these are not errors because one definition is that an error is unexpected behavior. Error codes play a significant role here. But you can also use exceptions for this.

*   Unexpected state
    An unexpected state is an error that you do not want to anticipate everywhere—for example, because a check is costly and the consequences of its occurrence do not justify the increased effort of error handling. Memory is running out; the configuration file that was just read has disappeared. For robust software, you need to respond to more of these unexpected states. I wouldn't say that you expect them, but you are simply well prepared. This is where exceptions usually come into play.

*   Program error
    It is quite possible that your program may enter an undefined state in certain situations. This usually leads to a crash, but not always. You can be aware of this when writing the program and intentionally choose to forgo error handling. You might restrict the input in the documentation, but the documentation is part of the program. There you can write “Do not enter more than 100 numbers”, but nothing prevents users from doing so anyway. Not every program error is a programming error, because it is possible that the program was used incorrectly.

*   Programming errors
    Programming errors are mistakes that you have unknowingly introduced and that produce faulty behavior. Divide by zero? Array one element too small? Your program then has a bug. If you are lucky, you can protect yourself from fatal consequences—with error codes, but more often with exceptions.

*   Quality errors
    Quality errors are those issues that, while not preventing the correct end result for end users, still impose compromises for users or programmers. For users, this might mean that the program runs too slowly or has difficult-to-use dialogs. For programmers, it could mean that the software becomes hard to maintain, potentially leading to future programming errors. This broad category also involves subjective factors like code readability, testing, documentation, and more.
    Quality errors often stem from a lack of adherence to coding standards and best practices, which can result in a disjointed and inconsistent codebase. This inconsistency can make collaborative development more difficult and increase the likelihood of introducing new bugs when making changes. As a result, addressing quality errors is crucial not only for ensuring a smooth and enjoyable user experience but also for maintaining a sustainable and efficient development process.

You can see here that the term error encompasses a lot of completely different things. In this chapter, we do not deal with quality errors at all, little with programming and program errors, partly with unexpected states, and mostly with undesirable states. When you handle errors, you are in a way anticipating them—and this chapter is about error handling.

## 10.1    Error Handling with Error Codes

When working with error codes, use return values and error parameters to convey information about error states. It looks something like the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/EWqqGjnnz
#include <iostream>  // cout, cerr
#include <fstream>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
using std::vector; using std::string; using std::cout; using std::cerr;

int countWords(const string& filename) {  // return negative on error
    std::ifstream file{filename};
    if(!file) {     // was there an error opening the file?
        cerr << "Error opening " << filename << "\n";
        return -1;  // report an error to the caller using a special value
    }
    int count = 0;
    string word;
    while(!file.eof()) {      // not at the end yet?
        file >> word;
        ++count;
    }
    return count-1;           // one more word was read at EOF
}
bool process(const vector<string>& args) { // return true if all okay
    if(args.size() == 0) {   // expecting parameters
        cerr << "Command line argument missing\n";
        return false;        // report an error via return
    } else {
        bool result = true;  // for the final result
        for(const string filename : args) {
            cout << filename << ": ";
            int count = countWords(filename);
            if(count < 0) {  // special return indicates error
                cout << "Error!\n";
                result = false;        // at least one error
            } else {
                cout << count << "\n"; // output normal result
            }
        }
        return result;                 // return overall result
    }
}

int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    bool result = process(             // return value contains error indicator
        {argv+1, argv+argc} );         // const char*[] to vector<string>
    if(result) {                       // evaluate return value
        return 0;
    } else {
        cerr << "An error occurred.\n";
        return 1;                      // indicate error externally
    }
} 
```

**Listing 10.1**     Respond to many states with different types of return values.

You will often see that states that are not optimal are checked with <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>:

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">if(!file)</samp>, I check if the file opening was successful.

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">if(args.size()==0)</samp>, I check if the user has provided at least one command line parameter.

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">if(count < 0)</samp>, I use the special return value of the function to react to the error.

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">if(result)</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, I check the forwarded result.

Each case is handled differently:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">countWords</samp> returns a count (always zero or greater), so in <samp class="listingcharacter">countWords</samp> the <samp class="listingcharacter">return -1;</samp> with the special value of <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp> indicates an error to the caller.

*   The return value is checked in <samp class="listingcharacter">process</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">if(count < 0)</samp>, possibly specially handled, and finally passed outward at <samp class="listingcharacter">return result;</samp>.

*   The test in <samp class="listingcharacter">process</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">if(args.size() == 0)</samp> can directly lead to a negative return via <samp class="listingcharacter">return false;</samp>.

*   And if an error occurs somewhere, it ultimately reaches <samp class="listingcharacter">bool result = process();</samp> and is even passed to the callers of the program at <samp class="listingcharacter">return 1;</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>.

If you react to errors in this way, you pass the error state through function calls using <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> codes or—in extreme cases—separate error objects.

I want to quickly explain the argument <samp class="listingcharacter">{argv+1, argv+argc}</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">process</samp>: The function <samp class="listingcharacter">process</samp> receives a <samp class="listingcharacter">const vector<string>&</samp> as a parameter. However, the given argument is an initializer list consisting of <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>. The compiler can convert this without problems using the appropriate constructors of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>.

To show you how to use the program, here is how it reacts in different cases:

```
$ touch empty_file
$ echo "Two words" > two_words.txt
$ ./28-codes.x
Command line argument missing
An error occurred.
$ ./28-codes.x empty_file two_words.txt 28-codes.cpp
empty_file: 0
two_words.txt: 2
28-codes.cpp: 252
$ ./28-codes.x two_words.txt DOES_NOT_EXIST.txt empty_file
two_words.txt: 2
DOES_NOT_EXIST.txt: Error opening DOES_NOT_EXIST.txt
empty_file: 0
Error!
An error occurred. 
```

First, prepare two files with zero and two words of content using <samp class="listingcharacter">touch</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">echo</samp>. When you run <samp class="listingcharacter">./28-codes.x</samp> without arguments, you get an error. Running it with three arguments (<samp class="listingcharacter">empty_file …</samp>) works and counts the words in each of the files. A file name that does not exist leads to an error when running with <samp class="listingcharacter">DOES_NOT_EXIST.txt</samp>.

No matter what you implement—error codes, exceptions, or neither—the behavior of a function in the event of an error is part of the interface. As part of the interface, you must document it just like returns, parameters, and regular behavior. In the standard library, you will see many examples of how to accomplish this documentation.

## 10.2    What Is an Exception?

You cannot avoid the really important checks for error states: you have to teach the computer what an error is and what is not. But the passing on of codes is tedious and long-winded. You can also centralize handling for errors that occur in multiple places with a different approach.

Instead of generating and passing on error codes, you can trigger an exception—or, in other words, throw an exception.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/j8abxvvvo
#include <iostream>            // cout, cerr
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <fstream>             // ifstream
#include <stdexcept>           // invalid_argument
using std::vector; using std::string; using std::cout; using std::ifstream;
size_t countWords(const string& filename) { // 0 or greater
    std::ifstream file{};      // create unopened
    // register for exceptions:
    file.exceptions(ifstream::failbit | ifstream::badbit);
    file.open(filename);       // could throw an exception
    size_t count = 0;
    string word;
    file.exceptions(ifstream::badbit); // EOF no longer an exception
    while(!file.eof()) {       // not at the end yet?
        file >> word;   ++count;
    }
    return count-1;            // one more word was read at EOF
}
void process(const vector<string>& args) {
    if(args.size() == 0) {     // process expects parameters
        throw std::invalid_argument{"Command line argument missing"}; // trigger
    } else {
        for(const string filename : args) {
            cout << filename << ": " << countWords(filename) << std::endl;
        }
    }
}
int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    try {                                      // block with error handling
        process(
          vector<string>{argv+1, argv+argc} ); // const char*[] to vector<string>
        return 0;
    } catch(std::exception &exc) {             // error handling
        std::cerr << "An error occurred: " << exc.what() << "\n";
        return 1;
    }
} 
```

**Listing 10.2**     Exceptions are triggered with “throw” and handled with “try-catch”.

At <samp class="listingcharacter">file.open(filename)</samp>, I no longer check if opening the file was successful, because now something else happens: <samp class="listingcharacter">file.open()</samp> triggers an exception if there was an error. This means that the program is immediately interrupted and the current function—here, <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream::open</samp>—is exited. However, this does not happen in the normal way via <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>, but rather on the fly. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">countWords()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">process()</samp> are “unwound” in this manner—until the <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> block in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> is reached, which contains the call to <samp class="listingcharacter">process()</samp>. There it is stated what needs to be done with <samp class="listingcharacter">catch(std::exception) in this case</samp>. Here I output an error, and, as in the previous example, <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>.

That was exception handling in a nutshell. For you to really understand it, I need to go into a bit more detail.

### 10.2.1    Throwing and Handling Exceptions

The keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> triggers an exception. A value is associated with it, representing the exception. At the beginning of <samp class="listingcharacter">process()</samp>, you see an example of this: after the <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>, I create an instance of the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::invalid_argument</samp> class, which now represents the error.

In the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">file.open()</samp>, it is not me who triggers the exception with <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>; <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> itself does. Therein, in the case of an error, <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> raises an <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::failure {…}</samp> exception, and <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> exits this way.

I called this exit above “in passing.” This means that no <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> is used, and it has nothing to do with the declared return type of the function. The return is, so to speak, replaced by the value of the exception.

The program does not leave the functions uncontrollably. On the contrary: all objects are carefully cleaned up, as is the usual case when leaving a block normally. So it is still ensured that every created object is completely cleaned up. This includes all types of the standard library and also types that you have created yourself (see [Chapter 16](#16_001.html_h16)).

#### Raw Pointers Are Not Properly Unwound

Wait a moment—I need to clarify something: pointers that you have created with <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> are only safe if you have wrapped them in a smart pointer (like <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp>; see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20)).

### 10.2.2    Unwinding the Call Stack

Neither <samp class="listingcharacter">countWords()</samp> nor <samp class="listingcharacter">process()</samp> handle exceptions that are thrown within their bounds.
