That is done by <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, which contains a <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> block there. Everything that happens within the curly braces <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> is now checked when an exception is thrown—and within here also means that it could have happened somewhere deep in the basement of a function call.

The check consists of going through the <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> commands associated with the <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> one by one. The compiler tries to convert the value of the exception into the type specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>. In my <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>, it says <samp class="listingcharacter">std::exception</samp>, which feels responsible for quite a lot—at least for both <samp class="listingcharacter">std::invalid_argument</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::failure</samp>.

My own exception handling now consists of outputting an error message. I add the text with what is attached to the exception value. For example, I get the text with <samp class="listingcharacter">exc.what()</samp> that I specified as an error message with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::invalid_argument{…}</samp>.

So that you can also see this program in action, here is the screen output:

```
$ ./28-exc01.x
An error occurred: Command line argument missing

$ ./28-exc01.x empty_file two_words.txt 28-exc01.cppp
empty_file: 0
two_words.txt: 2
28-exc01.cppp: 171

$ ./28-exc01.x two_words.txt DOES_NOT_EXIST.txt empty_file
two_words.txt: 2
An error occurred: basic_ios::clear 
```

Here too, calling <samp class="listingcharacter">./28-exc01.x</samp> without parameters leads to an error. If all files can be opened, then the program counts the words. If a file does not exist, then you will get an error again when calling with <samp class="listingcharacter">DOES_NOT_EXIST.txt</samp>.

## 10.3    Minor Error Handling

Unlike in the first example, the processing now completely stops; for <samp class="listingcharacter">empty_file</samp>, you see no result. This is because the exception from <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> is only caught in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>—and thus the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop in <samp class="listingcharacter">process</samp> was also prematurely terminated.

If you want the same behavior—that is, continuing the processing with the next file—then you must not leave the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop in passing. You need error handling within the loop.

```
void process(const vector<string>& args) {
    if(args.size() == 0) {                 // expect parameters
        throw std::invalid_argument{"Command line argument missing"};
    } else {
        for(const string filename : args) {
            cout << filename << ": ";
            try {
                cout << countWords(filename) << "\n";
            } catch(std::exception &exc) {
                cout << "Error: " << exc.what() << "\n";
            }
        }
    }
} 
```

**Listing 10.3**     A “catch” can also be within a loop.

Now the error is caught and handled, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop can continue normally with the next file.

The rest of the program remains the same. The <samp class="listingcharacter">throw std::invalid_argument</samp> is outside the <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> block and reaches <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> unchanged to be handled.

## 10.4    Throwing the Exception Again: “rethrow”

If you want both options—local error handling, but also error handling in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>—then you can use a <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> without any argument within the <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> block to rethrow the currently handled exception unchanged (hence the name rethrow).

```
try {
    cout << countWords(filename) << "\n";
} catch(std::exception &exc) {
    cout << "Error: " << exc.what() << "\n";
    throw; // rethrow
} 
```

**Listing 10.4**     Using “throw” without parameters rethrows the currently handled exception.

You might need this if you have some specific local cleanup to do but still want to use the main error-handling routine—perhaps to present a sophisticated error dialog to users.

## 10.5    The Order in “catch”

With the single <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> from [Listing 10.2](#10_002.html_l10.2), I caught all possible exceptions in my program. Both <samp class="listingcharacter">std::invalid_argument</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::failure</samp> can be converted to the specified <samp class="listingcharacter">std::exception</samp>. However, you can also use two separate handlers:

```
int main() {
    try {
        //… Code as before …
        return 0; // if everything is okay, return ok as well
    } catch(std::invalid_argument &exc) {  // first handler
        cerr << "Invalid argument: " << exc.what() << "\n";
    } catch(std::ios_base::failure &exc) { // second handler
        cerr << "File error: " << exc.what() << "\n";
    } catch(std::exception &exc) {         // third, very general handler
        cerr << "An error occurred: " << exc.what() << "\n";
    } catch( ... ) {  // fourth and last handler for the rest
        cerr << "A strange error occurred\n";
    }
    return 1;         // you only get here after a catch: report error
} 
```

If an <samp class="listingcharacter">invalid_argument</samp> exception occurs between <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> blocks, then the <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> handlers are tried in order—and the first one, <samp class="listingcharacter">invalid_argument</samp>, matches. The handler is executed and then the entire handler block is exited; the next line is therefore <samp class="listingcharacter">return 1</samp>. Unlike with <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp>, there is no fall-through to the next handler here.

If the code throws an <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::failure</samp> exception, then <samp class="listingcharacter">invalid_argument</samp> does not match, and the second handler is tried. It matches and is executed. Even after this handler, the program continues after the last <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>.

The handler for <samp class="listingcharacter">std::exception</samp> would have also matched the other two exceptions, but it is not reached in either case. How this conversion works is explained in [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15). You will only reach this point if you extend the program and other exceptions are thrown that match—or if you have overlooked something.

And indeed, we have. An exception that you should always expect is <samp class="listingcharacter">std::bad_alloc</samp>. This is thrown when <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> requests more memory than is available (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20)). This can happen either if your program has really consumed the memory or, often, if an error elsewhere leads to a memory request of size <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp> or similar. Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_alloc</samp> indicates a serious problem. In any case, <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_alloc</samp> can also be converted into <samp class="listingcharacter">exception</samp> and—theoretically—be thrown by many parts of the standard library. With the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::exception</samp> handler shown here, you at least catch the error.

The last clause with <samp class="listingcharacter">catch(...)</samp> captures everything that still comes in here. With <samp class="listingcharacter">exception</samp>, I have actually handled everything that can be triggered by and with the standard library, but theoretically, there could be more.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">catch(...)</samp> clause must be the last one in a <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> list. Another one could not be reached afterward anyway. Because you cannot give the caught exception a name as in the more specific clauses, the information you can obtain here is very limited. Sometimes, however, there are still important cleanup tasks to be done.

### 10.5.1    No “finally”

If you come from another programming language (such as Java), then you might now be waiting for the <samp class="listingcharacter">finally</samp>. Do you miss a block that is executed when leaving a range, whether by exception or regularly? That does not exist in C++; instead, you use the destructor of an object (see [Chapter 16](#16_001.html_h16)). There, the resource wrapper is also described if you really want to simulate a <samp class="listingcharacter">finally</samp> block.

### 10.5.2    Standard Library Exceptions

You don't have to deal with an excessive number of exceptions in the C++ standard library. Nevertheless, some can occur almost anywhere. I only want to mention the most important ones here; the documentation of the functions always describes possible exceptions:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_alloc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_array</samp>
    Triggered by <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">new[]</samp> when there is a lack of memory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">logic_error</samp> These are errors that are more likely to be in the program code and that you might have been able to discover before starting the program.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">invalid_argument</samp> You already know these exceptions. They belong to <samp class="listingcharacter">logic_error</samp> and are rarely triggered in the standard library.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">out_of_range</samp> This exception is also a <samp class="listingcharacter">logic_error</samp> and is triggered by <samp class="listingcharacter">vector::at(n)</samp> when <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is too large.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">runtime_error</samp> These include errors that can only occur at runtime.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">overflow_error</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">underflow_error</samp>
    These are exceptions that you can trigger yourself if your function receives an inappropriate integer argument. The standard library rarely triggers these exceptions. They belong to <samp class="listingcharacter">runtime_error</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">range_error</samp> You can trigger this exception if your function receives an inappropriate floating-point argument. The standard library rarely throws this exception. It belongs to <samp class="listingcharacter">runtime_error</samp>.

This list is not exhaustive. You can always see in the documentation of the standard library functions which exceptions they throw.

In larger projects, it is quite common to create your own exception classes. Refer to [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15) for more information. It is best to derive your own class from <samp class="listingcharacter">std::exception</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">std::runtime_error</samp> for this purpose.

## 10.6    Types for Exceptions

What else can there be besides <samp class="listingcharacter">std::exception</samp> and everything that can be converted into it? In principle, you can use values of any type with <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>. However, it is recommended to use the exception types from the standard library whenever possible.

If that is not possible, then use <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/67cd5bhhE
#include <string>
#include <iostream> // cout
using std::string; using std::to_string; using std::cout;
void triggerError(int errorCase) {
   try {
       if(errorCase < 10) throw (int)errorCase;
       else if(errorCase < 20) throw 1.0/(errorCase-10.0);
       else throw string{"Error " + to_string(errorCase)};
   } catch(int eval) {
       cout << "int-error: " << eval << "\n";
   } catch(double eval) {
       cout << "double-error: " << eval << "\n";
   } catch(string eval) {
       cout << "string-error: " << eval << "\n";
   }
}
int main() {
    triggerError(3);   // Output: int-error: 3
    triggerError(14);  // Output: double-error: 0.25
    triggerError(50);  // Output: string-error: Error 50
} 
```

**Listing 10.5**     You can also throw exceptions of other types.

There is usually no reason to use types with <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> that cannot be converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">std:: exception</samp>. For understanding how exceptions work, it is useful to know that <samp class="listingcharacter">std:: exception</samp> is not really special when it comes to exception handling; it just comes with some helper functions, like <samp class="listingcharacter">what()</samp>.

## 10.7    When an Exception Falls Out of “main”

If you do not handle a thrown exception at all, so that it reaches <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> and is not caught there either, then your program will terminate. Most of the time, you will still see a message. Therefore, it is quite common to install only the necessary handlers in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>. Those that would do nothing anyway you do not implement at all. The objects you have created will all be properly cleaned up before the program terminates.

However, seeing a message is not mandatory for the system. So if you at least want to see the error type and text, then wrap the entire code in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> with a simple error output.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TsP33njar
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept> // exception

int main() {
    try {
        // … your other code …
    } catch(std::exception& exc) {
        std::cerr << "main: " << exc.what() << "\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 10.6**     At least output the error type and text instead of letting your program tumble out of “main”.

# 11    Good Code, 2nd Dan: Modularization

So long as you write a small program that fits into a single source file, a C++ project is simple. It becomes more difficult when you need to split your program to increase clarity. What goes where?

In this chapter, I use classes for explanation. If you are working through the book sequentially, please forgive the jumping ahead. But this should not distract from the principles of modularization. You can easily return to the dan chapters later.

## [Übung]  C++20: Modules

Since C++20, modules enable a clean separation of declaration and implementation. They also allow the compiler to import faster than with <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> included program parts. Look out for the new <samp class="listingcharacter">module</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">import</samp> keywords.

Although a lot has changed regarding modularization, in practice, much will remain the same: <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp>-based modularization will stay with us for various reasons for a long time. What you learn in this chapter will also be useful when working with modules.

## 11.1    Program, Library, Object File

When the compiler (or linker) assembles the executable program, it usually takes your translated source code and combines it with other libraries available in the system.

Each <samp class="listingcharacter">*.obj</samp> file represents a <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file translated by the compiler that you have written. The <samp class="listingcharacter">*.dll</samp> files are libraries present on your system that your program is aware of but does not need to fully integrate (hence the dashed line in [Figure 11.1](#11_001.html_f11.1)). The [Figure 11.1](#11_001.html_f11.1) <samp class="listingcharacter">*.lib</samp> files are also libraries, but ones that your program integrates fully—or at least parts of them. For example, libraries of the C and C++ compilers as well as a game library are shown here. You may have acquired the latter from a third-party vendor so that you don't have to develop essential parts of the program yourself.

As a Unix user, you are more familiar with the extensions <samp class="listingcharacter">*.o</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*.so</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">*.a</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">*.obj</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*.dll</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">*.lib</samp>, but the same applies to all systems: the final program is assembled from multiple libraries.

[![Apart from your code, a program consists of several libraries.](bilderklein/klein11_001.png)](img-f11.1.html)

**Figure 11.1**     Apart from your code, a program consists of several libraries.

Each library usually consists of individual modules. For example, the C++ standard library, from your perspective as a user, consists of several headers. Sometimes you include <samp class="listingcharacter">#include <vector></samp>, sometimes <samp class="listingcharacter">#include <iostream></samp>. These headers reflect that the library was probably not developed as a single huge <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file. The modules were combined into a single library for your convenience, so you only need to specify this one <samp class="listingcharacter">*.lib</samp> file to the compiler. The compiler then picks out the things that are actually used by itself.

## 11.2    Modules

Your task now is to sensibly divide the modules of your part of the program for your own project. For this, you need to answer the question, for example, “What belongs in <samp class="listingcharacter">main.obj</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">teil1.obj</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">teil2.obj</samp>?” And along with that: “What belongs in the <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">teil1.cpp</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">teil2.cpp</samp> source code files?”

<samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp> should probably contain <samp class="listingcharacter">int main()</samp>. Instead of naming the file <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">program.cpp</samp> is also a reasonable name if your program will later be called <samp class="listingcharacter">programm.exe</samp>.

Otherwise, you should break your project into parts based on functionalities. Each part goes into a separate set of <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> files. Each <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file, in turn, is complemented by a similarly named <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file. The exception is <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp>, for which you normally do not need to create a header file.

### Interface: Each .cpp File Also Gets a .hpp File

Write a similarly named <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> header file for each <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp>. Declare in it all the functions and other things that are directly used by other <samp class="listingcharacter">.cpp</samp> files: these form the interface. Intentionally keep certain elements only in the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file—specifically, those needed solely to implement the interface.

It is a good standard practice to have a corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file for every <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file. But there are more exceptions to this rule. Sometimes you combine headers for simplicity; sometimes the interface is also the implementation or contains only constants. You might consider separating such headers from the normal ones, naming them differently, or managing them in a different directory.

## 11.3    Separating Functionalities

That's easier said than done, because often the boundaries of functionalities are fluid.

When you break down your program into <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> files, the consequence is that the various <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> files include other <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> files via <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp>.

It gets bad when every file needs all the other files. Try to keep the number of required <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> directives small.

Cyclic dependencies are really tricky—where <samp class="listingcharacter">A.hpp</samp> includes <samp class="listingcharacter">B.hpp</samp>, but in <samp class="listingcharacter">B.hpp</samp> you then realize that you actually need <samp class="listingcharacter">A.hpp</samp> first. You solve this by separating one (or both) headers so that only the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file needs the other header.

I therefore recommend following these rules:

*   Separate your program into layers. One layer may only use things from the layers below. But skip as few layers as possible:

    *   An <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file should ideally only include something from the direct layer below. Another part of the program that wants to include this header will then also need all the others, and that can quickly become many. But the fewer there are, the better.

    *   A <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file can be more permissive. The disorder is localized to compiling this source file, so it doesn't have such a wide impact.

    *   There are exceptions. In [Figure 11.2](#11_003.html_f11.2), <samp class="listingcharacter">const.hpp</samp> has the role of consolidating central declarations. Probably every header needs these, and then it's good to have them in one place, in a single file, and not scattered across multiple files.

*   Avoid cyclic dependencies:

    *   A <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file must always include “its” <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file anyway.

        A <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file may use any other <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file at this level. <samp class="listingcharacter">teil2.cpp</samp> may include <samp class="listingcharacter">teil1.hpp</samp>, as shown in [Figure 11.2](#11_003.html_f11.2). There would also be nothing against <samp class="listingcharacter">teil1.cpp</samp> in [Figure 11.2](#11_003.html_f11.2) using <samp class="listingcharacter">teil2.hpp</samp> at the same time.

    *   This does not apply to <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> files. Include other headers of the same level only in exceptional cases. And if you do, strictly only in one direction. In the illustration, <samp class="listingcharacter">teil1.hpp</samp> may thus use <samp class="listingcharacter">teil2.hpp</samp>, but not vice versa.

If you follow these rules as much as possible, you will definitely avoid cyclic dependencies. The layering model is also beneficial to keep the number of required includes in later modules lower. It is not a panacea, but it is a step in the right direction.

[![Divide the components of your program into layers to avoid cyclic dependencies.](bilderklein/klein11_002.png)](img-f11.2.html)

**Figure 11.2**     Divide the components of your program into layers to avoid cyclic dependencies.

### [Übung]  Modularization and OOP

When you work cleanly with classes and traditional object orientation, it is a natural cut to create one “module” per class. In [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12), the description of object-oriented programming (OOP) in C++ begins, and in [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14), you will see a practical example of splitting a project into modules with classes.

**Table 11.1**     Structure of an example project.

I also use this example project later in [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14) on good code to demonstrate unit tests.

The project consists of a library that I pretend to deliver to a customer. For testing and demonstration purposes, I want to provide the customer with two small example programs to show how to use the library. Whether these example programs are given to the customer as source code or only as a finished program is irrelevant. The customer will receive the header files and the compiled library, but not the source code.

This example library shall mainly consist of a class that implements an index. It will function similarly to a dictionary: sequentially adding multiple entries that then make up the index. With this, you can query the index with a search pattern to check if a specific entry exists. An exact search would be boring, so we search “approximately.” The search should return the best match.

I don't want to tell the customer anything more. What the “best match” is should be an implementation detail. Here, I want to use q-grams for the search, where I choose the length of q to be 3\. This means that the search finds the entry where most of the three-character substrings of the search pattern match an index entry.

If the index contains, for example, Graumaus and Nagetierstamm, then with the Anagramm query you will find the latter, because both contain NAG and AMM, while the former does not have any three-letter group in common with Anagramm. I don't want to say more about the algorithm as an example here, because it is really a side issue in this chapter. (While translating this chapter, I discovered that German is an excellent language to do q-grams with!)

If you call <samp class="listingcharacter">make all</samp> in the main directory, then the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.a</samp> library in <samp class="listingcharacter">src/lib/</samp> and the programs in <samp class="listingcharacter">src/prog/</samp> will be built one after the other.

The library here consists only of a minimal set of files: a header file that is to be delivered with the library, as well as the implementation files. These, in turn, consist of two <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> files, <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.cpp</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap.cpp</samp>, as well as an internal <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file, <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap.hpp</samp>, which is not intended for delivery. Therefore, it is also located in <samp class="listingcharacter">src/lib/</samp>. If you deliver the library to a customer who uses a compiler compatible with yours, for static linking it is sufficient to deliver the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.a</samp> library file and on Windows <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.lib</samp> together with the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.hpp</samp> header file. If you want to support dynamic linking too, you provide a <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.so</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.dll</samp> library file.

### The Header File Must Match the Library File

It is crucial that you (and your customers) use the exact same header file that was used to build the library file when using your library. If you have different versions in use, the best thing that can happen is a compiler or linker error; in the worst case, the behavior will be unpredictable.

The main <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.hpp</samp> header file is shown in [Listing 11.1](#11_004.html_l11.1).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/e5GWbbq4Y
#ifndef QWORT_H // header guard
#define QWORT_H
#include <string>
#include <memory> // unique_ptr
namespace qw { // library namespace
    int version();
    namespace impl_multimap {
        class index_impl;
    }
    class index {
        using index_impl = impl_multimap::index_impl;
    public:
        index();
        ~index() noexcept; // needed for pimpl
        index(const index&) = default;
        index(index&&) noexcept = default;
        index& operator=(const index&) = default;
        index& operator=(index&&) = default;
    public:
        void add(const std::string &arg);
        size_t size() const;
        std::string getBestMatch(const std::string& query) const;
    public:          // public for tests
        std::string normalize(std::string arg) const;
    private:
        const std::unique_ptr<index_impl> pimpl;
    };
} // namespace qw
#endif // header guard 
```

**Listing 11.1**     The main header file of the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.hpp</samp> library.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getBestMatch</samp> methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> class are the actual interface of the library:

*   First, you create an empty index with the default <samp class="listingcharacter">index()</samp> constructor.

*   Then, you add entries one by one using <samp class="listingcharacter">add(const string&)</samp>.

*   When you are done, you can query as many times as you want with <samp class="listingcharacter">getBestMatch(const string&)</samp> for the best matching entry that you previously added.

### 11.4.1    Namespaces

Everything intended for the export of the library is defined in its own namespace <samp class="listingcharacter">qw</samp>. Therefore, the header also begins with a <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace qw</samp>, and all declarations and definitions are enclosed within it.

This is followed by a forward declaration of the <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap::index_impl</samp> class. A namespace is opened for it as well. All internal library components that should be as hidden as possible are contained within it. However, the name of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> class, which the <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> class uses further down, is needed here.

#### [Übung]  Switching Implementations with Namespaces

By the way, the namespace is called <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap</samp> because it contains only one of several possible implementations. In another directory, you will see the <samp class="listingcharacter">15p-unittest-100</samp> project in the download sources, which defines an <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_simple_map</samp> namespace with an <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> class contained within it. This is a different, simpler version of an index implementation.

In principle, you could run both namespaces in parallel and easily switch the implementation used in the main class. However, this is just a suggestion here, which is why I only show it in a rudimentary way. If fully developed, this switchability would involve a bit more programming effort and is not the focus of this chapter.

Now follows the actual main class of the <samp class="listingcharacter">class index</samp> library. At its core, it contains a <samp class="listingcharacter">pimpl</samp> field of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> class (as a pointer). With this “trick,” implementation details of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> interface class can be separated even better. Sometimes this is called the pointer to implementation (or Pimpl) pattern.

To avoid bothering users of the class with implementation details (or to keep them secret), all methods of the class are declared only. They are defined later in the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.cpp</samp> implementation file.

Normally, as you will see in [Chapter 17](#17_001.html_h17), you would not define a destructor, copy constructor, move constructor, assignment operator, or move operator (the “big five”). The compiler would generate them optimally for you. Unfortunately, that is not possible here: the compiler would need the definition of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> class for this, because how else would it know what to do with <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr<index_impl> pimpl</samp>? But so far, we have only declared it as a forward declaration. Therefore, the compiler can only help us here if we let it generate the code in the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.cpp</samp> file—especially for the constructor, destructor, and move constructor. You will see how this works shortly. We can simply let the compiler generate the other three here with <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp>. However, we must list them here, because according to C++ rules, they would otherwise be completely missing as we have defined at least one other member of the “big five” family.

### 11.4.2    Implementation

I chose to separate this chapter into the <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> interface class and the <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> implementation class for two reasons. On the one hand, I wanted to present the Pimpl pattern in practice; on the other hand, this example should not be trivial. With this separation, I have an excellent reason for a second class and a second <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file. I can then also handle both later in a second test module.

The header file of the interface class also includes the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file with the implementation, as you can see in [Listing 11.2](#11_004.html_l11.2).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TMExE8doz
#include "qwort/qwort.hpp" // self
#include <map>
#include <algorithm>       // transform
#include <cctype>          // toupper
#include "impl_multimap.hpp"
using std::map; using std::string;

namespace qw {
    int version() {
        return 1;
    }
    // administration
    index::index()
        : pimpl{ new index_impl{} }
        { }
    index::~index() noexcept = default;
    // interface
    void index::add(const string &arg) {
        pimpl->add(normalize(arg), arg);
    }
    size_t index::size() const {
        return pimpl->size();
    }
    string index::getBestMatch(const string& query) const {
        return pimpl->getBestMatch(normalize(query));
    }
    string index::normalize(string str) const {
        using namespace std; // begin, end
        transform(begin(str), end(str), begin(str), [](char c) {
                return ::isalpha(c) ? ::toupper(c) : '#';
            });
        return str;
    }
} // namespace qw 
```

**Listing 11.2**     The interface class forwards all calls to the implementation class.

First, all <samp class="listingcharacter">include</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> directives are tended to. A sensible order is to start with the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file that belongs to the current <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file—in this case, <samp class="listingcharacter">"qwort/qwort.hpp"</samp>. Note that the file name is enclosed with <samp class="listingcharacter">""</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter"><></samp> because the include is part of our own library. In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.hpp</samp> is located in its own subdirectory <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort/</samp>, which is a good idea in larger libraries with multiple header files.

The implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> class now requires the complete definition of the <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> class; therefore, its header file must also be included with <samp class="listingcharacter">#include "impl_multimap.hpp"</samp>.

Because everything that is part of this library is in its own namespace, everything in this file is also enclosed in <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace qw</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">version()</samp> free function is quickly implemented. Then the implementations of all contents of <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> follow. First, these are the constructors and destructors that have not yet been defined in <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp>. At this point, the <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> class is fully known, so we can ask the compiler to generate these constructors and destructors with <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp>. In the default constructor, that is not enough: the compiler would initialize <samp class="listingcharacter">pimpl</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">nullptr</samp>, but we need a <samp class="listingcharacter">new index_impl</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">getBestMatch()</samp> methods mainly delegate their calls to <samp class="listingcharacter">pimpl</samp>. Only <samp class="listingcharacter">normalize()</samp> is called beforehand each time, because <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> does not handle that, as the implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> is contained in the current file and therefore included last. Using <samp class="listingcharacter">transform()</samp>, all characters of <samp class="listingcharacter">str</samp> are individually converted to uppercase if they are letters; if not, a <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> is inserted. This is done in the fourth parameter of <samp class="listingcharacter">transform()</samp> using the <samp class="listingcharacter">isalpha()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">toupper()</samp> C functions for each individual character. This is a lambda—essentially, a function on the spot.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">normalize()</samp> function ensures that for <samp class="listingcharacter">e.g.</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">E#G#</samp> is stored in the index along with <samp class="listingcharacter">e.g.</samp>. If you later search for <samp class="listingcharacter">e.g.</samp>, then another <samp class="listingcharacter">normalize()</samp> ensures that it can also be found in the index.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp> helper class is defined in the corresponding header, which is included at the top of the file. This is, as mentioned, necessary so that the implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> can take place. However, it is an implementation detail of the library, and thus <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap.hpp</samp> is not found in the directory of <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.hpp</samp>, as it is not shipped with it. It is located right next to <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.cpp</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap.hpp</samp>. You can see the source code itself in [Listing 11.3](#11_004.html_l11.3).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ob9voovMx
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>
#include <map> // multimap
namespace qw::impl_multimap {

using std::vector; using std::multimap;
using std::string; using std::string_view;

class index_impl {
    vector<string> entries;
    multimap<string, size_t> qindex;

public:
    void add(string_view normalized, string_view original);
    string getBestMatch(string_view normalized) const;
    size_t size() const {
        return entries.size();
    }

private:
    vector<string> qgramify(string_view normalized) const;
    static constexpr size_t Q = 3;
    static const std::string PREFIX;
    static const std::string SUFFIX;
public: // test interface
    vector<string> _qgramify(string_view n) const { return qgramify(n); }
    static size_t _q() { return Q; }
    static std::string _prefix() { return PREFIX; }
    static std::string _suffix() { return SUFFIX; }
};
} // namespace qw::impl_multimap 
```

**Listing 11.3**     Header of the implementation class.

Because the focus here is not really on the algorithm, I will keep it brief. In the <samp class="listingcharacter">entries</samp> vector, the index stores all original (non-normalized) entries so that the search results can also be displayed. Thus, each entry has a number in the vector. In <samp class="listingcharacter">qindex</samp>, each three-word key has all the entry numbers in the index. For example, if you later search for <samp class="listingcharacter">HELLO</samp>, then the <samp class="listingcharacter">multimap</samp> will be examined sequentially for the keys <samp class="listingcharacter">HEL</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ELL</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">LLO</samp>. The values are numbers in the <samp class="listingcharacter">entries</samp> vector—that is, indexes of the entries there.

<samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> is used to insert new entries into the index, while <samp class="listingcharacter">getBestMatch()</samp> finds the best matching entry. Both methods expect an already normalized parameter. And both methods use the <samp class="listingcharacter">qgramify()</samp> helper function to split a string into its q-grams.

For testing purposes, I have also made a <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> section here again. Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">normalize()</samp>, which I also made <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> specifically for testing, I have left the parts to be tested here <samp class="listingcharacter">private</samp>. Instead, all things to be tested later are enriched with public access methods. As a convention, these methods start with an underscore <samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp>. I will go into this in [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14) on testing, but I need to mention it here so that you are not surprised by this <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> section.

I also want to mention that I have placed the entire class not only in the <samp class="listingcharacter">qw</samp> namespace but also in its own <samp class="listingcharacter">impl_multimap</samp> namespace. The class itself is called <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp>. If you want to provide an alternative, simply put your class in its own namespace and name it <samp class="listingcharacter">index_impl</samp>.

No magic happens in the header; you are more likely to see it in the implementation, as shown in [Listing 11.4](#11_004.html_l11.4).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/hWan33Go9
#include "impl_multimap.hpp" // header for this file
#include <map>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace qw::impl_multimap {

using std::vector; using std::multimap; using std::map; using std::string;
using std::string_view; using namespace std::literals::string_literals;

void index_impl::add(string_view normalized, string_view original) {
    /* TODO: Check for existence in 'entries' */
    const auto pos = entries.size(); // Index of the new entry
    entries.push_back(string(original));
    auto qgrams = qgramify(normalized);
    for(const auto& qgram : qgrams) {
        qindex.insert( make_pair(qgram, pos) );
    }
}
string index_impl::getBestMatch(string_view normalized) const {
    auto qgrams = qgramify(normalized);

    /* hits stores which words were hit how often */
    map<size_t, size_t> hits; /* 'entries-index' to 'hit-count' */
    size_t maxhits = 0z; /* always: max(hits.second) */
    for(const auto& qgram : qgrams) {
        auto [beg, end] = qindex.equal_range(qgram);
        for(auto it=beg; it!=end; ++it) {
            hits[it->second] += 1z; /* hit-count of the entry */
            if(hits[it->second] > maxhits) { /* simpler max-search */
                maxhits = hits[it->second];
            }
        }
    }

    /* Search first entry with maxhits. Improvement possible with PrioQueue */
    for(auto const &hit : hits) {
        if(hit.second == maxhits) {
            return entries[hit.first];
        }
    }

    /* only reached if entries is empty */
    return ""s;
}
const string index_impl::PREFIX = string(Q-1, '^');
const string index_impl::SUFFIX = string(Q-1, '$');

vector<string> index_impl::qgramify(string_view normalized) const {
    auto word = PREFIX+string(normalized)+SUFFIX; /* trick for better q-grams */
    vector<string> result {};
    auto left = word.cbegin();
    auto right = std::next(word.cbegin(), Q); /* okay: |"^^"|+|"$"| => 3 */
    for( ; right <= word.end(); ++left, ++right) {
        result.emplace_back(left, right);
    }
    return result;
}
} // namespace qw::impl_multimap 
```

**Listing 11.4**     The header of the implementation class.

As I said before, for this chapter, exactly how the algorithm is implemented is not so interesting. For the module, it is much more important that everything works as it should externally. Nevertheless, I would like to say a few words about the structure of this implementation file.

As always, I include the header of what is implemented in this file as early as possible. Then, only the necessary headers of the standard library follow.

The defined methods all belong to the <samp class="listingcharacter">qw::impl_multimap</samp> namespace, which is opened at the beginning and closed at the end.

<samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> stores the entry in <samp class="listingcharacter">entries</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">qindex</samp> after it has been dissected using <samp class="listingcharacter">qgramify()</samp>. In one aspect, this implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> behaves poorly: if you store exactly the same entry twice, you will never find one of them again. So it would be good if <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> checked whether the entry already exists before storing it, or if a search would find not only the best match but somehow also several good matches. However, I leave solving this problem to your tinkering spirit.

<samp class="listingcharacter">getBestMatch()</samp> also breaks down the search pattern using <samp class="listingcharacter">qgramify()</samp> into its components. In <samp class="listingcharacter">hits</samp>, it counts how often each original word was matched. At the end, the entry with the highest number of matches is selected and returned.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">qgramify()</samp>, I use a simple trick to slightly increase the number of generated q-grams: the entry or search pattern is framed by <samp class="listingcharacter">^^</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp> before being broken down. As a result, the list of q-grams for words of length three like <samp class="listingcharacter">NYC</samp> includes not only <samp class="listingcharacter">NYC</samp>, but also <samp class="listingcharacter">^^N</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">^NY</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">YC$</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">C$</samp>, thus having better chances of being matched.

All in all, creating q-grams for a similarity index is neither a very difficult task nor a perfect solution. There are many algorithms that achieve better results with more sophisticated methods. But for its simplicity, the q-gram index delivers surprisingly good results.

This entire functionality is then packaged into the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.a</samp> library. On other systems, it may also be called <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.so</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.lib</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.dll</samp>. Together with the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort/qwort.hpp</samp> header and documentation, this is the minimum delivery package for the customer.

### 11.4.3    Using the Library

Because you are my customers today, I will demonstrate how you can use the library in a program before we move on to the tests. [Listing 11.5](#11_004.html_l11.5) is pretty much the simplest example program to demonstrate the library.

After the <samp class="listingcharacter">include</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> directives, the <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> program follows immediately. First, two example entries are stored in the index. Then follows a loop over all command line arguments of the program. For each argument, a search for the best match is performed, which is then output.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zj91TshnY (includes all files)
#include <cstdlib>  // EXIT_SUCCESS
#include <iostream> // cout
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include "qwort/qwort.hpp"

using std::cout; using std::vector; using std::string;

int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    cout << "qwort version " << qw::version() << "\n";

    /* Build index */
    qw::index myindex{};

    /* - Demo data */
    myindex.add("Germany");
    myindex.add("Greece");

    /* Generate queries */
    vector<string> args(argv+1, argv+argc); // iterator-based initialization
    for(auto &querystring : args) {
        cout << "Searching for '" << querystring << "'... ";
        const auto match = myindex.getBestMatch(querystring);
        cout << match << "\n";
    }
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
} 
```

**Listing 11.5**     Pretty much the simplest example program of the library.

The compiler packs this <samp class="listingcharacter">query.cpp</samp> source file with <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.hpp</samp> (because it is included) and the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort.a</samp> library together into the <samp class="listingcharacter">query.x</samp> program. The Makefile essentially says the following (somewhat obfuscated by variables):

```
g++ -o query.x query.cpp -lqwort -I../../include -L../lib 
```

This means something like, “Create <samp class="listingcharacter">query.x</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">query.cpp</samp>, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">qwort</samp> library, and look for includes and libraries in the specified paths.”

If you run this program as follows, you will get this output:

```
$ ./query.x armada green
qwort version 1
Searching 'armada'... Germany
Searching green'... Greece 
```

In the downloadable content at [www.rheinwerk-computing.com/5927](http://rheinwerk-computing.com/5927), you will find another simple example in <samp class="listingcharacter">code/15p-unittest-200/src/prog/dictfile.cpp</samp>. There, I create the index from lines of any text file. With additional command line parameters, you can then output the best matching lines.

# Part II

Object-Oriented Programming and More

It's time for you to start building your own data types. This is the real strength of C++.

You can simply bundle multiple pieces of data together so that you can treat them as one. More importantly, you can design classes where data and behavior form a single unit. This ultimately leads you to learn about object-oriented inheritance.

In this part, you’ll also learn more about constant and static values, as these become particularly interesting in the context of classes.

# 12    From Structure to Class

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Aggregate
    An aggregate is a simple bundling of multiple data fields into a new type—specifically, a <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> that only has data fields and methods. A C-array is also an aggregate.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp>
    A <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> is a bundling of data fields. It may also have constructors, and private and static elements. It can be a simple aggregate or a more advanced structure.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp>
    A <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> is very similar to a <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp>, except that <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">private</samp> visibility; in common usage, a <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> is more data-focused, while a <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> is more behavior-oriented.

*   Structure
    A structure can be more than an aggregate; for example, it can have constructors. When I speak of a structure, I usually refer to both <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp>.

*   Data field, member variable, or attribute
    A variable within a structure.

*   Method, member function, or instance function
    A function that is bound to its structure.

*   Member
    Generic term for data fields and methods of a class.

*   Constructor
    A special method for initializing a structure.

*   Inline
    Give the compiler a hint to insert the code directly instead of using a function call.

*   Include guard
    Avoid double inclusion.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">private</samp>
    Protect methods and data fields from external access.

*   Encapsulation
    The clean separation of interface and implementation; possible in varying degrees.

*   Class as value
    Use the instance of a class as a value parameter (call-by-value) or as a return value.

*   Copy elision
    Compiler technique to avoid unnecessary copying of a return value.

*   Implicit type conversion
    Within an expression of type <samp class="listingcharacter">A</samp>, the compiler requires another type <samp class="listingcharacter">B</samp> and generates the desired <samp class="listingcharacter">B</samp> using its single-argument constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">B(A)</samp>.

*   Explicit type conversion
    When you explicitly call the single-argument constructor in an expression.

*   Conversion method
    A method of the form <samp class="listingcharacter">operator TargetType()</samp>, which allows you to convert an object to <samp class="listingcharacter">TargetType</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> method
    A method that does not change the state of the instance; it is marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> at the end.

*   Type alias
    Using <samp class="listingcharacter">using newType = oldType</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef oldType newType</samp> to introduce an alternative notation for a type—also locally within a class.

*   Type inference and <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>
    With <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, you can let the compiler deduce the type of a variable during initialization.

A custom data type can, for example, hold data about a <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp>. You then don't always have to gather the individual elements and pass them to functions one by one; you can bundle several into an aggregate. Use <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> for that.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/8YqoTEx58
#include <string>
#include <iostream>                      // cout
#include <format>
using std::string; using std::cout; using std::format;
struct Person {                          // defines the new type Person
    string name_;
    int age_;
    string city_;
};                                       // closing semicolon
void print(Person p) {                   // entire Person as one parameter
    cout << format("{} ({}) from {}\n",
      p.name_, p.age_, p.city_);         // access via dot
}
int main() {
    Person john {"John", 45, "Boston" }; // initialization
    print(john);                         // call as a unit
} 
```

**Listing 12.1**     Creating your own data type with “struct”.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">struct Person</samp>, the new <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> type is defined. It consists of the union of the three listed elements. As always, the type is named first, followed by the name. Under this name, you can then access the elements with a dot <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp>, as shown in <samp class="listingcharacter">p.name_</samp>.

I have ended the names of all elements here with an underscore <samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp>. This is just a convention to distinguish them from global variables and parameters.

As you can see in <samp class="listingcharacter">void print(Person p)</samp>, the parameter of the <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> function is now the entire person. You do not need to pass the <samp class="listingcharacter">name_</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">age_</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">city_</samp> elements separately. <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>, by the way, was newly introduced in C++20.

## Terminate Type Definitions with a Semicolon

You terminate the definition of a new type with a semicolon. Unlike compound statements, you place a <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> after the closing curly bracket here. Forgetting the semicolon is a common oversight.

In structures, it is called a definition when you list the entire content of the structure and a declaration when you only mention the name. This can sometimes be necessary when structures use each other.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zPbK16zWE
#include <memory>                   // shared_ptr
#include <vector>                   // vector
struct Employee;                    // class declaration
struct Boss;                        // class declaration
struct Employee {                   // class definition
    std::shared_ptr<Boss> boss_;    // pointer to Boss
    void print() const;             // method declaration
};
struct Boss {                       // definition
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Employee>> employees_; // Pointer to Employees
    void print() const;             // method declaration
};
void Employee::print() const {      // method definition
    // …
}
void Boss::print() const {          // method definition
    // …
} 
```

**Listing 12.2**     The declaration of a class initially only mentions its name, while the definition contains all its elements.

In this example, there are two classes that use each other. You can only use <samp class="listingcharacter">Boss</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">Employee</samp> if you have previously declared it.

Note that declarations method can occur in such a class definition. This makes the term class definition somewhat confusing.

## 12.1    Initialization

The initialization can now be done like this, <samp class="listingcharacter">Person john {"John", 45, "Boston" }</samp>, with the listing of the initialization values of the subelements in curly brackets. Alternatively, you can also use the empty list <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> for initialization; then all elements are value-initialized—that is, with zeros for numbers and with the empty string <samp class="listingcharacter">""</samp> for strings (see [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.4.2](#04_004.html_h4.4.2)).

If you do not specify enough elements in the initializer list, the remaining ones will also be value-initialized. However, you should avoid this as it looks like an oversight and always raises eyebrows. If you specify too many elements, the compiler will complain.

But you must not omit the initialization entirely. For example:

```
Person john; 
```

This does initialize the <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> attributes <samp class="listingcharacter">name_</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">city_</samp> (they are full-fledged classes), but not <samp class="listingcharacter">age_</samp>, as it is of the built-in data <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>; <samp class="listingcharacter">age_</samp> could receive a random value.

Note that you can also use an equal sign when listing all elements:

```
Person john = {"John", 45, "Boston" }; 
```

However, I recommend sticking to the form without the equal sign, which is more common.

Starting from C++20, you can also name the fields you want to set during initialization; this is the designated initializer. If the order of the fields in the class changes, the compiler will notify you.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/K8WePajvM
Person john1 {"John", 45, "Boston" }; // correct
Person john2 {"Boston", 45, "John" }; // oops, swapped, and no one notices
Person jack { .name_ = "Jack", .age_ = 23, .city_ = "Dallas" }; // okay
Person jimmi { .name_ = "Jimmi", .age_ = 48  }; // okay, not all specified
Person carl { "Carl", .age_ = 53  };  // all designated or none
Person paul { .age = 34, .name_ = "Paul", .city = "Reno" }; // swapped
Person jim(.name_="Jim", .age_=34, .city_="NYC"); // not with parenthesis 
```

**Listing 12.3**     With designated initializers, you specify the elements to be set.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">paul</samp>, the designated initializers must be specified in the correct order. As with <samp class="listingcharacter">jimmi</samp>, you can also omit fields, which will then be value-initialized. However, you must not mix fields with and without designated names, as with <samp class="listingcharacter">carl</samp>.

### Warning about Parentheses

You can also write the initialization elements in parentheses, like <samp class="listingcharacter">string name("x")</samp>. However, if you have no element for the list, then you must not use the parentheses: <samp class="listingcharacter">string name()</samp> unfortunately means something else (a function declaration). Therefore, it is better to consistently initialize with curly brackets: <samp class="listingcharacter">string name{}</samp> is a correct initialization.

In a few cases, initialization with curly brackets and parentheses means something different; <samp class="listingcharacter">std::vector</samp> is one such exception.

## 12.2    Returning Custom Types

Returning a <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> is just as simple as using it as a parameter:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/rrjPorT1o
// Snippet
Person create(string name, int age, string city) { // return type
    Person result {name, age, city};
    return result;
}
int main() {
    Person john = create("John", 45, "Boston");    // store return value
    print(john);
} 
```

There is actually nothing new for you here, except that you can see that you can return variables of your own type just as you can with built-in types and those of the standard library.

It may still be worth noting that just like with the types you already know, you don't always need a variable to store the value. You can use your new type as part of an expression. This then creates temporary variables of your type as usual:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ME76bfbWa
Person create(string name, int age, string city) {
    return Person{name, age, city};       // returned directly
}
int main() {
    print(create("John", 45, "Boston"));  // return value used directly
} 
```

This shouldn't be new to you. You do the same with built-in types—although not quite, because when you return an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, you don't write <samp class="listingcharacter">return int(12);</samp>, even though you could.

Therefore, instead of writing

```
return Person{name, age, city};, 
```

simply write

```
return {name, age, city};. 
```

The compiler knows from the return type of the function that you want to create a <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp>. So it tries to convert the list you provided into a <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp>; the two expressions are almost synonymous. You can choose which style you prefer.

There are cases where you need to specify <samp class="listingcharacter">Person{…}</samp>—for example, when using the syntax for function declaration available since C++14, <samp class="listingcharacter">auto create()</samp>. The next listing shows an example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jer44aWs9
auto create(string name, int age, string city) {
    return Person{name, age, city};  // auto requires constructor name
}
auto create2(string name, int age, string city) {
    return {name, age, city};        // auto with initializer_list does not work
} 
```

**Listing 12.4**     Here, specifying <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> is necessary.

Here, an <samp class="listingcharacter">initializer_list</samp> is returned in <samp class="listingcharacter">create2</samp>. That would be fine if you had specified a return type in the function header into which the <samp class="listingcharacter">initializer_list</samp> can be automatically converted. But here it says <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, and the compiler cannot infer the type from that.

## 12.3    Methods Instead of Functions

The <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> function in [Listing 12.1](#12_001.html_l12.1) requires a <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> to work; it is in fact specifically designed for <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> and nothing else. It might even be the case that the <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> type only really makes sense if you also provide a suitable set of functions that work with your new type.

These functions, along with the data in <samp class="listingcharacter">struct Person</samp>, belong to the interface of this type. It is a pity that <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> is not already listed in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> type—but you can do exactly this. Combine the functions of a type with the data to form an entity such that neither can exist without the other. Such a function always requires a variable, and a variable without the associated functions is almost useless.[[ 16 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn12_01) A variable that is part of the type is called an instance variable. A function that is part of the type is called a method.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5T1Er36P7
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
#include <format>
using std::string; using std::cout; using std::format;
struct Person {
  string name_;
  int age_;
  string city_;
  void print();            // function as a method of the type
};
void Person::print() {     // method name is extended by Person::
  cout << format("{} ({}) from {}\n",
    name_, age_, city_);   // in a method you can directly access fields
}
int main() {
  Person john {"John", 45, "Boston" };
  john.print();            // calling the method for a variable of the type
} 
```

**Listing 12.5**     Methods bundle data and behavior together.

Now <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> type and thus has become a method.

When one speaks of a method, they mean a function within a type. To be distinguished from this are functions outside of classes, which you have learned about so far.

Sometimes functions are also called free functions to distinguish them from methods. The term global functions is also sometimes used, but it is not entirely correct; a function can also be within a namespace and is still free, but not global. Conversely, the term member function is used for method.

Technically speaking, methods are also just functions. One of the differences is that the full identifier of a method includes the class name. If you define the method outside the type, then you call it—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">Person::print</samp>. Within the method, you can then access all data fields and methods of the class without further qualification: where before you wrote <samp class="listingcharacter">p.name_</samp>, now <samp class="listingcharacter">name_</samp> is sufficient.

Strictly speaking, the compiler internally translates this to <samp class="listingcharacter">this->name_</samp>—and here I come to the second important difference from functions: a method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> always has an implicit <samp class="listingcharacter">Type* this</samp> parameter,[[ 17 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn12_02) without it appearing in the method's parameter list. This parameter represents the memory address of the instance on which you call the method. <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> together with the data field you use gives the exact location you mean.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp>, the compiler must use the dereference operator <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> instead of the dot, as described in detail in [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20).

```
struct Person {
    //… rest as before …
    string greeting();
};
string Person::greeting() {
    return format("Hello {} from {}", this->name_, this->city_);
}
int main() {
    Person anna { "Anna", 33, "Eek" };
    Person nina { "Nina", 22, "Ojo" };
    anna.greeting();
    nina.greeting();
} 
```

**Listing 12.6**     The “greeting()” method uses fields; via “this”, it always refers to the field belonging to the called object.

Within a method, the compiler automatically tries to see if an identifier belongs to <samp class="listingcharacter">*this</samp>. Thus, you can implement <samp class="listingcharacter">greeting()</samp> more clearly:

```
string Person::greeting() {
    return format("Hello {} from {}", name_, city_);
} 
```

Although the program code during the execution of <samp class="listingcharacter">greeting()</samp> is the same in both cases, the implicit <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> parameter ensures that different <samp class="listingcharacter">name_</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">city_</samp> fields are accessed—namely, those belonging to the current object.

[![Each call to “greeting()” receives a different “this” parameter.](bilderklein/klein12_001.png)](img-f12.1.html)

**Figure 12.1**     Each call to “greeting()” receives a different “this” parameter.

And indeed, with a few small (but important) differences, you can rewrite a method and turn it into a free function by making the implicit <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> parameter explicit.

```
string greeting(Person * const p) {  // implicit parameter made explicit
    return format("Hello {} from {}", p->name_, p->city_);
} 
```

**Listing 12.7**     How to separate methods and data from each other.

You must not name the parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> because <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> is a keyword in C++; here, it is called <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp>.

There are cases where you also need to use <samp class="listingcharacter">this-></samp> for attribute access in a method—namely, when two or more identical identifiers conflict. Then you need to be explicit:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/hEvqWqqc6
int value = 5;                          // global variable
struct Wrap {
    int value = 3;                      // data field
    void set(int value) {               // parameter
        this->value = value + ::value;
    }
}; 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">this->value</samp> refers to the data field of <samp class="listingcharacter">Wrap</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> refers to the parameter, and <samp class="listingcharacter">::value</samp> refers to the global variable.

It is a good idea to bundle data and functions together. Whether you should always and consistently do this is a design question. For example, C++ allows the extension of existing functionality through new overloads of free functions, not just by adding methods to an existing data type. The <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ostream</samp> is a good example of this.

## 12.4    The Better “print”

It pains me every time I present you with something as impractical as <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> as an example of a function. There are several important things to note about <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> as a method or the corresponding free function, simple as it may be. You now know enough about C++ that I can explain the better alternative to you. Take another look at the method:

```
void Person::print() {
    cout << format("{} ({}) from {}", name_, age_, city_);
} 
```

Here, output is sent to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>. What if you want to output a <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> as an error (to <samp class="listingcharacter">cerr</samp>)? Would you write a separate function or method for that? The root problem is that you are accessing the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> global variable in the method. You cannot change this behavior from the outside if, for example, you wanted to write to a file via <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp> or to a <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp> for testing purposes.

### No Global Accesses

Avoid direct access to global variables in functions and methods.

Maybe you want to write automatic tests for <samp class="listingcharacter">Person::print</samp>. How annoying that you then have to monitor <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> with your eyes to check if the program ran correctly! I want to suggest that you can make automatic testing (see [Chapter 14](#14_001.html_h14)) easier, among other things, if you avoid using the global <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> specifically and global variables in general.

Pass the target of the output as a parameter. <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">cerr</samp> are of type <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ostream</samp>. And if you want to write to a file, then <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> is also suitable for that.

```
void Person::print(std::ostream& os) {
    os << format("{} ({}) from {}", name_, age_, city_);
} 
```

Note that you use the type <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>, which is a reference. You do not want to create a copy of the stream, but rather change its state. Outputting something to a stream is a state change.

Wonderful—having suggested this to you for the future already greatly eases my conscience! Now use the <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> function in the following listing as you like.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/bz6n3Pjrv
// Excerpt. Person as before
void Person::print(std::ostream& os) {
    os << format("{} ({}) from {}", name_, age_, city_);
}
int main() {
    Person carl {"Carl", 12, "Toledo"};
    carl.print(cout);          // on the screen
    cout << "\n";
    std::ofstream file {"persons.txt"};
    carl.print(file);          // to a file
    // automatic test:
    std::ostringstream oss{};  // writes to a string
    carl.print(oss);
    if(oss.str() == "Carl (12) from Toledo") {
        cout << "ok\n";
    } else {
        cout << "Error in Person::print!\n";
        return 1;              // propagate error outward
    }
} 
```

**Listing 12.8**     “print” takes a stream as an argument.

In particular, the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">ostringstream</samp> reveals a special aspect: if you want to automatically test whether a printing function works correctly, a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> is easy to handle and check for the desired result. How would you test that if you had written directly to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>? Extracting the output would have become difficult. One of the real advantages of passing the output stream is that the function is easy to test.

## 12.5    An Output Like Any Other

The next step is actually just cosmetic. To output an object to an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp>, there is a commonly used method in practice: overload the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> global operator for <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream&</samp> and your type.

```
std::ostream& Person::print(std::ostream& os) {
    return os << format("{} ({}) from {}", name_, age_, city_);
}
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, Person p) {
    return p.print(os);
} 
```

**Listing 12.9**     You can overload the standard operator for output.

Instead of calling <samp class="listingcharacter">p.print()</samp>, you can also output the fields directly:

```
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, Person p) {
    return os << format("{} ({}) from {}", p.name_, p.age_,  p.city_);
} 
```

Did you notice that the return type is not <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp>? By returning the <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> passed as a parameter, you can reuse this return value within an expression. You have done this often for <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>. See your new output operator in action in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/a7q5xsWGj
// Excerpt …
    std::ostream& print(std::ostream& os);
};
std::ostream& Person::print(std::ostream& os) {
    return os << format("{} ({}) from {}", name_, age_, city_);
}
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, Person p) {
    return p.print(os);
}
int main() {
    Person paul {"Paul", 23, "Irvine"};
    cout << "You are " << paul << ", right?\n";
} 
```

**Listing 12.10**     The output with <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> is achieved by overloading a free function.

And this is how you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> objects in the output just like other data types. As a complete output, you see the following:

```
You are Paul (23) from Irvine, right? 
```

## 12.6    Defining Methods Inline

Did you notice that when declaring and later defining the method of the class, I used a technique you already know—the forward declaration of the method? First, in the structure, only the method header is mentioned, and then later, outside, the actual definition takes place. (Strictly speaking, it is still an aggregate, but it will soon become a class. Everything is still public, without constructors or virtual methods.)

This is also the way you should usually go forward with structures and classes. However, if a method is very short, for example, then you can treat it the same way as normal functions. You can also define it right on the spot—within the structure.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Y3eW1Kh8v
#include <string>
#include <iostream>    // ostream
#include <format>

using std::string; using std::ostream; using std::format;

struct Person {
  string name_;
  int age_;
  string city_;
  ostream& print(ostream& os) {       // method defined inline
    return os << format("{} ({}) from {}", name_, age_, city_);
  }
}; 
```

**Listing 12.11**     Methods can also be defined inline.

However, use this option only when the method is really short.

By writing the method in a class this way, the compiler tries to insert the code of the implementation directly where you call the function: this is called inlining. While this potentially makes your code faster (a function call costs a lot of time), it also makes it larger.

If you inline too many functions, your code might become so large that the speed advantage is negated. It is best to inline only methods that are simple or called very, very frequently.

## 12.7    Separate Implementation and Definition

It is beneficial for the program's clarity if you separate definition and implementation. This even goes so far that you should put the structure definition in a header and the definition in an implementing <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file (see [Figure 12.2](#12_007.html_f12.2)).

[![Splitting a class into the header and implementation.](bilderklein/klein12_002.png)](img-f12.2.html)

**Figure 12.2**     Splitting a class into the header and implementation.

If you need <samp class="listingcharacter">Person</samp> in multiple parts of the program, use <samp class="listingcharacter">#include "person.hpp"</samp> there to make the data type known to the compiler.

Just in case you need to include <samp class="listingcharacter">person.hpp</samp> multiple times through various includes, the surrounding lines are there:

```
#ifndef PERSON_HPP
#define PERSON_HPP
// … actual content
```
