A small note on <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp>: even though the standard containers only require you to define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp> for your data type, you should at least consider defining the other operators, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>, if you define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp>. For such a group of operations, it is always practical to provide the complete set so that users do not have to struggle or look up what is available. At least if <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp> is not the only operation, you should support the entire group.

If you have good reasons to implement only <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp>, consider also implementing <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp>, which is needed for unordered associative containers. If you have <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp>, you can check “not <samp class="listingcharacter">a < b</samp> and not <samp class="listingcharacter">b < a</samp>” as the ordered associative containers do, but you might have a more efficient implementation for your data type.

### 12.13.1    Three-Way Comparison: The Spaceship Operator

With C++20, you can define greater, smaller, equal, smaller-equal, and so on for custom types without overloading a bunch of operators and potentially making mistakes. Simply define the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp>, and your data type will support the complete set of operators, especially <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, to be used in ordered containers.

If you insert the following definition for a custom data type, then the compiler generates <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> such that the elements are compared in the order in which they are defined in the class:

```
auto operator<=>(const X& other) const = default; 
```

If you desire different behavior, then implement the operator yourself.

#### A Custom-Defined <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> Also Requires a Custom-Defined <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp>

If you define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> yourself, you should also define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp> yourself. This is because if you do not let the compiler generate <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp> will not be generated automatically. It will be missing, and you will not be able to use <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> for your type.

The reason is that the result of the <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> check can often be computed faster than the result of <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp>, which covers the three <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> operators. So the compiler assumes that you have a better implementation for <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp> if you already know better than the compiler what is good for <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp>. Also, read the box in [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.8.1](#24_008.html_h24.8.1).

With an <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> (and possibly <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp>), the normal comparison operators <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> can then be derived by the compiler. This is done using the new mechanism of rewritten candidates.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> does not need to be a <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp>. A special case applies to it, allowing its implementation to access private elements without <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> and behave as if it were defined as a free function.

If you want to highlight that your data type does not support <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp>, then you can declare the operator with <samp class="listingcharacter">= deleted</samp>:

```
struct X {
    Data data_;
    /* Comparisons would be too expensive and are not supported */
    auto operator<=>(const X& other) const = delete;
}; 
```

Even without the <samp class="listingcharacter">auto operator<=>… = delete</samp> line, comparisons would not be possible, but with the line, you make it clear to readers that you consciously do not support comparisons.

# 13    Namespaces and Qualifiers

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp> Introduces a new namespace, either named or anonymous.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace std</samp>
    In the <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp> namespace, you will find all the identifiers of the standard library.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> Marks a variable, function, or method as file-local, shared, or persistent.

*   Singleton
    Popular design pattern in which only one instance of a type exists at most.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> Marks something as immutable at runtime.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> Marks a constant or function as computable at compile time.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp> Lets the compiler guarantee that a function is computable at compile time.

*   Const-correctness
    By using <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> on types, you can get help from the compiler in uncovering some typical errors.

*   Type safety
    The correct use of types, including <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, is enforced by the compiler with type safety.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">volatile</samp> Marker for volatile variables that can change without the compiler's knowledge.

In this chapter, you will learn about two quite different things: <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. However, due to the multiple meanings of many keywords in C++, there are overlaps. Therefore, I have decided to go from <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp> to the overlap with <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> within one chapter.

## 13.1    The “std” Namespace

All things in the standard library start with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp>; you have seen this often. <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::vector</samp> are all in the <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp> namespace. And in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.2](#04_002.html_h4.2), I explained how you can save the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp> prefix for a single identifier with <samp class="listingcharacter">using std::cout;</samp> and for all identifiers with <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std;</samp>.

But how does something get into a namespace in the first place? Simply enclose everything that should go into the namespace—let's say <samp class="listingcharacter">plant</samp>—within <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace plant {…}</samp>. This opens a scope, which behaves similarly to a class regarding identifiers: Within the range, you can omit <samp class="listingcharacter">plant</samp> for access to other elements; from outside, you need the <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::</samp> prefix, as you can see in [Listing 13.1](#13_001.html_l13.1).

Because this is about namespaces and <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>, I have refrained from using <samp class="listingcharacter">using std:: string</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">using std::ostream</samp>, and the like globally at this point. I do this in this book, as already explained, only for space reasons. In a real project, you should use each <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> at the global level very sparingly (up to complete abstinence).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/qo6W3bh5d
#include <string>
#include <iostream>                   // ostream, cout
namespace plant {
    class Tree {
        std::string name_;
    public:
        explicit Tree(const std::string_view name) : name_{name} {}
        void print(std::ostream& os) const { os << name_; }
    };
    std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Tree& arg)
        { arg.print(os); return os; }
    using ConiferTree = Tree;         // for future extensions …
    using BroadleafTree = Tree;       // … provide for
    namespace exampleNames {          // embedded namespace
        std::string oakName = "Oak";
        std::string beechName = "Beech";
        std::string firName = "Fir";
    } // end namespace exampleNames
} // end namespace plant

int main() {  // main must not be in a namespace
    using namespace plant::exampleNames; // make all example names available
    plant::ConiferTree fir{ firName };
    plant::BroadleafTree oak{ oakName };
    fir.print(std::cout); std::cout << "\n";
    using plant::operator<<;          // without it 'cout << oak' won't work
    std::cout << oak << "\n";
} 
```

**Listing 13.1**     You define a namespace with “namespace”.

I have packed all sorts of things into the <samp class="listingcharacter">plant</samp> namespace for demonstration purposes:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::Tree</samp> custom data type

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> free function

*   Two type aliases, <samp class="listingcharacter">ConiferousTree</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">BroadleafTree</samp>

*   Another namespace

The two type aliases are meant to suggest that you might plan to separate the classes <samp class="listingcharacter">ConiferousTree</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">BroadleafTree</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> in the future and write custom classes for them, but for now they are still identical.

You can, if it seems sensible to you, nest namespaces almost arbitrarily and group your project this way. I have packed another element into the <samp class="listingcharacter">exampleNames</samp> embedded namespace: variables such as <samp class="listingcharacter">oakName</samp> and the like.

You can also place constants and templates in a namespace. Only macros are not affected by namespaces; see [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21).

<samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> must be outside of any namespace; otherwise, the compiler will not find the function as an entry point. In this <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, I refer to <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::ConiferTree</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::BroadleafTree</samp> with the namespace qualifier. Alternatively, the following would have worked:

```
using plant::ConiferTree; using plant::BroadleafTree;
ConiferTree pine{ pineName };
BroadleafTree oak{ oakName }; 
```

Or simply:

```
using namespace plant;
ConiferTree pine{ pineName };
BroadleafTree oak{ oakName }; 
```

I also chose this approach for <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace plant::exampleName</samp>. As a reminder: you should only include an entire namespace with <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace</samp> locally—for example, within a function—but never globally in a <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file—and certainly not in a header file.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter">fir</samp> is a local variable in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, you can call <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> as a method:

```
fir.print(std::cout); std::cout << "\n"; 
```

It's a bit trickier with <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>. If you simply write <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << tanne</samp>, it will cause an error because the compiler looks for a suitable free function in all available namespaces (for operators, <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp> is also searched). So it looks for the following:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">::operator<<(std::ostream&, const Tree&);</samp>—globally, the level where <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> is

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::operator<<(std::ostream&, const Tree&);</samp>—where <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp> is searched

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::exampleNames::operator<<(std::ostream&, const Tree&);</samp>—because <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace plant::exampleNames</samp> was previously declared

The overload for <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> is in <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace plant</samp>:

<samp class="listingcharacter">plant::operator<<(std::ostream&, const Tree&);</samp>

To use an operator defined within a namespace, you must first make it available so that it is included in the search. There are two options here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using plant::operator<<;</samp>—to only fetch the operator

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace plant;</samp>—to fetch everything from the namespace

Namespaces are also useful for separating things that might otherwise conflict. Operators are good candidates here. You might have two <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> variants, as in the following listing.

```
namespace plant {
    // … as before …
    std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&, const Tree&) {…};
    namespace debug {
        std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&, const Tree&) {…};
    }
}
plant::Tree tree{"MyTree"};
void run() {
    using namespace plant;
    cout << tree << "\n";
}
void diagnostic() {
    using namespace plant::debug;
    cout << tree << "\n";
}
int main() {
    run();
    diagnostic();
} 
```

**Listing 13.2**     In separate namespaces, you can define the same operators.

Depending on the need, you include the desired <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> using a <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> directive. Unlike functions or types, you cannot specify the scope with operators; <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::Tree tree{"x"};</samp> works, but <samp class="listingcharacter">cout plant::<< tree;</samp> does not work. Instead, you could write <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::operator<<(cout, tree)</samp>, but that makes operators pointless, as you might as well define a function or method.

So if you are tempted to always define operators in the global namespace, you don't need to do that if you know that <samp class="listingcharacter">using plant::operator<<</samp> also helps.

### Use Namespaces

If you want to structure your project cleanly, use namespaces. I recommend using one main namespace per custom library. Whether you want to subdivide this namespace further depends on the requirements.

By the way, you can extend a namespace later without any problem and split it into two or more files. Simply put everything you want in each file into <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace plant {…}</samp>, and the namespace will fill up from file to file.

## 13.2    Anonymous Namespace

You can also define a namespace without its own identifier. This then has a special meaning. For the purposes of the next listing, assume that you have several files here.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/e3d55zvT8
// modul.hpp
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
namespace plant {
    class Tree {
        std::string name_;
    public:
        explicit Tree(const std::string_view name);
        void print(std::ostream& os) const;
    };
    std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Tree& arg);
}

// modul.cpp
#include "module.hpp"
namespace {  // anonymous namespace
    std::string PREFIX = "TREE:";
    void printInfo(std::ostream& os) {
        os << "Author: Torsten T. Will\n";
    }
}

bool debug = false;  // global, no namespace
namespace plant {
    Tree::Tree(const std::string_view name)
        : name_{name} {}
    void Tree::print(std::ostream& os) const {
        os << PREFIX << name_;
    }
    std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Tree& arg) {
        if(debug) printInfo(os);
        arg.print(os); return os;
    }
}

// main.cpp
#include "module.hpp"
int main() {
    plant::Tree x{"x"};
    x.print(std::cout); std::cout << "\n";
} 
```

**Listing 13.3**     An anonymous namespace makes definitions local to the current file.

You see three files here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">module.hpp</samp>—interface to <samp class="listingcharacter">class Tree</samp> with the method declarations

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">module.cpp</samp>—implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> class, with some helpers in an anonymous namespace and a global <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp> variable

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp>—uses the interface

So, you have two modules and a header. If you were to list all the identifiers defined in all modules, you would find that there are no overlaps. There must not be any. All defined identifiers of all modules must be distinct from each other.

For example, you could not define a <samp class="listingcharacter">int debug = 55;</samp> global variable in <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp>. The compiler would detect during linking that the identifier <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp> exists multiple times and would produce an error. This is because in <samp class="listingcharacter">modul.cpp</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp> is already defined; it is not in any namespace.

The set of identifiers can become very confusing in large projects, especially when you also use third-party libraries. You get a large number of identifiers delivered with them, which your identifiers must also not overlap with.

The first precaution for this is to use namespaces. The identifier of the namespace is part of the entire identifier name. This way, <samp class="listingcharacter">plant::Tree</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">algo::Tree</samp> would not interfere with each other.

The second measure is to use an anonymous namespace for what is not needed in other modules. <samp class="listingcharacter">main.cpp</samp> is not concerned with <samp class="listingcharacter">PREFIX</samp>. And the <samp class="listingcharacter">printInfo</samp> function is only used within <samp class="listingcharacter">modul.cpp</samp>. By encapsulating these two identifiers within a <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace {…}</samp>, they are only visible within the current module. They no longer interfere with another module.

## 13.3    “static” Makes Local

For exactly this purpose, you can also use the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. Instead of opening an anonymous namespace, you write <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> before the variables and functions. You achieve the same thing: the name of the variable or function is only visible within this module. Other modules can use the same name without the compiler complaining.

It would look like this for <samp class="listingcharacter">modul.cpp</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zfYzPjqrW
// modul.cpp
#include "modul.hpp"
static std::string PREFIX = "TREE:";
static void printInfo(std::ostream& os) {
    os << "Author: Torsten T. Will\n";
}
bool debug = false;
// rest as before 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp> variable is not yet <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. As a result, no other module can define a global function or global variable <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp>, but that is intentional here. Because although <samp class="listingcharacter">debug</samp> is not in the <samp class="listingcharacter">modul.hpp</samp> header, someone with enough insider knowledge (the author?) can manipulate the variable. Consider this an excursus as it should not be part of usual programming practice to hide and change variables in this way. In some other module of the project, someone can manipulate the variable with

```
extern bool debug; 
```

and declare and then manipulate it with <samp class="listingcharacter">debug = true;</samp>. This can be both good and bad. For a debugging switch, it might just be permissible. Otherwise, put identifiers that should not be exported into an anonymous namespace (or declare them <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>).

An anonymous namespace has the great advantage over <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> that it also protects its own types from spilling over into other modules. You cannot protect <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">using X = Y</samp> from export with a <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. Within a <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace {…}</samp>, however, these things are safe.

## 13.4    “static” Likes to Share

The fact that <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> is also used for a completely different purpose takes some getting used to. You can use it to mark a data field or a method of a class to share it among all instances of the class. Or to put differently:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> for a data field
    While there is always one instance of a normal data field per instance, all instances share a common data field marked as <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. Therefore, there is exactly one instance of this data field per class and not as many as there are instances.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> for a method
    A static method lacks the <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> pointer. Within the method, there is no connection to a specific instance of the class. Therefore, you do not call the method via an instance with <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp>, but rather via the class name with <samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp>.

Both variants are similar in that you can access both even if you have not created a single instance yet.

Typical applications are as follows:

*   A static data field can count the number of active instances of the class.

*   A static method can serve as a factory for controlled creation of instances (popular design pattern).

In the following listing, both application possibilities are in use.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/n4e8xdEGj
#include <iostream> // cout
#include <string>
using std::string;
class Tree {
    static size_t countConstructed_;
    static size_t countDestructed_;
    string kind_;
    Tree(string kind) : kind_{kind}      // private constructor
        { ++countConstructed_; }
public:
    Tree(const Tree& o) : kind_{o.kind_}
        { ++countConstructed_; }
    string getKind() const { return kind_; }
    ~Tree() { ++countDestructed_; }
    static Tree create(string kind) { return Tree{kind}; }
    static void stats(std::ostream& os) {
        os << "Constructed:+" << countConstructed_
           << " Destructed:-" << countDestructed_ << "\n";
    }
};
size_t Tree::countConstructed_ = 0;
size_t Tree::countDestructed_ = 0;

int main() {
    Tree birch = Tree::create("Birch");
    for(auto kind : {"Ash", "Yew", "Oak"}) {
        Tree temp = Tree::create(kind);
        std::cout << temp.getKind() << "\n";
    }
    Tree::stats(std::cout);
} 
```

**Listing 13.4**     All instances share their “static” data fields and methods.

First, I declared two counters <samp class="listingcharacter">countConstructed_</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">countDestructed_</samp>. Unlike normal data fields, you unfortunately cannot initialize static data fields within the class. Therefore, you see a repetition of the static data fields with the initialization values outside the class—here, <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> for each.

Note that if the class is defined in a header that may be included by multiple <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> files, you must place the initialization definitions in a <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file. Otherwise, the initialization would be performed multiple times in the entire program, or the linker would complain about duplicate definitions.

The static <samp class="listingcharacter">create</samp> method is in the public section of the class. This should now be used to create new <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> instances. To prevent anyone from calling it from outside, the constructor has been moved to the private section of the class.

Within the constructor, I increment the <samp class="listingcharacter">countConstructed_</samp> counter. To increment the <samp class="listingcharacter">countDestructed_</samp> counter, I also need the destructor. This should almost always be in the <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> section of the class.

<samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> still needs the copy constructor because <samp class="listingcharacter">create</samp> returns the newly created tree as a copy. Copying also creates a new object that should be counted with <samp class="listingcharacter">countConstructed_</samp>, so the <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp> copy constructor is not suitable. As the class currently stands, you could also do without the copy constructor and instead define the move constructor, but that's just a detail.

You see in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> that you can call <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree::create</samp> without a <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> instance already being created. When you are inside the <samp class="listingcharacter">create</samp> method, there is no instance whose data fields you can access. You can only access other static data fields and static methods—and constructors.

There is a distinction between calling a static <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree::create()</samp> method and a normal <samp class="listingcharacter">tree.getKind()</samp> method: the use of the class name instead of the instance variable, as well as the scope operator <samp class="listingcharacter">::</samp> instead of the access point <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> or the access arrow <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp>, if it is a pointer to an instance.

Similarly, I call <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree::stats()</samp> at the end. Again, only static data fields are accessed. And the output

```
Constructed:+4 Destructed:-3 
```

proves that each instance accessed the same counter variables in its constructor or destructor. The count is correct because all <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree temp</samp> objects in the loop were also destroyed again. Only the local <samp class="listingcharacter">birch</samp> variable still exists at the time of the <samp class="listingcharacter">stats()</samp> call.

### [Übung]  Copy Constructor and Move Constructor

How to make a class that copies itself is detailed in [Chapter 16](#16_001.html_h16). At this point, you should know that classes can be copied. Sometimes the compiler can set the rules for this, and sometimes you want or need to do it yourself. To do this, declare this constructor:

```
Keyboard(const Keyboard&); 
```

In the definition, you then specify how the copying should be done. If you explicitly want to prevent a copy from being possible, write the declaration like this:

```
Keyboard(const Keyboard&) = delete; 
```

The same applies to moving. The declaration that you use to declare and simultaneously prevent the move is this:

```
Keyboard(Keyboard&&) = delete; 
```

However, this is implicit if you have specified the copy constructor. For more on this, see [Chapter 16](#16_001.html_h16).

## 13.5    Remote Initialization or “static inline” Data Fields

Assume you have defined a <samp class="listingcharacter">Tree</samp> class in the <samp class="listingcharacter">tree.hpp</samp> header and used the header multiple times in your program. Then you must ensure that the initialization of the static data fields is done in exactly one <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file and not in the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.hpp</samp> file as they would otherwise be defined multiple times.

Therefore, starting from C++17, in addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, write the <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> keyword and set the field directly—that is, the declaration and definition together. Then the compiler ensures unique initialization:

```
class Tree {
    static inline size_t countConstructed_ = 0;
    static inline size_t countDestructed_ = 0;
    // … 
```

## 13.6    Guaranteed to Be Initialized at Compile Time with “constinit”

Starting from C++20, you can mark global or static variables with <samp class="listingcharacter">constinit</samp>. This ensures that the compiler guarantees that the variable can be initialized at compile time. The chances are then high that no initialization work needs to be done at runtime.

Even though the sequence of letters const appears in this keyword, the variable is not constant. One could say that “<samp class="listingcharacter">constinit</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> minus <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>”:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/b9arcEMM1
constinit auto SZ = 10*1000-1;                  // global variable
size_t autoincrement() {
    static constinit size_t i = 0;              // local static variable
    return i++;
}
class BraitenbergVehicle {
    inline static constinit size_t count_ = 0;  // class variable
public:
    size_t id_;
    BraitenbergVehicle() : id_{++count_} {}
    ~BraitenbergVehicle() { --count_; }
}; 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">SZ</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">count_</samp> variables are initialized at compile time. The <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">count_</samp> variables are also modified during the program's execution.

In practice, <samp class="listingcharacter">constinit</samp> solves the problem in which sometimes the order of initialization of static variables is not clear, and you might not realize that you are accessing a variable that has not been initialized yet. With <samp class="listingcharacter">constinit</samp>, it is guaranteed that the expression can be evaluated at compile time and is not affected by such problems.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">constinit</samp> together with <samp class="listingcharacter">extern</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">thread_local</samp>.

## 13.7    “static” Makes Permanent

Similar, but not the same, is the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> with local variables—that is, within a function. When you add <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> to the declaration of a local variable, this variable persists when the program flow leaves the scope and is reused when it is entered again.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/h5qond6db
#include <iostream>                     // cout
class Keyboard {
    Keyboard(const Keyboard&) = delete; // no copy
    const size_t nr_;                   // current number
public:
    static inline size_t count_ = 0;    // counts created instances
    explicit Keyboard() : nr_{count_++} {
        std::cout << "  Keyboard().nr:"<<nr_<<"\n";
    }
};
Keyboard& getKeyboard() {
    std::cout << "  getKeyboard()\n";
    static Keyboard keyboard{};         // static local variable
    return keyboard;
}
void func() {
    std::cout << "kbFunc...\n";
    Keyboard& kbFunc = getKeyboard();
}
int main() {
    std::cout << "kbA...\n";
    Keyboard& kbA = getKeyboard();
    func();
    std::cout << "kbB...\n";
    Keyboard& kbB = getKeyboard();
    std::cout << "count:" << Keyboard::count_ << "\n";
} 
```

**Listing 13.5**     A local static variable is initialized once and reused thereafter.

Here you see the implementation of the so-called Meyer’s Singleton pattern. A singleton is a way to always get the same instance of a class with each use. The uses can also come from different parts of the program, as seen here from <samp class="listingcharacter">func()</samp> and from <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>; because both use the <samp class="listingcharacter">getKeyboard()</samp> free function, they also receive the same <samp class="listingcharacter">Keyboard&</samp> reference and thus the same object.

Singletons are particularly popular in programs with multiple threads. For example, imagine that your program has multiple threads (simultaneously running program strands), and each wants to read from the keyboard—and for that, it needs a <samp class="listingcharacter">Keyboard</samp> class. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Keyboard</samp> class establishes the connection to the one keyboard actually connected to the computer. It would be helpful if it were always the same keyboard. This is what the <samp class="listingcharacter">getKeyboard()</samp> function is supposed to provide in the example.

```
Keyboard& getKeyboard() {
    cout << "  getKeyboard()\n”;
    static Keyboard keyboard{}; // static local variable
    return keyboard;
} 
```

**Listing 13.6**     The Meyers Singleton.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">getKeyboard()</samp>, you see the static local <samp class="listingcharacter">keyboard</samp> variable. Unlike global static variables, this one is not initialized beforehand at program start (or even earlier), but exactly at the first passage of the definition.

And unlike nonstatic local variables, the static variable is not cleared when leaving the block. The block here is the <samp class="listingcharacter">getKeyboard()</samp> function. The <samp class="listingcharacter">keyboard</samp> variable still exists upon reentry and is not reinitialized but reused.

There are many variants of the singleton design pattern and even more different implementations with various advantages and disadvantages. Some programmers even go so far as to say that the singleton itself is bad practice (an “antipattern”). This discussion is out of scope for this book, but it is true that you should not overuse the singleton design pattern.

Specifically, regarding the implementation of the singleton using a static local variable: the Meyer’s Singleton pattern has the advantage of being simple to implement and the disadvantage of not providing complete protection against multiple <samp class="listingcharacter">Keyboard</samp> instances. You could still create your own <samp class="listingcharacter">Keyboard{}</samp> using the public constructor. You could address this with a slightly modified interface if you find it to be a significant disadvantage.

The use of static local variables is also safe with multiple threads: It is guaranteed that only one thread initializes the variable.

## 13.8    “inline namespace”

The last way to define a <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp> is together with <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp>. You create an inline namespace as in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/115M1csEE
#include <iostream>
namespace mylib {
    namespace v1 {
        int version() { return 1; }
    }
    inline namespace v2 { // current version
        int version() { return 2; }
    }
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "Version " << mylib::version() << "\n";     // Output: 2
    std::cout << "Version " << mylib::v1::version() << "\n"; // Output: 1
    std::cout << "Version " << mylib::v2::version() << "\n"; // Output: 2
} 
```

**Listing 13.7**     The identifiers of an <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace</samp> also go into its surrounding namespace.

With the <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> before <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp>, you open a normal namespace. In addition, all identifiers are also included in the surrounding namespace. In this way, you can version your own library, for example: you pack the latest behavior into an <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace</samp>, making it the default behavior. You can see this in [Listing 13.7](#13_008.html_l13.7) with <samp class="listingcharacter">mylib::version()</samp>.

If users need old behavior, they can explicitly access an inner namespace, here with <samp class="listingcharacter">mylib::v1::version()</samp>. The new version is also available in an inner namespace, <samp class="listingcharacter">mylib::v2::version()</samp>, if users explicitly request it.

The standard library provides further examples of <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace</samp>. You can find a list in [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Section 28.4.2](#28_004.html_h28.4.2). For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::literals</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::literals::string_literals</samp> are both <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp>. To include <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""s</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">string_literals</samp>, you can use (among other things) one of the following <samp class="listingcharacter">using …</samp> options:

```
{ // direct addressing:
   using namespace std::string_literals;
   auto str = "abc"s;
}
{ // use inline namespace string_literals:
   using namespace std::literals;
   auto str = "abc"s;
}
{ // use both inline namespaces:
   using std::operator""s;
   auto str = "abc"s;
} 
```

## 13.9    Interim Recap

Because there can be so much confusion with <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, I will recapitulate the various usage scenarios here. For completeness, I will also include the type alias with <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>.

| Language Element | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace</samp> xyz <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> | New namespace xyz |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace {…}</samp> | Anonymous namespace; all identifiers file-local |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace</samp> xyz <samp class="listingcharacter">{…}</samp> | Embedded namespace |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> global variable | File-local variable |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> free function | File-local function |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> data field | Shared between all instances of the class |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> method | Method that you call without a specific instance |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> local variable | A variable that persists beyond the scope |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace</samp> xyz | Import all identifiers from namespace xyz |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> xyz::abc | Import identifier abc from namespace xyz |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> new <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> old<samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> | Introduce type alias new for type old |

**Table 13.1**     Variants of “namespace”, “static”, and “using”.

## 13.10    “const”

The <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> keyword should not be underestimated in C++. When used correctly, it can be very useful to programmers. With it, the compiler can help avoid careless mistakes and discover design problems.

In C++, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> in various places: whether passed as a parameter, as a local variable, or as a data field of a class. Here is a (not exhaustive) explanation of what is declared as “immutable” by a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">int MAX = 100;</samp>
    Together with <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, a constant is defined.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">string& getName();</samp>
    The return value must not be changed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void print(</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">string& msg);</samp>
    The parameter is not changed within the function.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void Widget::drawYourself()</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>
    The method does not change its object.

The last item has a special status, so to speak. It promises that the <samp class="listingcharacter">drawYourself</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp> class does not change the state of the instance it is called on within its function body. Technically speaking, this defines the <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> pointer within the method as <samp class="listingcharacter">this const * const</samp>, whereas a method without this trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> can change the state: <samp class="listingcharacter">this * const</samp>.

Yes, there is indeed still a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> in there. It is crucial where you write the <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> for the type.

The following list illustrates the subtle but important differences in usage together with pointers <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and references <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp>
    The <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp> is immutable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">&obj</samp>
    All data fields and methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp>, of which <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> is an object, are immutable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">* p_int</samp>
    The <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value pointed to by the pointer is immutable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">* const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">p_int</samp>
    The pointer <samp class="listingcharacter">p_int</samp> is immutable; the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value is mutable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">char const * const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">cstr</samp>
    Both the content and the pointer are immutable.

As a mnemonic, one could say that <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> always marks the entity as immutable behind which it stands. In the much more common notation, where <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> is mentioned first, you must mentally “move” the leading <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> one position to the right. The following notations are equivalent:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">int val</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">&obj</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">&obj</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">int * p_int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">* p_int</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">char * const cstr</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">* const cstr</samp>

### 13.10.1    Const Parameters

You have already learned in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.2](#04_002.html_h4.2) that you can mark a parameter with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, which often occurs together with call-by-reference passing of parameters with <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>:

```
void print(const vector<int> &primes) {
   for(auto prime : primes) {
       cout << prime << " ";
   }
} 
```

The parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">primes</samp> cannot be modified now. Any modification such as <samp class="listingcharacter">primes[7] = 4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">primes.push_back(12)</samp> will result in a compiler error. With classes and custom types, <samp class="listingcharacter">const MyClass& arg</samp> is often chosen as the passing method because the parameter does not need to be copied.

In the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass arg</samp>, it would be copied. You could safely modify <samp class="listingcharacter">arg</samp> within the function—because it is a copy, the changes do not affect the original object outside the caller—but copying a large object is costly.

If avoiding a copy is worthwhile, it is best to work with a <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> avoids the copy, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> prevents accidental modifications to the external object.

What applies to classes is no different for built-in types. However, their copy costs are negligible, which is why you rarely see <samp class="listingcharacter">const int&</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">const double&</samp>. The same rules apply as for classes. The compiler prevents changes to the values:

```
void nonsensicalParameter(const int& arga, const double& argb) {
    arga = 7;    // Assignment to constant
    argb = 3.14; // Assignment to constant
} 
```

As mentioned, you can do this with built-in types, but it is rather rare. Built-in types are almost always passed by value:

```
void valueParameter(int arga, double argb); 
```

Then you can change them in the function, which has no effect outside. Or you pass them by reference if the change should affect the outside:

```
void input(int &arga, double &argb); 
```

But it is better to choose return values here, for example:

```
std::pair<int,double> input(); 
```

In [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Section 28.1](#28_001.html_h28.1) on <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>, you will see in more detail how this works with <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>.

Finally, you can also choose value passing (which, as you know, has its advantages) and make this value constant:

```
void constantValues(const int arga, const double argb); 
```

The effect is that you get a copy when calling and at the same time ensure that you do not accidentally try <samp class="listingcharacter">arga = 5</samp>.

### 13.10.2    Const Methods

The compiler directly recognizes if you try to change an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. However, it becomes more difficult when you have an object equipped with methods:

```
void print(const vector<int> &primes) {
   if(primes.size() > 100)     // that's fine
       return;
   for(auto prime : primes) {  // that's fine too
       cout << prime << " ";
   }
   primes.push_back(4);        //  that's not fine
} 
```

How does the compiler know that <samp class="listingcharacter">primes.size()</samp> can be called on the <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> but that, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">primes.push_back(4)</samp> should result in an error message? This happens because the <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is marked with a trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>—essentially:

```
size_t vector<int>::size() const; 
```

This tells the compiler that this method call is allowed on a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> object.

For a custom data type <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp>, it might look like this:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/WTWxYa3rd
class Widget {
    unsigned x = 0, y = 0, w = 0, h = 0; // for example
public:
    unsigned getLeft() const;
    unsigned getTop() const;
    unsigned getRight() const;
    unsigned getBottom() const;
    void setWidth(unsigned w);
    void setHeight(unsigned h);
}; 
```

If you now pass <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp> as a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> object (reference) into a function, you can call the <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp> methods:

```
void show(const Widget& widget) {
    drawBox(
      widget.getLeft(), widget.getTop(),
      widget.getRight(), widget.getBottom()
    );
} 
```

The attempt to call <samp class="listingcharacter">widget.setWidth(100);</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">show</samp> will be met with a compiler error as the method is not marked as <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>.

At the same time, the trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> has another effect: you cannot change data fields within the implementation of such a method. This also includes calling a non-<samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> method:

```
unsigned Widget::getLeft() const {
    x = 77;                 //  data fields cannot be changed
    setWidth(88);           //  do not call non-const methods
} 
```

Taken together, these three effects are a very important tool for the compiler to detect careless errors and design problems. You should be careful when marking methods as <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. You will find that as a result, you will also need to carefully either make parameters <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> or pass them by value. Accidental <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>s, which open the door to careless errors, are then no longer possible.

Once again for practice: Technically speaking, the implicit <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> parameter is transformed by the trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget* const this</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget const* const this</samp>. Can you already read the <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>s in the different positions? The <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> refers to <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp>, which precedes it. Thus, everything in <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp> is off-limits for changes within the method.

### 13.10.3    “const” Variables

You can also apply <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> to variables. This applies to both local variables in a function or globally as well as to data fields in a class. A <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> variable can only be initialized, but you cannot assign it a new value or change its value (through a non-<samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> method call):

```
class Widget {
    const int id_;
public:
    explicit Widget(int id) : id_(id) {}
    Widget() : id_(0) {}
    void reset();
};
const Widget widget_a = Widget{12}; 
```

After these lines of code, you cannot write <samp class="listingcharacter">widget_a = Widget{24};</samp>. In the implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">reset()</samp>, the compiler also forbids

```
void Widget::reset() {
    id_ = 36;
} 
```

because <samp class="listingcharacter">id_</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>—just as if you had passed it as a parameter to the function.

Use <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> variables when it seems sensible to you, with discretion. For variables that are valid in a long section of code, where it is easy to lose track of which variables exist at all, a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> can be an effective protection against accidental modification.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/bxPaz9aW5
#include <vector>
namespace {                         // anonymous namespace for constants
    const unsigned DATA_SIZE = 100; /* number of elements in data */
    const double LIMIT = 999.999;   /* max value during initialization */
};
std::vector<int> createData() {
    std::vector<int> result(DATA_SIZE);
    double currVal = 1.0;
    for(auto &elem : result) {
        elem = currVal;
        currVal *= 2;          // next value is larger
        if(currVal > LIMIT) {
            currVal = LIMIT;   // no value should be larger
        }
    }
    return result;
} 
```

**Listing 13.8**     Local constants of a file fit well into an anonymous namespace.

This is especially true for global variables that, for example, define certain program parameters. It is best to put them in an anonymous namespace. The effect of this is that the identifier cannot be seen by other modules; in large projects, this is important to prevent global variables and constants from conflicting.

This allows you to easily tweak certain sizes of the program while also documenting the size well.

### 13.10.4    Const Returns

Normally, functions return a value, not a reference. This means that a copy of what you had in the function is returned. At least, you can think of it conceptually this way. In reality, the compiler can often avoid the copy (see [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12), [Section 12.11](#12_011.html_h12.11)):

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/fM4nsx9GP
struct Widget {
    int num_ = 0;
    void setNumber(int x) {    // a non-const method
        num_=x;
    }
};
Widget createWidget() {        // Return by value
    Widget result{};           // Create
    return result;
}
int main() {
    Widget w = createWidget(); // Return by value creates a copy
    w.setNumber(100);          // changing is naturally okay, w is non-const
} 
```

Because a copy of <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> exists outside of <samp class="listingcharacter">createWidget()</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget w = createWidget();</samp>, it is no longer the function's concern whether its content is modified. Therefore, it makes little sense to also mark the return type with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/98x3YsnKc
const Widget createWidget() {  // return as const value
    Widget result{};
    return result;
}
int main() {
    Widget w = createWidget();  // copied into new non-const w
    w.setNumber(100);           // w is non-const, changing is okay
} 
```

**Listing 13.9**     Although the return type is marked with “const” here, it has no effect because it is always copied.

Although the return type is <samp class="listingcharacter">const Widget</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> can never have an effect because the return is always copied as a value—and the caller has control over where it is copied. Here it is copied again into <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget w</samp> (non-<samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>), and thus the caller can do whatever they want with their copy.

It is quite different with references (and pointers): a reference means “no copy.”

#### Pay Attention to the Lifetime of the Referenced Object

I can't say it often enough: if you return a reference, you must ensure that the object the reference points to exists for as long as you use it externally.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/3EG1ovcev
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
using std::string; using std::string_view;

class Widget {
    string name_ = "";
public:
    void setName(string_view newName) {
        name_ = newName;
    }
    const string& getName() const {    // const& return
        return name_;
    }
};
int main() {
    Widget w{};
    w.setName("Title");
    string name1 = w.getName();        // new string, thus a copy
    name1.clear();                     // you are allowed to modify the copy again
    const string& name2 = w.getName(); // const reference to internal string name_
    /* name2.clear(); */               // name2 is const, so it doesn't work
    string& name3 = w.getName();       //  Function returns const&, not &.
    auto name4 = w.getName();          // identical to name1
    const auto& name5 = w.getName();   // identical to name2
} 
```

**Listing 13.10**     Constant references in returns.

In the preceding listing, I call a function five times that returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">const string&</samp>. The caller should store the result in variables of different types:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">name1 = w.getName();</samp>
    Here <samp class="listingcharacter">const string&</samp> is converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, which means the compiler should copy the return value. And as previously explained with the return of values, the caller has control over the copy.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const string&</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">name2 = w.getName();</samp>
    This is exactly the type that is also returned, so no conversion is necessary. A <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> points to exactly the same <samp class="listingcharacter">name_</samp> that exists in <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter">w.name_</samp> changes due to any influences, it would also be visible in <samp class="listingcharacter">name2</samp>. Only <samp class="listingcharacter">name2</samp> itself cannot be changed from the outside because it is a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> reference.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">string&</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">string& name3 = w.getName();</samp>
    Are you thinking “But I want to change <samp class="listingcharacter">w.name_</samp>” and therefore wanting to try to store the return value in a <samp class="listingcharacter">string&</samp>? The compiler does not allow this; a conversion from a <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> is not permitted. This is not like <samp class="listingcharacter">name1</samp>, where a <samp class="listingcharacter">const& string</samp> was converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> by copying it.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto name4 = w.getName();</samp>
    The compiler sets <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> to the type <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. Thus, the type of the variable is <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const string&</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">const auto& name5 = w.getName();</samp>
    Again, the compiler substitutes <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>. The overall type is then <samp class="listingcharacter">const string&</samp>.

When a class returns a reference, it is quite common to also mark it with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. You often do not want external changes to values that reside within the class. Therefore, you first choose to return by value, and if that is inappropriate, by reference. Whether it is <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> or not depends on the intended use.

For reference returns, both are conceivable. Sometimes you want the value to be changeable from outside, sometimes not.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/9MTj3rP5d
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
using std::string; using std::cout;

class Widget {
    string name_{};
public:
    const string& readName() const;         // const&-return, const-method
    string& getName();                      // &-return
};

const string& Widget::readName() const { return name_; }
string& Widget::getName() { return name_; }

int main() {
    Widget w{};
    const string& readonly = w.readName(); // const&, immutable
    cout << "Name: " << readonly << "\n";  // still "" empty.
    string& readwrite = w.getName();       // &, mutable
    readwrite.append("attached");          // also changes name_ and readonly
    cout << "Name via readwrite: " << readwrite << "\n"; // "attached"
    cout << "Name via readonly: " << readonly << "\n";   // also "attached"
} 
```

**Listing 13.11**     References can be returned as constant and nonconstant.

Because both <samp class="listingcharacter">readonly</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">readwrite</samp> are references to <samp class="listingcharacter">w.name_</samp>, changing <samp class="listingcharacter">readwrite</samp> affects <samp class="listingcharacter">w.name_</samp> and also <samp class="listingcharacter">readonly</samp>.

Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">readName()</samp> method, which has a <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> return type, is also marked with a trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>: because you can be sure that the return value will not be modified by anyone, calling this method does not change the state of the object—exactly what the trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> signifies.

It's different with <samp class="listingcharacter">getName()</samp> with its <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> return type (non-<samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>): you cannot mark this method with a trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. Because a part of the internal state (<samp class="listingcharacter">name_</samp>) is exposed through reference return, the internal state is no longer under the control of the method. Such a method can therefore never be <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>.

I have intentionally named the two methods differently in this example. However, you can also name them the same—that is, overload them. The compiler will then choose the appropriate variant:

```
class Widget {
    string name_{};

public:
    const string& getName() const;
    string& getName();
}; 
```

Depending on whether you are allowed to modify the return value at all, the appropriate overload will be chosen. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp> variable itself is <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, the compiler will choose the first variant. Or in other words, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp> variable on the right side of the assignment is relevant, not the <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> on the left.

Remember: <samp class="listingcharacter">*this</samp> is a hidden parameter in the method call—and the trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> is its parameter type after <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget const</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">* const</samp>. This way, the compiler can also call one method or the other depending on the <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> property of the actual <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp>:

```
Widget wid{};
cout << wid.getName(); // chooses non-const, because wid is not const
const Widget vot{};
cout << vot.getName(); // chooses const, because vot is const 
```

For starters, I recommend avoiding such overloads and making the distinction clear in the function name. You will find some overloads of this kind in the standard library, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">vector::front()</samp>.

### 13.10.5    “const” Together with “static”

You will often see that a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> variable is also marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. Let me show you three variants:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/4dnTs4vPx
namespace {
    const int MAX_A = 12;       // the same as MAX_B, but no static needed
}
static const int MAX_B = 10;    // in the global namespace
struct Data {
    static const int SIZE = 14; // as a data field in a class
};
void func() {
    static const int LIMIT = 16; // as a local constant
} 
```

The distinction mainly arises because <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> has a different meaning in each of these cases:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> in an anonymous namespace—<samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_A</samp>
    First without <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>. The constant <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_A</samp> is only known in this <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file. You cannot access it from another file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> in the global namespace—<samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_B</samp>
    Instead of an anonymous namespace, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> to define a constant. This has the same effect and is the older syntax. The disadvantage is that you cannot make classes local this way. Prefer an anonymous namespace.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static const</samp> as data field—<samp class="listingcharacter">SIZE</samp>
    The <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> ensures that all variables of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Data</samp> share a single <samp class="listingcharacter">SIZE</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> makes it immutable also.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static const</samp> as local variable—<samp class="listingcharacter">LIMIT</samp>
    For a local variable, <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> means that it retains its value when the function is exited. The variable is initialized only on the first pass. Together with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, it becomes a constant that is initialized only when needed.

### 13.10.6    Even More Constant with “constexpr”

In some cases, the compiler requires you to use a constant expression—one that it can evaluate at compile time. This happens, for example, when you want to create an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> of a certain size, as in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/E6MWxY1f7
#include <array>
int main() {

    std::array<int, 5> arr5{};     // literal and thus a constant expression
    std::array<int, 2+3> arr23{};  // 2+3 can be evaluated by the compiler

    const size_t SIZE = 5;         // defines a constant
    std::array<int, SIZE> arrSC{}; // can often be used by the compiler

    size_t size = 7;
    std::array<int,size> arrVar{}; // you cannot use a variable
} 
```

**Listing 13.12**     Some expressions must be known at compile time.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">SIZE</samp>, I define a constant with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, and then I can use it as a constant expression. A variable like <samp class="listingcharacter">size</samp> is not possible at this point—nor in some other places.

So far, so good. Can you use anything that is constant as an array size? Unfortunately, no. There are cases where it is not enough to mark something with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. Because the actual semantics of <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> say, “This must not be changed at runtime.” This is a big difference from saying, “The compiler must be able to calculate it at compile time,” even though they often coincide.

The following listing shows an example in which it the constant goes wrong.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xPzcWPdMa
#include <array>
struct Data {
    static const size_t LATE;             // declare constant
    static const size_t EARLY;            // declare constant
};

void func() {
    int x = Data::LATE;                   // use constant
}

const size_t Data::EARLY = 10;            // define constant

std::array<int, Data::EARLY> arrEARLY {}; // use constant
std::array<int, Data::LATE>  arrLATE {};  // use constant
const size_t Data::LATE = 10;             // define constant

int main() {
    func();
} 
```

**Listing 13.13**     Whether the compiler can use a constant in a constant expression is not always immediately apparent.

Here, the <samp class="listingcharacter">EARLY</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">LATE</samp> constants are defined in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Data</samp> class. <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> here means that all <samp class="listingcharacter">Data</samp> variables share a common constant or variable. As you already know, I first made the definitions outside the class for <samp class="listingcharacter">EARLY</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">LATE</samp>; within <samp class="listingcharacter">Data</samp>, only the “space” for them is defined.

However, because the <samp class="listingcharacter">arrLATE</samp> definition comes after its usage, the—seemingly—constant expression cannot yet be evaluated by the compiler here. And although the <samp class="listingcharacter">int x = LATE;</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">func()</samp> appears in the program code before the definition, it is not a problem here: the simple initialization of a variable does not need to be computed by the compiler in advance; it is sufficient that it can be done at runtime.

This “reverse order” is not always as clear as in this simple example. Definitions and declarations can indeed be in different <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> files. You can also write <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> before many more things than the compiler can compute in advance. For example, you can write and use

```
const double sin0 = sin(0.0);, 
```

but the compiler cannot compute sine at translation time.

Is this all quite confusing? I agree with you. Therefore, I recommend declaring constants of this kind not only with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, but with <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>—an enhancement of it.

For values you declare with <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, the compiler checks if it can compute them at compile time. If that is not the case, you will receive an error message.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, [Listing 13.13](#13_010.html_l13.13) looks like the following listing.

```
struct Data {
    static constexpr size_t LATE; // does not work without direct initialization
    static constexpr size_t EARLY = 10;
};
constexpr size_t Data::LATE = 10; // with constexpr, definition is different 
```

**Listing 13.14**     With “constexpr”, the compiler sees when an expression is not computable early.

You cannot declare <samp class="listingcharacter">LATE</samp> without also defining it—that is, initializing it at the same time. This ensures that you can use the constant as soon as its name is known.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> variables almost anywhere you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. Try to get used to using <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> for these purposes.

#### “constexpr” as Return Type

Another exciting feature of <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> is that you can also mark functions with it. Write <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> for the return type. In fact, this <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> affects the entire function:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Yv85s9T6v
constexpr size_t doubleIfTooSmall1(size_t value) {
   return value < 100 ? value*2 : value; // returns double if less than 100
}
std::array<int, doubleIfTooSmall1(50)> arr {}; 
```

This is huge progress! A self-written function that simply returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> value cannot be used as a constant expression:

```
const size_t doubleIfTooSmall2(size_t value) {
    return value < 100 ? value*2 : value;
}
std::array<int, doubleIfTooSmall2(50)> arr {}; //  not constant enough 
```

Why is there a distinction being made again here? The reason is so that the compiler ensures that it can calculate <samp class="listingcharacter">doubleIfTooSmall1(50)</samp> at compile time.

Here are two examples of what the compiler does not allow before C++23:

```
#include <cmath> // sin, cos, sqrt
constexpr unsigned myLog2(unsigned number) { // function has static variable
    static int count_calls = 0;              // not allowed in constexpr
    count_calls += 1;
    unsigned count = 0;
    while(number > 1) { number /= 2; }
    return count;
}
constexpr double one(double x) {             // uses non-constexpr
    return sqrt(sin(x)*sin(x) + cos(x)*cos(x));
} 
```

Since C++14 and especially since C++20 and C++23, the rules for what can be in a <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> function are much less strict. For example, since C++14, simple <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops are allowed. Since C++20, you can even allocate memory with <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> within them. Since C++23, the <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> local variable is allowed. This in turn has allowed many methods and constructors like <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> to be defined as <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, so you can now use them in <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> functions—but only if their memory is also freed at compile time. Many algorithms in <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><numeric></samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter"><utility></samp> are now also <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>.

Conveniently, <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> implies <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> for functions and member variables and <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> for member functions.

### 13.10.7    “if constexpr” for Compile-Time Decisions

Sometimes you want to decide which code to execute at compile time rather than at runtime. You do this all the time with overloads. “If the argument is a pointer, then dereference it; otherwise, return the value itself.” This problem could be solved with an overload, but it can also be done with <samp class="listingcharacter">if constexpr</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zMbnYzo17
template<typename T>
auto deref(T t) {
    if constexpr (std::is_pointer_v<T>) {
        return *t;
    } else {
        return t;
    }
}
int main() {
    int i = 42;
    std::cout << deref(i) << '\n';         // directly the value
    auto p = std::make_unique<int>(73);
    std::cout << deref(p.get()) << '\n';   // dereferenced pointer
} 
```

**Listing 13.15**     With “if constexpr”, you can decide at compile time what code will be executed.

Here it is decided at compile time what code will be executed. For <samp class="listingcharacter">I</samp>, it is <samp class="listingcharacter">return t</samp>—because <samp class="listingcharacter">is_pointer_v<int></samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">false.</samp> For <samp class="listingcharacter">p.get()</samp>, it is <samp class="listingcharacter">return *t</samp>.

Overloads, or template specializations, can also be replaced with <samp class="listingcharacter">if constexpr</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/eo468MvMo
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
struct S {
   int n;
   std::string s;
   float d;
};
template <std::size_t N> auto& get(S& s) {
    if constexpr (N == 0) return s.n;
    else if constexpr (N == 1) return s.s;
    else if constexpr (N == 2) return s.d;
}
int main() {
    S obj { 0, "hello", 10.0f };
    std::cout << get<0>(obj) << ", " << get<1>(obj) << "\n”; // Output: 0, hello
} 
```

**Listing 13.16**     <samp class="listingcharacter">"if constexpr"</samp> also works with “<samp class="listingcharacter">else”.</samp>

Before <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr if</samp>, you needed to write three template specializations, like <samp class="listingcharacter">template<> auto& get<0>(S& s)</samp>. The new approach can be more concise.

With this feature, you can very easily calculate Fibonacci numbers—a favorite example of this book—at compile time:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/44KMf1fWr
template<auto N>
constexpr auto fibonacci()    {
    if constexpr (N>=2) {
        return fibonacci<N-1>() + fibonacci<N-2>();
    } else {
        return N;
    }
}

int main() {
    std::cout << fibonacci<10>() << '\n';  // Output: 55
    std::cout << fibonacci<20>() << '\n';  // Output: 6765
} 
```

However, because this is written as a nasty recursion, it may, depending on the implementation, cause the compiler to hang. But maybe you want to test the compiler's performance?

### 13.10.8    C++20: “consteval”

Since C++20, there has been a superlative of <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>. If you declare a function with <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp>, you have an immediate function. The compiler then executes the function code at compile time and inserts the result at the call site.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/v3x7nGs3f
int get_input() {
    return 50;  // or read something from a file or so
}
constexpr auto calculate_1(int input) {
    return input * 2;
}
consteval auto calculate_2(int input) {
    return input * 2;
}
int main() {
    int input = get_input();
    auto a = calculate_1(77);     // at compile time … maybe computable
    auto b = calculate_1(input);  // … computable, but valid
    auto c = calculate_2(77);     // … computable
    auto d = calculate_2(input);  // … not computable, invalid
} 
```

**Listing 13.17**     With “consteval”, you can execute functions at compile time.

While <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> merely offers the possibility to be computed at compile time, <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp> is explicitly intended for that purpose. A <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp> function can only be called with constant expressions. There is a good chance that the compiler will actually use the result at that point and the function will not need to be called at runtime.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter">calculate_2(</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">input</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> depends on a variable whose value is not known at compile time, the compiler does not allow the function call.

Therefore, a <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp> function can only perform <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> computations. Such a function can be quite complex in itself (you can follow the Compiler Explorer link in the next listing to see the machine code and confirm that the calculated primes are part of the compiled program).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Wbr7n8M4q
#include <iostream>
#include <array>
constexpr bool isPrime(int n) { // computable at compile-time
  if(n < 2) return false; // 0, 1 are not prime
  for (int i = 2; i*i <= n; i += i>2 ? 2 : 1) { // 2,3,5,7,9,11,13,15…
    if (n % i == 0) return false;
  }
  return n > 1; // for 0 and 1
}
template<int Num>
consteval std::array<int, Num> primeNumbers() { // only at compile-time
  std::array<int, Num> primes{};
  int idx = 0;
  for (int val = 1; idx < Num; ++val) {
    if (isPrime(val)) primes[idx++] = val;
  }
  return primes;
}
int main() {
  // initialize with prime numbers
  auto primes = primeNumbers<100>();  // 1000000 doesn't work
  for (auto v : primes) {
    std::cout << v << ' ';
  }
  std::cout << '\n';
} 
```

**Listing 13.18**     Even more complex functions can be computed at compile time with “consteval”.
