You probably want a different behavior; for example, you may want to keep the indentation depth of the original. To do this, implement a special method with the following signature:

```
MyValue& MyValue::operator=(const MyValue&); 
```

Note that this is a method and not a constructor. The object to which something is assigned already exists; its content is to be overwritten by this assignment operator. Because it is not a constructor, you do not perform the transfer of the data fields in an initializer list, but like a method in the body.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/s65GvY9xj
struct MyValue {
    // … everything else as before
    MyValue& operator=(const MyValue& right) {
        if(this != &right) { // 1\. check for self-assignment
            // 2\. Release previous resources; none here
            // 3\. element-wise transfer by assignment or similar
            name_ = right.name_ + "-Assignment (previously " + name_ + ")";
            /* number_ remains, and thus the original indentation */
        }
        return *this; // 4\. return self
    }
}; 
```

**Listing 16.16**     The schema for implementing a custom assignment operator.

If you insert this into the definition of <samp class="listingcharacter">struct MyValue</samp>, you will get the following output:

```
Constructor ABCD
 Constructor WXYZ
 Destructor WXYZ
Destructor WXYZ-Assignment (previously ABCD) 
```

And so the world is back in order: You can see from the text and indentation which original was overwritten and when it was cleared away.

If you define the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp> assignment operator for your class yourself, be sure to follow the implementation pattern shown previously:

1.  Check with <samp class="listingcharacter">if(this != &right)</samp> whether <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> has the same address as <samp class="listingcharacter">&right</samp>. If you don't do this, problems can arise with self-assignments like <samp class="listingcharacter">value1 = value1</samp>.

2.  Release all previous resources of the object to be overwritten. This is indicated in [Listing 16.16](#16_007.html_l16.16) at <samp class="listingcharacter">2.</samp> because there is nothing to do for <samp class="listingcharacter">MyValue</samp> here.

3.  Transfer all elements from right to left as under <samp class="listingcharacter">3.</samp>. This is often done by assignment or some other form of copying. Because you intentionally omitted the transfer of <samp class="listingcharacter">number_</samp> in this case, add a comment about the unusual nature.

4.  Then return a reference to the current object with <samp class="listingcharacter">return *this</samp>. This allows assignment chains like <samp class="listingcharacter">value1 = value2 = value3 = value4;</samp>.

The similarities of the assignment operator to the copy constructor are very extensive:

*   Normally, you do not need a self-defined assignment operator; the compiler-generated one is at least as good for built-in data types, standard containers, and most types of the standard library.

*   If you define (or need to define) a copy constructor or destructor yourself, you usually also need your own assignment operator—and vice versa.

Besides the different way you implement the assignment operator, there is another crucial difference: if you have <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> data elements in your class, then the assignment operator is removed from the list of available operations—or “deleted.” The consequence is that you can no longer overwrite an instance by assignment. To illustrate, I reduce the <samp class="listingcharacter">MyValue</samp> class to a constructor and a constant data field.

```
struct MyNumber {

    const int number_;         // constant data field

    explicit MyNumber(int v)
        : number_{v}           // initialization of the constant data field
        {}
};

int main() {
    MyNumber c1{4};
    MyNumber c2{7};
    c1 = c2;                   // Error: Assignment removed by compiler
} 
```

**Listing 16.17**     The “const” data element is initially without an assignment operator.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">c1 = c2</samp> assignment is not possible here. The compiler tries to generate an assignment operator; it tries to assign <samp class="listingcharacter">number_ = other.number_</samp>. This is not possible because <samp class="listingcharacter">number_</samp> is declared with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. So instead of generating an assignment operator, the compiler deletes it. This results in the <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> operator not being available for this class.

## 16.8    Removing Methods

This has the same effect as if you had defined <samp class="listingcharacter">MyNumber</samp> as shown in the next listing. Note that I have again made <samp class="listingcharacter">number_</samp> non-<samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>, and the compiler would have generated an assignment operator again.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/398GhcbaE
struct MyNumber {
    int number_;           // variable data field

    explicit MyNumber(int v)
        : number_{v} {}
    MyNumber& operator=(const MyNumber&) = delete; // remove assignment
    MyNumber(const MyNumber&) = delete;            // remove copy
};
int main() {
    MyNumber c1{4};
    MyNumber c2{7};
    c1 = c2;               // Error – assignment removed by programmer
    MyNumber c3{c1};       // Error – copy removed by programmer
} 
```

**Listing 16.18**     Use “= delete” to manually remove operations.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp> is a way for programmers to prevent the compiler from generating a method. And as you can see from the second <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">MyNumber(const MyNumber&) = delete;</samp>, you can also remove a constructor with it. Thus, a copy of <samp class="listingcharacter">MyNumber</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">MyNumber c3{c1};</samp> is also no longer possible.

In our <samp class="listingcharacter">MyValue</samp> examples, it wasn't too problematic that I gradually addressed the necessary implementation of the copy constructor and assignment operator. The copy constructor or assignment operator generated by the compiler at worst produced incorrect output on the screen.

[Listing 16.7](#16_003.html_l16.7) did not address copying and assignment, which resulted in an error-prone class. What happens if you copy or assign a <samp class="listingcharacter">Database</samp> instance? You end up duplicating a database handle or overwriting an existing one:

*   If you duplicate it, then the destructor will call <samp class="listingcharacter">db_close</samp> on the same handle twice.

*   If you overwrite it, then you miss a <samp class="listingcharacter">db_close</samp>, and a handle is not released.

Both are serious errors that occur if your listing does not adhere to the following rule: If you define a destructor yourself, you almost always need your own copy constructor and your own assignment operator as well.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp>, you can quickly get the problem under control for <samp class="listingcharacter">Database</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/vb5a3EjcY
#include <iostream>              // cout
#include "database.hpp"          // include the foreign API

class Database {
    const db_handle_t db_;                         // make constant
public:
    explicit Database(const char* filename);
    ~Database();
    int execute(const char* query);
    Database(const Database&) = delete;            // prohibit copying
    Database& operator=(const Database&) = delete; // prohibit assignment
};
// … Implementations as before …
int main() {
    Database db{ "customers.dat" };
    std::cout << "Count: "<< db.execute("select * from cust") << "\n";
    Database db2{ db };          // compiler prevents dangerous copy
    db = db2;                    // compiler prevents dangerous assignment
} 
```

**Listing 16.19**     With the deleted functions, the compiler prevents incorrect usage of the class.

I also have marked the <samp class="listingcharacter">db_</samp> data field with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. This alone would prevent the compiler from generating an <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp>, making the program safe in this regard. Because I manually remove the copy constructor with <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp> anyway, it doesn't hurt to play it safe and treat the assignment operator the same way.

## 16.9    Move Operations

You have learned two ways to copy a class instance. Let's assume your class is called <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Image(const Image& other)</samp>—the copy constructor
    This can only happen during the initialization of a new object.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Image& operator=(const Image& other)</samp>—the assignment operator
    This overwrites and only happens with an already existing object.

In most cases, all data fields from the source are copied into the target. Of course, this can be very costly.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/75Kh5Ws45
#include <vector>
class Image {
    std::vector<std::byte> data_;
public:
    explicit Image(const char *fn) { /*...*/ }
    // Compiler generates (among others):
    // Copy constructor, assignment, but also moves
};
std::vector<Image> loadCollection(bool empty) {
    if(empty) return std::vector<Image>{};
    std::vector<Image> result {};                 // for return; initially empty
    // three images in the collection … copy?
    result.push_back( Image{"MonaLisa.png"} );
    result.push_back( Image{"TheScream.png"} );
    result.push_back( Image{"BoyWithPipe.png"} );
    return result; // return collection by value
}
int main() {
    // store return in variable
    std::vector<Image> collection = loadCollection(false);
} 
```

**Listing 16.20**     The class probably contains large amounts of data that are expensive to copy. But what is being copied here?

I have written a sample data type <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> that likely holds large amounts of data in <samp class="listingcharacter">data_</samp>. The compiler-generated operations for copy and assignment will completely copy this data field from the source to the target. So the data is duplicated after copying: I expect that, and thus it is fine.

Does it surprise you, then, when I tell you that at no point in [Listing 16.20](#16_009.html_l16.20) are image data duplicated in <samp class="listingcharacter">data_</samp>? If not, then you either have already read something about move operations or expect too much from C++. I would like to illustrate where duplicate data could exist due to copying, and then explain why this is not the case here:

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">Image{"MonaLisa.png"}</samp>, I create a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> including its data. The <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> takes this <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> and places it where it stores its own data. This is a good candidate for a complete copy.

*   With <samp class="listingcharacter">return result;</samp>, I return the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> by value. What was previously a local variable is to be passed outside. In this case, it should be stored in another variable with <samp class="listingcharacter">collection = …</samp>. Such a scenario is another very good candidate for a copy—which here would be the copy of all <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> elements.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has its own area where it stores its data. The new <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> instances within <samp class="listingcharacter">loadCollection()</samp> are, of course, unaware of this and certainly store their data elsewhere. The <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> copies this data to where the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> wants it. The good news is that this copy can be omitted under certain circumstances—as in this example. <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> can save the expensive copying of data for objects designed with <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp>. To achieve this, it is—as always—sufficient to use only built-in types, standard containers, or most types from the standard library, and then to not define a copy constructor, destructor, or assignment operator.[[ 40 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn16_02)

After <samp class="listingcharacter">return result;</samp>, it no longer makes sense to keep <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> as a local variable. When leaving the function, <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> is discarded; the destructor is called, and all contents are destroyed. It is good that the content was copied to <samp class="listingcharacter">collection</samp> beforehand for the return. Should you first make a complete copy and then destroy the original? This is not necessary in C++ either. In the case shown here, the content of <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> can be directly transferred—moved—to <samp class="listingcharacter">collection</samp>. This effect during return is called copy elision.

Neither is self-evident and both are subject to certain conditions. C++ can in no way forgo calling the destructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> as that would contradict the RAII principles. And when the destructor is called, you can expect the data fields to be removed as well. The solution to the puzzle is that a special form of copying is applied—not the one you already know, but one that only works with temporary values.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> symbol here denotes a special form of reference, the temp-value reference (technically, the rvalue reference). For the moment, please consider this like the normal reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>, but remember that when dealing with moving you need <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Image(Image&& other)</samp>—the move constructor
    Like the copy constructor, except that <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> is not <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. Therefore, its data can be taken away from it. Used by the compiler only when <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> will not exist for much longer, which is why taking away the data is acceptable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Image& operator=(Image&& other)</samp>—the move assignment operator
    Like the assignment operator, except that <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> is not <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. Data is taken away from it. The compiler automatically uses this operation when it is sure that <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> will be destroyed soon.

In [Listing 16.20](#16_009.html_l16.20), the compiler uses both to avoid copies:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> must first create an empty object with <samp class="listingcharacter">Image{}</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp>. Containers use this default creation without arguments when they need it. The newly created <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp> is then assigned using the move assignment operator.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<Image> collection = …</samp> is initialized with the move constructor. That means the return value, and thus <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp>, takes the data instead of copying the entire object.

How do the two operations you just learned about do this? The matter becomes clear when you consider the following facts:

*   The compiler ensures that <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> is short-lived and will be destroyed soon anyway.

*   Therefore, <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> no longer needs its data, and they can serve a better purpose—like avoiding a copy of the data.

*   The object that is supposed to receive the data is usually freshly created—almost empty.

*   The receiving object is supposed to have its data overwritten; it no longer needs its old—mostly empty—data.

*   Both involved objects must be valid before the operation. <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> is at least initialized empty; <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> contains the valuable data.

*   Both objects must be valid after the operation. <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> contains the data; <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> can be empty, ready for the destructor call.

If you had to implement the operations yourself with these requirements—which you don't have to, as the compiler does it—you could do it as in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/aoqW86vs8
#include <vector>
class Image {
    std::vector<std::byte> data_;              // byte has been available since C++17
public:
    explicit Image(const char *fn) { /*...*/ }
    Image(Image&& other) noexcept              // move constructor
        : data_{} // create empty
    {
        using std::swap;
        swap(data_, other.data_);
    }
    Image& operator=(Image&& other) noexcept { // move operator
        using std::swap;
        swap(data_, other.data_);
        return *this;
    }
}; 
```

**Listing 16.21**     Implementation of the two move operations.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp>, you exchange almost any element in the most efficient way imaginable. Normally, you can also directly use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::swap</samp>, but it has become an idiom that a prior <samp class="listingcharacter">using std::swap</samp> leaves the possibility open to use an even better <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp> variant. More important, however, is the question of what is being swapped here. Actually, everything has already been said with the preceding bulleted list: before swapping, <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> contains the data, afterward <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> does; before, <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> is (mostly) empty, afterward it is <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp>. Assuming that <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp> does not copy any data, you have very effectively transferred the data from <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> and left both objects in a correct state.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp> function is useful, but in some cases, the similar <samp class="listingcharacter">exchange</samp> function is more appropriate:

```
Image(Image&& other) noexcept            // move constructor
    : data_{ std::exchange(other.data_, {}) }
{ } 
```

Effectively, <samp class="listingcharacter">r = exchange(old, new)</samp> performs <samp class="listingcharacter">r=old</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">old=new</samp> sequentially where possible, using <samp class="listingcharacter">move</samp>. Thus, you can usually initialize all members in the move constructor.

If you do not write a copy constructor, assignment operator, or destructor because you do not need them, then you usually do not need either of the move operations. In that case, the compiler generates the move operations for you.

Or the compiler prohibits moving, similar to how it would prohibit copying. For example, if you have a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> data field, it cannot be moved from.

If you manage to create a movable data type, it is ideal for return values and for being put into standard containers. The compiler ensures that sorting, swapping, pushing, and resizing use the move operations. The noble goal of a data type that is to be put into a container is to be movable. You can achieve this in two ways:

*   Give your class only data fields that are themselves movable—for example, built-in types, standard containers, or types from the standard library.

*   You take on the thankless task of implementing the move operations yourself.

You should not do the latter, really. And if you do, then let me tell you that you must also write <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> after those operations—such a profound topic that I have only touched on it in this book (see [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7)).

### 16.9.1    What the Compiler Generates

It is important to understand when the compiler takes over the work of generating a constructor or <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp> for programmers and when it does not. The rules are not trivial, but they are written in such a way that your program becomes as safe and fast as possible automatically.

Here, automatically generated means that the compiler implicitly declares the special function in question as if you had marked it with <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp>:

*   The default constructor
    <samp class="listingcharacter">C()</samp> is automatically generated if you do not declare any constructor yourself.

*   The destructor
    <samp class="listingcharacter">~C()</samp> is automatically generated if you do not declare a destructor.

*   The copy constructor
    <samp class="listingcharacter">C(const C&)</samp> is automatically generated if you do not declare either of the move operations.

*   The copy assignment
    <samp class="listingcharacter">C& operator=(const C&)</samp> is automatically generated if you do not declare either of the move operations.

*   The move constructor
    <samp class="listingcharacter">C(C&&)</samp> is automatically generated if you do not declare either of the copy operations and all elements can be moved.

*   The move assignment operator
    <samp class="listingcharacter">C& operator=(C&&)</samp> is automatically generated if you do not declare either of the copy operations and all elements can be moved.

From this, you can conclude that the copy operations are independent of each other: if you declare one of them, the compiler could still generate the other. So, for example, if you declare the copy constructor but not the copy assignment, and then write code that requires <samp class="listingcharacter">C& operator=(const C&)</samp>, the compiler will generate it.

This does not apply to move operations; these are not independent of each other. If you declare one of the two, the compiler will not generate the other.

## 16.10    Operators

You have now learned about the special <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp> method, which is called by the compiler when you write the following:

```
Data data{};
Data newData{};
data = newData; 
```

The equal sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> of the assignment is also just a binary operator with a right operand and a left operand. It is called infix notation when the operator symbol is between the two operands. The compiler translates this into the following method call:

```
data.operator=(newData);  // method notation 
```

Although <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp> is not a normal identifier, it is allowed in this usage form—but only if you have actually defined such a method.

However, you have also redefined another operator: the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> output operator. To output <samp class="listingcharacter">Year</samp> to an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp>, you have overloaded a free function:

```
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Year&); 
```

If you do not want to use the infix notation, you can use the function notation analogously to the method notation:

```
cout << year;            // infix notation
operator<<(cout, year);  // function notation 
```

If you use the infix notation, the compiler automatically selects the method or free function, depending on what you have defined for your class. If you use the function or method notation, you choose it yourself. This can be useful in cases of doubt, for example, if you have both.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/P99563KoP
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::ostream;
struct Widget {
    bool operator<(const Widget&) const {      // method notation
        return true;                           // always true
    }
};
bool operator<(const Widget&, const Widget&) { // function notation
    return false;                              // always false
}
int main() {
    Widget x{};
    Widget y{};
    cout << (operator<(x, y)      // calls function notation
        ? "Method1\n" : "Function1\n");
    cout << (y.operator<(x)       // calls method notation
        ? "Method2\n" : "Function2\n");
    cout << (x < y                // infix notation, allows choice, here function
        ? "Method3\n" : "Function3\n");
} 
```

**Listing 16.22**     Infix, function, and method notation for operators.

For the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">Widget</samp>, two variants are implemented: the free function and the method. To observe the difference in invocation, the two implementations return different values. The first two callers in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> explicitly choose the respective implementation: <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<(x, y)</samp> calls the free function, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Function1</samp> is printed. <samp class="listingcharacter">y.operator<(x)</samp> is the method call and results in <samp class="listingcharacter">Method2</samp>. With the infix notation <samp class="listingcharacter">x < y</samp>, the compiler can choose. Here, GCC prefers the function, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Function3</samp> is printed, while Clang++ produces an error.

As you saw in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.3](#04_003.html_h4.3), there are more operators. And just like <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp>, you can define most of them for your class yourself. But how? As a free function or as a method? Most of the time, you can choose whether to define an operator for your own classes as a method of the class or as a free function. In practice, however, one or the other has become established for each operator. The following rules of thumb will help you choose:

*   Unary operators should be implemented as methods. This includes <samp class="listingcharacter">operator++</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator--</samp>, but also <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp>, and the unary forms of <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>.

*   Binary operators that do not modify any of the arguments should be defined as free functions. These are primarily the bitwise and arithmetic operators, including <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>, which are used for input and output. Comparison operators are implemented via <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp> and optionally also <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>.

*   Binary operators that modify the left argument are best suited as methods—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">operator+=</samp>.

*   Assignment, index operator, and call operator must be methods—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp>.

There are a few more operators that I won't mention here because they are only used in special cases. These are just general guidelines.

A disadvantage of implementing as a free function is that it does not give access to the private data fields and methods of the class the function is supposed to work on. However, often with these operators, delving into the internals is helpful or necessary. Then you have three options:

*   You can take a detour via a public method that offers a similar function—as seen in [Chapter 12](#12_001.html_h12), [Listing 12.27](#12_011.html_l12.27) with <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Year::print</samp>.

*   You can write the operator as a <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> within the class.

*   The worst way would be to make the private internals <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp>, as this contradicts encapsulation.

Whether you choose the first or second approach depends on the circumstances.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> function is a special notation of a free function that you write inside a class.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Wvr3aK75G
#include <compare>               // for <=>
class Value {
    int value_;
public:
    explicit Value(int value) : value_{value} {}

    // free functions, but declared as friend
    friend Value operator+(const Value& li, const Value& re);
    friend Value operator-(const Value& li, const Value& re) {
        return Value{li.value_ - re.value_};  // also defined inside
    }
    // operator<=> does not need to be friend.
    // for all comparisons: <, >, <=, >= as well as == and !=
    auto operator<=>(const Value& re) const = default;
};
// Definition of the previously declared friend function:
Value operator+(const Value& li, const Value& re) {
    return Value{li.value_ + re.value_}; // access to private members allowed
}
int main() {
    Value seven{7}; Value three{3}; Value two{2};
    if((three+two) < seven) {    // operator+, then operator< via <=>
        return 0;                // okay
    } else {
        return 1;                // something went wrong
    }
} 
```

**Listing 16.23**     A “friend” function is not a method, even if it is inside the class or defined there.

Even if the functions, here <samp class="listingcharacter">operator+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator-</samp>, are now inside the <samp class="listingcharacter">Value</samp> class, they are free functions—as if you had written them outside. The differences are as follows:

*   In the function body, you can access everything you could access from a method.

*   Other free functions can be added to your data type by anyone as they wish. For <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> functions, however, the following applies: because this special form is written within the class definition, you as the class designer determine which free <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> functions exist.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">operator+</samp>, I have separated the function declaration within the class from the function definition outside—as is also common with a normal method. When defining, you do not repeat the <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> keyword. At that point, you do not see that it is a friend and why it suddenly has private access rights. Perhaps that is why it is quite common for <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> functions to also perform the definition within the class, as was done with <samp class="listingcharacter">operator-</samp>. Of course, you should only consider this for short functions.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> is a special case because it does not need to be declared as a <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> function. More on this is to come in the next section.

## 16.11    Custom Operators in a Data Type

Many operators can theoretically be implemented in a variety of ways. And you are almost completely free to choose the argument and return types. For a <samp class="listingcharacter">Value</samp> class, you can certainly have <samp class="listingcharacter">operator++</samp> return <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp>, as it is practical to be able to use the incremented value immediately.

### Meaning over Convenience

When adding operators to your class, you should avoid creating surprises. Maintain the approximate meaning of the operator symbol. Let's take this code as an example:

```
Image img1{}; Image img2{};
auto x = img1 + img2; 
```

Nothing would be more confusing than if the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">img1 + img2</samp> did not merge the two images but, for example, displayed them sequentially on the screen. It is better to use descriptive function or method names.

Personally, I follow the rule that I only define operators if I use the operation in expressions and the readability of the overall expression increases.

Here, I will show you the most common argument and return types of most operators and indicate whether it is common to implement them as member functions or free functions. Because there are quite a few operators, [Listing 16.24](#16_011.html_l16.24) provides a longer example.

I have defined most operators directly in the class, but some, mainly for space reasons, outside the class. By the way: you should also mark such short implementations of operators outside the class with the <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> keyword. The compiler then strives more for speed. Users often expect performance from operators. When implemented within the class, the method is implicitly <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> for the compiler. In both cases, you can also consider <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, which allows computation at compile-time and also implies <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp>.

There are some peculiarities to consider with operators:

*   Binary arithmetic operators return new objects
    All binary arithmetic and bitwise operators must always return a new object. Do not be tempted to trick with references or even pointers. Avoid hard-to-find errors by adhering to this rule.

*   Compound assignments as methods
    Because <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp> and its relatives modify the left operand, they are best suited as methods.

*   Implementing binary operators using compound assignments
    When you implement <samp class="listingcharacter">a+b</samp>, make it easy on yourself by also implementing <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>. Then pass the left parameter by value—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">Num a</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">const Num& a</samp>—and let the compiler create a copy. Apply <samp class="listingcharacter">a += b</samp> to this copy—and you can return its <samp class="listingcharacter">Num</samp> directly with <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>.

*   Overloading operators for argument types
    For the operator <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>, I have defined two overloads. One takes a <samp class="listingcharacter">const Num&</samp> as a parameter, the other an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. Normally, you should prefer the current class as the parameter type, as it is the most natural. However, you would have to write <samp class="listingcharacter">a += Num{7};</samp>. Where it makes sense, you can add overloads and allow <samp class="listingcharacter">a += 7;</samp>—that is, with an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>.

*   Comparisons via <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp> or individually as free functions
    Since C++20, there is the spaceship operator <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp>, which implements all comparisons at once. If you define it, the compiler derives all comparisons <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> from it. If you cannot or do not want to use it, you should implement the operators as free functions with two <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> references.

*   If you define <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp> yourself, then also define <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>
    If you define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=>(…) = default</samp>, the compiler will also derive <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> from it. If you implement it yourself, you should also define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp> yourself.

*   Ordered types implement the <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> operators
    Your class is equipped to handle sorting standard containers like <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> if you only implement <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>. But you can also go so far as to offer all comparison operators. And then it is easiest if you define <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> implies <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>
    Since C++20, it is sufficient if you implement <samp class="listingcharacter">a == b</samp>. If the compiler needs <samp class="listingcharacter">a != b</samp>, it will try <samp class="listingcharacter">!(a == b)</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are of different types, it will also try <samp class="listingcharacter">b != a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!(b == a)</samp>. If you do not want this, then define the corresponding overloads yourself.

*   Use <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>
    If you can, mark your operators with <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp>. Member functions should at least be marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>.

*   Preincrement and predecrement
    <samp class="listingcharacter">operator++()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator--()</samp> modify the object immediately and then return it as a reference. This allows, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">++a</samp>. If you use <samp class="listingcharacter">a++</samp> instead (postincrement), then a copy of the old value needs to be created and returned; you should avoid this and prefer the pre variants. If you still want to provide the post variants, you need to define <samp class="listingcharacter">operator++(int)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator--(int)</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> parameter is just a dummy and is not used; it only serves to distinguish the overload. The implementation would look like this:

    ```
    //The less efficient a++ and a--
    Num Num::operator++(int) { Num res{*this}; val_++; return res; }
    Num Num::operator--(int) { Num res{*this}; val_--; return res; } 
    ```

*   Dereference operator
    The unary <samp class="listingcharacter">operator*</samp> is typically used to access the “real value” of a class. Good examples of this are <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp>, all iterators, and raw pointers. So if you write <samp class="listingcharacter">Num a{7};</samp>, you can now write <samp class="listingcharacter">*a</samp> to access <samp class="listingcharacter">val_</samp>. Because I also return a reference with <samp class="listingcharacter">int&</samp>, you can even do <samp class="listingcharacter">*a = 99;</samp> to change the value.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/YonbGKj8M
#include <iostream>  // istream, ostream, cout
class Num {
  int val_ = 0;
public:
  int& operator*();  // Dereference: Direct access to the value
  const int& operator*() const; // Dereference: Read access to the value
  Num() {}
  explicit Num(int value) : val_{value} {}
  // unary operators
  Num& operator++(); // Preincrement
  Num& operator--(); // Predecrement
  Num operator+();   // Positive
  Num operator-();   // Negate
  Num operator~();   // Bitwise invert
  // binary operators
  // - compound assignments, arithmetic
  Num& operator+=(const Num& re) { val_ += *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator-=(const Num& re) { val_ -= *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator*=(const Num& re) { val_ *= *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator/=(const Num& re) { val_ /= *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator%=(const Num& re) { val_ %= *re; return *this; }
  // - compound assignments, bitwise
  Num& operator|=(const Num& re) { val_ |= *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator&=(const Num& re) { val_ &= *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator^=(const Num& re) { val_ ^= *re; return *this; }
  Num& operator<<=(int n) { val_ <<= n; return *this; }
  Num& operator>>=(int n) { val_ >>= n; return *this; }
  // - Variation of compound assignments for easier handling
  Num& operator+=(int re) { val_ += re; return *this; }
  Num& operator-=(int re) { val_ -= re; return *this; }
  // binary operators, with call-by-value for the first parameter
  // and using compound assignment for assistance
  // - Arithmetic
  friend Num operator+(Num li, const Num& re) { return li += re; }
  friend Num operator-(Num li, const Num& re) { return li -= re; }
  friend Num operator*(Num li, const Num& re) { return li *= re; }
  friend Num operator/(Num li, const Num& re) { return li /= re; }
  friend Num operator%(Num li, const Num& re) { return li %= re; }
  // - bitwise
  friend Num operator|(Num li, const Num& re) { return li |= re; }
  friend Num operator&(Num li, const Num& re) { return li &= re; }
  friend Num operator^(Num li, const Num& re) { return li ^= re; }
  // - comparisons
  // - … fundamental for standard containers and algorithms
  friend bool operator==(const Num& li, const Num& re) { return *li == *re; }
  auto operator<=>(const Num& re) const {return val_ <=> *re; } // C++20
  // - input and output
  friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Num& arg);
  friend std::istream& operator>>(std::istream& is, Num& arg);
};

// unary operators
Num& Num::operator++() { ++val_; return *this; }
Num& Num::operator--() { --val_; return *this; }
Num Num::operator+() { return Num{val_}; }
Num Num::operator-() { return Num{-val_}; }
Num Num::operator~() { return Num{~val_}; }
int& Num::operator*() { return val_; }
const int& Num::operator*() const { return val_; }

// Input and Output
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&os, const Num& arg) { return os<<*arg; }
std::istream& operator>>(std::istream&is, Num& arg) { return is>>*arg; } 
```

**Listing 16.24**     A data type almost fully equipped with all operators.

Note that it is not necessary to declare <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> as a <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp>. You could also implement it as a free function with two parameters. This will automatically implement <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>. My implementation is identical to <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp>—which would have also saved me from implementing <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> is derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>.

I have omitted <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> everywhere to avoid impairing readability. Now you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">Num</samp> as you are accustomed to.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/YonbGKj8M
#include <iostream>                       // cout
int main() {
    using std::cout;
    Num a{1};
    *a = 7;                               // operator* also returns int&
    a += Num{3};                          // Increment with Num
    cout << ( ++( ++a ) ) << "\n";        // Output: 12
    a -= 2;                               // Variation with int
    cout << --(--a) << "\n";              // Output: 8
    Num b{99};
    cout << (a<b ? "yes\n" : "xxx\n");    // Output: yes
    cout << (a>b ? "xxx\n" : "no\n");     // Output: no
    b /= Num{3};           // b: 33
    b %= Num{10};          // b: 3
    b <<= 4;               // b: 48
    b >>= 2;               // b: 12
    Num c = b / Num{3} + a * Num{2};      // c: 20
} 
```

**Listing 16.25**     You use the data type equipped with operators as usual.

According to these principles, you can also implement the operators for Boolean logic in a more suitable data type.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/vjrr6d5TW
#include <iostream>               // istream, ostream, cout
class Bool {
    bool val_ = false;
    bool& operator*()             // dereference; mutable
        { return val_; };
    const bool& operator*() const // dereference; read-only
        { return val_; }
public:
    constexpr Bool() {}
    explicit constexpr Bool(bool value)
        : val_{value} {}
    // unary operators
    Bool operator!() const        // not operator
        { return Bool{!val_}; };
    // binary operators
    friend Bool operator&&(const Bool &re, const Bool &li)
        { return Bool{*re && *li}; }
    friend Bool operator||(const Bool &re, const Bool &li)
        { return Bool{*re || *li}; }
    // input and output
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Bool& arg);
    friend std::istream& operator>>(std::istream& is,  Bool& arg);
};
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Bool& arg)
    { return os << *arg; }
std::istream& operator>>(std::istream& is, Bool& arg)
    { return is >> *arg; }
// Constants
static constexpr Bool False{false};
static constexpr Bool True{true};
int main() {
    Bool yesno = True && ( Bool{false} || !Bool{} ); // uses &&, ||, and !
    std::cout << yesno << "\n"; // Output: 1
} 
```

**Listing 16.26**     This data type demonstrates the Boolean operators.

The unary not operator <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> is also implemented as a method, and the binary logical operators <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> as free functions.

I also define the <samp class="listingcharacter">True</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">False</samp> constants so that I can use them like literals in expressions more easily. To be able to do this everywhere, it is advisable to use the consistent declaration with <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> and do the same for the constructors of <samp class="listingcharacter">Bool</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> on the constructor makes <samp class="listingcharacter">Bool</samp> a literal data type. This allows you to use <samp class="listingcharacter">Bool</samp> in other <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> expressions as well. You can learn more about this in [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), [Section 18.6](#18_006.html_h18.6).

I should go into more detail about <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp>. Here is the definition again:

```
constexpr auto operator<=>(const Num& re, const Num& li) {
    return *re <=> *li;
} 
```

Instead of letting the compiler deduce the return type with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, you can also specify an explicit return type. This must be one of the comparison category types from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><compare</samp>> header. If you now write <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> with an explicit return type, the predefined constants in the corresponding category are suitable:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">strong_ordering</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">equal</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">greater</samp>
    You use this when every value of your type can be compared with every other value of your type—including itself—as less, equal, or greater. A typical example of this is <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>; any <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values can always be compared.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">weak_ordering</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">equivalent</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">greater</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">strong_ordering</samp>, but some values are equivalent instead of equal. Strings, when case is ignored, are an example.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">partial_ordering</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">equivalent</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">greater</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">weak_ordering</samp>, but there can be values of the type that cannot be compared at all. Floating-point numbers with <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp> are an example.

This might look like the following listing for your data type.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/KxWb4q8q9
#include <compare>  // partial_ordering etc
#include <set>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
struct Fraction {
  int z, n;  // numerator / denominator
  partial_ordering operator<=>(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    if(n==0 || rhs.n==0) return partial_ordering::unordered;
    return (double)z / n <=> (double)rhs.z / rhs.n;
  }
};
int main() {
  set<Fraction> fractions{ {1,2},{2,4},{1,3},{2,3},{1,4},{2,5},{3,8},{99,0} };
  for(auto f : fractions)
    cout << f.z << "/" << f.n << " ";
  cout << "\n”; // Output: 1/4 1/3 3/8 2/5 1/2 2/3
} 
```

**Listing 16.27**     The comparison categories contain constants for the return.

I know, my <samp class="listingcharacter">fraction</samp> is not really competitive compared to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ratio</samp>.

As you can see, the output is sorted by size. The incomparable element ends up at the end. You also see that <samp class="listingcharacter">2/4</samp> is missing in the output because it corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">1/2</samp>. The fraction <samp class="listingcharacter">99/0</samp> does not appear at all due to incomparability.

It is best to rely on the built-in overloads of <samp class="listingcharacter"><=></samp>, as shown here with <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>.

You can compare the return of <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<=></samp> with zero to see if the comparison resulted in equal, less, or greater. For example, you can implement comparison chains with multiple criteria:

```
auto operator<=>(const Address& re) const {
  auto cmp = street <=> re.street;
  if(cmp != 0) return cmp;  // not equal, result is clear

  cmp = zip <=> re.zip;
  if(cmp != 0) return cmp;  // not equal, result is now clear

  return city <=> re.city;
} 
```

For this case, there is also the practical <samp class="listingcharacter">lexicographical_compare_three_way(a,b)</samp> algorithm.

```
auto operator<=>(const Address& re) const {
  array a{street, zip, city};
  array b{re.street, re.zip, re.city};
  return lexicographical_compare_three_way(begin(a), end(a), begin(b), end(b));
} 
```

**Listing 16.28**     You can use this helper function to implement a simple ordered comparison.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">lexicographical_compare_three_way</samp> algorithm takes two pairs of iterators, which is why I create two <samp class="listingcharacter">arrays</samp> here that contain elements to compare.

Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">a <=> b</samp>, there is also the <samp class="listingcharacter">compare_three_way(a,b)</samp> functor, which in most cases does the same thing but may handle pointers better.

## 16.12    Special Class Forms

In C++, there are special class forms that help you structure your code. Abstract classes and methods allow you to define an interface first without implementing it. Enumeration classes, in turn, bundle possible values of a class.

### 16.12.1    Abstract Classes and Methods

You learned about virtual methods in [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15). With these, you can do something very special—namely, methods without implementation.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/1zq4jfdYb
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
using std::string; using std::ostream;

class Shape {
    string color_;
public:
    virtual double calcArea() const = 0; // pure virtual method
    string getColor() const { return color_; }
    void setColor(const string& color) { color_ = color; }
    virtual ~Shape() {}
};

class Square : public Shape {
    double len_;
public:
    explicit Square(double len) : len_{len} {}
    double calcArea() const override { return len_*len_; }
};

class Circle : public Shape {
    double rad_;
public:
    explicit Circle(double rad) : rad_{rad} {}
    double calcArea() const override { return 3.1415*rad_*rad_; }
};

struct Calculator {
    Shape& shape_;
    Calculator(Shape& shape) : shape_{shape} { }
    void run(ostream& os) const {
        os << "The area of the shape is " << shape_.calcArea() << "\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    Square square {5.0};
    Calculator ti { square };
    ti.run(std::cout); // Output: The area of the shape is 25
} 
```

**Listing 16.29**     A virtual method that is <samp class="listingcharacter">= 0</samp> is called pure virtual or abstract.

The base <samp class="listingcharacter">Shape</samp> class knows that <samp class="listingcharacter">calcArea</samp> is supposed to calculate the areas of shapes. However, it does not know how. Therefore, the method is pure virtual, marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">= 0</samp>. Note that you should define a <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp> destructor if you mark at least one method as <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp>, even if you do not write any source code in the destructor. The compiler will insert cleanup code there. If you do not write <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp> yourself, the destructor generated by the compiler will not be <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp>.

The derived <samp class="listingcharacter">Square</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Circle</samp> classes know how to calculate <samp class="listingcharacter">calcArea</samp> and therefore implement this method.

A class with at least one pure virtual method is called an abstract class. It is not possible to instantiate an abstract class directly. The compiler will respond to the attempt with an error:

```
Shape form {}; // abstract class 
```

Classes that inherit from an abstract class must override all pure virtual methods if they do not want to be abstract themselves. Only then can you instantiate them.

In practice, users of the class then store a pointer or a reference to the abstract base class, just as <samp class="listingcharacter">Calculator</samp> does with <samp class="listingcharacter">Shape& shape_</samp>. A reference or pointer is necessary here to enable polymorphism. Without it, the value would be converted, and parts of it would be copied—which wouldn't even compile with abstract base classes.

As with polymorphic instances in general, you will often see that a base pointer is initialized with a concrete pointer:

```
Shape* shape1 = new Circle{5.0};
delete shape1; // don't forget, please
unique_ptr<Shape> shape2 = make_unique<Square>( 7.0 ); // safer 
```

In [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20), you will also see that for a <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> for a raw pointer, the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp> is of immense importance.

### 16.12.2    Enumeration Classes

You have learned that integer types like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and the string type <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> are very useful data types. For example, if you wanted to write a <samp class="listingcharacter">Stoplight</samp> class, you could use it to represent the current light. With an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, you would “remember” that <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> stands for red, <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> for yellow, and <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp> for green. Or you could use a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and consistently use the literals <samp class="listingcharacter">"red"</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">"yellow"</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">"green"</samp>. You can avoid typos by defining constants like <samp class="listingcharacter">const string RED = "red";</samp>.

However, the ubiquitous <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> types are often referred to as type sinks—which roughly means “black holes for types.” Let's assume you wrote a method that takes a traffic light color:

```
Stoplight createStoplight(string lightColor, string lightName); 
```

Many things can go wrong here:

```
createStoplight("AX-001", YELLOW);        // Arguments swapped
createStoplight("yellowgreen", "AX-002"); // Undefined color used
createStoplight("grren", "AX-003");       // Typo in color 
```

These are all errors that the compiler does not notice—and perhaps you don't either, but only the customer does.

The solution is to write a <samp class="listingcharacter">StoplightColor</samp> enumeration class that defines the exact valid range—no more and no less.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xhd7s1YhE
#include <string>
using std::string;
enum class StoplightColor {
    RED, YELLOW, REDYELLOW, GREEN
};
struct Stoplight {
    StoplightColor color_;
    Stoplight(StoplightColor color, string name) : color_{color} {}
};

Stoplight createStoplight(StoplightColor color, string name) {
    return Stoplight{color, name};
}

int main() {
    Stoplight stoplight = createStoplight(StoplightColor::RED, "AX-001");
} 
```

**Listing 16.30**     With an “enum”, you define a type with its own value range.

Now you can implement different behaviors depending on the traffic light color. This is often used in <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statements or <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> chains:

```
string drivingSchool(Stoplight light) {
    switch(light.color_) {
      case StoplightColor::RED:
          return "stop";
      case StoplightColor::REDYELLOW:
          return "get ready";
      case StoplightColor::YELLOW:
          return "brake";
      case StoplightColor::GREEN:
          return "go";
    }
    abort(); // exhaustive switch, should not happen
} 
```

We've handled all possible cases in the switch, so the <samp class="listingcharacter">abort()</samp> should not occur. Alternatively, we could have defined a <samp class="listingcharacter">default:</samp> case.

It's good that with <samp class="listingcharacter">enum class</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">RED</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">YELLOW</samp> no longer enter the surrounding namespace, but having to always write the <samp class="listingcharacter">TrafficLightColor::</samp> prefix is cumbersome, especially in such a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp>. Therefore, since C++20, there is the possibility to bring the enumeration class into the current namespace with <samp class="listingcharacter">using enum TrafficLightColor</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/f8on7bs1Y
string drivingSchool(Stoplight light) {
    switch(light.color) {
      using enum StoplightColor;   // "StoplightColor::" can now be omitted
      case RED:
          return "stop";
      case REDYELLOW:
          return "get ready";
      case YELLOW:
          return "slow down";
      case GREEN:
          return "go";
    }
    abort(); // exhaustive switch, should not happen
} 
```

Individual values like <samp class="listingcharacter">using StoplightColor::RED</samp> can also be imported. This can be important to avoid name conflicts.

In other applications, the possible <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> values are backed by specific numerical values. You can access these with a type conversion. You can specify the numerical values in the enumeration class.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Yjbzrrnob
enum class Weekday {
    MO=1, TU, WE, TH, FR, SA, SU         // TU becomes 2, WE becomes 3, etc.
};
enum class Level {
   TRACE=1, DEBUG, INFO=10, ERROR, FATAL // gaps are also possible
};
void log(Level level) {
   int intLevel = (int)level;            // explicitly cast to an int
   if(intLevel > 10) { /* ... */ }
} 
```

**Listing 16.31**     In an “enum”, you can also specify the desired numerical values.

The C++ compiler assigns values incrementally after each explicitly specified value. Thus, in <samp class="listingcharacter">Level</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">DEBUG</samp> becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ERROR</samp> becomes 11, and <samp class="listingcharacter">FATAL</samp> becomes 12\. If, as a user, you need the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value of an element when using it, you can obtain the value through explicit type casting like <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)level</samp>.

# 17    Good Code, 4th Dan: Security, Quality, and Sustainability

In this chapter, I want to summarize some things that can particularly help you in the development of good software. Throughout the book, you will find many more tips, and, especially in [Chapter 29](#29_001.html_h29), a long collection, but each is only briefly touched upon.

The special thing about the tips in this chapter is that they are best applied from the very beginning. If you incorporate the ideas behind the rules into your daily programming routine, your perspective on C++ and your thinking with C++ will change in such a way that better code will automatically emerge.

## 17.1    The Rule of Zero

A class can be equipped with many functions for special purposes. You can initiate an automatic conversion, you can specify how a class should be copied, and so on.

Read the following paragraphs at ease—because at the end I will tell you that you should not implement any of these functions.

### 17.1.1    The Big Five

Pay special attention to the following special functions:

*   Destructor <samp class="listingcharacter">~Type()</samp>
    The compiler generates a destructor for you that cleans up member variables but does not call <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp> for raw pointers or <samp class="listingcharacter">delete[]</samp> for C-arrays (see [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20)). If your class has such fields, you need to write a destructor.

*   Copy constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">Type(const Type&)</samp>
    If you do not write a copy constructor yourself, the compiler generates one. However, this only copies all fields. This is bad for raw pointers, for example, because then two objects point to the same memory object; it looks like both “own” the object. And if you (rightly) wrote your own destructor, then both will call <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp> on the same memory object. You need to write a copy constructor yourself that copies the content of pointers.

*   Assignment operator <samp class="listingcharacter">Type& operator=(const Type&)</samp>
    If you do not write the assignment operator yourself, but raw pointers belong to the class, then the compiler generates an assignment that simply overwrites the current pointers without deleting them first. In addition, after the assignment, both objects point to the same memory area: doubly bad. Therefore, with raw pointers, you need to intervene yourself and copy the content again.

*   Move constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">Type(Type&&)</samp>
    Again, raw pointers are a problem here. The code the compiler generates for raw pointers in a move constructor just copies the pointer itself. This would mean two pointers to the same data. If you really want to move, you have to implement it yourself. If the compiler doesn’t generate the copy constructor, it also doesn’t generate the move constructor.

*   Move operator <samp class="listingcharacter">Type& operator=(Type&&)</samp>
    Just like with the move constructor, a move operator generated by the compiler does not handle raw pointers satisfactorily. You have to take matters into your own hands. Also, if the compiler doesn’t generate the assignment operator, it also doesn’t generate the move operator.

It is said that if you need to implement even one of these five functions, then you must implement the others as well. This is the rule of five. This is because all these functions need to handle unclear ownership scenarios. And if you need to manage such ownership in one of the functions, then you must do so in the others as well.

You may have noticed that what the compiler can generate was mentioned each time. And each time, raw pointers and dynamically allocated C-arrays are the member variables that need special attention.[[ 41 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn17_01)

### 17.1.2    Helper Construct by Prohibition

Instead of tackling the not-so-simple task of implementing all these functions, you can at least prohibit them. If you disable all copy and move operations, then ownership cannot get mixed up.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/K1714eWr9
struct Type {
    char* data_;             // raw pointer can cause unclear ownership
    explicit Type(int n) : data_(new char[n]) {}
    ~Type() { delete[] data_; }             // you need the destructor

    Type(const Type&) = delete;             // do not allow copying
    Type& operator=(const Type&) = delete;  // no assignment please
    Type(Type&&) = delete;                  // no moving
    Type& operator=(Type&&) = delete;       // no move assignment operator
}; 
```

**Listing 17.1**     Prohibit four of the big five with “= delete”.

So, if you unfortunately have a type that has a problematic field (which you cannot or do not want to get rid of), then for your safety, your first step should be to prohibit accidental copying and moving, as shown in [Listing 17.1](#17_001.html_l17.1).

By using <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp> after critical operations, you prevent the compiler from generating inappropriate functions.

### 17.1.3    The Rule of Zero and Its Application

Am I scaring you away from using raw pointers? Good! Because the solution to the puzzle, the philosopher's stone, the holy grail is this: take advantage of the compiler's ability to generate functions for you. You just need to allow it to do so correctly.

This is a dan chapter, and you won't learn how to handle raw pointers until [Chapter 20](#20_001.html_h20). But as I want to discourage you from using raw pointers anyway, this preview has its advantages. First, memorize the alternatives. However, you will encounter one or another raw pointer in the following paragraphs.

The most important thing is that you do not use raw pointers that own data—that is, having requested them with <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and thus being implicitly responsible for calling delete. Instead, use what the standard library offers you:

*   For large amounts of data, there are containers. You no longer need to build linked structures yourself; you have a wide selection.

*   Every <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> should only go directly into a smart pointer. Better yet, use <samp class="listingcharacter">make_shared</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">make_unique</samp>.

*   With smart pointers, you no longer need <samp class="listingcharacter">delete</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">delete[]</samp>. These are abolished for you.

*   Do not define any of the big five operations. Let the compiler handle it. This is the rule of zero.

*   There are objects that cannot be copied, such as a stream or a mutex. If your class holds such fields, the compiler does the right thing: it forbids copying. Under certain circumstances, the ability to move may remain. Stick to the rule of zero here.

The C++ Core Guidelines also place great emphasis on the identification of ownership. The Guideline Support Library defined therein offers tools such as <samp class="listingcharacter">owner<T></samp> to mark an owning raw pointer. Raw pointers without <samp class="listingcharacter">owner<T></samp> do not own their target and are less problematic when copying. In [Chapter 30](#30_001.html_h30), I discuss these guidelines.

#### Write Your Classes Such That You Can Apply the Rule of Zero

If you use the corresponding structures of the standard library instead of the fields with ownership problems, the compiler will generate suitable copy and move operations as well as the destructor for your class.

Then you do not define or declare any of the big five operations for your class.

The previous example now becomes almost trivial. Depending on the use case, simply use a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> or smart pointers.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/nbh9aozPM
#include <vector>
#include <memory>            // unique_ptr, shared_ptr
struct Type1 {               // automatic complete copy of the resource
    std::vector<char> data_;
    Type1(int n) : data_(n) {}
};
struct Type2 {               // copy prohibited, move allowed
    std::unique_ptr<int[]> data_;
    Type2(int n) : data_(new int[n]) {}
};
struct Type3 {               // copy allowed, resource is then cleanly shared
    std::shared_ptr<Type1> data_;
    Type3(int n) : data_(std::make_shared<Type1>(n)) {}
}; 
```

**Listing 17.2**     Instead of using a raw pointer, use a standard construct and do not define any of the big five operations.

### 17.1.4    Exceptions to the Rule of Zero

First: Third-party libraries in particular often contain things that leave incorrect ownership after copying—for example, GUI window and database handles. Often, developers do not consider harmful copies and do not prohibit them. Here, I recommend two techniques:

*   Resort to manually prohibiting copying and moving. The destructor you write must then handle the correct removal, just like with a raw pointer.

*   If you feel confident with C++ and smart pointers, you can use their custom deleters to handle the wrapped resource instead of the raw one. The smart pointer then manages the correct removal, and you can dispense with the big five. In some cases, the compiler even generates usable copy and move operations.

Second: When writing a class hierarchy that includes virtual methods, you must write the destructor of the base class and mark it with <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp> (see [Chapter 15](#15_001.html_h15)). The body can be empty—and it will be, if you have followed the other guidelines of the rule of zero.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6vsqnWeWh
struct Base {
    virtual ~Base() {};  // define the destructor, make it virtual
    virtual void other()
};

struct Derived : public Base {
    void other() override
};

int main() {
    Base *obj = new Derived{};
    /* ... more lines of code here ... */
    delete obj;          // works because Base::~Base is virtual
} 
```

**Listing 17.3**     In a hierarchy with virtual methods, you must define and mark the base class destructor as virtual.

If you don't declare the destructor, the compiler will generate one. The compiler would generate it as non-<samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp>, and that would be bad: If the destructor is not <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual</samp>, deleting a pointer to a derived class could call the wrong destructor, as shown in the example with the <samp class="listingcharacter">delete obj</samp> line in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>. If you omit <samp class="listingcharacter">virtual ~Base() {}</samp>, the program would be incorrect.

But wait: the preceding program does not follow the rule of zero guidelines. I used a raw <samp class="listingcharacter">Base *obj</samp> pointer as an owner. That needs to be remedied. You can do this, for example, by using a <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp>. The good news is that if you use it, you won't have a problem with incorrect cleanup even if you forget the virtual destructor. The <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp> has built-in mechanisms that do more than the compiler alone: when removing its ward, it always calls the correct destructor, virtual or not.

```
int main() {
    shared_ptr<Base> obj{ new Derived{} };
    /* ... more lines of code here ... */
} // obj is correctly cleaned up 
```

**Listing 17.4**     <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp> always calls the correct destructor, virtual or not.

That's one more reason not to use raw pointers as owners.

If you need a polymorphic pointer, use <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp> instead of raw pointers.

You will know when a pointer is polymorphic: when you create pointers within an object hierarchy where the classes have virtual methods—that is, when the type of the pointer variable (here <samp class="listingcharacter">Base*</samp>) is different from the type of the <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> (here <samp class="listingcharacter">Derived*</samp>). With <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp>, this does not work without additional mechanisms.

You can implement assignment and move assignment together by passing the argument by value (as a compiler-generated copy) and swapping the contents via <samp class="listingcharacter">swap()</samp>:

```
struct Data {

    // … other special functions and implementation …
    Data& operator=(Data copy) { // by value, assignment, move assignment
        copy.swap(*this);
        return *this;
    }

    void swap(Data& other) { // member function
        using std::swap;
        // … element-wise swap …
    }

    friend void swap(Data&a, Data&b); // friend: free function
} 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp> function is useful anyway. To work well with containers, it is best to also provide the free <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp> function.

### 17.1.5    Rule of Zero, Rule of Three, Rule of Five, Rule of Four and a Half

There are many tips on which of the big five special functions you should implement. I will summarize the various aspects here:

*   Rule of zero
    First, check if it is possible not to implement any of the special functions. Let the compiler generate them or declare them with <samp class="listingcharacter">= default</samp> (this documents that you have not forgotten the aspect). This is applicable if your class does not need to manage resources itself.

*   Rule of four and a half
    If your class manages resources, starting with a destructor, implement all five—but you can combine assignment and move assignment (so, four). Use a self-implemented <samp class="listingcharacter">swap()</samp> (four and a half).

*   Rule of five
    Implement assignment and move assignment separately and optionally provide <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp>.

*   Rule of three
    Your class manages resources, but the benefit of moving is not so relevant: write a copy constructor, assignment operator, and destructor. If the compiler wants to move, it will copy instead.

## 17.2    Resource Acquisition Is Initialization

RAII means that when creating an object—a resource—its initialization is also done. In C++, this happens in the constructor. It is important to always leave a valid object when exiting the constructor.

This means, in particular, that even an error must not leave an invalid object lying around. If an error occurs during the initialization of the object in the constructor, you must not leave half-created data structures lying around or still blocking resources. Resource can mean many things here, such as a pointer to reserved memory, an open file, or a lock for mutual exclusion of multiple processes.

In case of an error, the constructor should be exited with an exception so that higher levels can also release their resources, such as requested memory. However, the exception must also be carefully triggered: previously requested resources must be released beforehand (or in a separate <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> with rethrow) as the current instance does not (normally) regain control after the <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>.

One aspect of valid is that the associated destructor must be able to completely remove the object in any case on its own and release all still existing resources. Taken together, this very effectively implements stack-based resource management.

### 17.2.1    An Example with C

A typical C API often shifts administrative tasks into the program code that uses the API. A file object or a database connection must be opened and closed again with a symmetric call. Handles for fonts, brushes, or audio-video codecs are obtained and explicitly released again. If the releasing call is not made—due either to an unforeseen event or simply forgetting—the associated resources are not released. The file remains open; the database connection is not closed; the handles on brushes and fonts run out.

Correspondingly, in the C world, special return values are often used to indicate an error. As a sign that the client should refrain from using the resource, many functions use specific error codes. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">mktime()</samp> returns a –1 instead of the requested conversion in case of an error. And you must check the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">malloc()</samp> against the null pointer.

Usually, the error case in the check is the rarely expected result. One might almost omit the check because this case “never happens anyway.” Then one can only hope that the code is never used in a safety-critical environment.[[ 42 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn17_02)

And as it is rarely expected, we come to the exception: in the C++ world, exceptions are available for such errors. The return value does not need to be checked because a constructor must leave an object in a valid state. If the constructor exits via an exception, the preallocated memory is released by the compiler. If the exception passes through multiple constructors on the stack (the list of current function calls) upward without being caught by a matching <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>, then all previous constructions are undone. Only exactly then, when a constructor has been completely executed, is the object considered valid and fully created.

A small, lean example class that is only supposed to encapsulate a character buffer could look like the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/9eeG575Wz
struct Buffer {
  const char *data;
  explicit Buffer(unsigned sz): data(new char[sz]) {}
  ~Buffer() { delete[] data; }
  Buffer(const Buffer&) = delete;
  Buffer& operator=(const Buffer&) = delete;
}; 
```

**Listing 17.5**     An RAII character buffer class.

It should be mentioned that—true to the idea that there are “sixteen ways to stack a cat”—the same task could be better accomplished using <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr<char[]></samp>; this is just a simple example.

In C, this would usually involve a <samp class="listingcharacter">malloc</samp>, and (careful or paranoid[[ 43 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn17_03)) programmers would need to check the return value to see if the memory was allocated correctly. If not, the process must be aborted somehow. In C++, <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> always returns a valid pointer or throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_alloc</samp> exception. So there are two possible outcomes from the constructor:[[ 44 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn17_04)

*   Normal run
