Therefore, <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX2</samp> also works on <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and even on <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5zrfvovaW
#include <string>
#include <cmath> // sin, cos
#define MAX2(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))
int main() {
    double e = MAX2(sin(3.141592/2), cos(3.141592/2));
    int i = MAX2(10+12+45, 100/5+20);
    std::string s = MAX2(std::string("Ernie"), std::string("Bert"));
} 
```

However, type variability is better achieved in C++ with overloading. You can define <samp class="listingcharacter">max2</samp> for each type you use:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6xzTx83zE
#include <string>
#include <cmath> // sin, cos
constexpr double max2(double a, double b) { return  a > b ? a : b; }
constexpr int max2(int a, int b) { return  a > b ? a : b; }
std::string max2(const std::string &a, const std::string &b)
    { return  a > b ? a : b; }

int main() {
    double e = max2(sin(3.141592/2), cos(3.141592/2));
    double i = max2(10+12+45, 100/5+20);
    std::string s = max2("Ernie", "Bert");
} 
```

As you can see, in the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">max2("Ernie", "Bert")</samp>, it has even more advantages. First, the function does not reevaluate the arguments, and second, you save the explicit type conversion from <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[] "Ernie"</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string("Ernie")</samp>. The function <samp class="listingcharacter">max2()</samp> takes <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> as arguments, and the compiler recognizes that it can convert <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>.

Perhaps you want to implement <samp class="listingcharacter">max2</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> but with more intelligence than for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>—possibly without distinguishing between uppercase and lowercase. As a macro, there can only be a single <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX2</samp>, and with overloaded functions, you can make each implementation look different if necessary.

However, if the body of all <samp class="listingcharacter">max2</samp> functions is identical, then the necessary duplicate code is cumbersome and does not comply with the guidelines for good code. Therefore, I would like to provide you with a recipe that shows you how to avoid using macros in this case—as that would be even less in line with the guidelines for good code (according to the rules of this book).

If it comes to the point where you need to implement a function identically for all possible (or at least several) types, write the function as a simple function template. This is a preview, but don't worry, it's quite simple:

*   First, write one of the implementations with a specific type like <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>.

*   Take the type that changes in all implementations and replace it with the word <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp>.

*   Write <samp class="listingcharacter">template <typename TYPE></samp> in the line before the function.

Done. It looks like the following listing for <samp class="listingcharacter">max2</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/acMjvxcM5
#include <string>
#include <cmath> // sin, cos
template<typename TYPE>
constexpr TYPE max2(const TYPE &a, const TYPE &b)
    { return  a > b ? a : b; }
int main() {
    double e = max2(sin(3.141592/2), cos(3.141592/2));
    double i = max2(10+12+45, 100/5+20);
    std::string s = max2(std::string("Ernie"), std::string("Bert"));
} 
```

**Listing 21.6**     A simple function template is much better than a macro.

Congratulations! You have written your first function template. This implementation is as flexible as a macro, as fast as overloaded functions, and most importantly, type-safe.

And starting from C++20, even abbreviated function templates are possible:

```
constexpr auto max2(const auto &a, const auto &b) { return  a > b ? a : b; } 
```

If you want, you can even add overloads for individual types. And that's exactly what you should do if you want to get rid of the annoying explicit conversions to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> for the arguments <samp class="listingcharacter">"Ernie"</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">"Bert"</samp>. If you omit them here, the compiler will try to find an overload for <samp class="listingcharacter">max2(const char[6], const char[5])</samp>. It won't succeed because they are two different types—but in the template, I used only one <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp>, and it must match exactly in both places. So the template does not match the call. Therefore, simply add another overload:

```
const char* max2(const char* a, const char* b) {
    return  std::string(a) > std::string(b) ? a : b;
} 
```

This also immediately solves the problem that comparing two <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> is by no means a comparison of the texts, but only of the addresses of the pointers. Converting to <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> specifically for the comparison with <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> solves the problem—albeit not elegantly. Unfortunately, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, unlike for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, is not <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>, and the compiler thus does not allow the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> on <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> in a function marked as <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>. But at least you now have a template for almost all cases—and an extra overload for a useful special case.

### [Übung]  C++20: “consteval” and “constinit” Bring Even More Macro Replacements

With <samp class="listingcharacter">consteval</samp>, you can mark functions from C++20 onward that the compiler can guarantee to compute at compile time. Normally, it will then use the result at the point of use. With <samp class="listingcharacter">constinit</samp>, you can declare variables from C++20 onward that the compiler guarantees to compute at compile time.

By the way, you can save yourself the conversion of the <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp> literal because the compiler automatically interprets string literals with the <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> suffix as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp>. So you can write the following:

```
std::string s = max2("Ernie"s, "Bert"s); 
```

However, you must have included <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""s</samp> beforehand—for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std::literals</samp>.

## 21.7    Summary

For clarity, [Table 21.1](#21_007.html_t21.1) lists the most important preprocessor directives once again. I have added a few more with a brief explanation.

| Directive | Explanation |

| <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> | Include another file |

| <samp class="listingcharacter">#elifdef</samp> | Alternative check if an identifier is defined (C++23) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#elifndef</samp> | Alternative check if an identifier is not defined (C++23) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#if</samp> | Check preprocessor expression |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#else</samp> | Alternative source code to one of the preprocessor <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>s |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#elif</samp> | Alternative source code and another check |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">#endif</samp> | End of the alternative source code |

# 22    Interface to C

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   C library with C interface
    Extension often provided by third parties.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">extern "C"</samp>
    Mark a function so that it can be used by C++ programs.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> pointer
    Non-type-safe raw pointer type, to and from which all raw pointer types can be converted; often part of C interfaces.

*   Custom delete function or custom deleter
    Feature of <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp>, which can be useful for releasing C resources.

If you are writing a program that uses third-party libraries, then there is a good chance that these libraries come with a C interface. Fortunately, C++ is written in such a way that you can definitely include libraries for C as well. So your choice is not limited.

What is limited is your choice of language features. If you want to use a C library, you can only use C language elements. Here is a by no means exhaustive list of restrictions that you have to accept:

*   You have no classes. Structures can only have certain elements; for example, constructors are omitted, and everything must be public. For simplicity, you should only have data elements.

*   There are no references. You pass a value or raw pointer.

*   Many things from the C++ standard library are taboo. You cannot use standard containers, strings, or streams, but the C++ language designers have thought about interaction possibilities.

*   C functions do not throw exceptions. You usually deal with error codes as return values or parameters.

*   There are no overloaded functions in C; each name has a fixed set of parameter types (this has partially changed with C11). <samp class="listingcharacter">operator</samp> functions do not exist either.

*   You will rarely encounter <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> with parameters. When <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> is present, it is more for documentation purposes. You cannot be sure that the C function does not modify your parameter passed by pointer.

After this theoretical list, we dive into practice. As an example, I have chosen the zlib[[ 52 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn22_01) C library, which I want to integrate.

The zlib library contains functions for compressing data. This means that redundant information is removed, leaving a smaller package of data that you can, for example, transfer over the internet or store on a hard drive. A group of functions in the library is used for reading and writing <samp class="listingcharacter">*.gz</samp> files—a widely used data format. If you have a program on your computer for packing or unpacking files (e.g., 7zip or WinZip), you can most likely also unpack <samp class="listingcharacter">*.gz</samp> files. One difference of <samp class="listingcharacter">*.gz</samp> compared to other packing formats is that each packed file may contain only exactly one original file. It is common to simply append <samp class="listingcharacter">.gz</samp> to the original file name when the file has been compressed.

## 22.1    Working with Libraries

A C library that you include consists of the following components:

*   Library file
    You link your program with the library file to  use the third-party functions. These are one or more <samp class="listingcharacter">*.a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*.dll</samp> (Windows), or <samp class="listingcharacter">*.so</samp> files (Linux). In rare cases, you also receive the source code and link the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.o</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">*.obj</samp> object files to your program.

*   Header files
    You are usually provided with several <samp class="listingcharacter">*.h</samp> files. You need to include these in your source code with <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp>.

*   Documentation
    Sometimes you get a separate document; sometimes you only have the header.

How you make the library and header known during translation is very compiler-dependent. Refer to the documentation on how to adjust the library and include path and how to link a specific library.

With g++, this example is translated as follows:

```
g++ gzpack.cpp -o gzpack.x -lz -Lzlib -Izlib/include 
```

You should already be familiar with the <samp class="listingcharacter">g++ gzpack.cpp -o gzpack.x</samp> part. The remaining parameters are as follows:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">-lz</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">-l</samp> means that a library should be linked. Here it is <samp class="listingcharacter">z</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">libz</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">-Lzlib</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">-L</samp> specifies search paths for libraries; here <samp class="listingcharacter">libz.a</samp> is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter">zlib</samp> directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">-Izlib/include</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">-I</samp> specifies search paths for header files; here <samp class="listingcharacter">zlib.h</samp> is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter">zlib/include</samp> directory.

## 22.2    C Header

The demonstration program creates a compressed output file from any input file. Only three functions from zlib are needed for this. The documentation contains a lot of information about those functions, which I recommend you read. I focus here on the information in the header file or the function signatures from the documentation (some things are simplified). For your own experiments and to replicate the examples, you should of course use the original library:

```
typedef struct gzFile_s *gzFile;
extern "C" gzFile gzopen (const char *path, const char *mode);
extern "C" int  gzwrite (gzFile file, voidpc buf, unsigned len);
extern "C" int  gzclose (gzFile file); 
```

These and many other types and functions are available to you when you include the following in your source code:

```
#include <zlib.h> 
```

First, the <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef</samp> introduces the new <samp class="listingcharacter">gzFile</samp> type. This is a pointer to <samp class="listingcharacter">struct gzFile_s</samp>. Its internal details are intentionally not mentioned because they are irrelevant. Consider <samp class="listingcharacter">gzFile</samp> simply as a handle  that allows you to access the <samp class="listingcharacter">*.gz</samp> file.

The three functions are free functions, and all parameters and returns are either built-in types or raw pointers—very common in C.

Each function is introduced with <samp class="listingcharacter">extern "C"</samp> so that as a C++ author, when you include that header, you can distinguish C++ functions from C functions. This is necessary because C++ uses different mechanisms when searching for the appropriate function; this is important for overloading and the like. So, coming from C++, every function signature you want to use must be marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">extern "C"</samp>. If this is missing in a header, you can alternatively include it in your source code in a slightly more cumbersome way:

```
extern "C" {
    #include <zlib.h>
} 
```

So you wrap the entire <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp> in a large <samp class="listingcharacter">extern "C"</samp>.

After you have the header, you continue with the rest of the program. In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter"><zlib.h></samp>, you also need some of the usual C++ headers from the standard library. For error handling with zlib, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><cerrno></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstring></samp> C headers are necessary. The former allows querying the global error code variable, <samp class="listingcharacter">errno</samp>, which zlib uses; this is stated in the documentation. The latter provides <samp class="listingcharacter">strerror</samp> to convert an error code into a readable text message. Both headers are part of the C standard library. Therefore, each header exists in two variants: In C++, you use <samp class="listingcharacter"><cerrno></samp> when <samp class="listingcharacter"><errno.h></samp> is specified in the C documentation. Similarly, the C include <samp class="listingcharacter"><strings.h></samp> becomes <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstring></samp> for C++ programs. The “prefix with <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>, remove the <samp class="listingcharacter">.h</samp>” rule applies to most headers of the C standard library—but only to those, not to third-party libraries. The C++ variants are part of the C++ standard library and guarantee, for example, that each function also gets its <samp class="listingcharacter">extern "C"</samp>. In addition, all C functions imported this way are provided in the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp> namespace. Therefore, you can also call the function via <samp class="listingcharacter">std::strerror()</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/9Trh8h8Mb
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <span>      // C++20
#include <fstream>   // ifstream
#include <stdexcept> // runtime_error
#include <iostream>  // cerr
// C-Header:
#include <zlib.h>    // gzXyz; sudo aptitude install libz-dev
#include <cerrno>    // errno
#include <cstring>   // strerror
namespace {
using std::string; using std::span; using std::byte; 
```

**Listing 22.1**     The “gzpack.cpp” program uses a C library. Here you see the section with the includes.

In the second-to-last line, I start with <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace {</samp>—an anonymous namespace. This hides all variables, types, and functions in this <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file from potential conflicts with others. Instead of free functions, you could also write <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, but for data types, this is only possible through an anonymous namespace, which is often a good idea.

With the two <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> declarations, I save typing effort for the rest of the source code. Another advantage of the anonymous namespace is that the two <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp> declarations also apply only within the namespace and do not affect the outside.

Next, I define the class that bundles the main functionality of the C library. In this example, all three relevant C functions are already included. Based on the names, you can probably already guess the meanings and some of the operating rules:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Gzopen()</samp> opens a file. If it fails, the function returns a special value according to C conventions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Gzclose()</samp> closes a correctly opened file. The call is not necessary if <samp class="listingcharacter">gz-open</samp> failed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Gzwrite()</samp> writes data to the output. A return value greater than zero indicates success.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Yh7j1WEGc
class GzWriteStream {                         // RAII wrapper
public:
    gzFile gz_ ;                              // C struct from zlib.h
    explicit GzWriteStream(const string& filename)
        : gz_{gzopen(filename.c_str(),"wb9")} // 'w': write, 'b':binary, '9':level
    {
        if(gz_==NULL) throw std::runtime_error(std::strerror(errno));
    }
    ~GzWriteStream() {
        gzclose(gz_);
    }
    GzWriteStream& operator<<(const span<char> &data) {
        write(data);
        return *this;
    }
private:
    void write(span<char> data) {
        auto bytes = std::as_bytes(data);                    // C++20
        auto res = gzwrite(gz_, bytes.data(), size(bytes));
        if(res==0) throw std::runtime_error("Error writing");
    }
    GzWriteStream(const GzWriteStream&) = delete;            // no copy
    GzWriteStream& operator=(const GzWriteStream&) = delete; // no assignment
}; 
```

**Listing 22.2**     This part of “gzpack.cpp” contains all the C functions used.

As a data field, <samp class="listingcharacter">GzWriteStream</samp> contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">gz_</samp> handle as a connection to zlib and thus to the opened file. In the constructor's init list, <samp class="listingcharacter">gzopen()</samp> opens the file and assigns the result to the handle. The documentation states that a return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">NULL</samp> indicates an error. Then the global <samp class="listingcharacter">errno</samp> variable shows the exact error. You can decode this code with <samp class="listingcharacter">strerror</samp>. More importantly, you should also throw an exception and exit the code this way, instead of jumping out with a <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> or running to the end.

If <samp class="listingcharacter">gzopen()</samp> fails, then <samp class="listingcharacter">gzclose()</samp> is not necessary. Therefore, this is an optimal use case for using the destructor. If an exception leaves the constructor instead of running normally, the <samp class="listingcharacter">GzWriteStream</samp> object is considered not created. Thus, no destructor is called—and no <samp class="listingcharacter">gzclose()</samp> either.

The first parameter that <samp class="listingcharacter">gzopen()</samp> receives is the file name as a C string. From the <samp class="listingcharacter">filename</samp> parameter of <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, you can obtain the file name as a C string using the <samp class="listingcharacter">c_str()</samp> method. The second parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">"wb9"</samp> indicates that the file is opened for writing (<samp class="listingcharacter">'w'</samp> for write). The <samp class="listingcharacter">'b'</samp> stands for binary format. The alternative <samp class="listingcharacter">'t'</samp> for text format would potentially convert individual characters. The final <samp class="listingcharacter">'9'</samp> stands for maximum data compression.

## 22.3    C Resources

Packing the <samp class="listingcharacter">gzopen()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">gzclose()</samp> function pair together in the constructor and destructor of a class is particularly suitable here, as these two always need to be called in pairs. There is no (successful) <samp class="listingcharacter">gzopen()</samp> without <samp class="listingcharacter">gzclose()</samp>, and no <samp class="listingcharacter">gzclose()</samp> without <samp class="listingcharacter">gzopen()</samp>.

You deal with such pairings in many C interfaces. Whether it's initializing the entire library or acquiring and releasing a paintbrush for the window frame—such function pairs are common, and such a wrapper class is then appropriate.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">GzWriteStream</samp>, I have included even more functionality. Sometimes, however, you only need the pairing of two functions. Then it might be tedious to write a separate wrapper class for each pair. If that is too much work for you, you can fall back on your old acquaintance <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp>: you can use it in the variant where the constructor takes not one but two arguments.

The second argument here is a function object, which is called within the destructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp> calls this a custom deleter.

I will make a brief digression here, because as a function object you see a lambda—a function without a name—and within it <samp class="listingcharacter">gzclose()</samp> is called:

```
std::shared_ptr<gzFile_s> gz(
    gzopen(fNameOut.c_str(), "wb9"),
    [=](gzFile_s* f) { gzclose(f); } );
if(gz.get() == NULL) throw std::runtime_error("Error"); 
```

You will learn more about this in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.3](#23_003.html_h23.3).

You can almost always use this pattern with the <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp> constructor with two arguments for simple pairings of C functions.

## 22.4    “void” Pointers

The third function, <samp class="listingcharacter">gzwrite()</samp>, takes two parameters: a <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> to the data and the length of the data. The return value is the amount of data written; a value of zero indicates an error.

But what exactly is <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp>? Did you notice that our own <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> function, using the <samp class="listingcharacter">as_bytes</samp> function, created a <samp class="listingcharacter">span<byte></samp> whose <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp> method returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">const byte*</samp>, which I then passed to the <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">gzwrite()</samp>? Normally, C++ always complains when you take a variable of one type and try to use it as something else. Imagine if <samp class="listingcharacter">gzwrite()</samp> took an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>: then the <samp class="listingcharacter">const byte*</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">write</samp> wouldn't fit, and I would have had to define the parameter differently—or use a trick. And what if the data to be written are <samp class="listingcharacter">int*</samp> data or <samp class="listingcharacter">double*</samp>? Do you then need a <samp class="listingcharacter">gzwrite()</samp> function for each pointer type? Yes and no: <samp class="listingcharacter">gzwrite()</samp> doesn't really care whether the pointer points to <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned char</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> data, so long as you also provide the correct length of the data. And this is exactly where <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> comes into play: all raw pointer types can be converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> without the compiler complaining. What the respective function then does with these absolute raw data is entirely its own business. Here, it takes the raw data, whose length it knows, compresses it, and then writes it to the output file.

In a C function, it is more common to pass raw data of unspecified types as parameters. Often, you also pass the length of the raw data, and sometimes you pass a specific marker that describes the data in more detail. Less frequently, you don't need to provide any additional information. In that case, the address is only stored for later use, or the exact meaning is derived from the context.

When you work with <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp>, you unfortunately lose all type safety. The compiler accepts all raw pointers when converting to and from <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> and doesn't even warn you. Why would it? It assumes you know what you're doing when working with <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp>. I hope this will continue to be the case for you: use <samp class="listingcharacter">void*</samp> only when dealing with C programming interfaces. In the C++ world, you have type-safe means to handle variant data, such as function overloading or templates.

## 22.5    Reading Data

The following listing presents two simple helper functions that handle reading and writing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/84TcTbWjj
std::vector<char> readFile(const string& fName) {
    std::ifstream file{ fName, std::ifstream::binary };
    if(!file) throw std::runtime_error("Error opening input");
    file.seekg(0, file.end);           // jump to the end of the file
    const auto length = file.tellg();  // current position is file size
    if(length > 1024*1024*1024)
        throw std::runtime_error("No more than 1 GB please");
    file.seekg(0, file.beg);           // back to the beginning
    std::vector<char> data(length);    // allocate space
    file.read(data.data(), length);    // read in one go
    return data;                       // not copied (keyword: RVO)
}
void pack(const string& fNameIn, const string& fNameOut) {
    auto data = readFile(fNameIn);     // read input
    GzWriteStream gz{fNameOut};        // initialize output
    gz << data;
} 
```

**Listing 22.3**     This part of “gzpack.cpp” handles reading and writing the files.

It is somewhat tricky to read the data in one go into a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<char></samp>. First, <samp class="listingcharacter">tellg()</samp> determines the position of the end of the file, which was previously jumped to with <samp class="listingcharacter">seekg()</samp>. Another <samp class="listingcharacter">seekg()</samp> brings the read position back to the beginning so that <samp class="listingcharacter">file.read()</samp> reads from the start of the file. There could have been other ways to determine the file size, but they are not necessarily less complicated than this.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<char>::data()</samp> function returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp>, into which <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream::read()</samp> reads the data directly into the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> must have enough space allocated beforehand; that's why you create it with the <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> constructor argument in the appropriate size.

Besides <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, only <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> has such a <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp> method. No other standard container guarantees that its data is contiguous, allowing it to be read in one go with <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> and similar functions.

A word about <samp class="listingcharacter">return data;</samp>, where the return type is <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<char></samp>—a value, not a reference or pointer. Potentially, returning such a value type could require a large copy operation. However, the compiler and the standard library work together here to “avoid the copy” (copy elision). This is guaranteed in this case because all <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statements within the function return the same local variable; here it's trivial because there's only a single <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp>. In this case, the compiler never needs to create a copy for the return, even if it is returned by value. Before the standard mandated copy elision in this situation, this scenario was commonly referred to as return value optimization (RVO).

The <samp class="listingcharacter">pack()</samp> function starts with two trivial lines. The first line, <samp class="listingcharacter">readFile()</samp>, reads the input, and the second line, <samp class="listingcharacter">GzWriteStream gz</samp>, prepares the output. This is done using the overloaded <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>. For simplicity, I implemented it as a method. A free <samp class="listingcharacter">friend</samp> function would have been possible as well, but it is not necessarily needed here as the stream class is under my control—unlike with <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp>, where you can only work with a free function overload of <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>.

## 22.6    The Main Program

The conclusion is then formed by <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp> from [Listing 22.4](#22_006.html_l22.4). You will not encounter any surprises. You need to close the anonymous namespace opened in the first listing, then <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> begins.

A comprehensive <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp>-<samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> handles any exceptions that you might have thrown elsewhere in the program. <samp class="listingcharacter">exc.what()</samp> outputs an appropriate error message.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">fNamen</samp> vector stores all command-line arguments, which the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop then iterates over. In it, <samp class="listingcharacter">pack()</samp> calls the compression function.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5bWx6PzdP
} // namespace
int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    try {
        const std::vector<string> fNamen {argv+1, argv+argc};
        for(auto fName : fNamen) {
            std::cout << "packing " << fName << "... ";
            pack(fName, fName+".gz");
            std::cout << fName << ".gz"<< "\n";
        }
    } catch(std::runtime_error &exc) {
        std::cerr << "Error: " << exc.what() << "\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 22.4**     With “main” in “gzpack.cpp”, the example is complete.

## 22.7    Summary

Let’s conclude with a brief recap:

*   Virtually every third-party extension consists of a library and headers.

*   Include the header(s) with <samp class="listingcharacter">#include</samp>.

*   Look at the parameters and return types of the functions and choose the appropriate C++ ones.

*   Texts in <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> can usually be provided using <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>.

*   Large dynamic data sets with a raw pointer interact well with <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp>.

*   Specifically, look out for function pairs for resource management and consider managing them with a wrapper class or a custom deleter function via <samp class="listingcharacter">shared_ptr</samp> using C++ language features.

# 23    Templates

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Template
    A class template or function template.

*   Function template
    A template that takes a type as a template parameter to become a function.

*   Template function
    A complete function that is instantiated from a function template.

*   Class template
    Synonym for a parameterized type.

*   Template parameter
    A type that is fixed at compile time for a template; instead of a type, a template parameter can also be a constant number.

*   Parameterized type
    A class that takes another type (or a constant number) as a template parameter.

*   Instantiate template
    The moment of using a template with specific types (or constants); the compiler generates the program code at this moment.

*   Concept
    The <samp class="listingcharacter">concept</samp> language element allows templates to be constrained. This can make templates more consistent and generally leads to more understandable compiler error messages.

*   Function parameter, callback, or callback function
    A function that is passed as a parameter to a “worker function” and then called within the worker function.

*   C function pointer
    Pass a function parameter by address to a previously defined function.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">function<></samp> The C++ type of a function parameter.

*   Function object or functor
    A class that defines <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp>, or an instance of it.

*   Anonymous function or lambda expression
    A locally defined function without a name.

*   Capture clause
    List of outer variables that you can access from within a lambda expression.

*   Formal data type
    The type parameter in a template declaration.

*   User-defined literal
    When you override <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""</samp>, you define a suffix for custom character or numeric literals.

*   Fold expression
    Within a template with a variable number of arguments, the use of an operator like <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> together with <samp class="listingcharacter">...</samp> , which the compiler automatically concatenates.

I won't hide it: templates are difficult. But I want to make it easy for you, because if you completely avoid templates, you will miss out on most of the good things in C++.

The good news: You don't need to fully understand templates to use them. I would even argue that there are few people who have completely understood templates. However, you can still use them without too much mental gymnastics and thus get the most benefit from them. In fact, you have already used templates—namely, <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. And I very much hope that you have come to know and love <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> by now. The second faithful companion through most pages of this book, with whose help you have already used templates, is <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>—in its <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<double></samp>, or even <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<Car></samp> form.

So you have already dealt with the first aspect of templates: you use them as parameterized types. And that's exactly what a template is: a class that takes another type as a parameter is a class template. <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is one of them, and so is <samp class="listingcharacter">basic_string</samp>. Give <samp class="listingcharacter">basic_string</samp> a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> as a parameter, and you get this:

```
using string = basic_string<char>; 
```

Voilà! This is simplified, because <samp class="listingcharacter">basic_string</samp> can do a bit more. I will explain how to create templates—the class templates—once you have learned about function templates.

## 23.1    Function Templates

The second aspect of templates is function templates. Here, it is not a new class that takes a type as a parameter, but a function. You will learn this part just as quickly as using <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, because what you will be doing here is also not new: you are overloading functions. I will begin the explanation with this topic.

### 23.1.1    Overloading

Strictly speaking, a function parameter consists of two parts: the value and its type. At runtime, you can call a function with different values: sometimes with 5, sometimes with 42, sometimes with -10\. However, the type always remains the same.

A function where the type itself is variable is called a function template: Here, you must specify the type of a parameter in addition to its value when calling.

But first, let's consider a normal function like this:

```
void print(int value) {
    cout << value;
} 
```

You call it at runtime with the following:

```
print(5);
print(42);
print(-10.25); 
```

Here, the value of the parameter changes. Even if you pass a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> value like in <samp class="listingcharacter">print(‐10.25)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">void print(int)</samp> is still called, and the parameter<samp class="listingcharacter">-10.25</samp> is converted to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value <samp class="listingcharacter">-10</samp> for the call. So, for the last line, <samp class="listingcharacter">-10</samp> would be output instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">-10.25</samp>.

This is not a problem for you, because you can write a function overload for the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> type:

```
void print(double value) {
    cout << value;
} 
```

With this additional definition of <samp class="listingcharacter">print(double)</samp>, you also get the output <samp class="listingcharacter">-10.25</samp>. What do you get for the following line?

```
print("Flamingo"); 
```

You get an error message stating that there is no suitable overload for <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp>. Said and done:

```
void print(const char* value) {
    cout << value;
} 
```

And now <samp class="listingcharacter">print("Flamingo");</samp> works as well. But I'm starting to notice that the function body is always the same. It always says <samp class="listingcharacter">{ cout << value; }</samp>. If the program gets more types that you want to output to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp>, it becomes tedious. You also get a lot of code duplication, and you should avoid that.

### 23.1.2    A Type as Parameter

If you write it in such a way that the type is also flexible, it looks like this:

```
template<typename TYPE>
void print(TYPE value) {
    cout << value;
} 
```

One could say the function now has two parameters: <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> for the type of the argument and <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> for its value.

When calling it specifically, you now need to specify both things. As such, you write the type argument after the function name in angle brackets:

```
print<int>(5);
print<double>(-10.25);
print<const char*>("Flamingo"); 
```

But the compiler already knows that <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-10.25</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">"Flamingo"</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>. And when the compiler can make the choice for you, you can also omit the angle brackets and the explicit type when calling this function:

```
print(5);
print(-10.25);
print("Flamingo"); 
```

These lines are equivalent to the previous example. However, it is important to note that you now actually have three functions: one for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> as a parameter, one for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and one for <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>.

Note that whether you write <samp class="listingcharacter">template<</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">template<</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE></samp> is irrelevant. Both notations are equivalent, and it is a matter of taste or agreement to use one or the other. The standard library prefers <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> here, while I personally prefer <samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp>.

### 23.1.3    Function Body of a Function Template

The function body of <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> takes advantage of the fact that the output operator <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> is defined for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>. This is, of course, not true for all types.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/aMPj3K7EE
#include <iostream>
struct Number {
    int value_;
};
template<typename TYPE>
void print(TYPE value) {
    std::cout << value << "\n";
}
int main() {
    print(5);
    print(-10.25);
    print("Flamingo");
    Number seven { 7 };
    print(seven);    // cout << seven does not exist
} 
```

**Listing 23.1**     The call to a function template works so long as the function body is valid with the template parameters.

The compiler also generates a new function here—essentially:

```
void print(Number value) {
    std::cout << value;
} 
```

But for <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp>, there is no <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>. Therefore, the compilation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">print(seven);</samp> statement fails.

There is an important term you should remember: you instantiate a function template at the moment you actually call it with a specific type. This is important because it is only at that moment that the compiler checks whether the template's source code can be translated.

For example, you can make the listing compilable after the fact by adding:

```
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, Number z) {
    return os << z.value_;
} 
```

Think of it roughly as the compiler looking at the content of the function only at the moment you use it concretely. This “looking at” consists of the concrete type parameter being applied at all points and the function being truly generated—as if you had written it into the source code. This may not be a completely accurate perspective, but it is useful and sufficient for getting started.

If your terminology is to be precise, then use the following terms:

*   A function template is the blueprint.

*   You instantiate the function template by specifying the template parameters.

*   Then it becomes a function—more precisely, a template function.

The last distinction is only important in the context of overloads. When the compiler tries to determine the correct function for a call, it first goes through the real functions before considering the template functions. An instantiated function template ranks below normal functions without type parameters in the overload resolution hierarchy.[[ 53 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn23_01)

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/816Ys17aT
#include <iostream>
using std::cout;
template<typename TYPE>
  void func(TYP a) { cout << a <<" TYP\n"; }
void func(int a) { cout << a << " int\n"; }
int main() {
    func<int>(8); // Output: 8 TYP
    func(8);      // Output: 8 int
} 
```

**Listing 23.2**     With and without explicit type specification during the call.

This program first outputs <samp class="listingcharacter">8 TYP</samp> because the template function was explicitly requested with angle brackets.

However, both definitions would fit the second call. If there is both a matching function and a matching template function, the function is preferred during overload resolution.

#### [Übung]  C++20: Abbreviated Function Template

For the simple way to define a function for any parameter types, C++20 offers that you write an abbreviated function template. You can then omit <samp class="listingcharacter">template<…></samp> and instead use <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> as the argument type:

```
#include <iostream>
void show(auto a) { std::cout << a; } // no template<…>
int main() {
    show(8);
    show(6.66);
} 
```

Here, the compiler recognizes from <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> as the argument type that you actually mean and interprets it as the following code:

```
template<typename T> void show(T a) { std::cout << a; } 
```

So, using <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> as an argument type also introduces a function template.

### 23.1.4    Values as Template Parameters

In most cases, it is types that are template parameters of functions. However, there are indeed cases where the parameter is a value. You can use numbers like <samp class="listingcharacter">10</samp>, characters like <samp class="listingcharacter">'a'</samp>, and since C++20 also floating-point numbers like <samp class="listingcharacter">12.89</samp> as well as strings like <samp class="listingcharacter">"abc"</samp> and instances of structure types (literal and public) like <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> as template parameters.

You already know this with classes. <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> takes a constant number as its second parameter. <samp class="listingcharacter">array<int,10></samp> creates space for exactly <samp class="listingcharacter">10</samp> values of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. What happens if you want to write a function that sometimes creates an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> of size 10 and sometimes an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> of size 100? You already know that this doesn't work because <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is a variable and not a constant—or to be precise, not a <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>:

```
array<int,n> createArray(size_t n); 
```

But it almost works this way. Turn <samp class="listingcharacter">createArray</samp> into a function template and <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> into a template parameter instead of a simple function parameter, as in the next listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/c9xzM7EhP
#include <array>
#include <iostream> // cout
using std::array; using std::cout;
template<size_t SIZE>
array<int,SIZE> createArray() {
    array<int,SIZE> result{};
    return result;
}
int main() {
    auto data = createArray<5>();
    data[3] = 33;
    for(auto e : data) cout << e << " ";
    cout << "\n";
} 
```

**Listing 23.3**     A template parameter can also be a constant number.

The output will unsurprisingly be <samp class="listingcharacter">0 0 0 33 0</samp>. The mechanism is exactly the same as for types as parameters: the moment you use the function, you instantiate it. The compiler replaces all occurrences of the template parameter with what you specified at the call, and you get a completely new function. Essentially, the instantiated function for <samp class="listingcharacter">createArray<5>()</samp> looks like this:

```
array<int,5> createArray() {
    array<int,5> result{};
    return result;
} 
```

And because <samp class="listingcharacter">array<int,5></samp> as opposed to <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t n = 5; array<int,</samp>n<samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> is valid, the example works.

Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> works for values as template parameters. Then the value can take any valid type. However, this feature is rarely used.

```
template <auto value> void f() { }
f<10>();                // value gets type int
f<'a'>();               // value gets type char 
```

**Listing 23.4**     With <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> as a template parameter, you can specify any simple value.

Together with the variable number of template arguments <samp class="listingcharacter">...</samp>, you can specify any number of different types and values as template parameters. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> together with <samp class="listingcharacter">...</samp> is rarely needed.

```
template<auto ... vs> struct MixedList {};
using Three = MixedList<'a', 100, 'b'>;
Three three{}; 
```

**Listing 23.5**     With “auto” and <samp class="listingcharacter">…,</samp> you can specify any values as template parameters.

### 23.1.5    Many Functions

Instantiating a function template actually means that the compiler generates the entire function: function header and function body. If you call—sorry, instantiate—a function template with 20 different template parameters within a <samp class="listingcharacter">*.cpp</samp> file, then you actually get the function body 20 times, even if the function body always looks the same. However, the machine code that is generated often looks very different—for example, for <samp class="listingcharacter">print(5)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">print("Flamingo")</samp>. The output of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is certainly implemented very differently from the output of a string. For this reason, the compiler needs all these function variants (or template functions, as previously explained).

But don't worry: if the compiler notices that 18 of these variants produce the same machine code and only two variants are really different, then it will compress the duplicates of the functions before assembling the overall program. This is not a must, but any reasonably modern compiler is capable of doing this.

However, this “unrolling” of the function body at the moment of instantiation of the function has a huge advantage: the function body is tailored to the place of the call. The compiler can use this and actually save the call of the function. It can directly insert the function body of the function templates where you actually called a function.

This inlining has considerable speed advantages. An executed function call is always a huge slowdown during the runtime of any program. Not only do parameters have to be prepared, but the jump into the function and out of the function must also be executed. For current CPUs, a function call is like a construction site on the highway: internal memory areas can only be slowly refilled, planned overtaking maneuvers have to be aborted, and so on.

All in all, it is often very worthwhile if the compiler saves a function call. And function templates are the ultimate sign to tell the compiler to “inline, please.” Here, the compiler puts in a lot of effort.

### 23.1.6    Parameters with Extras

Some functions use the “pure” formal type of the template, while others qualify it:

```
template<typename TYPE>
TYPE add(TYPE a, TYPE b) {       // use the pure type
    return a + b;
}

template<typename TYPE>
void print(const TYPE& value) { // type enriched with const and &
    cout << value;
} 
```

It depends on what you want to do with the parameters in the function. Because the <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> function probably only makes sense for numbers, it will very likely only be applied to built-in types. Thus, passing parameters by value is very sensible: simply use <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp> function, on the other hand, looks like it could be used for all sorts of types—and you certainly want to avoid a copy if possible. By qualifying <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">const &</samp>, you ensure that the function generated by the compiler also declares the parameter as <samp class="listingcharacter">const &</samp>—for a by-reference parameter passing.

Establishing a general rule for when to use what is difficult. After all, you might overload <samp class="listingcharacter">operator+</samp> for a custom data type. And if you then call your new <samp class="listingcharacter">add()</samp> template—say, for <samp class="listingcharacter">Matrix</samp>—then a by-value parameter might be very costly.

Therefore, I want to give you the following guidelines:

*   If you are quite sure that your function template will only be called with very specific types, write the function—regarding the enrichments—as you would without templates.

*   If you don't have control over the type arguments, prefer to perform a calculation with a newly generated return value by value, as with <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp>.

*   Choose a reference (not <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>) if you want to modify the parameters. This is rather rare with templates, as you don't know exactly what type you will get.

*   You will often have <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> references, because if you only need to read, that is the most flexible option.

However, I don't want to hide from you that dealing with qualifiers is sometimes not that simple. Imagine that the <samp class="listingcharacter">TYP</samp> template parameter is completely replaced by the type that is present at the moment of instantiation. So if you already have a constant reference (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp>), then <samp class="listingcharacter">TYP</samp> is also a constant reference when instantiated.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/fev879zaK
#include <iostream>
const int& a_or_b(int choice) {
    static const int a = 42;
    static const int b = 73;
    if(choice==1)
        return a; // return const& to inner variable a
    else
        return b; // return const& to inner variable b
}
template<typename TYPE>
TYPE add(TYPE a, TYPE b) {
    return a + b;
}
int main() {
    auto res = add(
        a_or_b(0),   // const int&
        a_or_b(1) ); // const int&
    std::cout << res << "\n"; // Output: 115
} 
```

**Listing 23.6**     For “TYPE”, the compiler determines “const&”.

Because the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">a_or_b</samp> is always a <samp class="listingcharacter">const int&</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> for the compiler in the call to <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> is exactly this <samp class="listingcharacter">const int&</samp>. And because <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> is also the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp>, it is this <samp class="listingcharacter">const int&</samp>. A reference as a return value is very dangerous. Where does the reference point to? Well, in this example, fortunately, it's not a problem because <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> references are always somewhat less problematic than mutable references. In this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> has created a new value, and as we only access it as <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp>, the compiler is smart enough to retain the immutable value for the output on <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>.

Actually, it's quite simple: the compiler replaces exactly <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> with what you instantiated the template with. All embellishments that the type already has are preserved and passed through. In some cases, this can lead to unexpected results. Often, it's compiler error messages that you need to interpret, especially when using the standard library. Therefore, I wanted to be clear on this point about how the compiler proceeds, so you can correctly interpret the error messages.

You might now wonder what happens if the type is already <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> when instantiated but—as in <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp>—you also enrich it with <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp>. Well, the rules are quite simple:

*   When two <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>s meet, the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>.

*   When two <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>s collide, the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>.

So if it happens that you pass the return of <samp class="listingcharacter">a_or_b</samp> into <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp>, the compiler instantiates <samp class="listingcharacter">void print(const int&)</samp>—not <samp class="listingcharacter">void print(const const int & &)</samp>, which wouldn't make sense.

There is another case I need to mention. When you pass a temp-value as a parameter, it is a <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp>. A temp-value is usually treated like a normal reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> in terms of template parameters. Here, for example, the compiler instantiates <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">Image&</samp>, even though this temp-value is actually an <samp class="listingcharacter">Image&&</samp>:

```
print( Image{"my-image.png"} ); 
```

Only when you write your own template where the type parameter itself is qualified with <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> do you need to consider special cases—so very likely not for the time being. If you believe you need to write such a template to manage your project, refer to the literature on universal references and perfect forwarding as well as reference collapsing.

Until then, remember: do not write templates with <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> as type parameters, because you might not get what you expect. If an actual argument that is a reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> matches a <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> template parameter, it becomes a normal reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>. Only if both the actual argument is an rvalue reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> and the template parameter is <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> will the parameter in the instantiated function be an rvalue reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp>.

### 23.1.7    Method Templates are Just Function Templates

You can write a method template just as you can write a function template. Is that enough? Almost, right?

There is really nothing special about methods compared to functions, except that the first parameter with the invisible <samp class="listingcharacter">this*</samp> is already set, meaning its value and type. I think you just need an example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/bfofn76Ke
#include <iostream>
class Printer {
    std::ostream& trg_;
public:
    explicit Printer(std::ostream& target)
        : trg_(target)
        {}
    template<typename TYPE>
    Printer& print(const TYP& arg) {
        trg_ << arg;
        return *this;
    }
};
int main() {
    Printer normal(std::cout);
    normal.print(7).print(" ").print(3.1415).print("\n");
    Printer error(std::cerr);
    error.print(8).print(" ").print(2.7183).print("\n");
} 
```

**Listing 23.7**     A method can also be a template.

I have deliberately chosen a comparable example, again with <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp>. This time, the only difference is that you need to create an object—an instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">Print</samp>. You decide with the constructor's parameter where the output goes. If you pass <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp> goes to the standard output; if you pass <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cerr</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp> goes to the error stream.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter">Printer::print()</samp> method, there is no difference from a normal function, except that you can access the <samp class="listingcharacter">trg_</samp> data field.

The compiler generates a separate method for each argument type with which you call <samp class="listingcharacter">print()</samp>. In this example, these are <samp class="listingcharacter">print(int)</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">8</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">print(double)</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">3.1415</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">2.7183</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">print(const char*)</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">"\n"</samp>. The functionality is the same as with functions.

## 23.2    Function Templates in the Standard Library

In the standard library, you will find function templates everywhere. You have already seen some examples, especially from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><numeric></samp> headers.

The functions from these headers are particularly interesting because they work with the standard containers. If you pass an entire container as a parameter, starting from C++20, it becomes a range (see [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.1.7](#24_001.html_h24.1.7)). Alternatively—and before C++20—you pass a pair of iterators, as in the next listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/oTn1K4sGG
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>  // cout, ostream
#include <algorithm> // sort, copy
#include <iterator>  // ostream_iterator
int main() {
    std::ostream_iterator<int> oit(std::cout," ");
    std::vector data { 100, 50, 1, 75, 25, 0 };       // vector<int>
    std::sort(std::begin(data), std::end(data));      // Iterator pair
    std::copy(std::begin(data), std::end(data), oit); // Iterator pair
    std::cout << '\n';                                // Output: 0 1 25 50 75 100
    std::ranges::reverse(data);                       // Range
    std::ranges::copy(data, oit);                     // Range
    std::cout << '\n';                                // Output: 100 75 50 25 1 0
} 
```

**Listing 23.8**     You will also find various function templates in the standard library.

After <samp class="listingcharacter">sort()</samp>, I use <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream_iterator</samp> together with <samp class="listingcharacter">copy()</samp> to output the contents of <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream_iterator</samp> is an adapter that converts each element assignment into a <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">copy()</samp> thus actually leads to stream output.

Here I used <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> and obtained the iterators from it with <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp>, which <samp class="listingcharacter">sort()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">copy()</samp> require as parameters. These are the template arguments. And because they are template arguments, the whole thing works (almost always) with all standard containers and with all iterators. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp>, you could just as well have used <samp class="listingcharacter">list<string></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">array<double></samp>. You would not have had to change the rest of the program. It also works with a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<Image></samp> if you have overloaded <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">Image</samp>.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse()</samp> and the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">copy()</samp>, I used the range variants. Here, the entire container is passed, not the iterators as a pair.

### 23.2.1    Ranges instead of Containers as Template Parameters

If you want to write a function that operates on a container, it is advisable to do it the same way as the standard library: do not pass the container as a parameter, but as a range, which has been available in the standard since C++20\. The effect is that your function does not care whether the range belongs to a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> or a <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/h3baE65od
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <set>
#include <bitset>
#include <ranges>
namespace rng = std::ranges;
std::ostream& printBinary(std::ostream& os, rng::input_range auto&& range) {
    for(auto&& elem : range) {
        std::bitset<4> x(elem); // Copy number into bitset
        os << x << " ";
    }
    return os;
}
int main()
{
    std::vector vdata { 2, 0, 15, 12 };
    printBinary(std::cout, vdata) << "\n";
    // Output: 0010 0000 1111 1100
    std::set sdata { 2, 0, 12, 15 };
    printBinary(std::cout, sdata) << "\n";
    // Output: 0000 0010 1100 1111
    int adata[] = { 0,1,2,13,14,15 };
    printBinary(std::cout, adata) << "\n";
    // Output: 0000 0001 0010 1101 1110 1111
} 
```

**Listing 23.9**     Pass your own algorithm ranges as arguments, not the container.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> as the second parameter, you have defined a template. Before C++17, you had to put <samp class="listingcharacter">template<typename T></samp> before the function and then <samp class="listingcharacter">T&&</samp> for the parameter—as described in the previous section. The <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> ensures that you can pass both values directly from variables and temp-values from expressions. Before <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> is the <samp class="listingcharacter">ranges::input_range</samp> concept. It works without it, but you tell the compiler and the user of the function a lot when you write it down. In particular, the compiler's error messages will be better. You can find more about ranges as parameters in [Chapter 25](#25_001.html_h25), [Section 25.6](#25_006.html_h25.6), under the subheading “Ranges as Parameters (and More).”

The <samp class="listingcharacter">printBinary()</samp> function converts all elements of the range into a <samp class="listingcharacter">bitset<4></samp>, which is then printed. The conversion to <samp class="listingcharacter">bitset</samp> naturally only works if the container from which the iterators originate contains integer types, which is the case here with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. If you try <samp class="listingcharacter">printBinary()</samp> with a container that contains <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, the compiler will report an error exactly where the conversion is attempted with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::bitset<4> x(elem);</samp>.

As for the type of container, using ranges is flexible. Try it with a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> like <samp class="listingcharacter">vdata</samp>, and you will get the content output as binary numbers. With a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> like <samp class="listingcharacter">sdata</samp>, the elements are also sorted—a property of the <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> class. And because raw pointers are just a certain form of iterators, you can even call the <samp class="listingcharacter">printBinary()</samp> function with a C-array like <samp class="listingcharacter">adata</samp>. Ranges work for standard containers as well as for C-arrays.

Note that I have omitted the template arguments for <samp class="listingcharacter">vector data</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">set data</samp> here and let the compiler deduce them, which has been possible since C++17.

If you are programming for a compiler that does not yet support ranges, you need to “unpack” the range—that is, get the two iterators and call the function with the iterators.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/13eMxKTfj
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <set>
#include <bitset>
template<typename IT>
std::ostream& printBinary(std::ostream& os, IT begin, IT end)
{
    for(IT it=begin; it != end; ++it) {
        std::bitset<4> x(*it); // Copy number into bitset
        os << x << " ";
    }
    return os;
}
int main()
{
    std::vector<int> vdata { 2, 0, 15, 12 };
    printBinary(std::cout, vdata.cbegin(), vdata.cend()) << "\n";
    // Output: 0010 0000 1111 1100
    std::set<int> sdata { 2, 0, 12, 15 };
    printBinary(std::cout, std::begin(sdata), std::end(sdata)) << "\n";
    // Output: 0000 0010 1100 1111
    int adata[] = { 0,1,2,13,14,15 };
    printBinary(std::cout, std::begin(adata), std::end(adata)) << "\n";
    // Output: 0000 0001 0010 1101 1110 1111
} 
```

**Listing 23.10**     Pass your own algorithm iterators as arguments, not the container.

Specifically, <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> is instantiated by <samp class="listingcharacter">printBinary()</samp> in this example with three different types:

*   For <samp class="listingcharacter">vdata.cbegin()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int>::const_iterator</samp>, as this is what the function <samp class="listingcharacter">cbegin()</samp> returns.

*   For <samp class="listingcharacter">std::begin(sdata)</samp>, it is a <samp class="listingcharacter">set<int>::iterator</samp>, as that is the return type of <samp class="listingcharacter">set<int></samp>. You would have gotten a <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp> if you had declared <samp class="listingcharacter">sdata const</samp>.

*   For <samp class="listingcharacter">std::begin(adata)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">TYP</samp> will be a raw pointer <samp class="listingcharacter">int*</samp>. The loop in the <samp class="listingcharacter">printBinary()</samp> function, which looks like it specializes in iterators, also works on raw pointers—precisely because they are just a form of iterators.

I also did not use <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> for the parameter here, did not specify a concept, and did not use template argument deduction. This is now C++14 compatible.

Writing your own functions on containers in this manner increases the flexibility of your program in the long run. Of course, this is not suitable everywhere. So long as you only read the elements in the range, everything will definitely work. Here, we only let the loop run forward. Maybe you want to write an algorithm that accesses the elements of the range backward or even randomly. Then it may be that some containers do not cooperate with your function or behave undesirably. A <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> does not allow random access to its elements. With the choice of the right range concept, you can document that.

So long as you keep this in mind, you are definitely on the safe side for functions that only read. If you also need write access, you need to be a bit more cautious. When you describe an element with a new value, you must consider that, for example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> wants to keep its elements sorted—and it will do so, causing the order of elements to change and thus the range as well.

### 23.2.2    Example: Information about Numbers

In the following example, you will not only see the use of a function template but also that there is a very interesting helper template, <samp class="listingcharacter">numeric_limits<></samp>. With it, you can find out all sorts of useful internals and use them in your program. If you want to initialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> large enough to hold all possible values of <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned short</samp>, you can do it like this:

```
const auto sz = std::numeric_limits<unsigned short>::max();
std::vector<string> dictionary(sz); 
```

If the <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned short</samp> type on your system has a width of 16 bits, then <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned short</samp> variables can hold values from 0 to 65536\. The <samp class="listingcharacter">sz</samp> variable takes this value, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector dictionary</samp> is initialized with this size.

A few examples of what else you can find out using <samp class="listingcharacter">numeric_limits</samp> are shown in [Listing 23.11](#23_002.html_l23.11).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/r83Yeon7r
#include <iostream>                            // cout
#include <limits>                              // numeric_limits
template<typename INT_TYP>                     // Template with type argument
void infos(const char* name) {
    using L = typename std::numeric_limits<INT_TYP>; // rename for brevity
    std::cout
        << name
        << " number of bits:" << L::digits     // Bits without sign bit
        << " sign:" << L::is_signed            // stores sign?
        << " min:"<< (long long)L::min()       // smallest possible value
        << " max:"<< (long long)L::max()       // largest possible value
        << "\n";
}
int main() {
    infos<signed char>("char");                // smallest int type
    infos<short>("short");
    infos<int>("int");
    infos<long>("long");
    infos<long long>("long long");             // largest int type
} 
```

**Listing 23.11**     How to find the range of integer types.

Although this example is only designed for integer types, there are also many information functions for the <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> floating-point types.

#### [Übung]  What Is “typename”?

So far, you have only seen <samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp> for template parameters—for example, before functions in <samp class="listingcharacter">template<typename T></samp>. In such cases, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> instead: <samp class="listingcharacter">template<class T></samp> means exactly the same thing.

Since C++20, you can also use the name of a concept instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp> to restrict the type of a template parameter. If <samp class="listingcharacter">infos</samp> is supposed to work only for integer types, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::integral</samp> concept from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><concepts></samp> header instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp>.

Outside of angle brackets, a <samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp> appears exactly when you are writing a template and a type you are using is itself a template type in which you are using one of your template parameters. You can see this in [Listing 23.11](#23_002.html_l23.11) at <samp class="listingcharacter">typename std::numeric_limits<INT_TYP></samp>. Then you need the additional word <samp class="listingcharacter">typename</samp> before the name of the template type you are using. Otherwise, the compiler cannot know, before you assign a value/type to <samp class="listingcharacter">INT_TYP</samp>, whether <samp class="listingcharacter">numeric…<…></samp> is a variable, a type, or something else. You then have to tell it: “Hey, by the way, this is a type.”

## 23.3    A Class as a Function

So far, you can do two things with a function: you can define it, and you can call it. It becomes exciting and truly flexible only when you consider functions not just as a piece of outsourced program code but as objects like all other C++ objects. When you pass a function as a parameter, receive it as a return value, or simply store it in a variable for later use, you are using functions as objects.

I'll start with a very simple example. Say you want to write something that performs either an addition or a multiplication operation depending on a parameter. In the context of this chapter, I would like to call the thing that sometimes performs one operation and sometimes another a procedure to conceptually distinguish it from the variable function (addition or multiplication).

I don't even want to explicitly write down the crudest solution as a listing here. You could pass a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> as a parameter, which performs an addition for a <samp class="listingcharacter">'+'</samp> sign and a multiplication for a <samp class="listingcharacter">'*'</samp> sign. You would then probably implement the functions themselves in a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> within the procedure. You already did that skillfully in [Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8), [Listing 8.18](#08_010.html_l8.18). By now, you would just be a bit more suspicious and use an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum class</samp> with enumeration elements for the types of functions.

I would much rather throw you straight into the deep end. The function itself is passed as a parameter. As a result, it gets the name of the parameter in the procedure, and you then call it normally with parentheses and parameters.

```
#include <functional> // function
int calculate(int a, int b, std::function<int(int,int)> binop) {
    return binop(a,b);
} 
```

**Listing 23.12**     A function as a parameter.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">binop</samp> parameter has a somewhat peculiar type: <samp class="listingcharacter">function<int(int,int)></samp>. This refers to any function that takes two <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values as parameters and returns one. <samp class="listingcharacter">function<…></samp> is a template, that much is clear. But the function must have the correct signature. And if you take a normal function declaration like

```
int plus(int arg1, int arg2); 
```

and remove all names, <samp class="listingcharacter">plus</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">arg1</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">arg2</samp>, you are left with <samp class="listingcharacter">int(int,int)</samp>. That is exactly the template argument for <samp class="listingcharacter">function<…></samp>. You have determined the type of a function.

Here you need to take a deep breath first, because this is quite a chunk. Then let the actual invocation of the function parameter sink in:

```
binop(a, b); 
```

The parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">binop</samp> behaves like a function. If you had defined <samp class="listingcharacter">binop</samp> as a global function, the call here would look the same.

### 23.3.1    Values for a “Function” Parameter
