This is the case, for example, when an iterator reads from <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp>—which changes the state of <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> upon input and is therefore certainly not multipass capable.

*   Bidirectional iterators
    These are forward iterators, but can also be decremented with <samp class="listingcharacter">--it</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">it--</samp>.

*   Random access iterators
    Random access iterators are bidirectional and support addition <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp> and subtraction <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">-=</samp> with integers, as well as comparisons with <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>. The combination of addition and dereferencing also implies that dereferencing with an offset <samp class="listingcharacter">it[…]</samp> is supported.

*   Contiguous iterators
    Contiguous iterators are random access and guarantee that the elements are arranged contiguously in memory. For example, you can pass a block of elements to a C function by memory address.

In [Table 24.2](#24_002.html_t24.2), you can see which iterator categories are provided by which containers or streams.

In the ranges library, there is a corresponding concept for each of these iterator categories. The <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_iterator</samp> corresponds to the <samp class="listingcharacter">ranges::forward_range</samp> range concept and so on.

### 24.2.1    Iterators from Containers

Each container has two different iterator types that you can obtain using various methods:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> This allows you to modify the value in the container upon dereferencing—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">*it = 12;</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp> This allows you read-only access to the elements—for example, for <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << *it</samp>.

Depending on what you intend to do with the iterator, you should use either one type or the other. There are two variants of the <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp> methods. For the <samp class="listingcharacter">Container</samp> container, they would look like this:

```
struct Container {
    iterator       begin();
    iterator       end();
    const_iterator begin() const;
    const_iterator end() const;
    const_iterator cbegin() const;
    const_iterator cend() const;
}; 
```

If your container is, for example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> parameter of a function, you can only get back a <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp>. If the container is mutable, you should decide which iterator type you need.

Do you not always want to have to type “std::vector<std::string>::const_iterator” when programming a loop? You don't have to. <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> helps you here; the compiler uses it to calculate the correct type:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/dxb98rWzo
#include <iostream>                // cout
#include <vector>
using std::vector;
vector<int> createData(size_t sz) {
  return vector<int>(sz);          // sz x null
}
void fibonacci(vector<int> &data) {
  for(auto it = begin(data)+2; it != end(data); ++it) { // iterator it
    *it = *(it-1) + *(it-2);
  }
}
std::ostream& show(std::ostream &os, const vector<int> &data) {
  for(auto it=begin(data); it != end(data); ++it)      // const_iterator it
    std::cout << *it << " ";
  return os;
}
int main() {
  vector<int> data = createData(10);
  data[0] = 1;
  data[1] = 1;
  fibonacci(data);
  show(std::cout, data) << "\n";
} 
```

**Listing 24.8**     For “const” objects, “begin()” and “end()” return a “const_iterator”.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">fibonacci()</samp>, the parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp> is not constant. Therefore, <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp> return an iterator of type <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int>::iterator</samp>. Thanks to <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, you don't need to type this for <samp class="listingcharacter">it</samp> yourself; the compiler does it for you.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">show()</samp>, the parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp> is constant, and in that case, you get a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int>::const_iterator</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp>—well-suited for read-only output.

### 24.2.2    More Functionality with Iterators

Many methods of the standard containers do not take an index or pointer as a parameter when referring to an element. After all, it is only <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> that know the concept of an index with an integer. Therefore, throughout the entire standard library, you need to specify iterators for positions. Do you want to delete an element from a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, for example? Try this:

```
vector<int> data { 2,5,99,8,3, };
data.erase( data.begin()+2 ); // deletes 99 
```

This is even more common for ranges. You can delete everything from <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">8</samp>:

```
vector<int> data { 2,5,99,8,3, };
data.erase( data.begin()+1, data.begin()+4 ); // deletes 5,99,8 
```

It should be noted that the end of the range always points to the element after the last element of the range. <samp class="listingcharacter">data.begin()+4</samp> refers to the <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp>; therefore, deletion occurs from <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> up to before <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp>. This applies to all methods of all standard containers and free functions with iterators, with the exception of some methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>.

This is also the reason that the <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp>s of all containers point behind the last element. Thus, they can be used easily in algorithms for range specification.

There are many algorithms. In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><numeric></samp> headers, you will find very, very many of them. For example, you can sort almost any standard container by calling (essentially) the following:

```
#include <algorithm>
int main() {
   // …
   std::sort(begin(container), end(container));
   // or with ranges:
   std::ranges::sort(begin(container), end(container));
} 
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> you don't need to try that, because they are already sorted. But <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> can be sorted this way.

Finally, you can extend iterators and equip them with new functionalities. For example, in the next listing, see how you can use an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream_iterator</samp> output iterator to output the contents of any container to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/7xYcqqh68
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>   // cout
#include <iterator>   // ostream_iterator
#include <algorithm>  // copy

int main() {
  std::vector data { 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 10 };
  std::ostream_iterator<int> out_it (std::cout,", "); // when assigned to cout
  std::copy(data.begin(), data.end(), out_it); // all elements to the iterator
  std::cout << "\n";                           // Output: 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 10,
  // or from C++20 with Ranges:
  std::ranges::copy(data, out_it);
  std::cout << "\n";                           // Output: 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 10,
} 
```

**Listing 24.9**     Iterator adapters change the behavior of operations.

Every time the iterator <samp class="listingcharacter">out_it</samp> of type <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream_iterator</samp> is dereferenced and then assigned something, it outputs it to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>. Between the elements, it prints a comma with a space <samp class="listingcharacter">", "</samp>. So a <samp class="listingcharacter">*out_it = 42</samp> results in the output <samp class="listingcharacter">42,</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">copy</samp> algorithm from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> header now performs exactly this assignment for all elements within the range between <samp class="listingcharacter">data.begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">data.end()</samp>. As a result, you get to see all elements on <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><iterator></samp> header, there are other useful things for iterators. For example, you can reverse a range with <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse_iterator</samp> or use <samp class="listingcharacter">make_move_iterator</samp> to turn a copying algorithm into a moving one. For the exact functionalities, I refer you to the standard library reference, e.g., [https://cppreference.com](https://cppreference.com).

## 24.3    Allocators: Memory Issues

Containers constantly request new memory to store their elements. This can be a complex task, especially for noncontiguous containers like <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>. To give users the ability to intervene, each container is equipped with an <samp class="listingcharacter">allocator</samp>. If you do not specify one, it defaults to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::allocator<Elem></samp>.

### [Übung]  Allocators Are an Expert Topic

I recommend that you use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::allocator</samp> and do not implement your own allocator. If you do, use ones from the Boost project or other major providers. The concept of allocators implemented in the current standard library is much debated and does not make all experts happy. You should not bother delving deeply into this subject unless you really have to.

To show you how to use allocators, I will now define a very simple allocator. There are much more sophisticated ones, both for general and specific situations.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/3dYhh6n5f
#include <set>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

template<class T> class GobAllocator  {
public:
    using value_type = T;
    T* allocate(size_t count) {
        size_t add = sizeof(T)*count;
        std::cout << "allocate("<<add<<"/"<<(buf_.size()-current_)<<")\n";
        if(current_+add > buf_.size()) throw std::bad_alloc{};
        char* result = buf_.data()+current_;
        current_ += add;
        return reinterpret_cast<T*>(result);
    }
    void deallocate(T* p, size_t count) {
        size_t del = sizeof(T)*count;
        std::cout << "deallocate("<<del<<")\n";
        if(del==current_ && p==reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_.data())) {
            std::cout << "...all free.\n";
            current_ = 0;                // release everything again
        }
    }

    GobAllocator() : GobAllocator{1024} {}
    explicit GobAllocator(size_t mx)
      : buf_(mx, 0), current_{0} { }

private:
       std::vector<char> buf_;
       size_t current_;
};

int main() {
    constexpr size_t CNT = 1*1000*1000;
    using Gob = GobAllocator<int>;
    try {
        Gob gob(CNT*sizeof(int));        // prepare allocator
        std::vector<int,Gob> data(gob);
        data.reserve(CNT);               // get memory in one go
        for(int val=0; val < (int)CNT; ++val)
            data.push_back(val);
    } catch(std::bad_alloc &ex) {
        std::cout << "Memory exhausted.\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 24.10**     A (too) simple allocator and its usage.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">GobAllocator</samp> acquires a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<char></samp> as a memory reservoir upon creation. It can allocate memory when the using container requests it via <samp class="listingcharacter">allocate()</samp>, but it rarely deallocates it. The container requests this via deallocate. Only if <samp class="listingcharacter">deallocate()</samp> wants to release all the requested memory will <samp class="listingcharacter">GobAllocator</samp> actually do something and releases all its memory for new requests.

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">current_</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">GobAllocator</samp> keeps track of how much memory it has already managed. When it is asked to allocate memory for <samp class="listingcharacter">count</samp> objects via <samp class="listingcharacter">allocate()</samp>, it simply increases the <samp class="listingcharacter">current_</samp> counter by the number of bytes these objects need. The old position is returned as data storage and converted into a raw pointer of the desired type. This means the container stores its elements here at this location.

It is also important to note that the allocator throws <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_alloc</samp> as an exception if it fails to obtain the requested memory. This can then be caught using <samp class="listingcharacter">try/catch</samp>. For example, omit <samp class="listingcharacter">data.reserve(ANZ);</samp> in [Listing 24.10](#24_003.html_l24.10) and observe how the <samp class="listingcharacter">GobAllocator</samp> runs out of space: the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> now wants to grow continuously and alternates between <samp class="listingcharacter">allocate()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">deallocate()</samp> calls to request increasingly larger memory and release the old memory. However, this dumb allocator cannot do that and must eventually give up.

What this could theoretically be used for is reusing memory that has been obtained once.

Here, the memory from <samp class="listingcharacter">gob</samp> would be used twice completely, but only under the condition that <samp class="listingcharacter">data1</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">data2</samp> do not grow beyond <samp class="listingcharacter">CNT</samp> elements:

```
Gob gob(CNT*sizeof(int));  // prepare common allocator
{
    std::vector<int,Gob> data1(gob);
    data1.reserve(CNT);
    // ...
}
{
    std::vector<int,Gob> data2(gob);
    data2.reserve(CNT);
    // ...
} 
```

All in all, this simple allocator is quite useless in practice. But at least it shows you how to equip a container with an allocator.

### [Übung]  All Containers Support Allocators

All containers of the standard library use an allocator. If you do not specify one, the standard library uses <samp class="listingcharacter">std::allocator<Elem></samp>. You can specify your own by passing its type as a template parameter. In addition, you can optionally pass an instance of your allocator to the constructor or let the container create a new one if you do not want to.

The classical allocators described here have a weakness: two containers that are essentially the same but have different allocators are of different types, because an allocator is part of the container type. This means in practice that you cannot assign between them.

The solution is containers with polymorphic allocators. Two containers that use these are of the same type even if they use different allocators. Therefore, since C++17, all containers are also available in the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::pmr</samp> namespace—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::pmr:: vector</samp> (polymorphic memory resource). Here, you do not specify the allocator with the type but pass it as an additional constructor parameter.

Ahead, I will omit mentioning the allocator as a template argument and constructor parameter for all containers, as well as the mention of the <samp class="listingcharacter">pmr</samp> variant.

## 24.4    Container Commonalities

In [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), [Listing 6.12](#06_004.html_l6.12), I used iterators for a loop over the contents of a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. This brings me to the commonalities of all containers. If you simply replace <samp class="listingcharacter">std::vector</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::list</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::set</samp>, or use <samp class="listingcharacter">std::array<int,5></samp>, then the rest of the program remains the same. This would not have been possible with <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>, for example, if you had accessed it with an index <samp class="listingcharacter">[idx]</samp>.

The range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop also works internally on iterators and is therefore also possible on all containers. However, it can only ever work on the entire container, whereas an iterator that you obtained with <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> is almost arbitrarily manipulable. You will see many examples of this throughout this chapter. As a reminder: I use <samp class="listingcharacter">italic code</samp> for features from C++23 that might be too recent for some compilers (see [Chapter 1](#01_001.html_h1), [Listing 1.1](#01_004.html_l1.1)).

When designing this part of the standard library, great care was taken to provide a common interface for the containers where it makes sense and works. I do not list the special cases here—they are explained with the specific container—but only give a rough overview:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">begin() end()</samp>
    All containers offer these two functions to get iterators. Among other things, this allows you to use them in the range-based <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, because they also exist as free functions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">size() empty() std::ssize()</samp>
    Get the number of elements in any container. Since C++17, they also exist as free functions, and from C++20, there is the free function <samp class="listingcharacter">ssize()</samp>, which returns <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp>. This avoids warnings about comparisons between <samp class="listingcharacter">signed</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> in statements like <samp class="listingcharacter">for (int i=0; i<cont.size(); ++i)</samp>. Just write <samp class="listingcharacter">i<ssize(cont)</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">resize() reserve() clear()</samp>
    You can resize or shrink sequence-based containers (except <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>) with a single call. <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered</samp> containers can be preinformed with <samp class="listingcharacter">reserve</samp> about how many elements you intend to store approximately. This saves administrative effort later when actually inserting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[] at() data()</samp>
    Read and write at arbitrary positions of a container with <samp class="listingcharacter">cont[where]</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">cont.at(where)</samp>. Not all containers support this. Sequence-based ones require a number for <samp class="listingcharacter">where</samp>, while associative ones need the data type you chose as the key. With <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp>, you can access the contiguous memory of elements in some containers. This is useful for C functions, among other things. <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp> is also available as a free function.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">insert()</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">insert_range()</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace()</samp>
    Use these to insert or delete elements at arbitrary positions. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> can do this, but it is slow. With <samp class="listingcharacter">insert()</samp>, the element already exists and is copied (or moved in the case of temp-values), while with <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace()</samp>, it is created in place within the container. The range variant is available from C++23.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">push_front() push_back() emplace_front() emplace_back()</samp>
    Use these to add individual elements to sequence-based containers. Here, a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is also fast.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">assign()</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">assign_range()</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">swap() merge()</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">assign()</samp> allows you to reinitialize a container. With <samp class="listingcharacter">swap()</samp>, you can very efficiently exchange the entire contents of two similar containers. <samp class="listingcharacter">Merge()</samp> combines two similar and presorted containers. <samp class="listingcharacter">assign_range()</samp> is available from C++23.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">prepend_range() append_range()</samp>
    Since C++23, you can also insert entire ranges into sequence-based containers.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">erase() extract()</samp>
    Remove individual elements or ranges with <samp class="listingcharacter">erase()</samp>. With <samp class="listingcharacter">extract()</samp>, you remove an element with the intention of inserting it elsewhere.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">find() count() contains()</samp>
    Find a specific element in an associative container or count how often it occurs. As of C++20, there is also <samp class="listingcharacter">contains</samp>.

Methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">c.size()</samp>, which are also available as free functions like <samp class="listingcharacter">size(c)</samp>, allow for more generic code. Instead of having to modify an existing container type (perhaps from a third party), you can overload the free function and implement the functionality there.

## 24.5    An Overview of the Standard Container Classes

First, the containers can be roughly divided into four groups:

*   Sequence-based containers
    Access and insertion in these containers occur either in order or element-wise with an index as a number. <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> are examples. Typically, you delete and add elements at one or both ends. Some support efficient direct element access with <samp class="listingcharacter">[int]</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">at(int)</samp>.

*   Associative ordered containers
    Instead of numbers, these use any data type for access. For example, associate the name of a city with its historical German postal code by writing <samp class="listingcharacter">cities["Berlin"s] = 1000</samp>. In such containers, you can insert elements at arbitrary positions. The associative containers are kept permanently sorted by their keys. Like sequence-based containers, you can read all elements in order—and because the keys are always kept sorted, you get them delivered in sorted order when iterating. All operations on associative containers have a guaranteed upper bound for resource consumption, regardless of the data you feed into the container.

*   Associative unordered containers
    From the outside, associative unordered containers look like normal associative containers and have almost the same interface. The difference, however, is that their most important operations are usually faster, but not guaranteed. They are based on hashing instead of sorting. This hashing can degrade and significantly reduce performance. I recommend using ordered associative containers in normal cases and only consciously switching to unordered variants for special cases.

*   Container adapters
    The existing sequence-based and associative containers are so powerful and equipped with such rich interfaces and good performance guarantees that you could also use them for simpler containers. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has all the methods that a stack needs. It would be unnecessary to offer a separate container for <samp class="listingcharacter">stack</samp> that does not support iteration. For this purpose, there is a small set of adapters that internally hold another container but offer a reduced or slightly redesigned interface externally.

### 24.5.1    Type Aliases of Containers

Ahead, it is sometimes important to know which type we are talking about. A container deals with multiple types. There is of course the container type itself. This consists of a template that becomes an instantiated type at the moment you write it with its template arguments. With at least one template argument, you specify the types of the elements that are stored in the container. So, for example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> container with the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> element type together becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> and thus the type of the container.

In addition to data and methods, all containers also contain some type aliases. I have compiled the most important ones in [Table 24.3](#24_005.html_t24.3). On the one hand, I will use these terms when I tell you about the containers; on the other hand, you can use the type aliases to write consistent code with different container types—and perhaps later use them in your own templates. In some cases, the type is really just an alias for another more or less simple type; for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">value_type</samp> of a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> is an alias for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. In other cases, like <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator</samp>, the underlying type is not specified by the standard and is only described by its properties. You must then use the alias because you could not (portably) write the concrete type.

It is not always easy to apply the terms clearly here. For <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp>, the term “value” is ambiguous, because it is often used like “it maps a key to a value”. But the <samp class="listingcharacter">value_type</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> is actually together defined as <samp class="listingcharacter">pair<key_type,mapped_type></samp>. Therefore, I prefer using the term “target” in that case. I strive to use the following clear terms in the book:

*   Value or element of <samp class="listingcharacter">value_type</samp>

*   Key of <samp class="listingcharacter">key_type</samp>

*   Target of target type or mapped type for <samp class="listingcharacter">mapped_type</samp>

| Type Alias | Meaning | <samp class="listingcharacter">vector <int>::…</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">set <int>::…</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">map<int, string>::…</samp> |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">value_type</samp> | Elements of the container | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">pair<const int, string></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">key_type</samp> | Key part of the elements | – | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">mapped_type</samp> | Mapped part of the elements | – | – | <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">size_type</samp> | Size or index | <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">reference</samp> | Reference to element | <samp class="listingcharacter">int&</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int&</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">pair<const int, string>&</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator</samp> | Iterator in the modifiable container | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp> | Iterator in the immutable container | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse_iterator</samp> | Reverse iterator | Yes | Yes | Yes |

**Table 24.3**     Overview of the most important type aliases of containers.

Even if you forgo <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, you can use these aliases to write code that looks the same for every container type or create your own templates.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/c97qra3M7
#include <vector>
#include <map>
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::ostream;
template<typename K, typename T>
ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, std::pair<const K,T> value) {
    return os << '[' << value.first << ':' << value.second << ']';
}
int main() {
  {
    using Cont = std::vector<int>;
    Cont cont{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 };
    Cont::size_type sz = cont.size();
    cout << "size=" << sz << " content= ";
    for(Cont::const_iterator it = cont.begin(); it != cont.end(); ++it)
        cout << *it << ' ';
    cout << '\n';
  }
  {
    using Cont = std::map<int,char>;
    Cont cont{ {1,'a'}, {2,'b'}, {3,'c'}, {4,'d'}, {5,'e'}, {6,'f'} };
    Cont::size_type sz = cont.size();
    cout << "size=" << sz << " content= ";
    for(Cont::const_iterator it = cont.begin(); it != cont.end(); ++it)
        cout << *it << ' ';
    cout << '\n';
  }
} 
```

**Listing 24.11**     Type aliases are sometimes clearer than the concrete types.

Here I use the aliases provided by the containers <samp class="listingcharacter">size_type</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp>. In this simple case, <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> would have worked, but this demonstrates the aliases.

#### Interlude: “pair” and “tuple”

As shown in [Table 24.3](#24_005.html_t24.3), some containers internally use <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp>. As you progress through the chapter, you will encounter several methods that also return a <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> as a return type. This is nothing more than bundling two data types and their values together—essentially:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xcrbvM1jz
struct PairIntDouble {
    int first;
    double second;
};
int main() {
    PairIntDouble p{ 2, 7.123 };
} 
```

What I have done here specifically for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> is possible with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::pair</samp> as a template class for any types. You can access the first element with <samp class="listingcharacter">first</samp> and the second with <samp class="listingcharacter">second</samp>.

A generalization of <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> for any number of elements is <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>. For example, you use <samp class="listingcharacter">get<3>(t)</samp> to access the fourth element of <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp>.

That should suffice for a discussion of <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> for this chapter. A complete discussion of these two data types can be found in [Chapter 28](#28_001.html_h28), [Section 28.1](#28_001.html_h28.1).

## 24.6    The Sequential Container Classes

Let’s walk through the sequential container classes (see [Table 24.4](#24_006.html_t24.4)):

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">array<</samp>ElementType,Size<samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> A fixed number of elements is stored here. Adding and removing is only possible by overwriting. The elements are stored directly next to each other in memory. Therefore, <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> is suitable for both a few huge and many tiny element types, as it has virtually no memory overhead.

[![An “array” can neither grow nor shrink, but it is compact.](bilderklein/klein24_002.png)](img-f24.2.html)

**Figure 24.2**     An “array” can neither grow nor shrink, but it is compact.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<</samp>ElementType<samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> This all-rounder grows automatically. You can insert anywhere, but efficiently only at the back end.

[![Schematic representation of a “vector”.](bilderklein/klein24_003.png)](img-f24.3.html)

**Figure 24.3**     Schematic representation of a “vector”.

Reading the elements is done sequentially forwards, backward, or randomly by index. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> stores its elements directly next to each other in memory, making it practical for both a few large and many tiny elements. Optimally used, it has virtually no memory overhead; in nonoptimal cases, it is still acceptable as it does not fragment memory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">deque<</samp>ElementType<samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> You can easily add elements to the end of a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, but less easily to the beginning, as all existing elements must be shifted one place to the right. The double-ended queue <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> is suitable for quickly adding elements at both ends. As a disadvantage, it does not store its elements directly next to each other, but still usually more compactly than <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>. If possible, prefer <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>.

[![A “deque” can be extended at both ends, but the elements are not contiguous in memory.](bilderklein/klein24_004.png)](img-f24.4.html)

**Figure 24.4**     A “deque” can be extended at both ends, but the elements are not contiguous in memory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">list<</samp>ElementType<samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> The list is simpler than a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and is very well suited for frequent insertions in the middle. However, the elements are not contiguous in memory but are internally linked. You do not have index access available. If you want to iterate over ranges, it is fast.

[![A “list” can be traversed forwards and backward. Insertion is easy.](bilderklein/klein24_005.png)](img-f24.5.html)

**Figure 24.5**     A “list” can be traversed forwards and backward. Insertion is easy.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list<</samp>ElementType<samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> This exotic type mimics the fundamental structure of a linked list from C and therefore requires minimal additional resources. However, it has a slightly different interface than all other containers. Even insertion works somewhat differently. You can only iterate forwards. Both <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> are specialists in splicing—that is, transferring some consecutive or all elements from one list to another.

[![Elements of the “forward_list” only know their successor.](bilderklein/klein24_006.png)](img-f24.6.html)

**Figure 24.6**     Elements of the “forward_list” only know their successor.

| Container | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> | Fixed size; similar to C-array ElementType<samp class="listingcharacter">[</samp>Size<samp class="listingcharacter">]</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> | All-rounder; similar to <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> ElementType<samp class="listingcharacter">[</samp>Size<samp class="listingcharacter">]</samp>, but dynamically growing; inserting and removing at the back is very efficient |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> | Inserting and removing at the front and back is very efficient |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> | Inserting everywhere is efficient; no <samp class="listingcharacter">[i]</samp>; forward and backward iterable |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> | Efficient insertion everywhere; low memory overhead; no <samp class="listingcharacter">[i]</samp>; no <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp>; only forward iterable |

**Table 24.4**     Profiles of the sequence containers.

### 24.6.1    Commonalities and Differences

Among the sequence-based container classes in C++, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> are the ubiquitous all-rounders. If you are considering using a sequence container, one of these two should always be your first choice.

| Property | <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dynamic size | – | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Key type* | <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> | – | – |
| Iterate forward | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Iterate backward | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | – |
| Overhead per element | None | Special* | Very Little | Yes | Little |
| Efficient insertion | Not at all | Back | Front/back | Everywhere | Special* |
| Where to insert | – | Everywhere | Everywhere | Everywhere | Everywhere |
| Splicing | – | – | – | Yes | Yes |
| Memory layout | Stack | Contiguous | Open | Fragm. | Fragm. |
| Iterators/ranges | Contiguous | Contiguous | Random access | Bidirectional | Forward |
| Algorithms | All | All | All | Special* | Special* |

**Table 24.5**     Properties of sequence containers. For the * entries, see the explanation ahead.

You use <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> when you know at compile time how many elements the container should hold. <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, on the other hand, has a dynamic size: you can add elements to it or remove them.

[Table 24.5](#24_006.html_t24.5) lists the main properties that distinguish the sequence-based containers from each other. The following notes apply to the entries marked with an asterisk *:

*   Key type
    You can only use a <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp>. Key is not quite the right term here, because shifting elements changes the association of the keys to the container elements. However, I include this property here to compare it with associative containers.

*   Overhead per element of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>
    In the optimal case, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has virtually no additional memory consumption other than that of the bare elements it manages. If you know in advance that you will store 1,000 elements, you can prepare the vector to exactly this size with <samp class="listingcharacter">reserve(1000)</samp> and then add elements. You will achieve optimal performance in terms of time and memory consumption. If you do not reserve a size in advance, the vector will be slightly larger than needed, and new space will have to be allocated from time to time when adding elements. However, the internal algorithms ensure that, on average, you spend at most twice as much time or memory as without the advanced reservation.

*   Efficient insertion into the <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>
    Unlike all other containers, when you insert into the <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>, you do not insert at the position you indicate, but rather one element after. Why this is the case will be shown later in an example. For this reason, this container, unlike any other (except <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>), does not have <samp class="listingcharacter">insert</samp> but instead has <samp class="listingcharacter">insert_after</samp>. This inconvenience is due to the desire to use as little memory per element as possible.

*   Splicing of <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>
    These two containers have the unique property compared to all others that you can merge two containers of the same type extremely quickly. Making one out of two does not cost a single copy operation of the elements contained within these two, and the administrative information to be changed is independent of the number of elements in the lists.

*   Memory layout
    On many occasions, the elements of the container need to be packed closely together to work with them optimally. For example, when writing to the hard drive, it is advantageous to pass all the data to be written to the operating system as one large block. And other C functions also struggle with complex C++ data structures. They require a starting point in memory and a length (hello, <samp class="listingcharacter">span</samp>!). Of all the containers, only <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> store their elements in such a way that this type of data exchange works, with <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> being the only container that can use only the stack and does not need to request heap space with <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp>.

*   Algorithms
    The containers that offer random access iterators work with all free functions that take an area in the form of a pair of iterators as parameters. However, lists do not offer random access and refuse to work with algorithms. Special methods that they provide instead solve this problem.

*   Spans
    You can access contiguous sequence containers (including C-array) with <samp class="listingcharacter">span</samp> since C++20\. This class contains an iterator to the first element and the number of elements in the container. Both are immutable and set upon creation. Conversions of a container to a <samp class="listingcharacter">span</samp> happen implicitly, for example, when passing it to a function that expects a <samp class="listingcharacter">span</samp>. For <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, there is <samp class="listingcharacter">string_view</samp> for this purpose. In C++23, <samp class="listingcharacter">mdspan</samp> is introduced to create a multidimensional view like a matrix or cube from a one-dimensional <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> (or similar).

### 24.6.2    Methods of Sequence Containers

In this section, <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">C</samp> stands for one of the container types like <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">array<Hobbit,4></samp>. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">cont</samp> stands for an instance of a container, as in <samp class="listingcharacter">list<double></samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">cont</samp><samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp>. For element type, I use <samp class="listingcharacter">Elem</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp>, and for iterator types, I abbreviate with <samp class="listingcharacter">It</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">rg</samp> stands for a range.

To save space and increase clarity, I am not always very precise or detailed with the function signatures here. If I do not include the parentheses with <samp class="listingcharacter">method</samp>, there are usually multiple overloads:

*   Constructors: <samp class="listingcharacter">C()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C(size_t)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C(size_t, E e)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C{…}</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C(It, It)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C(from_range, rg)</samp>
    The default constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont()</samp> creates an empty container. With <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont(size_t)</samp>, you can create a container of a predetermined size filled with default-initialized elements, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<int>(5)</samp>, which creates a vector with the value <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> five times. If you do not like the default value, specify your own: <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<double>(5,42.0)</samp> will contain the value <samp class="listingcharacter">42.0</samp> five times, for example. With a pair of iterators from any other container, you can copy its contents. Since C++23, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">from_range</samp> marker to initialize from a range. You can specify an initializer list that your container should contain at the beginning. Exception: You always create an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> using an initializer list.

*   Copy and Move: <samp class="listingcharacter">C(const C&)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C& operator=(const C&)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">assign</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">assign_range</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C(C&&)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">C& operator=(C&&)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp>
    You can pass a different <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont</samp> as an argument to the copy and move constructors and operators. There is an <samp class="listingcharacter">assign</samp> method in several variants to reinitialize the container similarly to one of the constructor options, with <samp class="listingcharacter">assign_range()</samp> existing since C++23\. All containers implement <samp class="listingcharacter">swap(Cont& other)</samp> efficiently (in constant time, independent of the number of elements), which allows for great performance tricks when used skillfully; see [Listing 24.51](#24_007.html_l24.51). Exception: <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> has no <samp class="listingcharacter">assign</samp> methods, and <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp> takes linear time for <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>.

*   Destructor: <samp class="listingcharacter">~Cont()</samp>
    All containers have destructors that remove the contained elements. Note that this does not apply if you pack raw pointers into containers. Use smart pointers for that, or manage the dynamic objects elsewhere. The destructors do not implicitly throw exceptions.[[ 57 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn24_01)

*   Iterate forward: <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp> and backward: <samp class="listingcharacter">rbegin()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">rend()</samp>
    You get an iterator with <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> that points to the first element, and with <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp> one that points behind the last element; you can use these iterators for a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop to iterate forward. For the backward loop, use <samp class="listingcharacter">rbegin()</samp>, which points to the last element, and <samp class="listingcharacter">rend()</samp>, which points before the first element. In sequence containers, you always iterate over the elements in the order in which you inserted them or where you inserted them. All these methods return a <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont::iterator</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont::const_iterator</samp>, and they also come in variants with a <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> prefix, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">cbegin()</samp>, which always returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Cont::const_iterator</samp>. Exception: <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> has neither <samp class="listingcharacter">rbegin()</samp> nor <samp class="listingcharacter">rend()</samp>.

*   Element access: <samp class="listingcharacter">E& operator[]</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">E& at(size_t)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">E& front()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">E& back()</samp>
    With <samp class="listingcharacter">cont[i]</samp>, you can access the i-th element unchecked. The <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> method first checks whether the container contains the element and throws an <samp class="listingcharacter">out_of_range</samp> exception if it does not. <samp class="listingcharacter">c.front()</samp> is equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">*(c.begin())</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">c.back()</samp> is equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">*(prev(c.end()))</samp>. Exceptions: <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> have neither <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> nor <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> has no <samp class="listingcharacter">back()</samp>.

*   Size: <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">empty()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">resize(size_t)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">max_size()</samp>
    With <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp>, you get the current number of elements in the container; <samp class="listingcharacter">empty()</samp> is true if this number is zero. When you call <samp class="listingcharacter">resize</samp>, the container shrinks or grows and may remove or create elements accordingly. With <samp class="listingcharacter">max_size()</samp>, you get the theoretical maximum size of the container. Note that this does not consider the current state of the program or the machine but is a library-dependent constant. Exceptions: <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> has no <samp class="listingcharacter">size()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> has no <samp class="listingcharacter">resize</samp>.

*   Capacity: <samp class="listingcharacter">capacity()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">reserve(size_t)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit()</samp>
    Only <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has a capacity different from its size that you can influence. <samp class="listingcharacter">capacity()</samp> returns the number of elements that <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> can hold without needing to request new dynamic memory. If you pack more than <samp class="listingcharacter">capacity</samp> elements into it, this capacity automatically increases. Internally, this results in all elements being copied or moved. This sounds worse than it is, but if you know in advance how many elements you will pack into a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, it is worth requesting this capacity once with <samp class="listingcharacter">reserve()</samp>. If you do not know this in advance but can estimate when you are done adding elements, you can get rid of excess capacity with a <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit()</samp> call. However, this approach can also trigger an internal copy or move, and <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> does not have to comply with the request. Exceptions: As <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> is usually based on <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, it also has a <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit()</samp>.

*   Adding and removing at one end: <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back(E)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">push_front(E)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_back()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_front()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">prepend_range()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">append_range()</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp> adds an element at the back, <samp class="listingcharacter">push_front</samp> at the front. The <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_…</samp> methods remove an element. For <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>, you must expect that references and iterators to the container become invalid after these operations. The <samp class="listingcharacter">range</samp> methods are available from C++23\. Exceptions: <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> does not have any of these methods, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> lacks the <samp class="listingcharacter">front</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">prepend</samp> methods, and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> lacks the <samp class="listingcharacter">back</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp> methods.

*   Adding and removing with emplacement: <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace_front(…)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace_back(…)</samp>
    While the <samp class="listingcharacter">push_…</samp> methods take a ready-made element as an argument, which is then copied into the container, <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace_…</samp> can save you this copy. Simply provide these methods with the desired constructor arguments of <samp class="listingcharacter">Elem(…)</samp>, and the new object will be created directly in place. Exceptions: <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> lacks these methods, and <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> lacks <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace_front</samp>. The container <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> lacks <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace_back</samp>.

*   Other modifications: <samp class="listingcharacter">clear()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">erase</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">insert</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">clear()</samp> simply removes all elements from the container, leaving it with a size of zero. With <samp class="listingcharacter">erase</samp>, you can remove a single element using an iterator or an entire area using a pair. Similarly, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">insert</samp> and an iterator as a position to insert something at a specific spot—a single element (or multiple copies of it), the elements of an initializer list, or an area from another container using a pair of iterators. With <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace</samp>, you can create one or more elements at a specified position in the container without copying. Exceptions: <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> has none of these methods, and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> instead has <samp class="listingcharacter">…_after()</samp> methods (but does have <samp class="listingcharacter">clear()</samp>).

*   List operation: <samp class="listingcharacter">splice</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">splice_after</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">merge</samp> and algorithm methods
    Only <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> can easily merge ranges of different containers with <samp class="listingcharacter">splice</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">splice_after</samp>—removing from one and adding to the other. And among the sequence containers, only these two can merge two presorted lists in sorted order using <samp class="listingcharacter">merge</samp>. Because the two list containers do not offer random access iterators, the free functions from <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> are not applicable to them. As a substitute, they offer methods that mimic the algorithms: <samp class="listingcharacter">merge</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">remove</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">remove_if</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">unique</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">sort</samp>. Note that unlike their counterparts in <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">remove</samp> methods of the lists actually remove the found elements rather than just changing their position.

### 24.6.3    “vector”

<samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> should be the first thing that comes to mind when you need a container that must be able to grow and shrink. You can add elements to it—preferably at the back, but elsewhere if necessary. The elements are in the order you specify in the container, so they are not automatically sorted.

Because it guarantees to store its elements in a contiguous block, it is suitable for use with C functions and similar, which receive input or output data in this manner. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> works well with the <samp class="listingcharacter">span</samp> introduced in C++20, as it bundles a pointer to the beginning and the length, as often expected by C APIs. You can determine and pass on the address of an element. Just like the container's iterators, addresses to its elements remain valid as long as you do not change the size or capacity of the container.

The space for the elements of a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is automatically adjusted, increased, or decreased as needed. Space is reserved for upcoming elements so that the size does not need to be adjusted for each individual insertion. This happens in such a clever way that even in the worst case, each insertion on average proceeds at O(1). You can determine how much space the vector currently holds with <samp class="listingcharacter">capacity()</samp>. If you know in advance how many elements will end up in the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, request the memory with <samp class="listingcharacter">reserve(size_t)</samp> to avoid future expansions.

You can access the elements of the vector randomly in O(1)—that is, with optimal speed.

#### Tip: Locality

For the CPU, it is better to access registers than cache. Cache is better than main memory, and main memory is faster than the hard drive. The more compact the memory areas needed for a computation are, the more likely it is that the computer can use fast memory for it. Even better for locality is if the memory is mainly used in one direction rather than back and forth. Often, the same computation using a strategy with better locality is many times faster: factors of x10 or x100 are possible!

A <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has better locality than, for example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>, if no special precautions with specific allocators are taken. If you can also use a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> in ascending order, then that is even better for locality. To do this, let the iterator only move forward in the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> or increment the index for access only.

If you want to keep data always sorted, you usually use a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>. However, that is not good for memory. If this is important to you, take a look at the <samp class="listingcharacter">flat_set</samp> adapter for a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, which has been available since C++23.

You can pack almost anything into a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> that is possible in C++ types. It depends on the operations you will use and whether the type is allowed or not. The element type must either be copyable or movable; the standard library will choose the appropriate operation. However, there must be a destructor for <samp class="listingcharacter">Elem</samp>, either one generated by the compiler or one you wrote yourself—so you cannot mark the destructor with <samp class="listingcharacter">= delete</samp>.

In practice, it is recommended that the element type be movable and guaranteed not to throw exceptions when moved—that is, either marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> move operations or generated by the compiler. If you can, stick to the rule of zero for the element type; see [Chapter 17](#17_001.html_h17), [Section 17.1](#17_001.html_h17.1) as a reminder.

Assume that all the following examples in this section for <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> are embedded in the code from [Listing 24.12](#24_006.html_l24.12).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/WK86eaz1x
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
using std::vector; using std::cout;
template<typename T>
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&os, const vector<T>& data) {
    for(const auto &e : data) {
        os << e << ' ';
    }
    return os;
}
int main() {h
   // Example code here
} 
```

**Listing 24.12**     This is the template for the example listings in this section for <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>.

#### Operator “<samp class="listingcharacter"><<=</samp>”

In some examples in this chapter, I use a self-defined <samp class="listingcharacter">cout <<= …</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << … << '\n'</samp>. I do this only for brevity in the presentation in this book.

Do not mix the two operators in an expression: <samp class="listingcharacter"><<=</samp> has a lower operator precedence than <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and would be executed last. Use it at most at the end of the food chain, perhaps in tests.

#### Initialize

I will exemplarily go through the various ways to initialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> with you. These are mostly repeated for the other containers, especially the sequence containers. Elsewhere, I will briefly touch on the common initializations and then focus on the differences.

You can initialize a vector with the default constructor.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/7zMP5fo7c
vector<int> dataA;
vector<int> dataB{};
vector<int> dataC = {};   // no assignment
cout << format("{} {} {}\n", dataA.size(), dataB.size(), dataC.size()); // 0 0 0 
```

**Listing 24.13**     The default constructor initializes an empty <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>.

I have applied the C++20 <samp class="listingcharacter">format()</samp> here.

You can also copy a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. Here you can also see that since C++17, the compiler deduces the template parameter <samp class="listingcharacter"><int></samp> from the constructor arguments.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/cE6G1aErs
auto count(vector<int> arg) { return arg.size(); }
// …
vector input{1,2,3};           // vector<int>
vector outputA(input);         // copy
vector outputB = input;        // also copy, no assignment
cout << count(input) << '\n';  // call by copy-by-value 
```

**Listing 24.14**     Copying a vector using the constructor or implicitly.

Whether automatically by the compiler or intentionally with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::move</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> can also steal the data of another <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. With the help of <samp class="listingcharacter">make_move_iterator</samp>, you can modify any iterator so that it applies <samp class="listingcharacter">std::move</samp> to each individual element. Thus, you can move not only all elements of another container but also those of a range.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/fv5WEe97M
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <iterator>                     // make_move_iterator
using std::make_move_iterator; using std::string;
vector<int> create() { return vector<int>{8, 9, 10}; }
size_t count(vector<int> d) { return d.size(); }
// …
vector input{1,2,3};
vector outputA(std::move(input));       // move
vector outputB = std::move(input);      // also move, not assignment
vector data = create();                 // Return-Value-Optimization
cout << count(input) << '\n';           // call by Copy-by-Value
// move elements from another container
std::list<string> source{ "a", "a", "a", "BB", "CC", "DD", "b", "b" };
auto from = source.begin();
std::advance(from, 3); // 3 forward, but slow in list
auto to = from;
std::advance(to, 3);   // another 3 forward
vector target(make_move_iterator(from), make_move_iterator(to));
// source is now {"a", "a", "a", "", "", "", "b", "b"}, target is now {"BB", "CC", "DD"} 
```

**Listing 24.15**     For return values, the compiler can often also move.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">move_iterator</samp> created by <samp class="listingcharacter">make_move_iterator</samp> ensures that every <samp class="listingcharacter">a = b</samp> during the element-wise initialization of <samp class="listingcharacter">target</samp> becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">a = std::move(b)</samp>. And this means for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> that <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> will contain the empty string afterward. Moving from <samp class="listingcharacter">source</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">target</samp> for three elements does not move the entire elements, but rather applies a move operation element-wise—meaning that the content of the elements is moved, not the element itself.

All containers support initialization with an initializer list and can usually deduce the template parameter for you since C++17\. However, avoid the pitfall of putting C string literals into the initializer list. In such a case, explicitly write <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<string></samp> to force a conversion or use the <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> suffix for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> (or even <samp class="listingcharacter">""sv</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">string_view</samp>).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6rG393Wa5
vector<int> primes{ 2,3,5,7,11 };
vector evens{ 2,4,6,8,10 };
vector<int> notLikeThis{ 'a', 4.3, 8L }; // "Narrowing" double not okay
vector<string> names{ "are", "only" };   // converts arguments
vector sound{ "smoke", "fume" };         // dangerous: vector<const char[]>
vector wet{ "rain"s, "water"s };         // vector<string>
vector cold{ "ice"sv, "pole"sv };        // vector<string_view> 
```

**Listing 24.16**     Using an initializer list to prefill a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. Pay attention to the correct types in the list.

##### Narrowing and Initialization Lists

Narrowing is the implicit conversion of a numeric data type <samp class="listingcharacter">A</samp> into another type <samp class="listingcharacter">B</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">B</samp> is not capable of holding the entire range of values of <samp class="listingcharacter">A</samp>, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>.

In an initialization list, the compiler does not allow such conversions to protect you from typical and hard-to-find errors.

In [Listing 24.15](#24_006.html_l24.15), the compiler complains that you are trying to convert the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> value <samp class="listingcharacter">4.3</samp> into an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. For the <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> value <samp class="listingcharacter">8L</samp>, it does not complain because it is smart enough to realize that an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is sufficient for this. <samp class="listingcharacter">800000000L</samp> will allow it for a 32-bit <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> but not otherwise.

All standard containers can copy data from other containers when fed with iterators.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/h8Pze74ME
#include <deque>
#include <ranges>                       // C++20
// …
std::deque in{1,2,33,34,35,99};
vector thirty(in.begin()+2, in.begin()+5);
for(auto &e : thirty) {
    cout << e << ' ';
}
cout << '\n';
namespace vs = std::ranges::views;      // C++20
auto v = in | vs::drop(2) | vs::take(3);
vector otuz(v.begin(), v.end());
vector trente(std::from_range, in);     // C++23 
```

**Listing 24.17**     Copy values from any other container or C-array during initialization.

Since C++20, this is also possible with the iterators of ranges and views, and from C++23 even without iterators, if you additionally pass the <samp class="listingcharacter">from_range</samp> marker to the constructor.

Specifically for <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, there are constructors that preinitialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> with a number of elements.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/addobjfsK
vector<int> zeros(10);        // 10 zeros
vector<int> sixes(10, 6);     // 10 sixes
vector<int> ten{10};          // Attention! Only one 10
vector<int> tenSix{10, 6};    // Attention! Two elements 10 and 6 
```

**Listing 24.18**     Preinitializing with a fixed number of values is (almost) only available with “vector”.

In these cases, you must use the round brackets <samp class="listingcharacter">()</samp> during initialization; otherwise the elements will be interpreted as an initializer list.

#### Assignment

Like all containers (except <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has overloaded the assignment operator <samp class="listingcharacter">operator=</samp> for copying and moving. With the help of <samp class="listingcharacter">assign</samp>, you can usually apply all those initializations to a container even after construction that you can apply during the “first” initialization. Starting from C++23, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">assign_range</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Yb4jEdaKj
vector<int> from{ 2,3,4 };
vector<int> to{};
to = from;                  // Assignment with operator=, now both are the same

vector<int> drain{};
sink = std::move(from);           // Move, now 'from' is empty
vector<int> v;
v.assign(4, 100);                 // v is now {100, 100, 100, 100}
v.assign(to.begin(), to.end());   // v is now {2,3,4}
int z[] = { 10, 20, 30, 40 };
v.assign(z+1, z+4);               // v is now {20, 30, 40} 
```

**Listing 24.19**     You can assign to “vector” or reinitialize it later with “assign”.

#### Accessing a “vector”

Somehow you need to get to the data that is in the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. There are mainly these possibilities:

*   Iterator
    You use an indirection, mainly an iterator. Because the elements are contiguous, pointers also work.

*   Index
    You use an index to directly address an element. For this purpose, use <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp>.

*   Beginning and end
    <samp class="listingcharacter">front</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">back</samp> return references to the first and last element. As the result is undefined for an empty container, you must combine the query with, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">!empty()</samp> if necessary.

*   Span
    A span is easier to handle than two separate iterators or an iterator and a count. Hence, <samp class="listingcharacter">span</samp> bundles this into a single entity. This class has been available since C++20, and since C++23, there is also the multidimensional variant <samp class="listingcharacter">mdspan</samp>. For more on this, see the “Access via Spans” section ahead.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> container has several member functions that return an iterator, primarily <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp>, as with all containers. And just like with all other containers, you dereference an iterator to get a reference to the actual element, as shown in [Listing 24.20](#24_006.html_l24.20).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/freaK1Pea
vector vowels { 'A', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u' };
const vector even { '0', '2', '4', '6', '8' };
auto it1 = vowels.begin();           // vector<char>::iterator
*it1 = 'a';                          // '*it1' returns 'char&'
auto it2 = even.begin();             // vector<char>::const_iterator
auto it3 = vowels.cbegin();          // enforces const_iterator
*i2 = '9'; *i3 = 'x';                // 'const char&' is not modifiable
for(auto it=vowels.cbegin()+1; it!=vowels.cend(); ++it)
    { cout << *it; } cout << '\n';   // Output: eiou
for(auto it=vowels.crbegin()+1; it!=vowels.crend(); ++it) // ++ despite reverse!
    { cout << *it; } cout << '\n';   // Output: oiea 
```

**Listing 24.20**     With “begin”, “end”, and their relatives, you get iterators.

With the variants <samp class="listingcharacter">cbegin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">cend</samp>, you always get a <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp> back, which does not allow you to modify the element upon dereferencing. <samp class="listingcharacter">begin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp>, on the other hand, return either a <samp class="listingcharacter">const_iterator</samp> or an <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator</samp> depending on the container's modifier.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">r…</samp> variants of these functions allow reverse iteration through the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. Note that you need to increment <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse_iterator</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">const_reverse_iterator</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> to actually iterate backward.

##### [Übung]  Notation for “begin()”, “cbegin()”, “rbegin()”, and “crbegin()”

To be more concise, I write

*   [c]<samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">cbegin()</samp>;

*   [r]<samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">rbegin()</samp>; and

*   [cr]<samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">begin()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cbegin()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">rbegin()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">crbegin()</samp>.

The same applies to the variants of <samp class="listingcharacter">end()</samp>.

Access via iterator is universal for all containers. <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has iterators with random access—that is, via <samp class="listingcharacter">random_access_iterator_tag</samp>. In practice, this means that you can add a positive or negative offset to a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> iterator, as you can see in [Listing 24.21](#24_006.html_l24.21).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/srczx737G
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>               // ranges::sort
using std::vector; using std::cout;
double median(vector<int> data) {  // copied
    std::ranges::sort(data);       // C++20, otherwise std::sort()
    auto it = data.begin();
    auto sz = data.size();
    if(sz==0) return 0;            // special case
    // Determine median:
    auto m = (it+sz/2);            // approximately the middle
    if(sz%2 != 0) {                // odd number of elements
        return *m;
    } else {                       // even number of elements
        return double(*m + *(m-1)) / 2;
    }
}
int main() {
    vector data1 { 12, 22, 34, 10, 1, 99, 33 };
    cout << median(data1) << '\n'; // 22
    vector data2 { 30, 2, 80, 99, 31, 3 };
    cout << median(data2) << '\n'; // 30.5
} 
```

**Listing 24.21**     With “vector” iterators, you can perform random access.

<samp class="listingcharacter">it</samp> points to the beginning of the vector. With <samp class="listingcharacter">m = it+sz/2</samp>, you move forward by half the vector, and <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> points approximately to the middle. For an odd number of elements like <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sz/2</samp> naturally results in <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">it+3</samp> corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">data[3]</samp>, which is the middle of <samp class="listingcharacter">7</samp> elements. If the number is even like <samp class="listingcharacter">6</samp>, then the middle lies between the elements <samp class="listingcharacter">data[2]</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">data[3]</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> points to <samp class="listingcharacter">data[3]</samp>, and thus <samp class="listingcharacter">(*m + *(m-1)) / 2</samp> calculates the average of the surrounding values. To ensure that the division also occurs with floating-point numbers, I convert the intermediate result beforehand with <samp class="listingcharacter">double(…)</samp>.

While every container works with iterators, only <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> allow access to the integer position in the container using <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp>. (Of course, that’s aside from the fact that you can also use an associative container with integers as keys.)

The frontmost element always has the index zero, and the last in the container has the index <samp class="listingcharacter">size()-1</samp>:

*   Unchecked access
    When you access a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">Elem& operator[](size_t idx)</samp>, you immediately get back the element at the stored position—that is, in O(1). It is not allowed to access an element beyond <samp class="listingcharacter">size()-1</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. That would be a programming error and would lead to undefined behavior. You must ensure that this does not happen in your program.

*   Checked access
    <samp class="listingcharacter">Elem& at(size_t idx)</samp> is very fast, in O(1), but the library checks at runtime whether you are using an index within the allowed range of the container. If not, then it is not a programming error, but it throws an exception of type <samp class="listingcharacter">std::out_of_range</samp>.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> both for reading and on the left side of an assignment for writing the element.

In a loop, it is smart to avoid <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> and use <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp>, because typically the loop condition already includes a check.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jjWx3d375
vector d{ 1, 2, 4, -1, 1, 2, -2 };
for(size_t idx=0; idx < d.size(); ) {  // checks vector boundary
    cout << d[idx] << ' ';             // additional check with at not necessary
    idx += d[idx];                     // same here
}
cout << '\n';
// Output: 1 2 -1 4 -2 1 2 
```

**Listing 24.22**     Normally you access with [], because you already check the boundaries elsewhere.

Here, the loop's termination condition <samp class="listingcharacter">idx < d.size()</samp> already checks if access in the loop body is allowed. Using <samp class="listingcharacter">d.at(idx)</samp> would be wasted effort.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">const vector</samp>, both <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp> naturally return <samp class="listingcharacter">const Elem&</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jGx51caTj
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
void printAndMore(const std::vector<int>& data) { // by-const-ref
    std::cout << data[0] << std::endl;
    data[0] = 666;         // doesn't work because 'const int&'
}
int main() {
    std::vector numbers {1,2,3};
    printAndMore(numbers);
} 
```

**Listing 24.23**     Constant container returns constant reference.

Unlike associative containers, the position of elements changes when you delete or insert items.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/s9P1Y6jhv
vector<string> cars{ "Diesel", "Petrol", "Super", "Gas" };
cout << cars[1] << '\n';                   // Output: Petrol
```
