```
#include <algorithm> // copy
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>  // ostream_iterator
#include <vector>
#include <ranges>    // iota, take, stride
using std::accumulate; using std::cout; using std::vector;
namespace vs = std::views;
struct Generator {
    int state_;
    void operator++() { state_ += state_; }
    operator int() { return state_; }
};
int main() {
    std::ostream_iterator<int> os{std::cout, " "}; // Stream output iterator for int
    vector<int> data(7);
    std::iota(data.begin(), data.end(), 10);
    std::copy(data.begin(), data.end (), os);
    cout << '\n';           // Output: 10 11 12 13 14 15 16
    vector<int> seq(7);
    std::iota(seq.begin(), seq.end(), Generator{2});
    std::copy(seq.begin(), seq.end(), os);
    cout << '\n';           // Output: 2 4 8 16 32 64 128
    for(auto i: vs::iota(0) | vs::stride(3) | vs::take(6))
        cout << i << ' ';
    cout << '\n';           // Output: 0 3 6 9 12 15
} 
```

**Listing 25.17**     “iota”, “stride”, and “take”.

Even though it looks like you can only generate sequences of ascending numbers here (which is already quite useful), with a suitable <samp class="listingcharacter">operator++</samp> you can generate quite interesting sequences. Helper type <samp class="listingcharacter">Generator</samp> stores a state that is retrieved during the implicit conversion to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>—specifically when <samp class="listingcharacter">iota</samp> wants to write the value to the output iterator. <samp class="listingcharacter">operator++</samp> on the helper type can execute any function; here I just double the value of the internal state. The result is an almost arbitrary output sequence that can be generated over a changing state.

At the end, you will see the <samp class="listingcharacter">vs::iota</samp> range generator. Here I start at 0 and generate infinitely many values. With <samp class="listingcharacter">stride</samp>, I only take every third value. Because the process is lazy, it can simply be stopped with <samp class="listingcharacter">take</samp> after the sixth value. The last two range adapters are new in C++23.

In the next listing, I perform <samp class="listingcharacter">inclusive_scan</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">exclusive_scan</samp> on a dataset.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/enj3znvTs
#include <numeric> // *_scan
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using std::inclusive_scan; using std::exclusive_scan;
std::ostream& operator<<=(std::ostream&os, const std::vector<int>&data) {
    for(auto &e : data) os << e << ' '; return os << '\n';
}
int main() {
  std::vector data{ 1, 3, 10, 18, 30, 50 };
  std::vector<int> result(6);    // 6 elements
  auto plus = [](auto a, auto b) { return a+b; };
  inclusive_scan(data.begin(),data.end(), result.begin(), plus, 100);
  std::cout <<= result;
  // Output: 101 104 114 132 162 212
  exclusive_scan(data.begin(),data.end(), result.begin(), 100);
  std::cout <<= result;
  // Output: 100 101 104 114 132 162
} 
```

**Listing 25.18**     “inclusive_scan” and “exclusive_scan”.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">inclusive_scan</samp>, the first element of the output already contains <samp class="listingcharacter">100+1</samp>, so the i-th result already includes the i-th input in the sum.

The result of <samp class="listingcharacter">exclusive_scan</samp> starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp>, so the i-th result does not include the i-th input, thus it is exclusive of the i-th element. You always need an initial value for the first result here. I defined <samp class="listingcharacter">plus</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">inclusive_scan</samp> only so that I could use a comparable overload: if you want to specify an <samp class="listingcharacter">init</samp> value for <samp class="listingcharacter">inclusive_scan</samp>, you also need an operator as an argument.

## 25.8    Copy instead of Assignment: Values in Uninitialized Memory Areas

All functions from <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> use assignment with <samp class="listingcharacter">E& operator=(const E&)</samp> when moving elements. With <samp class="listingcharacter">move_iterator</samp>, you can make an algorithm use the move assignment <samp class="listingcharacter">E& operator=(E&&)</samp> instead. But in both cases, an object must already exist at the destination. That means you need to initialize the entire target range with valid objects first. This can be cumbersome and unnecessary as you know that <samp class="listingcharacter">copy</samp> will overwrite the entire range anyway.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><memory></samp> header, there are a handful of additional algorithms that do not require a valid object at the destination. The objects are then created with the copy constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">E(const E&)</samp> in uninitialized memory, not overwritten. The size of this memory must still be sufficient. The ranges variants are also available starting from C++20.

To obtain uninitialized memory, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">get_temporary_buffer</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">malloc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">alloca</samp> C function. To create an object at a specific location, all these algorithms use placement new, a special form of <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> in which the programmer, not the compiler, decides where the object should be created.

Assume that the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> element type is a data type that is really expensive to create, where it would be worthwhile to save the unnecessary initialization. Then you would use <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_copy</samp> as follows:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/dKPbjj1f8
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>    // uninitialized_copy
#include <alloca.h>  // alloca (Linux)
#include <list>
int main () {
  const std::list input{1,9,2,6,6,6,8};
  const auto SZ = input.size();
  // uninitialized memory area:
  int* target = (int*)alloca(sizeof(int) * SZ); // space for 7 ints
  std::uninitialized_copy(input.begin(), input.end(), target);
  // test output
  for(int idx=0; idx<SZ; ++idx) {
    std::cout << target[idx] << ' ';
  }
  std::cout << '\n'; // output: 1 9 2 6 6 6 8
} 
```

The call to <samp class="listingcharacter">alloca</samp> allocates space for seven <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> on the stack (which is automatically freed when the function exits). The memory area is uninitialized—default for the built-in <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> anyway, but unlike usual, real C++ objects would also be uninitialized.

Then the elements from <samp class="listingcharacter">input</samp> are copied to <samp class="listingcharacter">target</samp>—and this time with the copy constructor instead of the assignment operator. Therefore, it is okay that there are no valid objects at the target location. For real classes, this could make a difference.

By the way, <samp class="listingcharacter">alloca</samp> should only be used with extreme caution, so only in functions where nothing can go wrong.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_copy</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: in/fw
    Copies elements of a range using the copy constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_copy_n</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: in/fw
    Copies <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> elements from a starting point to a target point using the copy constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_fill</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Fills a range with a specific value using the copy constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_fill_n</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Creates n copies of a value from a starting point using the copy constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_move</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Moves elements into an uninitialized range.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_move_n</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Moves n elements into an uninitialized range.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_default_construct</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Fills a range with the values of the default constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_default_construct_n</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Creates n objects using the default constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_value_construct</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Fills a range with value-constructed objects.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">uninitialized_value_construct_n</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Creates n objects using value constructor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">destroy_at</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Calls the destructor of an object at a specific address.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Destroy</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Destroys a range of objects.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">destroy_n</samp>
    Usage: special; iterators: fw
    Destroys n objects.

## 25.9    Custom Algorithms

If you want to write such useful functions yourself that you store them in a header for the future of your programming career and then reuse them in all projects, it is quite simple to do. Well, you will need one or two angle brackets <samp class="listingcharacter"><></samp>, but with functions, it's not that bad. The template parameters are mainly iterators and sometimes a function or a functor.

Assume you wanted to write an algorithm that calls a function for all adjacent pairs of a container range. That is, it does something similar to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::for_each</samp>, but for two adjacent elements of the container. Then the following applies:

*   A container range is represented as usual by a pair of iterators.

*   The two iterators are of the same type and a template parameter.

*   The function takes two parameters of the same type.

*   The function is a template parameter.

Let's call the algorithm <samp class="listingcharacter">adjacent_pair</samp>. Its signature can be derived from these considerations as follows:

```
template<typename It, Func>
void adjacent_pair(It begin, It end, Func func); 
```

Thus, the function is flexible regarding the type of iterators and also the type of function. The implementation here is also not difficult.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/n8ErWj7j6
template<typename It, typename Func>
void adjacent_pair(It begin, It end, Func func) {
    if(begin != end) {
        It prev = begin;    // first argument
        ++begin;            // second argument
        for(; begin != end; ++begin, ++prev) {
            func(*prev, *begin);
        }
    }
} 
```

**Listing 25.19**     A custom algorithm.

I use the <samp class="listingcharacter">begin</samp> parameter as the loop variable here, so I don't need to introduce another variable. What I do need, however, is a variable to remember the predecessor in my loop, so I can call <samp class="listingcharacter">func</samp> with it, as promised, with two adjacent elements.

The check at the beginning ensures that the call also works with an empty range. For a range with one element, it also works—no call to <samp class="listingcharacter">func</samp>—because it catches the loop's termination condition.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/91jj8Toqs
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
// … adjacent_pair from above here …
int main() {
    std::vector v{1,2,3,4};
    auto f = [](auto a, auto b) { std::cout << (a+b) << ' '; };
    adjacent_pair(v.begin(), v.end(), f); // 3 5 7
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::vector x{4,8};
    adjacent_pair(x.begin(), x.end(), f); // 12
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::vector w{4};
    adjacent_pair(w.begin(), w.end(), f); // nothing
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::vector<int> y{};
    adjacent_pair(y.begin(), y.end(), f); // nothing
    std::cout << '\n';
} 
```

**Listing 25.20**     The use of <samp class="listingcharacter">adjacent_pair</samp>.

Some basic rules should be observed when implementing algorithms:

*   Only require the properties of forward iterators. That means you should prefer the <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> increment. This way, you can use the new algorithm the most broadly.

*   Compare iterators only with equal <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and not equal <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp>.

*   When defining ranges using iterators, adhere to the rule that the end of a range is exclusive; <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp> therefore points behind the last element.

*   Consider edge cases, especially the empty range as a parameter.

*   Prefer operations that do not generate temporary values—so instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">it++</samp> use <samp class="listingcharacter">++it</samp>.

Depending on the type of iterators you write your algorithm for, you determine which containers the algorithm can then work on. If you stick to forward iterators, the function works with all containers; with bidirectional iterators, it still works with <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>, but as soon as you require random access, you are limited to <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>.

If forward iterators do not fit in your algorithm—because, for example, you want iterators to move forward and backward—then you prefer decrement <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp> over addition <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and subtraction <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> or over <samp class="listingcharacter">advance()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">distance()</samp>. So you are still using bidirectional iterators, but not yet random-access iterators.

If you would use <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> for iterator comparisons, for example, you would also need random-access iterators.

In [Chapter 26](#26_001.html_h26), [Section 26.3](#26_003.html_h26.3), you will see that you can be even more general: input iterators cannot be stored like <samp class="listingcharacter">Iter prev = begin</samp> and reused later. If you want to write an algorithm for these, it is certainly possible. At the latest in this case, you should consider specialization via traits so that you do not lose performance with an overly ubiquitous implementation.

## 25.10    Writing Custom Views and Range Adapters

If you want to write your own range adapters for use in <samp class="listingcharacter">operator|</samp> chains, you need two things: an adapter class that implements your operation, and an instance of it, which is then the adapter itself. This is used to create closure objects. These objects are then instances where your adapter is “bound” to a specific range.

So you write a class <samp class="listingcharacter">MyAdp</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp> and then create an instance <samp class="listingcharacter">myAdp</samp> of it. If you now have a range <samp class="listingcharacter">rng</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">myAdp(rng)</samp> is a range adapter closure object (or just a closure for short). The alternative way to create such a closure is to write <samp class="listingcharacter">rng | myAdp</samp>. You can then chain this closure with other <samp class="listingcharacter">operator|</samp> and ranges.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/e54xzT9dW
#include <ranges>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

using namespace std::literals;
using namespace std; 
namespace vs = std::views; namespace rs = std::ranges;

// Example 1
class Add_1: public rs::range_adaptor_closure<Add_1> { // derive from helper class
public:
  template<rs::input_range R>
  constexpr auto operator()(R&& r) const {        // universal reference
    return forward<R>(r)                          // preserve universal reference
      | vs::transform([](auto i) {return i+1;});  // Your implementation
  }
};
Add_1 add_1{};                                    // Create range adapter

// Example 2
class Dna_to_rna: public rs::range_adaptor_closure<Dna_to_rna> { // derive
public:
  template<rs::input_range R>
  constexpr auto operator()(R&& r) const {        // universal reference
    return forward<R>(r)                          // preserve universal reference
      | vs::transform([](char c)                  // Your implementation
      {
        switch(c) {
          case 'T': return 'U';
          case 't': return 'u';
          default: return c;
        }
    });
  }
};
Dna_to_rna dna_to_rna{};                          // Create Range-Adapter
// Use examples
int main() {
  vector vec{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
  for(auto i: vec | add_1)                        // use
    cout << i << ' ';
  cout << '\n';          // Output: 2 3 4 5 6
  auto telo_rep = "TTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGT"sv;
  for(auto c: telo_rep | dna_to_rna)              // use
        cout << c;
  cout << '\n';          // Output: UUAGGGUUAGGGUUAGGGUUAGGGU
} 
```

**Listing 25.21**     Custom range adapters for views.

Note the following things for your own adapter classes:

*   Your operation must be wrapped in an adapter class, and it must have an <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp> method that takes a range as a parameter.

*   The range parameter should be a universal reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> so that you can work with temp-values and variables.

*   You will likely pass the range parameter along. To preserve the universal reference, you should use <samp class="listingcharacter">forward<R></samp> for that.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">forward</samp> needs the concrete type <samp class="listingcharacter">R</samp>, which is why you cannot use an abbreviated function template with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, but must write out the template. For this, use an appropriate range concept such as <samp class="listingcharacter">input_range</samp>.

*   You should derive from the <samp class="listingcharacter">range_adaptor_closure</samp> base class, which was added in C++23\. You may have noticed that you need to pass your closure class as a template parameter to it. This is the curiously recurring template pattern (CRTP), which helps the base class generate code for your adapter class.

*   Use as much <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp> as possible.

Then create an instance of your adapter class for use in pipelines. In the example, <samp class="listingcharacter">dna_to_rna</samp> is an instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">Dna_to_rna</samp>.

# 26    Good Code, 6th Dan: The Right Container for Each Task

Here I provide a decision aid on which container is right for which task. In the end, I will once again concretely bring together the application of containers and algorithms, because algorithms are part of solving tasks with containers.

## 26.1    All Containers Arranged by Aspects

It is possible to find comprehensive descriptions of the behavior of any given container in a multitude of places. This allows you to select the most appropriate container for a particular scenario “simply” by reading all the documentation.

Or you can read this section, where I do it the other way around: given a scenario or important aspect, and I tell you the strengths and weaknesses of the individual containers for it. Then you can choose the container that fits the given situation.

### 26.1.1    When Is a “vector” Not the Best Choice?

The first rule of thumb is this: use a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. Only if that is not suitable should you use something else.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has so many good properties that there must be a good reason to decide against it:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>
    If you don't want the elements to end up on the heap, but rather be managed on the stack like automatic variables, you can consider an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> does not guarantee that the memory is always managed in the same place, but in practice it is very likely to be the stack. Alternatively, you can also use a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> with a special allocator.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>
    If <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_back</samp> are not enough when inserting, because you also need <samp class="listingcharacter">push_front</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_front</samp>, then use <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>
    If a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> grows dynamically, copying elements is expensive or impossible, and you don't know beforehand how many elements will come, then you can switch to <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>. It guarantees that once inserted, elements stay in place. A second reason could be that you often need to insert in the middle. In both cases, you should be aware of the management overhead of <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>
    If all elements always need to be kept sorted, then use a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>. However, read in the next section that it is worth considering whether you can split your work into a writing phase and a reading phase, because then <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">sort</samp> between the phases are the best solution.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp>
    If you need an association from a key to a target, a <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> is usually the best choice.

There are a few key tips to keep in mind when using <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>.

You should add new elements to the back as often as possible. You do this with <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace_back</samp>. You should also remove elements from the back. The method for this is called <samp class="listingcharacter">pop_back</samp>.

If you already know or can estimate how many elements you will insert, you should request this amount with <samp class="listingcharacter">reserve</samp>. The automatic growth of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is surprisingly efficient, but if you can avoid it, why not?

### 26.1.2    Always Sorted: “set”, “map”, “multiset”, and “multimap”

Before using <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>) to keep elements constantly sorted, you should prefer one of the ordered associative container types. An <samp class="listingcharacter">insert</samp> in the middle of a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> is really expensive. Because the elements in a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> are stored contiguously, in the case of an insertion that does not occur at the end, all elements must be shifted one position to the right. This also applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>, and although the latter does not guarantee completely contiguous storage for the elements, inserting in the middle is also suboptimal.

If you decide on a constantly sorted <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, starting from C++23, <samp class="listingcharacter">flat_set</samp> is available. It is as easy to use as a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> but stores its elements in a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. This does not nullify the cost of an insertion in the middle; if you do not have too many elements, and they are also small, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">flat_set</samp>.

Against keeping sorted with <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> or even <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>, it argues that finding the insertion position takes a while. Even if a <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> is sorted, you usually have to traverse from the beginning to the desired element when searching. This is faster in a sorted <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>. And the associative sorted containers are specifically made for this task.

### 26.1.3    In Memory Contiguously: “vector”, “array”

For most applications, it is a huge advantage if the elements are densely packed in memory—and also nicely in a contiguous manner. This is exactly what <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> guarantee.

There are two main reasons for this:

*   Locality
    When you iterate through the elements of a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, you usually start at the beginning and move toward the end in small or large jumps. The closer the memory accesses are within a unit of time, the better for the computer: memory is accessed in medium-sized blocks. For example, if you want to read only one byte, the CPU will still load a four-kilobyte page. The next time you read memory near the first byte, which is on the same page, it does not need to be loaded again. A huge time saver. The strategy of an implementation under this aspect is called locality behavior.

*   Shared access
    Wouldn't it be useful if you only needed to know a single memory address to process a million elements? This is possible with <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>. If you know that your container holds a million elements, a single call to <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp> is enough, and you have all the information you need. From that point on, the elements lie neatly next to each other. You can use this, for example, to pass all elements together to a C function. Many C functions take a raw pointer plus a count to receive multiple elements. This is not only useful for interacting with C: writing a single large block of data from memory to disk is much faster than multiple small ones, and some C++ functions also take advantage of this.

#### The “deque” Does Not Guarantee Contiguous Storage

Regarding the locality of elements, <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> is as good as <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. The elements are very likely stored directly next to each other and therefore require very little additional management overhead. When you iterate through them, it is memory-friendly in one direction.

But not all elements are guaranteed to be stored next to each other. There can be several large chunks. This means there is no way to access the single memory area of the elements with <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp>, as is the case with <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. Therefore, this application is unfortunately ruled out for <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>.

### 26.1.4    Cheap Insertion: “list”

Inserting a single element somewhere in the middle of a <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> (and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>) always costs a constant amount of time—called O(1) (see [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.1.4](#24_001.html_h24.1.4)). No other container can exhibit this property:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> (and <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>) can insert at the end (and beginning) in O(1), but require linear time in the middle—called O(n).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> (and the <samp class="listingcharacter">multi_…</samp> variants) guarantee O(log n), and the position is determined by the sorting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered_map</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered_set</samp> usually insert in O(1), but in the worst case, which is hard to predict, in O(n). The position of the insertion also cannot be determined and may change with further insertions.

### 26.1.5    Low Memory Overhead: “vector”, “array”

If you want to store a million small elements like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, it can't be done more compactly than in <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>. You need exactly zero bytes of additional memory per element. That's not much and can't be beaten by any other container—except perhaps <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp>, which requires a little additional memory for block management, but very little.[[ 68 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn26_01)

All other containers require more additional memory per element. Rarely can this be reduced with tricks:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> stores two additional pointers per element. On a current Linux system, an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> requires four bytes and a pointer requires eight bytes of memory. For one million <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> elements, you need four megabytes of memory with a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. In a <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp>, you would occupy 20 megabytes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> is specifically designed for low memory overhead. If <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> (without any overhead) does not work, but the smallest possible additional footprint per element is crucial, then <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> is preferred. However, keep in mind that you will have to deal with its specialized interface, which I advise against unless necessary.

*   The ordered associative containers store their elements in a tree. Typically, this means that three additional pointers are required per element (although optimizations exist).

*   The unordered associative containers maintain a hash table and a set of buckets with the actually inserted elements. The hash table holds pointers and, when well-filled, has about as much space for pointers as you have elements in the container.[[ 69 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn26_02) The buckets are usually implemented as <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp>. All in all, you need an estimated two additional pointers of space per element in your container.

Besides the additional memory required per element, there is another factor you need to consider: It is much worse to request 1,000 bytes 1,000 times than to request 1,000,000 bytes once. This is because the system also requires some memory for each requested memory block. It gets even worse if you also release blocks in between. Then it depends on how well your system can reuse memory—and that is an arbitrarily difficult problem.

What can happen is that the memory fragments. The bad thing is that it happens without you noticing, hidden from you. Your program has no way to detect fragmentation. You only notice it when you request memory that is theoretically available but can no longer be provided to you. Yes, there are solutions for this, but they are situation-dependent. One of the possible solutions is this: use a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>.

#### Noteworthy Special Case: “vector<bool>”

A <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<bool></samp> is optimized for low memory usage. It packs the elements tightly—that is, eight <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>s per byte. [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Table 24.12](#24_011.html_t24.12) presents the different alternatives for storing many <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> values.

### 26.1.6    Size Dynamic: All Except “array”

<samp class="listingcharacter">array<int,5></samp> means space for five. Not four, not six, but five. You can neither remove elements from the <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> nor add any. All other containers grow with their tasks: they start empty and with possibly preallocated memory and grow dynamically as you add more elements. In most cases, you don't have to worry about the additional overhead when growing.

But there are exceptions. Here are the facts about the growth of containers in the C++ standard library:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> cannot grow.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> manage singly linked elements. They behave optimally when growing: the elements are inserted individually and independently into the data structure. However, many small memory allocations can cause memory fragmentation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> can grow well, but it is not optimal. Occasionally, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has to double its size and temporarily occupies three times the memory than actually needed for the elements, but immediately releases one-third of it. However, the memory does not fragment, even if you store many small elements.

*   The ordered associative containers link elements individually in a tree-like structure. This is also good for growth. However, parts of the tree need to be rearranged when inserting, which involves some effort.

*   The unordered associative containers also store the elements individually linked, which is good for adding elements one by one. However, the hash table occasionally needs to be resized. To estimate the effort of resizing, assume the hash table is a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> with approximately as many pointers as the container has elements.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> has the most degrees of freedom when it comes to implementation. It grows well, at worst like a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. However, it is more likely that memory is requested in larger chunks and not as much temporary storage is needed.

That's all there is to say about growth. But what about shrinking?

*   You can't remove anything from an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_list</samp> as well as all associative containers manage their elements individually, and removing an element also frees its memory. Only in the case of unordered associative containers might the hash table not be affected by shrinking.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> does not shrink when you remove elements. The maximum space that a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> once required it will continue to require, even if you delete elements. You can explicitly call <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit</samp>, which releases (parts of) the excess memory. The implementation may do this, but it doesn't have to. However, all implementations known to me support <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit</samp> to the next larger power of two. Note that you should not call <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit</samp> after every removal.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">deque</samp> can be implemented like <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> and therefore has <samp class="listingcharacter">shrink_to_fit</samp>, but it can also be implemented with blocks and automatically behave better regarding removal.

## 26.2    Recipes for Containers

After the general guide to container selection, I will show you some specific recipes for handling containers. I have chosen problems that frequently occur in practice:

*   Is a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> really the right container for a sorted collection?

*   How do I output the contents of a container?

*   Can I really not add an element to an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>?

Answering these questions in the following sections also helps in understanding some fundamental aspects of C++ and the standard library: the linear memory layout of <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>, the interaction between streams and containers, and the moving of values.

### 26.2.1    Two Phases? “vector” as a Good “set” Replacement

Note that whenever your use of <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> splits into two distinct phases for filling and reading, you should prefer using a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. A <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> keeps its elements sorted at all times and incurs some overhead with every insertion. Often, it is better to first dump all elements into a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter">push_back()</samp> and then sort them in one go with <samp class="listingcharacter">sort()</samp> from the header <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/T4d4jdqox
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using std::vector; using std::ostream; using std::cout;
int main() {
    vector<int> data{};
    data.reserve(400);                    // Space for 400 elements
    // Phase 1: fill
    for(int idx = 1; idx <= 20; ++idx) {
        for(int val = 0; val < 20; ++val) {
            data.push_back(val % idx);    // something between 0 and 19
        }
    }
    cout << data.size() << '\n';          // 400 elements between 0 and 19
    // Post-processing Phase 1: create set-equivalent
    std::sort(data.begin(), data.end());  // preparation for unique
    auto wo = std::unique(data.begin(), data.end()); // duplicates to the end
    data.erase(wo, data.end());           // remove duplicates
    data.shrink_to_fit();
    cout << data.size() << '\n';          // only 20 elements left
    // Phase 2: use
    for(auto &e:data)
        cout << e << ' ';                 // Output: 0 1 2 .. 18 19
    cout << '\n';
    auto it = std::lower_bound(data.begin(), data.end(), 16); // search value
    if(it!=data.end() && *it == 16)
        cout << "found!\n";
    if(std::binary_search(data.begin(), data.end(), 7))   // yes or no
        cout << "also found!\n";
} 
```

**Listing 26.1**     With a “vector”, you can simulate a “set”.

If you then iterate over the elements of the vector, you get the same result as with a <samp class="listingcharacter">multiset</samp>. To simulate a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>, follow the call to <samp class="listingcharacter">sort()</samp> with a call to <samp class="listingcharacter">unique()</samp> from the header <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> and then remove duplicates with a call to <samp class="listingcharacter">erase()</samp>.

Then you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> almost as if it were a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>. The elements are sorted, which means you can read them out in the same order. Instead of using <samp class="listingcharacter">find()</samp> to search for elements, you now use, for example, the functions <samp class="listingcharacter">lower_bound()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">binary_search()</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp>. This is done using binary search and is therefore just as fast as <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>—probably even faster as <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has better locality behavior, meaning the data is stored in a more CPU-friendly manner in memory.

#### Binary Search

This is a standard procedure to ensure that a desired element can be found in a sorted sequence of elements with a few steps. In this process, the middle element of the sequence is successively selected and then searched either to the right or left, depending on whether the middle element is greater or smaller than the desired element. This guarantees that the desired element is found after a maximum of log n steps or it is known that it is not in the list.

The disadvantage of this procedure is that you keep more elements in the <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> during the insertion phase than in a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp>. This means that <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> loses its speed advantage over <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> if you expect many duplicates. When exactly this happens depends on many factors. As a rule of thumb, I would recommend that using <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> as a <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> replacement is worthwhile if you expect more than about 1,000,000 elements and more than half of them remain unique. For fewer elements, the additional effort in implementation is hardly worthwhile, and for fewer unique elements (i.e., more duplicates), <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> saves memory.

### 26.2.2    Output the Contents of a Container to a Stream

This recipe is needed repeatedly: for example, for debugging or during unit tests. Of course, there are a thousand ways to output the elements of a container to a stream: from a simple loop to a ranged <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop to a specialized overload of the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>.

The most elegant way, however, is to copy the contents of the container to the stream—for this, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ranges::copy()</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> is used, or std::copy before C++20\. Then, all that is needed is the <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream_iterator</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><iterator></samp> as an adapter, and the output is a one-liner:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/fGKsfs1Y4
#include <iostream>  // cout
#include <algorithm> // copy
#include <iterator>  // ostream_iterator
#include <vector>
int main() {
  std::vector<char> path{};
  for (char ch = 'a'; ch <= 'z'; ++ch) {
    path.push_back(ch);
  }
  std::ranges::copy(path, // here everything, but it also works with other ranges
    std::ostream_iterator<char>(std::cout, " ") // copy to cout, separator " "
  );
} 
```

### 26.2.3    So “array” Is Not That Static

After reading the chapter on containers, you might think that <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> always has a fixed size. While this is true, you don't have to completely discard <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> if you need one more or one less element. It is generally quite simple to add an element to an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>, merge two together, or shrink it.

Almost. You cannot turn an <samp class="listingcharacter">array<int,1000></samp> into an <samp class="listingcharacter">array<int,1001></samp> without copying the integers once. But for (large) elements like perhaps <samp class="listingcharacter">Picture</samp>, which you can move, you can indeed turn an <samp class="listingcharacter">array<Picture,50></samp> into an <samp class="listingcharacter">array<Picture,51></samp> without copying a lot of data.

It is quite easy to enlarge any <samp class="listingcharacter">array<T,n></samp> by one element.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Yde6azqoc
#include <iostream>
#include <array>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
using std::array; using std::move; using std::forward;

// == enlarging array ==
template<typename T, size_t S, std::size_t... Idx>
constexpr array<T, S+1>
help_append(array<T, S>&& data, T&& elem, std::index_sequence<Idx...>) {
  return { std::get<Idx>(forward<array<T, S>>(data))..., forward<T>(elem) };
}
template<typename T, size_t S>
constexpr auto
append(array<T, S> data, T elem) {
  return help_append(move(data), move(elem),
                  std::make_index_sequence<S>{});
}

// == Example ==
class Picture {            // rule of zero; movable
  std::vector<char> data_; // lots of data
  std::string name_;
public:
  explicit Picture(const std::string& name) : data_(1000,0), name_{name}
    { /* ... load picture here ... */ }
  auto name() const { return name_; }
};
int main() {
  // before
  array pics{Picture{"Mona"}, Picture{"Scream"}, Picture{"Vincent"}};
  std::cout << pics[0].name() << '\n'; // Output: Mona
  // enlarge
  Picture new_pic { "Clocks" };
  auto more = append(move(pics), move(new_pic));
  // after
  std::cout << pics[0].name() << '\n'; // Output:
  std::cout << more[0].name() << '\n'; // Output: Mona
  std::cout << more[3].name() << '\n'; // Output: Clocks
} 
```

**Listing 26.2**     You get back an array enlarged by one element.

First, let me explain what happened in <samp class="listingcharacter">main()</samp>. In the middle, you see a call to <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp>. It is important here that you pass both arguments with <samp class="listingcharacter">move</samp>; otherwise, the <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp> function could not move the data out of its parameters. As a reminder: with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::move</samp>, you convert an lvalue reference into an rvalue reference—a temp-value—and thereby tell the compiler that it is allowed to “steal” the data from the argument. If you omit this, you still get a larger <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> back, but the original <samp class="listingcharacter">pics</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">new_pic</samp> parameters would remain unchanged. However, the data was moved out of them, which you can see by the fact that <samp class="listingcharacter">pics[0].name()</samp> is empty. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">pics[0].data_</samp> is now empty.

You still have three <samp class="listingcharacter">Picture</samp> elements in <samp class="listingcharacter">pics</samp>, but they are all empty and are now in the first three slots of the <samp class="listingcharacter">array<Picture,4></samp> named <samp class="listingcharacter">more</samp>.

How did that happen? The key lies in the helper function <samp class="listingcharacter">help_append</samp> and in <samp class="listingcharacter">index_sequence</samp>. First, <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp> calls the helper function:

```
return help_append(move(data), move(elem), std::make_index_sequence<S>{}); 
```

I'll write this in pseudocode, where the functionality of <samp class="listingcharacter">make_index_sequence</samp> becomes a bit clearer. The call effectively results in the following:

```
return help_append(move(pics), move(new), tag<0,1,2>); 
```

With the template function <samp class="listingcharacter">make_index_sequence<S></samp>, you generate a tag type at compile time that somehow contains a sequence of numbers—specifically, the numbers needed to directly access the individual elements from <samp class="listingcharacter">pics</samp>.

The helper function now constructs a new array:

```
return { std::get<Idx>(forward<array<T, S>>(data))..., forward<T>(elem) }; 
```

The braces <samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp> form an initializer list. And because the return type is given as <samp class="listingcharacter">array<T,S+1></samp>, it specifically initializes an <samp class="listingcharacter">array<Picture,3+1></samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp> is central here. The ellipses <samp class="listingcharacter">...</samp> refer to the passed <samp class="listingcharacter">index_sequence</samp>, which is <samp class="listingcharacter"><0,1,2></samp> (pseudocode). The compiler expands this to <samp class="listingcharacter">get<0>(d), get<1>(d), get<2>(d)</samp>. Finally, <samp class="listingcharacter">elem</samp> is added to the initializer list—in this case, <samp class="listingcharacter">new_pic</samp>.

But not quite: to actually move, each <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> is actually <samp class="listingcharacter">forward(data)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">new_pic</samp> is actually <samp class="listingcharacter">forward(new_pic)</samp> (with the respective template arguments). Using <samp class="listingcharacter">forward</samp> and the universal reference <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> in the parameter list, the function works for both values to copy and temp-values to move.

So if you have movable values in an <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>, you can still manipulate the <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> cost effectively.

Consider the following implementation using <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp> for comparison.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/MMP16Mj3W
#include <iostream>
#include <array>
#include <string>
using std::array;
template<typename T, size_t S>
auto append(const array<T, S>& data, T elem) {
    array<T, S+1> result {};
    for(auto i=0u; i < data.size(); ++i)
        result[i] = data[i];
    result[S] =elem;
    return result;
}

int main() {
    // before
    array pics { 3, 4, 5 };
    std::cout << pics[0] << '\n'; // Output: 3
    // enlarge
    auto more = append(pics, 77);
    // after
    std::cout << more[3] << '\n'; // Output: 77
} 
```

**Listing 26.3**     “append” at runtime.

Here is an implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp> that uses <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp>. For better clarity, I have removed everything related to moving, but that makes no difference for what I want to explain.

The main difference between <samp class="listingcharacter">get<></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp> is, of course, that the index for access with <samp class="listingcharacter">get<></samp> is decided at compile time, whereas with <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp> it is decided at runtime. And because of this, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">get<></samp> together with the ellipsis <samp class="listingcharacter">...</samp> which the compiler expands to index accesses at translation time. At runtime, you don't have this feature, so you have to resort to a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop.

There are only small speed advantages that you get with <samp class="listingcharacter">get<></samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp>. It is more likely that the compiler can optimize something better. Because with the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp> is now too complicated for <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>. And if there's one thing the compiler likes for its optimization attempts, it's <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>.

## 26.3    Implementing Algorithms That Are Specialized Depending on the Container

If you want to write algorithms that behave differently depending on the type of range (or container) they operate on, starting with C++20, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr if</samp> and the well-thought-out hierarchy of ranges concepts to write the appropriate implementation in the different <samp class="listingcharacter">if constexpr</samp> branches.

Within a single function, you can decide which algorithm you want to use for which range. All of this happens at compile time, as shown in [Listing 26.4](#26_003.html_l26.4).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/rqz1s6h11
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <list>
#include <ranges>
namespace rs = std::ranges;

template<rs::range R>
void alg(R&& range) {
  if constexpr(rs::random_access_range<R>)
    std::cout << "random access.\n";
  else if constexpr(rs::bidirectional_range<R>)
    std::cout << "bidirectional, but not random access\n";
  else static_assert(false, "unsupported range type");
}
int main() {
    std::vector<int> vec {};        // vector is random access
    alg(vec);
    std::list<int> lst;             // list is only bidirectional
    alg(lst);
    std::istreambuf_iterator<char> i1{std::cin}, i2{}; // not even bidirectional
    auto fwd = rs::subrange{i1, i2};
    alg(fwd);                       // Error: no matching implementation
} 
```

**Listing 26.4**     Different implementations of an algorithm, distinguished by concepts.

Before C++20 with its ranges, concepts, and <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr if</samp>, this was not so easily possible. The way then led through the iterator tags, with which you can offer multiple overloads of a function. The code would thereby become much more confusing.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr if</samp>, you have more flexibility than would be the case with overloads. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">random_access_range</samp> first checks the special case, then <samp class="listingcharacter">bidirectional_range</samp> the more general one.

# 27    Streams, Files, and Formatting

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Stream
    Model of a class for input and output.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">iostream</samp>
    Base classes for input and output streams.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>></samp>
    Important operators for output and input.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cerr</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">clog</samp>
    Standard streams for normal input, output, and error output.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><filesystem></samp> Header with utilities for working with files in the filesystem.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><format></samp>
    Function for flexible formatting from C++20.

*   print and println from <samp class="listingcharacter"><print></samp>
    Output using <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> from C++23.

Handling files and input/output in C++ is realized through a special and extensible stream model. This chapter will explain this fundamental stream model of C++ in more detail.

Streams sometimes—but not always—refer to files. Handling names and other attributes of files on the hard drive is described at the end of this chapter.

Sometimes, using streams feels a bit cumbersome, especially when it comes to changing formatting. From C++20, there is a new formatting library in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><format></samp> header, which allows convenient formatting attributes and is extensible. It is entirely independent of streams. Direct formatted output will be possible from C++23 with <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">println</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><print></samp> header. We will discuss both at the end of this chapter.

## 27.1    Input and Output Concept with Streams

On the following pages, you will very often read the term stream or stream object. <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> are examples of such (globally predefined) stream objects. A stream is a flow of data that moves in a specific direction. Each stream object has its own properties, which are defined by the corresponding stream class.

The entire principle is based on a hierarchy of class templates, with the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> class at the top of the class hierarchy, from which all other stream classes are derived. [Figure 27.1](#27_001.html_f27.1) shows a simplified representation of the input/output class hierarchy.

[![Simplified representation of the stream hierarchy.](bilderklein/klein27_001.png)](img-f27.1.html)

**Figure 27.1**     Simplified representation of the stream hierarchy.

The I/O stream library with all its facets is extremely extensive, so not all details of the library can be covered here.

### Specializations

In the representation in [Figure 27.1](#27_001.html_f27.1), the specializations for a base type have already been shown. Apart from <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">basic_</samp> prefix would appear before each class template here. A specialization thus looks as follows:

```
using ostream = basic_ostream<char>; 
```

This is a specialization for the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> data type from the <samp class="listingcharacter">basic_ostream</samp> class template. Such specializations can also be used for other character types like <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">char16_t</samp>, and so on.

## 27.2    Global, Predefined Standard Streams

The I/O stream library provides predefined and global stream objects that you have used practically since your first C++ program without knowing what they are. Of course, we are talking about the standard stream objects <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cerr</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">clog</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">std</samp>.

For output, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ostream></samp> header file contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> (standard output), <samp class="listingcharacter">cerr</samp> (standard error output, unbuffered), and <samp class="listingcharacter">clog</samp> (standard error output, buffered) stream objects. For input, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><istream></samp> header file contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> stream object, which can be used for typical user inputs (e.g., from the keyboard).

### 27.2.1    Stream Operators << and >>

Basically, a data stream is initially nothing more than an unreadable sequence of bytes, which is formatted for output by specializing <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> and for input by specializing <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>></samp>.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ostream></samp> header file, you will find <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> overloaded multiple times for all built-in types:

```
ostream& operator<<(bool val);
ostream& operator<<(short val);
ostream& operator<<(unsigned short val);
ostream& operator<<(int val);
// … 
```

The same applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>></samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><istream></samp> header file:

```
ostream& operator>>(bool val);
ostream& operator>>(short val);
ostream& operator>>(unsigned short val);
ostream& operator>>(int val);
// … 
```

By returning the stream as a reference with the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>></samp> operators, it becomes possible to use the operators multiple times in a row, as in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/WaEGdnWvq
#include <iostream> // cin, cout
int main() {
    int val1, val2;
    std::cout << "Please enter 2 int values: ";
    std::cin >> val1 >> val2;
    std::cout << val1 << " : " << val2 << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 27.1**     Returning the stream by reference allows chaining.

#### Using Custom Types

Many standard classes like <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> also have the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>></samp> operators implemented. For custom classes, you need to implement these yourself if you want <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and/or <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> to work with streams.

The standard input/output operators support almost all fundamental types in C++. Exceptions are <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">nullptr_t</samp>. Of course, input and output do not occur arbitrarily. There are also a few things you need to consider:

*   Numeric types
    When reading a numeric value, the input must start with at least one digit. If you specify the sign with <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">–</samp>, it must only appear before the first digit. However, there must be no space between the sign and the digit. Leading whitespace characters are ignored. In case of an erroneous input, the numeric value is set to 0 and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::failbit</samp> is set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> The use of <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> for input was already very critical in C. Input is read until the first whitespace or until end of file (EOF; more on this later). Leading whitespace is skipped, which can be changed with the <samp class="listingcharacter">skipws</samp> manipulator. The problem with reading <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> is that it can read beyond the buffer area (buffer overflow)—for example, char <samp class="listingcharacter">cval[20];std::cin >> cval</samp>. If you read in more than 20 characters here, <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> will dutifully do so and write into an undefined memory area. Therefore, with old C-strings (if you absolutely must use them), you must always ensure that the maximum length is not exceeded. For this, the <samp class="listingcharacter">setw</samp> manipulator from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><iomanip></samp> header is suitable—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">cin >> setw(20) >> cval</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> The output of <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> is converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> and to <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. For input, the same rules as for numeric values apply initially. When entering valid numeric values other than <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, it is converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> (= <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>). When entering <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> (for <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>) is used. In case of an erroneous input, the value is also set to <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">std::failbit</samp>.

## 27.3    Methods for Stream Input and Output

In addition to the usual <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>></samp> for streams, you can also use methods provided by the I/O stream library. However, unlike the <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> operators, these methods work with raw bytes and are therefore unformatted. The methods for standard input/output use the <samp class="listingcharacter">streamsize</samp> type from <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp>, which is usually <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t</samp>. This means, for example, that leading whitespace is not ignored during input.

### 27.3.1    Methods for Unformatted Output

For raw and unformatted output, the I/O stream library provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">put()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp>methods from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ostream></samp> header file. The <samp class="listingcharacter">put()</samp> method outputs individual characters, and <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> outputs a specified number of characters. The following code snippet demonstrates these methods briefly:

```
std::string sdata("raw data");
for(auto c : sdata)
    std::cout.put(c);
std::cout << 10 ;          // = 10
std::cout.put(10);         // = Newline '\n'
char cdata[] = {"raw data"};
std::cout.write(cdata, 4); // = raw
std::cout.put(10);         // = Newline '\n'
std::cout.flush(); 
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">put(c)</samp>, you output the individual characters of the <samp class="listingcharacter">sdata</samp> string unformatted on the screen. With <samp class="listingcharacter"><< 10</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">put(10)</samp>, you can clearly see the comparison between formatted and unformatted output. While <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout << 10</samp> outputs the formatted value 10, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout.put(10)</samp> outputs the unformatted (usually ASCII) value on the screen. A look at an ASCII table shows that the value 10 stands for the newline character.

Afterward, the unformatted output with <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> is demonstrated. It simply outputs a specified number of characters (here, four) from <samp class="listingcharacter">cdata</samp> unformatted to the screen. Here, of course, there is again a risk because more characters can be specified than are actually available. At the end, we also force all data still in the stream's buffer to be output immediately with <samp class="listingcharacter">flush()</samp>.

#### Positioning Stream

To position streams, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">tellp()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">seekp()</samp> methods, which are also included in <samp class="listingcharacter"><ostream></samp>. These methods only become really interesting when you work with files. You can learn more about this in [Section 27.6](#27_006.html_h27.6).

The following is an overview of the methods for unformatted output in <samp class="listingcharacter"><ostream></samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream& put(char c);</samp>
    Writes the <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> argument to the stream.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream& write(char* s, streamsize n);</samp>
    Writes <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> characters from <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> to the stream. The caller must ensure that the value of <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is not greater than the number of characters in <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. The termination character for C strings <samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp> does not end the output of <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream& flush();</samp>
    Flushes the stream buffer immediately. All characters in the buffer that have not yet been written must now be output.

All methods return the <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> stream. Whether the output was successful can and should be checked using the functions from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp> header file ([Section 27.4](#27_004.html_h27.4)).

### 27.3.2    Methods for Unformatted Input

When reading raw data with methods, unlike formatted reading with <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>, leading whitespace characters are not simply skipped and ignored. For unformatted input, the header file <samp class="listingcharacter"><istream></samp> offers several methods, some of which are overloaded multiple times.

The following is an overview of the methods for unformatted input in <samp class="listingcharacter"><istream></samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& get(char& c);</samp>
    Extracts a single character from the stream into <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& get(char* s, streamsize n);</samp>
    This reads n–1 characters from the stream and stores them as a C string in <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. If fewer than n–1 characters are used, reading continues until the first newline character <samp class="listingcharacter">'\n'</samp>. The newline character is not stored in <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. The null terminator <samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp> is automatically added at the end.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& get(char* s, streamsize n, char del);</samp>
    This reads n–1 characters from the stream and stores them as a C string in <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. If fewer than n–1 characters are used, it reads up to the first delimiter character contained in <samp class="listingcharacter">del</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">del</samp> character is not stored in <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. The termination character <samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp> is automatically appended at the end.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& getline(char* s, streamsize n[, char del]);</samp>
    The main difference from the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> versions is that the <samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> error flag is set if more than n–1 characters are read.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& read(char* s, streamsize n);</samp>
    This extracts n (not n–1) characters from the stream and stores them in C string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. Unlike the <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getline</samp> versions, the read sequence is not terminated with the null character <samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp>—a classic function for copying entire blocks of data.

For all versions where you extract <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>–1 characters from the stream into the address of <samp class="listingcharacter">char* s</samp>, you must ensure that there is enough memory space available in <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. All methods return the stream <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp>. Whether the input was successful can/should be checked using the mechanisms available in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp> header file ([Section 27.4](#27_004.html_h27.4)). Extracting characters from a stream is terminated in all input methods when EOF is read.

#### End of File

EOF is often defined with the value –1 and is used to indicate the end of a data stream or file. In an interactive shell, you can also generate EOF with a key combination. In classic Unix shells, you can reproduce this with (Ctrl)+(D). In the Windows command prompt, EOF is generated using (Ctrl)+(Z).

The following simple listing demonstrates some of the methods for unformatted input.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/MaEzcccTG
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::cin; using std::endl;
int main() {
    const unsigned int MAX = 10;
    char buffer[MAX] = {0};
    cout << "Input getline : ";
    cin.getline(buffer, MAX);
    cout << std::cin.gcount()
        << " characters were read\n";
    for(auto c : buffer) {
        if(c && c!='\0') cout.put(c);
    }
    cin.ignore(MAX, '\n');
    cout << "\nMake input (end with .) : ";
    char ch=0;
    while(cin.get(ch)) {
        if(ch == '.') break;
        cout.put(ch);
    }
    cout << "Input ended" << endl;
} 
```

**Listing 27.2**     Unformatted input from streams.

First, I extract up to <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX</samp> characters from the <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> stream and store them in <samp class="listingcharacter">buffer</samp>. The number of characters actually extracted from the stream is determined using the <samp class="listingcharacter">gcount()</samp> method. The <samp class="listingcharacter">gcount()</samp> method can also be used for all other methods of unformatted input.

Then I output the individual characters to the screen using <samp class="listingcharacter">put()</samp>.

In this example, I use the <samp class="listingcharacter">ignore()</samp> method to skip up to <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX</samp> characters from the input stream until the <samp class="listingcharacter">'\n'</samp> character and remove <samp class="listingcharacter">'\n'</samp> from the buffer. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">'\n'</samp>, another character can also be used here. In the example, I use this line to pull the newline character out of the buffer so that it is not used in the next read operation and can thus be simply skipped.

This “trick” does not work everywhere. On other systems (such as the Mac), you can insert the following lines:

```
cin.clear();
cin.ignore(cin.rdbuf()->in_avail());
cin.get(); 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop comes from the classic Unix framework, which simply reads all characters from the <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> stream unformatted and outputs them to the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> stream. Reading continues until a period is entered or EOF is reached.

The program during execution looks like this:

```
Input getline: Hello getline
9 characters were read
Hello get
Make an input (end with .): Hello get
Hello get
Another line
Another line
We end with a period.
We end with a period
Input ended 
```

#### std::string and getline()

In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><string></samp> header file, you will also find a <samp class="listingcharacter">getline()</samp> method that reads a line from a stream into a <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp>.

## 27.4    Error Handling and Stream States

For streams, it is often not enough to simply check whether something works (<samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>) or does not work (<samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>). Because various types of errors can occur, the I/O stream library provides mechanisms to check the state of the stream. For this, you will find a few constants with <samp class="listingcharacter">iostate</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_state</samp> (see [Table 27.1](#27_004.html_t27.1)).

The constants are defined in <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> members and can be accessed either directly via <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::goodbit</samp>) or through classes derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> or created objects (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::goodbit</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">cout.goodbit</samp>).

| Constant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp> | No problems with the stream. All other bits are not set. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">eofbit</samp> | EOF is set. The end of a data stream has been reached. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> | Error in an input/output function. An input/output operation could not be successfully executed. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">badbit</samp> | Severe error. The stream is in an undefined state. |

**Table 27.1**     Constants in iostate.

### 27.4.1    Methods for Handling Stream Errors

To query the individual states, C++ offers you various methods:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">bool good()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if everything is okay (<samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp> is set).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">bool eof()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the file stream has ended (<samp class="listingcharacter">eofbit</samp> is set).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">bool fail()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if an error has occurred (<samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">badbit</samp> are set).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">bool bad()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if a serious error has occurred (<samp class="listingcharacter">badbit</samp> is set).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void clear()</samp>
    Resets the state of <samp class="listingcharacter">iostate</samp>. Status is set to <samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void clear(iostate f)</samp>
    Resets the state of <samp class="listingcharacter">iostate</samp> and sets the status to <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void setstate(iostate f)</samp>
    The current state is combined with <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> using a bitwise OR.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">iostate rdstate()</samp>
    Returns the currently set status.

#### eofbit and failbit Set

Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> is also set when <samp class="listingcharacter">eofbit</samp> is set. The reason is that the <samp class="listingcharacter">eofbit</samp> state is only set after an attempt is made to perform another action past the EOF. This also means that the next operation fails, and therefore <samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> is set as well.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/exKMv8646
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::cin; using std::ofstream;
void checkIOstate(std::ios& stream) {
    if( stream.good() ) {
        cout << "All good\n";
    } else if( stream.bad() ) {
        cout << "Fatal error\n";
    } else if( stream.fail()) {
        cout << "I/O error\n";
        if( stream.eof()) {
            cout << "End of stream reached\n";
        }
    }
    stream.clear();
}
int main() {
    int val=0;
    cout << "Enter value: ";
    cin >> val;
    checkIOstate( cin );
    std::ifstream file;
    file.open("nonexistent.text");
    checkIOstate(file);
    std::fstream fstr;
    fstr.open("newFile.txt",
        ofstream::out | ofstream::in
        | ofstream::binary | ofstream::trunc);
    fstr << "Text in the file\n";
    fstr.seekp(std::ios_base::beg);
    char ch;
    while( fstr.good()) {
        fstr.get(ch);
        if(fstr.good()) cout.put(ch);
    }
    checkIOstate(fstr);
} 
```

**Listing 27.3**     State checks for streams.

Pass any stream to the <samp class="listingcharacter">checkIOstate()</samp> function to check its state. I check the individual methods to clarify the state. At the end, I reset the state with <samp class="listingcharacter">clear()</samp> back to <samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp>.

In the section starting from <samp class="listingcharacter">val=0</samp>, you will be prompted to enter a value. Correctly, you must enter an integer here. With <samp class="listingcharacter">checkIOstate</samp>, I then check the <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> stream. If the input is correct, <samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp> is set, and <samp class="listingcharacter">good()</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. For an incorrect input like <samp class="listingcharacter">blablubb</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">fail() true</samp>.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream file</samp>, I check a file stream <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ifstream</samp>, because with it I can open a file for reading. In the example, it is assumed that the file does not exist, which is why <samp class="listingcharacter">fail()</samp> is true here as well.

And finally, starting from <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream fstr</samp>, I demonstrate EOF. Between <samp class="listingcharacter">open</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">seekp</samp>, I create a file, write something into it, and reset the data stream to the beginning. In the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, I read characters from the <samp class="listingcharacter">fstr</samp> stream as long as the state of <samp class="listingcharacter">fstr</samp> is equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">good()</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp> set). If the state is no longer <samp class="listingcharacter">good()</samp>, either the end of the data stream has been reached (<samp class="listingcharacter">eofbit</samp> is set) or an error has occurred (<samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> is set).
