As already mentioned, <samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> is usually also set when <samp class="listingcharacter">eofbit</samp> is set.

#### Exception ios_base::failure

In case of errors in the I/O stream library, the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::failure</samp> exception can also be thrown (if <samp class="listingcharacter">badbit</samp> is set). However, this depends on the implementation of the compiler manufacturer. Nevertheless, it is possible to throw and catch this exception yourself using <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp>.

#### Checking Streams with “bool”

The state of the stream can also be tested with <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> operator. Both have been implemented as methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">operator bool()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">operator!()</samp>). Both methods return whether an error has occurred (<samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">badbit</samp> set).

For example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator bool</samp> is used as shown in the next listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Mr6E3Ez48
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    unsigned int val;
    std::cout << "Enter value: ";
    std::cin >> val;
    if( std::cin ) { // operator bool()
        /* ... */                                   // Input correct
    } else {
        std::cout << "Error with std::cin\n";   // Error with input
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.4**     Operator “bool” of streams.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">if(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)…</samp>, the stream, because it is used in an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>, is automatically converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">operator bool()</samp> is defined in the class specifically for such purposes. You can just as easily apply the <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> operator to streams.

## 27.5    Manipulating and Formatting Streams

How characters are input or output in a stream is controlled by so-called flags, which are defined in the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> base class. You can think of flags as an array of bits, where the values can be either 1 or 0. Individual bits, of course, do not make a value, so the bits are stored in a variable. Depending on the set bits, the value of the variable changes, and each value has a special meaning. All flags have a default setting, where, for example, without further specification, all integral values are output in decimal (<samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp>) notation.

You can directly change the format flags by using methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">setf()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">unsetf()</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">flags()</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> class. However, a better alternative has been available for a long time (specifically) with manipulators. With these, you can insert and call all flags directly as a function in an input or output stream. In practice, the use of manipulators is therefore usually preferable to direct access to the format flags with methods. Therefore, manipulators will be discussed first. The methods by which you can directly change the format flags will be briefly introduced in [Section 27.5.4](#27_005.html_h27.5.4).

### 27.5.1    Manipulators

Manipulators for streams are objects that you can insert with the standard input/output operators <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>. You are already familiar with the manipulator <samp class="listingcharacter">endl</samp>. This adds a newline character to the buffer to output a new line. The basic manipulators are listed in <samp class="listingcharacter"><istream></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><ostream></samp> in [Table 27.2](#27_005.html_t27.2).

| Manipulator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">endl</samp> | Outputs a new line and flushes the output buffer. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ends</samp> | Adds the null terminator character (<samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp>) to the buffer. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">flush</samp> | Flushes the stream's output buffer. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ws</samp> | Ignores leading whitespace when reading input. |

**Table 27.2**     Basic manipulators in <istream> and <ostream>.

#### Independent Manipulators in “<ios>”

You can find a considerable number of additional manipulators in the header file <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp>. These are manipulators to enable or disable certain states or to format the data during output. I summarized the manipulators in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), [Table 6.3](#06_002.html_t6.3).

Since C++20, you can often use <samp class="listingcharacter">format()</samp> instead of the manipulators. This allows you to convert built-in and custom types into a string. You can find the description in [Section 27.10](#27_010.html_h27.10).

It is easy to enable or disable states. Once (de)activated in a particular stream, the state remains until you call the opposite manipulator again. Consider the following simple example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/s1csa51z9
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
using std::cin; using std::cout; using std::endl;
void f(bool b) {
     cout << b << endl;                     // Output:  true
}

int main () {
    bool b=true;
    cout << std::boolalpha << b << endl;   // Output: true
    b=false;
    cout << b << endl;                     // Output: false
    f(true);
    cout << std::noboolalpha << b << endl; // Output: 0
    b=true;
    cout << b << endl;                     // Output: 1
} 
```

**Listing 27.5**     Outputting a Boolean as text or a number.

First, I push <samp class="listingcharacter">std::boolalpha</samp> into the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> stream to output <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> from Boolean variables literally, which the output in the same line also immediately proves. The <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << b</samp> afterwards also outputs the value of the Boolean variable literally. From this, you can see that the setting, once activated, remains active.

The output in the function <samp class="listingcharacter">f()</samp> shows that the setting is globally applicable. After the function call, I deactivate the setting again by sending <samp class="listingcharacter">std::noboolalpha</samp> into the stream. The output of the now numeric values of <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> confirm this process.

Even if the example doesn’t show it, you can certainly apply the manipulator on input streams like <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp> as well—for example:

```
bool b;
std::cin >> std::boolalpha >> b; 
```

Here you can now actually enter <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>, and it will be recognized as a Boolean value.

#### Manipulators for integers

Other manipulators are available that allow you to set the number base format between decimal, hexadecimal, and octal. In [Table 27.3](#27_005.html_t27.3), you will find an overview from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp> header file.

| Manipulator | Reading/writing integral values is done in … |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp> | … decimal number format (default setting). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hex</samp> | … hexadecimal number format. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">oct</samp> | … octal number format. |

**Table 27.3**     Manipulators for the format of integral types.

The following listing shows the three manipulators for changing the integer format.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/bEKaYdssE
#include <iostream>
#include <ios>
using std::cout; using std::endl;
void f() {
    int val = 100;
    cout << val << endl;                // Output: 0x64
}
int main() {
    int val = 255;
    cout << std::showbase;
    cout << std::dec << val << endl;   // Output: 255
    cout << std::hex << val << endl;   // Output: 0xff
    f();
    cout << std::oct << val << endl;   // Output: 0377
    cout << val << std::endl;          // Output: 0377
} 
```

**Listing 27.6**     Number formats in output.

First, I use the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::showbase</samp> manipulator so that the number base <samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp> for hexadecimal or <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> for octal values appears. I could have skipped the manipulator <samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp> at this point because it is the default setting, and thus the value is output in decimal form anyway.

Next is the <samp class="listingcharacter">hex</samp> manipulator, which causes the value to be output in hexadecimal notation. The setting then remains global for the stream, as confirmed by the output of the <samp class="listingcharacter">f()</samp> function. Then the value is output in octal representation after applying the <samp class="listingcharacter">oct</samp> manipulator. The very last output shows again that the setting remains for the stream. If you want to have the decimal notation again, you must reset the format with the <samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp> manipulator.

#### Manipulators for Floating-Point Numbers

There are also some manipulators (<samp class="listingcharacter">floatfield</samp> flags) for floating-point numbers, which are also included in <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp> and listed in [Table 27.4](#27_005.html_t27.4).

| Manipulator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">fixed</samp> | Output in floating-point notation: <samp class="listingcharacter">3.14159</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">scientific</samp> | Output in exponential notation: <samp class="listingcharacter">3.14159e+000</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hexfloat</samp> | Writes in hexadecimal format: <samp class="listingcharacter">0x1.921f901b866ep+1</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">defaultfloat</samp> | Writes the value in the default notation. |

**Table 27.4**     Manipulators for floating-point numbers.

#### Manipulators for Alignment

Finally, there are various manipulators that allow the stream output to be aligned. An overview of these <samp class="listingcharacter">adjustfield</samp> flags, which are also defined in <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp>, can be found in [Table 27.5](#27_005.html_t27.5).

| Manipulator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">internal</samp> | Fills the space between the sign and the value. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">left</samp> | Aligns the output to the left. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">right</samp> | Aligns the output to the right. |

**Table 27.5**     Manipulators for aligning output.

Using these manipulators to align the output is, of course, only useful if the output has been set to a specific width using <samp class="listingcharacter">setw()</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><iomanip></samp> header file. For better understanding, here is an example with the corresponding output on the screen:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TMdzrjvhd
#include <iostream>
#include <ios>        // left, right, internal
#include <iomanip>    // setw
using std::cout; using std::endl;

int main() {
    int val = -1000;
    cout << std::setw(10) << std::internal
         << val << endl;

    cout << std::setw(10) << std::left << val << endl;

    cout << std::setw(10) << std::right
         << val << endl;
} 
```

**Listing 27.7**     Different ways to pad output.

The program speaks for itself when executed:

```
-     1000
 -1000
      -1000 
```

#### Manipulators with Arguments

There are some manipulators with arguments in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><iomanip></samp> header file. You can find an overview of them in [Table 27.6](#27_005.html_t27.6).

| Manipulator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setiosflags(ios::fmtflags m)</samp> | This allows you to combine multiple flags with a bitwise <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;</samp> and set them to <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">resetiosflags(ios::fmtflags m)</samp> | Clears all flags specified by <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setbase(int base)</samp> | Sets the base for reading and writing integral values to 8, 10, or 16. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setfill(char ch)</samp> | If a fill width is used, the empty space is filled with the character <samp class="listingcharacter">ch</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setprecision(int n)</samp> | This allows you to set the number of decimal places for floating-point numbers. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setw(int w)</samp> | This allows you to set a fill width between two values in a stream. |

**Table 27.6**     Manipulators with parameters from the “<iomanip>” header file.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/sYK8oT33x
#include <iostream>
#include <ios>        // left, right, internal
#include <iomanip>    // setw

using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
    double dval = 3.14159;
    std::ios_base::fmtflags ff(std::ios::scientific|std::ios::uppercase);
    cout << std::setiosflags(ff);
    cout << dval << endl;                           // Output: 3.141590E+00
    cout << std::resetiosflags(ff) << dval << endl; // Output: 3.14159
    cout << std::setprecision(3) << dval << endl;   // Output: 3.14
    cout << std::setw(10);
    cout << std::setfill( '*' ) << 1246 << endl;    // Output: ******1246
} 
```

**Listing 27.8**     Number formats in output.

First, I store a few format flags in the bitmask of type <samp class="listingcharacter">fmtflags</samp>. You can combine multiple flags using the <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> operator. Then I set the flags so that a floating-point number appears in exponent format and the <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp> is capitalized. You don't necessarily have to create <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::fmtflags</samp>; you can also write the flags directly into <samp class="listingcharacter">setiosflags</samp>. Then I reset these settings with <samp class="listingcharacter">resetiosflags</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">setprecision()</samp> ensures that the floating-point number is truncated to three digits in the output. The <samp class="listingcharacter">dval</samp> value is not changed in the process. <samp class="listingcharacter">setfill()</samp> together with <samp class="listingcharacter">set()</samp> for the fill width demonstrates how it is extended to 10 characters, and the empty space is now filled with the <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> character.

##### setw() Is Different

Note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">setw()</samp> manipulator does not make the width setting permanent, as is the case with all other manipulators. The width is reset after each use and must therefore be set again before each use.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">get_money()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">put_money()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">get_time()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">put_time()</samp>, you have four more manipulators. You can use them for locale-specific tasks such as input/output of currency or date and time.

### 27.5.2    Creating Custom Manipulators without Arguments

You can also create your own manipulators. In practice, you only need to accept the stream as an argument and return a reference to this stream. In between, you can manipulate the stream (hence the name manipulator). Custom manipulators without arguments can be implemented with a few lines of code, as in the next listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/z8zc3ocd5
#include <iostream>
#include <ios>        // left, right, internal
#include <iomanip>    // setw
using std::cout; using std::cin; using std::endl;
std::ostream& tabl(std::ostream& os) {
    os << '\t';
    return os;
}
std::istream& firstNum(std::istream& is) {
    char ch;
    is.get(ch);
    if( (ch >= '0') && (ch <= '9') ) {
        std::cin.putback(ch);
    }
    return is;
}
int main() {
    int val=0;
    cout << "Text1" << tabl << "Text2" << endl; // Output: Text1 (tab) Text2
    cout << "Make an input: ";
    cin >> firstNum >> val;
    cout << val << std::endl; // Output: 12345
} 
```

**Listing 27.9**     Custom manipulators.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">tabl</samp> function manipulates <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp>. You can embed the function in an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> or, more precisely, give it to <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> because an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> is passed as an argument and the <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> is also returned by reference. Within the function, you can now modify the stream as desired. For example, you can use one of the many manipulators offered by the standard library. In the example, I wrote a simple <samp class="listingcharacter">tabl</samp> manipulator that generates a tab character <samp class="listingcharacter">\t</samp>. You see this in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> between <samp class="listingcharacter">Text1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Text2</samp>.

You can also manipulate the input, as <samp class="listingcharacter">firstNum</samp> demonstrates. There I pass an <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp> as an argument and return this <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp> as a reference. Within the function, you can now manipulate the input stream. In this example, I do something similar to what <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp> does when reading a leading whitespace—namely, ignore it. In this example, I check the first character of <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp> to see if it matches any of the characters 0 through 9\. If that is the case, I push it back into the input stream with <samp class="listingcharacter">putback</samp>. If it is not one of the characters 0 through 9, an incorrect first character was entered, and I simply let it be “swallowed.” In <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, you also see an example of this.

The fact that you can pass a custom-written manipulator through the input/output operators is due to the (complex) implementation of the operators:

```
ostream& ostream::operator<<(ostream& (*fp) (ostream&) ) {
    *fp(*this);
    return *this;
} 
```

Thanks to the function pointer <samp class="listingcharacter">*fp</samp>, our custom-written manipulators are called in the stream. <samp class="listingcharacter">*fp(…)</samp> then calls the passed function. <samp class="listingcharacter">fp</samp> is thus a pointer to a function that, as shown in the example, takes an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream&</samp> as an argument and returns an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream&</samp>. Thanks to automatic conversion of functors and lambdas to C function pointers, it also works as in the following listing.

```
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
    auto ddash = [](auto &os) -> std::ostream& { return os << "--"; };
    cout << "Text1" << ddash << "Text2" << endl; // Output: Text1--Text2
} 
```

**Listing 27.10**     Manipulator as lambda.

Here, instead of a function, I have defined a lambda as a manipulator. Note that you must specify the return type of the lambda with <samp class="listingcharacter">-> std::ostream&</samp> to ensure that it returns by reference and not by value.

It is the same for the input stream.

### 27.5.3    Creating Custom Manipulators with Arguments

You can also create manipulators with arguments without much effort using a functor.

The following listing is a simple example of how you can write manipulators with parameters.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/KKE6nWT49
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::endl;
class dendl { // Dots followed by newline
    int dendl_;
public:
    dendl(int n=1)
      : dendl_{n} {}
    std::ostream& operator()(std::ostream& os) const { // Functor
        for(int i=0; i<dendl_; ++i) os << '.';
        return os << '\n';
    }
};
std::ostream& operator<<( std::ostream& os, const dendl& elem) {
    return elem(os);
}
int main() {
    cout << "Text1" << dendl(4); // Output: Text1....
    cout << "Text2" << dendl(2); // Output: Text2..
    cout << "Text3" << dendl();  // Output: Text3.
} 
```

**Listing 27.11**     Manipulators with parameters.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">dendl</samp>, you see the typical class definition for defining the functor needed in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>. This functor itself does nothing more than output <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> dots followed by a newline.

As you can see in the <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> application, you will notice that using the functor alone is not yet possible. The equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << dendl(4)</samp> as a function call is the following:

```
operator<<(std::cout, dendl(4)); 
```

However, <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> does not yet have an overload for the second parameter of type <samp class="listingcharacter">dendl</samp>. This must still be provided—as in the example. In it, only the call to the passed function object needs to be made.

The implementation of a manipulator with arguments for the input stream can be implemented similarly.

#### Reference as Return Value

Here too, it is advisable to return a reference because this ensures that further operations can be chained with the operator.

### 27.5.4    Directly Change Format Flags

In addition to formatting streams using manipulators, you can also directly change the flags using methods. Although the use of manipulators is generally more common and considerably more convenient, we will briefly discuss the available methods here. The difference is also quite quickly explained. Consider the following listing, in which we use manipulators to format the output.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/csbPMYM19
#include <iostream>
#include <ios> // hex, dec
using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
    int val = 255;
    cout << std::showbase << std::hex << val << endl;   // Output: 0xff
    cout << std::noshowbase << std::dec << val << endl; // Output: 255
} 
```

**Listing 27.12**     Directly influencing format.

First, I use the two manipulators to output the hexadecimal value (<samp class="listingcharacter">ff</samp>) along with the number base (<samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp>). Then I deactivate the output of the number base and switch the base back to decimal.

The manipulators used here are equivalent to the following instructions, where the flags were directly changed using methods.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/1xzzMdjdM
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
    int val = 255;
    cout.setf(std::ios_base::hex, std::ios_base::basefield);
    cout.setf(std::ios_base::showbase);
    cout << val << std::endl; // Output: 0xff
    cout.unsetf(std::ios_base::showbase);
    cout.setf(std::ios_base::dec, std::ios_base::basefield);
    cout << val << std::endl; // Output: 255
} 
```

**Listing 27.13**     Influencing format with “setf” and “unsetf”.

Here the same thing happens as in [Listing 27.12](#27_005.html_l27.12), but first the bit for the hexadecimal number representation is set with <samp class="listingcharacter">hex</samp> in the group <samp class="listingcharacter">basefield</samp>. To ensure that the number base (<samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp>) is also output, I set this flag for the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> stream. I do the same in reverse order further down, where I clear the <samp class="listingcharacter">showbase</samp> bit again. At the end, I reset the flag in the <samp class="listingcharacter">basefield</samp> group back to decimal integer output (<samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp>).

I think the example shows the clearer and more convenient use of manipulators as opposed to the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">setf()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">unsetf()</samp> used here. With manipulators, you don't have to deal with cumbersome things like flags, bits, and bitmasks. And ultimately, a manipulator like <samp class="listingcharacter">std::showbase</samp> internally calls the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout.setf(std::ios::showbase)</samp> method anyway.

Some format of the flags can also be used in groups, as seen in the example of <samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">basefield</samp>. Specifically, there are three groups with <samp class="listingcharacter">adjustfield</samp> (and the flags <samp class="listingcharacter">left</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">right</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">internal</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">basefield</samp> (with the flags <samp class="listingcharacter">dec</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">oct</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">hex</samp>), and <samp class="listingcharacter">floatfield</samp> (with the flags <samp class="listingcharacter">scientific</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">fixed</samp>).

Independent flags, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">showbase</samp>, can be used alone (though with <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::</samp>). [Table 27.7](#27_005.html_t27.7) provides an overview of the methods in the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> class, which allow you to directly change the format flags.

| Method | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setf(flags)</samp> | Sets the format flags to <samp class="listingcharacter">flags</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">setf(flags, group)</samp> | Sets the format flags of the group <samp class="listingcharacter">group</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">flags</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">unsetf(flags)</samp> | Clears all <samp class="listingcharacter">flags</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">flags()</samp> | Returns the currently set format flags. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">flags(flags)</samp> | Sets the format flags to <samp class="listingcharacter">flags</samp>. |

**Table 27.7**     Methods for accessing format flags.

The next listing is the same example as the previous one, but now everything should be implemented using only the <samp class="listingcharacter">flags()</samp> method.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/4MY1Yznv9
#include <iostream>
using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
    int val = 255;
    std::ios::fmtflags ff = std::cout.flags();
    cout.flags(std::ios::hex | std::ios::showbase);
    cout << val << endl;  // Output: 0xff
    cout.flags(ff);
    cout << val << endl;  // Output: 255
} 
```

**Listing 27.14**     Saving and restoring flags.

I retrieve the current state of the format flags with <samp class="listingcharacter">flags()</samp> and store it in <samp class="listingcharacter">ff</samp>. Calling <samp class="listingcharacter">flags(…)</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">hex</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">showbase</samp> parameters for the <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> stream changes the format. Afterward, I restore the previously saved state of the format flags, which the output at the end confirms.

#### Further Methods for Formatting

You will also find suitable methods in the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base</samp> class (see [Table 27.8](#27_005.html_t27.8)) for some manipulators with parameters, primarily to format variable output (like precision or fill width).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int fill() const</samp> | Returns the currently set fill character. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int fill(int ch)</samp> | Sets the fill character to <samp class="listingcharacter">ch</samp>. Equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter"><< setfill(ch)</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int width() const</samp> | Returns the field width. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int width(int n)</samp> | Sets the field width to <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>. Equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter"><< setw(n)</samp>. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int precision() const</samp> | The current precision of floating-point numbers. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int precision(int n)</samp> | Sets the precision to <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>. Equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter"><< setprecision(n)</samp>. |

**Table 27.8**     Additional methods of the “ios_base” class for formatting.

##### width() Is Different

As with the manipulator <samp class="listingcharacter">setw()</samp>, the fill width setting using <samp class="listingcharacter">width()</samp> does not remain permanent, unlike all other flags. The fill width is reset after each use and must therefore be set again before each use.

## 27.6    Streams for File Input and Output

You've been using the computer for a while now, and you've found yourself working with variables in the system's memory. You've probably noticed that when you close the program, all those variables just disappear. Well, don't worry, because in this section, I am going to show you how you can save those variables permanently on an external storage device so that you can access them whenever you need them.

Before we get started, I just want to quickly go over how you can access files. To access files, you'll need certain functions. These are provided by the C++ standard library. When reading and writing files, you don't access them byte by byte. Instead, you access them in larger blocks to improve efficiency. For this kind of data transfer, we use a buffer as a temporary storage space in the RAM. You can think of the file or the file's contents as an array of bytes with a specific length.

And just like you write the data into a file, you can also read it back out again. So, you'll need to take care of the formatting and structure yourself. To make sure that reading and writing files works smoothly, there's a special place in the file (starting from 0) that you can use. This is called the file position, and it makes sure that files are processed in the right order. If you read 10 bytes from a file, the read position will be on the 10th byte. The same goes for writing.

### 27.6.1    The “ifstream”, “ofstream”, and “fstream” Streams

The streams for file input and output have been seamlessly integrated into the stream concept of the standard library. If you look at the beginning of the chapter and at the simplified class hierarchy in [Figure 27.1](#27_001.html_f27.1), you can see that the <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp> file streams all have well-known classes as base classes. This means that you can use all the well-known input/output operations (such as the operators <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>) with files as well. Basically, only the stream object changes. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp>, other stream objects associated with a file are now used. Here is a brief overview of the three available file stream classes:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp> is derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp> and is used for reading files.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp> is derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp> and is used for writing to files.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp> is derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">iostream</samp> and can be used for reading and writing to files.

For all file streams, you must include the <samp class="listingcharacter"><fstream></samp> header file in your program.

### 27.6.2    Connecting to a File

To do anything with a file, you must first instantiate an appropriate stream object of type <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp>. Furthermore, you must open the file. You can open the file either directly during instantiation with the appropriate constructor or with the <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> method by specifying the file name (optionally with path). You can specify the file name as a C string or <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp>. Specifying a mode in which you want to open the file is also optional.

#### No Path Specified

If you do not specify a path, the system assumes that the file is in the same directory where you are running the program.

The next listing shows some examples where a few file streams are created and files are opened.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/o7YP7or8s
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
int main() {
    std::string name = "textfile.txt";
    std::ifstream file01;
    file01.open(name);
    if( file01.fail() ) {
        std::cout << "Could not open " << name << "\n";
    }
    std::ofstream file02("data.dat");
    if( file02.good() ) {
        std::cout << "data.dat opened or created\n";
    }
    std::fstream file03;
    file03.open("database.db");
    if( !file03 ) {
        std::cout << "Could not open database.db\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.15**     Opening and creating files.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream file01</samp>, I create an <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp> object for reading using the default constructor. The <samp class="listingcharacter">file01</samp> stream object created this way is not yet associated with any file. I accomplish this with the <samp class="listingcharacter">open()</samp> method and the file name. I check whether the file could be opened using the <samp class="listingcharacter">fail()</samp> method.

Next, I create a new stream object for writing. I provide the file name directly in the constructor. If this file does not exist, it will be created. If this file does exist, it will be truncated to length 0 by default, and the old content will be overwritten. With <samp class="listingcharacter">good()</samp>, I check whether the file was successfully opened or created.

In the last example, I open a file <samp class="listingcharacter">database.db</samp> for reading and writing using <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp>. If the file does not exist, the <samp class="listingcharacter">!file03</samp> check will return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> and present an appropriate error message.

#### Error Checking

For error checking when opening a file, you can use both <samp class="listingcharacter">if(!file)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">if(file.fail())</samp>. In both cases, <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> will be returned if opening a file has failed and thus the <samp class="listingcharacter">failbit</samp> flag is set (see also [Section 27.4](#27_004.html_h27.4)). If a file is successfully opened, all error flags are cleared, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">goodbit</samp> flag is set. Therefore, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">good()</samp> method to test whether the file was successfully opened (<samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>) or not (<samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>).

#### Flags for Opening a File

When opening a file stream, you can either stick with the default values of the <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp> class, or you can set optional flags that determine how the file is opened. In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ios></samp> header file, you will find the definition of the type (specifically the bitmask) <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::openmode</samp>. The individual flags (see [Table 27.9](#27_006.html_t27.9)) can be combined with each other using the bitwise OR operator <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp>, where appropriate.

| Flag | Short | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp> | Input | Open for reading (default for <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp> | Output | Open for writing (default for <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::app</samp> | Append | Always add something at the end when writing. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::trunc</samp> | Truncate | The file length is set to 0, and existing content is deleted. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::ate</samp> | At end | Positions the read or write position at the end of the file immediately after opening. Without this flag, the read and/or write position is usually at the beginning of the file after opening. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::binary</samp> | Binary | Opens the file in raw binary mode. For example, line-end conversions are not performed, and raw bytes are transferred. Without this mode, a file is opened in a formatted text mode. |

**Table 27.9**     Various flags for opening a file.

##### Default Values of “ifstream”, “ofstream”, and “fstream”

The default value of <samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp> is essentially <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp>, that of <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out | ios::trunc</samp>, and that of <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in | ios::out</samp>.

You can write the flags either directly in the constructor after the file name or in the method after the file name. The following listing shows two simple examples.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/GoPddTWq6
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
using std::cout;
int main() {
    std::ofstream file01("testfile.txt", std::ios::out|std::ios::app);
    if(file01.fail()) {
        cout << "Could not open testfile.txt\n";
    } else {
        cout << "ok.\n";
    }
    std::fstream file02;
    file02.open("database.db", std::ios::out|std::ios::trunc);
    if( !file02 ) {
        cout << "Could not open database.db\n";
    } else {
        cout << "ok.\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.16**     Additional flags when opening files.

| Flags from <samp class="listingcharacter">ios</samp> | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">in</samp> | Read; file must exist. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> | Truncate and write; file will be created if necessary |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">out &#124; trunc</samp> | Truncate and write; file will be created if necessary |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">out &#124; app</samp> | Append data; file will be created if necessary |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">app</samp> | Append data; file will be created if necessary |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">in &#124; out</samp> | Read and write; file must exist; file position at the beginning |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">in &#124; out &#124; trunc</samp> | Truncate, read, and write; file will be created if necessary |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">in &#124; out &#124; app</samp> | Read and write; append data; file will be created if necessary |

**Table 27.10**     Meanings of different combinations for opening a file.

First, I open a file for writing (<samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp>) with <samp class="listingcharacter">"testfile.txt"</samp> and append the new content to the end of the file (<samp class="listingcharacter">ios::app</samp>). I also open the file <samp class="listingcharacter">"database.db"</samp> for writing (<samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp>), where the content of the file is deleted (<samp class="listingcharacter">ios::trunc</samp>). If this file does not yet exist, it will be created.

Confusion often arises about when and how to combine which flags. It can definitely be said that you should always use at least the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp> flag, which is also the default setting of the classes. For <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp>, the file must already exist. If you do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp>, the file will be newly created if it does not exist. [Table 27.10](#27_006.html_t27.10) provides an overview of various combinations of flags and what they do.

#### Close File

When you are done with the file, you should return the resources to the system and close the file. First, you do not have an infinite number of file streams available, and second, you ensure that data still in the buffer is finally processed. To close a file, the <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> method is used. The following listing briefly demonstrates <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TMzdWhE51
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::ofstream file01("data.db");
    if( file01.fail() ) {
        std::cout << "Could not open data.db\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "ok.\n";
    }
    file01 << "Text for the file\n";
    if( file01.is_open()) {
        file01.close();
    }
    file01.open("data001.db");
    // Automatically:
    {
        std::ofstream file02("data002.db");
    } // here file02 is closed
} // here file01 is also closed 
```

**Listing 27.17**     Explicitly closing a file stream.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp>, you cut the connection to the file. To avoid accidentally closing a file that is not (or is no longer) open, I use the <samp class="listingcharacter">is_open()</samp> method here, which checks whether the stream object <samp class="listingcharacter">file01</samp> is actually connected to a file. Otherwise, you might trigger an exception when attempting to close.

A file is also closed when the running program terminates or the scope of the stream variable is exited, as you can see with <samp class="listingcharacter">file01</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">file02</samp>.

You will find an overview of the basic methods for opening and closing files in [Table 27.11](#27_006.html_t27.11).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">open(filename)</samp> | Opens the file for a stream object in the default mode. The default mode depends on the class used (<samp class="listingcharacter">ifstream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">fstream</samp>). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">open(filename, flags)</samp> | Opens the file for a stream object and uses <samp class="listingcharacter">flags</samp> for the mode. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> | Closes the file. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">is_open()</samp> | Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if a stream object is open, otherwise <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. |

**Table 27.11**     Methods for opening and closing files.

##### You Cannot Copy Streams by Value

You can't copy stream objects, only move them. This means that you use references as parameters, for example. If you return the parameter, you can also do so by reference.

When you create a stream in a function, one possible approach is to return it by value (not by reference). In this case, you must either return a temp-value directly with <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> or pass a local variable to the outside using <samp class="listingcharacter">std::move</samp>.

### 27.6.3    Reading and Writing

After you have opened a file, you can use this stream object for reading and writing, just as you are already accustomed to with standard stream objects like <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>.

The simplest way to write something to a file or read something from it is likely to use the <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> operator for writing and the <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> operator for reading. With this, you can also use all known manipulators and methods for formatting. The following example is intended to demonstrate this.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/3756v8rzK
#include <fstream>
#include <iomanip> // setw
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::ofstream file("data.dat");
    if( !file ) {
        std::cout << "Could not open data.dat\n";
        return 1;
    }
    file << std::setw(10) << std::setfill( '*' )
         << 1234 << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 27.18**     Reading and writing with files.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">file("data.dat")</samp>, I open a file for writing. If the file already exists, the old content will be deleted. If this file does not exist, it will be created. Then I push the value <samp class="listingcharacter">1234</samp> with a field width of ten characters, filling the remaining characters with an asterisk, into the stream object <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp>, where everything is written to the file. Afterward, the content of the file <samp class="listingcharacter">data.dat</samp> looks as follows:

```
******1234 
```

In practice, however, formatted writing and reading with the operators <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> is rarely used. It is much more efficient to read from and write to files in whole blocks and in binary mode. I will go into more detail on the individual possibilities (character-wise, line-wise, and block-wise) in the next sections.

#### Byte-Wise Reading and Writing

If you want/need to read or write a file byte by byte, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">put()</samp> methods here. The usage is the same as with the stream objects <samp class="listingcharacter">cin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp>, except that you use the corresponding stream object with which you opened the file.

The following listing reads a file byte by byte and outputs each byte on the screen.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/sjaGaq48v
#include <fstream>
#include <iomanip> // setw
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::ifstream file("data.dat");
    if( !file ) {
        std::cout << "Error opening file\n";
        return 1;
    }
    char ch;
    while(file.get(ch) ) {
        std::cout.put(ch);
    }
    if( file.eof() ) {
        file.clear();
    }
    file.close();
} 
```

**Listing 27.19**     Byte-wise reading and writing.

First, I try to open the <samp class="listingcharacter">data.dat</samp> file. In the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, I start with byte-wise reading from the <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> file stream. Each character read with <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> is immediately output to the screen with <samp class="listingcharacter">put()</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop continues until EOF is reached.

It should now be no problem to copy a file byte by byte instead of outputting to the screen. To do this, you simply need to create a file stream for writing, open it, and write the read bytes there (byte by byte) instead of outputting to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp>. I don't want to withhold the example from you, so examine the following listing.

```
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
using std::cout;
int main() {
    std::ifstream file("data.dat");
    if( !file ) { /* Error */ cout << "ERR\n"; return 1; }
    std::ofstream filecopy("backup.dat");
    if( !filecopy ) { /* Error */ cout << "ERR\n"; return 1; }
    char ch;
    while(file.get(ch) ) {
        filecopy.put(ch);
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.20**     Copying a file byte by byte.

Similarly, you can also read data from the keyboard via the stream object <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cin</samp> instead of using the data stream <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> and write the typed data into the file stream <samp class="listingcharacter">filecopy</samp>. However, you must trigger EOF yourself using the key combination (Ctrl)+(D) or (Ctrl)+(Z).

##### Slow Copying

It should be obvious that byte-wise copying is not very efficient.

#### Line-by-Line Reading and Writing

Processing a file line by line naturally requires files that contain line breaks. Therefore, line-by-line reading or writing is more suitable for formatted files. It makes little sense to process a binary file line-by-line. For reading a stream line by line, the <samp class="listingcharacter">getline()</samp> method is suitable, and for formatted writing to the stream, the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<()</samp>.

Consider the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/hPaz3a3sE
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
using std::cout;
int main() {
    std::ifstream file("44fstream07.cpp");
    if( !file ) { /* Error */ cout << "ERR\n"; return 1; }
    std::ofstream filecopy("backup.cpp");
    if( !filecopy ) { /* Error */ cout << "ERR\n"; return 1; }
    std::string buffer;
    while( getline(file, buffer) ) {
        filecopy << buffer << std::endl;
        cout << buffer << std::endl;
    }
    if( file.eof() ) {
        file.clear();
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.21**     Line-by-line reading and writing.

This listing largely corresponds to the previous example, in which data was read byte by byte. Now you will find <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> as a buffer, into which I read a line from the <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> file stream using <samp class="listingcharacter">getline()</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. <samp class="listingcharacter">filecopy << buffer</samp> copies this read line into the <samp class="listingcharacter">filecopy</samp> file stream. The newline is automatically removed by <samp class="listingcharacter">getline()</samp>, so you need to add a newline to the stream here. I also output the line to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> (usually the screen). The <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop reads line by line until EOF is reached.

#### Block-Wise Reading and Writing

For reading and writing entire raw data blocks, the <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> methods are best suited.

The following listing allows you to copy a file in one go. Random access is also used here, which will be explained in the next section.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/P6MPabsKc
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using std::cout;
int main() {
    std::ifstream file("testfile.txt", std::ios::binary);
    if( !file ) { /* Error */ cout <<"ERR1\n"; return 1; }
    std::ofstream filecopy("backup.dat", std::ios::binary);
    if( !filecopy ) { /* Error */ return 1; }
    file.seekg(0, std::ios::end);
    auto size = file.tellg();
    cout << "File size: " << size << " bytes\n";
    file.seekg(0, std::ios::beg); // Important!
    std::vector<char> buffer(size);
    file.read(buffer.data(), size);
    if( !file ) { cout << "Error during read...\n"; return 1;}
    cout << "Read: " << file.gcount() << " bytes\n";
    filecopy.write( buffer.data(), size );
    if( !filecopy ) { cout << "Error during write...\n"; return 1;}
} 
```

**Listing 27.22**     Block-wise reading and writing with “read” and “write”.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">filecopy</samp>, I first opened a file for reading and another file for writing to copy (both in binary mode with <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::binary</samp>). Then I set the position of the file to be copied to the end (<samp class="listingcharacter">ios::end</samp>) using the <samp class="listingcharacter">seekg()</samp> method. Using the position at the end of the file, I get the byte offset from the beginning of the file with the <samp class="listingcharacter">tellg()</samp> method and later store the size of the file in the <samp class="listingcharacter">size</samp> variable for copying.

It is also very important now that I reset the read position to the beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter">seekg</samp>. Then I get a sufficiently large buffer to read the entire file. For this, I initialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> of size <samp class="listingcharacter">size</samp> with elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. A vector guarantees that all elements are stored consecutively in one block. This is useful and necessary to serve as a parameter for the following calls to <samp class="listingcharacter">read</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">write</samp>. For this very purpose, <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> has the <samp class="listingcharacter">data()</samp> method.

Often at this point, a dynamic C-array is fetched—for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">new char[size]</samp>. That works too, but you shouldn't forget the <samp class="listingcharacter">delete[]</samp> then. <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp> can offer support here, but <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> already has everything needed in one package, so I like to use it for this purpose. Later in [Listing 27.29](#27_008.html_l27.29), I will show you the <samp class="listingcharacter">char[]</samp> alternative.

##### Storing Vectors, Structures, or Classes

Although the listing only demonstrated how to copy a simple file in blocks, in practice, the ability to use <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> is also well suited for storing more complex data structures such as vectors, structures, or the properties of classes. It is always necessary to ensure that the type must be converted to and from <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp>.

Sooner or later, you will want to store the properties of classes. As this seems somewhat more complex, a simple recipe for practice will be shown here. As a basic framework, I use the class in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/b3W48s86z
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using std::cout; using std::string;
class DataClass {
    std::string text_;
    int data_;
public:
    DataClass(string t="", int i=0)
      : text_{t}, data_{i} {}
    std::ostream& write(std::ostream& os) const {
        os << text_ << std::ends;
        os.write(reinterpret_cast<const char*>(&data_), sizeof(data_));
        return os;
    }
    std::istream& read(std::istream& is) {
        std::getline(is, text_, '\0');
        is.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&data_), sizeof(data_));
        return is;
    }
    std::ostream& print(std::ostream& os) {
        return os << text_ << " : " << data_ << std::endl;
    }
};
int main() {
    std::ofstream file_w("data.dat", std::ios::binary);
    if( !file_w) { cout << "Error opening file\n"; return 1; }
    std::vector<DataClass> vec_dat;
    vec_dat.push_back(DataClass("A text", 123));
    vec_dat.push_back(DataClass("More text", 321));
    vec_dat.emplace_back("Much more text", 333);
    for(const auto &elem : vec_dat){
        elem.write(file_w);
    }
    file_w.close();
    std::ifstream file_r("data.dat", std::ios::binary);
    if( !file_r) { cout << "Error opening file\n"; return 1; }
    DataClass dat_r;
    while( file_r ) {
        dat_r.read(file_r);
        if( file_r.eof()) break;
        dat_r.print(cout);
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.23**     Block-wise reading and writing with a helper class.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">DataClass</samp> class contains two data fields that should be written and read in binary form. The main focus here is on the implementation of the two <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> methods.

At the method head of <samp class="listingcharacter">write</samp>, you can see that you are writing the properties of <samp class="listingcharacter">DataClass</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">os</samp> stream and returning it. <samp class="listingcharacter">text_</samp> is simply written away with <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>, but the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ends</samp> (=<samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp>) manipulator is appended as an end marker, which we need again to read the data.[[ 70 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn27_01) Keep in mind that <samp class="listingcharacter">text_</samp> is a subobject of the <samp class="listingcharacter">DataClass</samp> class, whose length can always vary.

<samp class="listingcharacter">data_</samp> refers to <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> elements as in <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. The data from <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> must first be converted into a raw data block of <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> because <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp> expects this as the first argument. This is done using <samp class="listingcharacter">reinterpret_cast<const char*></samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp> is used because the method is <samp class="listingcharacter">const</samp>. This means <samp class="listingcharacter">data_</samp> must not be changed. A conversion to <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> would not work, but <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp> would—thus ensuring that no one changes the data.[[ 71 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn27_02)

Similarly, this also works with the counterpart <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp>, just in the other direction. The method takes an input stream as a parameter and returns it. To read the first <samp class="listingcharacter">text_</samp> property, I use <samp class="listingcharacter">getline()</samp>. Here I read up to the <samp class="listingcharacter">'\0'</samp> character. I had previously appended this specifically for <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp>. When reading, you also need to convert the first argument to raw data for <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> expects it. This is done using <samp class="listingcharacter">reinterpret_cast<char*></samp> as the data is now changing.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, I then write away three <samp class="listingcharacter">DataClass</samp> elements, which I retrieve from a previously filled <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp>. For demonstration purposes, I read them back immediately and output them on the console—for your and my reassurance.

### 27.6.4    Random Access

In block reading in the previous section (in [Listing 27.22](#27_006.html_l27.22)), you have already become familiar with random access to file streams. This makes it possible to determine the current write or read position or to change the position. In [Table 27.12](#27_006.html_t27.12), you will find an overview of the available methods.

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& seekg(streampos)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">istream& seekg(streampos, ios::seekdir)</samp> | Sets the read position to a specific position from the beginning of the file or relative to the optionally specified second argument |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">streampos tellg()</samp> | Returns the current read position |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream& seekp(streampos)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream& seekp(streampos, ios::seekdir)</samp> | Sets the write position to a specific position from the beginning of the file or relative to the optionally specified second argument |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">streampos tellp()</samp> | Returns the current write position |

**Table 27.12**     Methods for random access.

The possible values for the second argument of <samp class="listingcharacter">seekg()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">seekp()</samp> (<samp class="listingcharacter">g</samp> stands for <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">put</samp>) for the reference position of type <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::seekdir</samp> are as follows:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::beg</samp>: position relative to the beginning of the file

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::cur</samp>: position relative to the current position in the file

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::end</samp>: position relative to the end of the file

Here are some examples:

```
// Position 10 characters forward from the current position
file.seekg(10, std::ios::cur);
// …
// Position at the beginning of the file
file.seekg(0, std::ios::beg);
// …
// Position 5 characters before the end
file.seekg(-5, std::ios::end); 
```

You must ensure that you set the file position to a valid range here. If you choose a position before the beginning or after the end, then the behavior is undefined.

### 27.6.5    Synchronized Streams for Threads

When working with multiple threads, outputs of the threads can overlap each other. To prevent a thread from interrupting the output of a stream, you need a synchronization mechanism. You could use a <samp class="listingcharacter">mutex</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_lock</samp> at all output points. Since C++20, there is a simpler solution for this: in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><syncstream></samp> header, there is the <samp class="listingcharacter">osyncstream</samp> class, which works similarly to <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_lock</samp>—following the RAII pattern. But instead of introducing an additional <samp class="listingcharacter">mutex</samp>, you use the respective stream whose output you want to synchronize as a parameter.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/GefKP5sj4
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <syncstream>
long fib(long n) { return n<=1 ? n : fib(n-1)+fib(n-2); }
void runFib(long from, long step, long to) {
    for (auto n=from; n<=to; n+=step) {
        std::osyncstream osync{ std::cout }; // Sync on cout as long as osync exists
        osync << "fib("<<n<<")=" << fib(n) << '\n';
    }
}
int main() {
    std::jthread f40{ runFib, 1, 3, 40 };
    std::jthread f41{ runFib, 2, 3, 41 };
    std::jthread f42{ runFib, 3, 3, 42 };
} 
```

**Listing 27.24**     Synchronizing output between threads with “osyncstream”.

Here, the Fibonacci numbers are calculated in three threads in steps of three from 1 to 42\. The variable <samp class="listingcharacter">osync</samp> locks the output to <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> for other threads for as long as it exists—but only if the other threads also use <samp class="listingcharacter">osyncstream</samp>. Apart from the order, the output is nice and clean line by line:

```
fib(2)=1
fib(5)=5
fib(8)=21
fib(11)=89
fib(14)=377
… 
```

If you did not synchronize the output, then the outputs would almost certainly be interrupted, especially before <samp class="listingcharacter"><< fib(n)</samp>, because the calculation takes time. This is how it would look without <samp class="listingcharacter">osyncstream</samp>:

```
fib(fib(3)=2)=21
fib(5)=5
fib(8)=21
fib(11)=89
… 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">osyncstream</samp> class is on one hand a wrapper for a stream, but on the other hand also a stream itself. You can use it like a stream, so you can output it with <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> as in the example. But it is also suitable as a parameter for functions that expect an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream&</samp>. However, you must pass it as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ref(osync)</samp> when calling. If you want to force an output before the destructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">osync</samp>, output <samp class="listingcharacter"><< std::flush_emit</samp>.

You can synchronize not only <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> or other standard streams, but also file streams that you open with <samp class="listingcharacter">ofstream</samp>.

## 27.7    Streams for Strings

If you look at the simplified class hierarchy of the stream class in [Figure 27.1](#27_001.html_f27.1), starting from <samp class="listingcharacter">ios</samp>, you will find three streams for strings: <samp class="listingcharacter">istringstream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ostringstream</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp>. For strings means that you are reading or writing a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> rather than outputting to or from a console or file.

For all three classes, you need to include the <samp class="listingcharacter"><sstream></samp> header. These streams are well-suited for converting different data types to and from strings—again, with all the advantages of the preceding streams and their methods and manipulators. [Table 27.13](#27_007.html_t27.13) lists the various string streams.

| Stream | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">istringstream</samp> | Creates a string stream that can be read from. The stream is opened in <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp> mode. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ostringstream</samp> | Creates a string stream for writing. By default, this stream is used with the <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp> mode. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp> | Creates a string stream for reading and writing. The default modes here are <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp>. |

**Table 27.13**     String streams of the standard library.

For all three constructors, you can use an empty constructor as an argument; the open mode, as with file streams (see [Table 27.9](#27_006.html_t27.9)); a string (<samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp>) with which the stream should be initialized immediately; or a combination of the string (first argument) and the open mode (second argument). It should be added to the open modes that for string streams, <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::in</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::out</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::ate</samp> make the most sense. The other values of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">ios::openmode</samp> are also implemented, but whether they actually have an effect on a <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp> object depends on the implementation.

### Old strstream

In the old C++98 standard, a stream class was still implemented with the <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp> type. Today, the <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> type (more precisely, <samp class="listingcharacter">basic_string</samp>) is used for this purpose. The old string stream classes <samp class="listingcharacter">istrstream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ostrstream</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">strstream</samp> are therefore only present for backward compatibility reasons and should no longer be used in new projects; they are deprecated, meaning that they are obsolete.

Because the string streams inherit all <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> methods from the base classes derived from them, all previously known and introduced methods with the string streams are also available to you here. However, the main methods for string streams are provided by the class itself with the <samp class="listingcharacter">str()</samp> method (see [Table 27.14](#27_007.html_t27.14)).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">string str() const</samp> | Returns the string stream buffer as a string |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">void str(const string& s)</samp> | Resets the content of the string stream buffer |

**Table 27.14**     “str()” is the centerpiece of the string stream.

This way, you can convert simple data types like <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> into a string, as in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TT13E3sz5
#include <sstream>  // ostringstream
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::ostringstream ostr;
    double dval = 3.1415;
    int ival = 4321;
    ostr << dval << " : " << ival;
    const std::string sval = ostr.str();
    std::cout << sval << std::endl;    // Output: 3.1415 : 4321
} 
```

**Listing 27.25**     Writing to a “stringstream”.

First, I create the string stream for writing, which we need for the conversion. Then I simply write the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> value and the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value separated by a colon into the string stream using <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp>. With the <samp class="listingcharacter">str()</samp> method, I copy the entire content of the string stream buffer into the <samp class="listingcharacter">sval</samp> string and then output it.

The same works in the other direction. The following listing shows how you can extract individual types from a string.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/1EMox3hW5
#include <sstream>  // istringstream
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::istringstream istr;
    std::string sval("3.1415 : 4321");
    std::string none;
    double dval=0.0;
    int ival=0;
    istr.str(sval);                 // initialize
    istr >> dval >> none >> ival;   // read
    if( ! istr.eof() ) {
        std::cout << "Error converting\n"; return 1;
    }
    std::cout << dval << " == " << none << " == " << ival << "\n";
    // Output: 3.1415 == : == 4321
} 
```

**Listing 27.26**     Reading from a “stringstream”.

First, I initialize an empty <samp class="listingcharacter">istringstream</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">istr</samp>, from which I will later extract values. I then set the content with <samp class="listingcharacter">str(…)</samp>. You could also pass the content directly to the constructor.

Extraction is done as with any other <samp class="listingcharacter">istream</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>. This means that for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, characters are consumed so long as they could be part of a floating-point number. Extraction stops at a whitespace. The colon <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> ends up in <samp class="listingcharacter">none</samp>, because when reading into a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> also stops at the next whitespace. Finally, it reads into an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> so long as there are <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">9</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> in the string stream.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">eof</samp>, I check if any errors occurred during the conversion. If the string stream is not at the end, that would be the case.

Conversion from binary to ASCII and vice versa is quite easy with string streams. However, because the conversion work is almost always quite similar, it is advisable to create a function template for this purpose. The following function template serves as a simple recipe that you can use to convert a C++ basic data type to a string or a string to a basic data type.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/vcoEcYYcx
#include <sstream> // stringstream
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept> // invalid_argument
template <class T1, class T2>
void myConvert(const T1& in, T2& out) {
    std::stringstream ss;
    ss << in;
    ss >> out;
    if( ! ss.eof() ) {
        throw std::invalid_argument("Error during conversion");
    }
}
int main() {
    std::string sval;
    float fval=3.1415f;
    std::string sdval("5.321");
    double dsval=0;
    std::string doesnotwork("does not work");
    try {
        myConvert(fval, sval);
        std::cout << sval << std::endl;  // Output: 3.1415
        myConvert(sdval, dsval);
        std::cout << dsval << std::endl; // Output: 5.321
        myConvert(doesnotwork, dsval);   // triggers "Error during conversion"
    }
    catch(const std::invalid_argument& e) {
        std::cout << e.what() << std::endl;
    }
} 
```

**Listing 27.27**     Type conversion using “stringstream”.

The main focus in this example is on the <samp class="listingcharacter">myConvert</samp> function template. This should convert values of type <samp class="listingcharacter">T1</samp> to type <samp class="listingcharacter">T2</samp>. For this, I simply send the data with <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> into the string stream <samp class="listingcharacter">ss</samp> and then retrieve it with <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>.

To check if everything worked, I use <samp class="listingcharacter">!eof()</samp> and throw an <samp class="listingcharacter">invalid_argument</samp> exception in the case of an error.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> block in <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> value is converted to a string and then a string value to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. The third conversion throws an exception because converting the text sequence <samp class="listingcharacter">"does no work"</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> fails.

### String Streams Instead of File Streams

String streams can indeed be used excellently for converting to and from strings, but in practice, they are even more frequently used for buffering purposes to avoid temporary files. Basically, you just need to use a corresponding string stream instead of a file stream. The advantage is obvious: string streams are significantly faster (as they are in main memory) than slow temporary files, which require rather slow access to a storage medium. However, this depends on the use case. It should also be clear that data that only resides in the buffer of the main memory will be lost in the event of a program crash.

### 27.7.1    Difference from “to_string”

With <samp class="listingcharacter">ostringstream</samp>, you can convert all objects to a string for which you or someone else has defined <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream&</samp>.

Alternatively, there is also the <samp class="listingcharacter">to_string(…)</samp> free function with predefined overloads for all built-in integer and floating-point types. However, the output may differ in detail from what would appear on an <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream</samp>. The implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">to_string</samp> overloads is based on what the <samp class="listingcharacter">printf</samp> C function would output and uses its <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> formats.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/z6sYqM48e
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
void show(double f) {
    std::cout << "os: " << f
       << "\t to_string: " << std::to_string(f) << "\n";
}
int main() {
    show(23.43);     // Output: os: 23.43    to_string: 23.430000
    show(1e-9);      // Output: os: 1e-09    to_string: 0.000000
    show(1e40);      // Output: os: 1e+40    to_string: 100…0752.000000
    show(1e-40);     // Output: os: 1e-40    to_string: 0.000000
    show(123456789); // Output: os: 1.23457e+08  to_string: 123456789.000000
} 
```

**Listing 27.28**     The “to_string” function.

The output of <samp class="listingcharacter">1e+40</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">to_string</samp> has been abbreviated here with <samp class="listingcharacter">…</samp>.

### 27.7.2    “to_chars” and “format” Are More Flexible than “to_string”

Because you cannot influence the detailed output format with <samp class="listingcharacter">to_string</samp>, it is of little use, especially for floating-point numbers.

Since C++17, there is the <samp class="listingcharacter">to_chars</samp> function (to-char-sequence), which allows you to write a number into a preinitialized string. This function has additional overloads for further formatting options.

The most versatile way to convert to a string is via the <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> function, which has been available since C++20.

### 27.7.3    Reading from a String

If you want to convert a string to a number, you can again use <samp class="listingcharacter">istringstream</samp> and read from it with <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp>. There are overloads of <samp class="listingcharacter">operator>>(istream& is, …)</samp> for all built-in numeric types.

Alternatively, there is a whole family of functions for directly converting a character string to a number. You can see a list in [Table 27.15](#27_007.html_t27.15).

| Function | Numeric Type |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stoul</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stoull</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned long long</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stoi</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stol</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stoll</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stof</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stod</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stold</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> |

**Table 27.15**     Conversion functions for strings to numbers.

## 27.8    Stream Buffers

Although you will rarely need to access them directly, the stream buffer classes should be briefly described here to conclude the stream classes. If you look at the class hierarchy in [Figure 27.1](#27_001.html_f27.1), you will find them somewhat pushed to the edge with <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">filebuf</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">stringbuf</samp>. In reality, however, these stream buffer classes are more like the core of the I/O stream library. If you have always wondered where the individual bytes of the stream classes are processed, you will find the answer in the stream buffer classes.

The stream buffer classes provide basic methods for buffering streams without extensive formatting options. Every stream (string stream, file stream, and standard I/O stream) works with stream buffers. The abstract <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> base class is used by all other parts of the I/O stream classes. For buffering the input and output of files, <samp class="listingcharacter">filebuf</samp> is used, and for buffering strings in memory, <samp class="listingcharacter">stringbuf</samp> is used. Both are derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp>.
