With buffering, individual characters are not sent to the stream; instead, the data is transmitted in blocks. The output occurs only when a block unit of the buffer is full. However, you can also manually intervene to explicitly empty the buffer using the <samp class="listingcharacter">flush()</samp> method, for example:

```
#include <fstream>
int main() {
    std::ofstream file("logfile.log");
    file << "Text for the log";
    file.flush();
} 
```

If the data has not yet been transferred to the file stream <samp class="listingcharacter">file</samp> because the block unit of the buffer was not yet ready, a simple call to the <samp class="listingcharacter">flush()</samp> method will handle it.

However, <samp class="listingcharacter">flush()</samp> is implicitly called anyway when a stream is closed. And that, in turn, happens automatically in the destructor—that is, when the stream is removed, here when exiting <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>.

### Application Area

For normal household use, you will rarely access the stream buffer classes directly. They play a more important role when you want to create new classes of streams for input and output (e.g., sockets or GUIs). Or if you want to redirect streams, direct access to the stream buffer is very useful. Likewise, it is possible to combine streams using stream buffer classes (e.g., encrypting the output before it is written to another stream).

### 27.8.1    Access to the Stream Buffer of “iostream” Objects

The most important thing for you to know is that for every <samp class="listingcharacter">iostream</samp> object, there is a pointer to a <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> object. Using this pointer, it is always possible to directly access the raw bytes in the stream buffer. There are several methods that can be called with a <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> object.

To access a stream buffer, each I/O stream object provides a method called <samp class="listingcharacter">rdbuf()</samp>, which returns a pointer to the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> object. With this, you can now access the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> methods. For example, you can connect the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> pointer to another stream by using <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<<</samp>:

```
std::ifstream file("logfile.log");
std::cout << file.rdbuf(); 
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << file.rdbuf()</samp>, the entire content of the file is pushed to <samp class="listingcharacter">cout</samp> and displayed in one go. This method of passing the entire content to another stream in one go is even significantly more efficient than outputting the entire content using <samp class="listingcharacter">read()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp>, as you did in [Listing 27.23](#27_006.html_l27.23).

In the following listing, I will show you how to place the contents of a file from the buffer into a raw <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array and possibly further process it there. In the example, we simply output the content to the screen with <samp class="listingcharacter">write()</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/8hK9Y4vhd
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory> // unique_ptr

int main() {
    std::fstream file("27Streams.tex");          // Open file for reading
    auto bufptr = file.rdbuf();                  // std::streambuf*
    auto size = bufptr->pubseekoff(0, file.end); // std::streamsize
    bufptr->pubseekoff(0, file.beg);             // back to the beginning
    auto buffer = std::unique_ptr<char[]>(new char[size]); // allocate memory
    auto n = bufptr->sgetn(buffer.get(), size);  // transfer number of chars
    std::cout << "Characters read: " << n << "\n";
    std::cout.write(buffer.get(), size);         // Output char[]
} 
```

**Listing 27.29**     Transferring data from the “rdbuf”.

Thanks to <samp class="listingcharacter">bufptr = file.rdbuf()</samp>, you now have full control over the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> buffer with the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> pointer. First, I use <samp class="listingcharacter">pubseekoff</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">file.end</samp> to set the stream buffer pointer to the end of the buffer to obtain the <samp class="listingcharacter">size</samp> buffer size. Because I also want to read from the buffer afterward, I then set the position of the stream buffer pointer back to the beginning of the buffer with <samp class="listingcharacter">file.beg</samp>.

In a <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr<char[]></samp>, I now reserve memory from the heap in which I can store the entire contents of the buffer. With the <samp class="listingcharacter">sgetn()</samp> method, I now copy <samp class="listingcharacter">size</samp> bytes from the stream buffer into the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array. That's it. In this way, I would have transferred the entire stream buffer into a raw <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array. For demonstration purposes, I use <samp class="listingcharacter">cout.write(…)</samp> to output the contents of <samp class="listingcharacter">char[]</samp> to the console.

This time I used <samp class="listingcharacter">char[]</samp> as a data buffer together with a <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp>. Without <samp class="listingcharacter">unique_ptr</samp>, you would have had to take care of <samp class="listingcharacter">delete[]</samp> in a larger program. This solution here is an alternative to using a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector</samp> as a buffer, as you saw in [Listing 27.22](#27_006.html_l27.22).

You now know how to use the <samp class="listingcharacter">rdbuf()</samp> method to get a stream buffer (of any kind). With the returned pointer, you can now use various methods within the stream to change the position, read characters or entire blocks, and write or reset characters in the stream buffer.

### 27.8.2    “filebuf”

The <samp class="listingcharacter">filebuf</samp> class derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> also contains methods to directly open a file and create a stream buffer. The following code snippet is intended to briefly demonstrate this:

```
std::ofstream file;
std::filebuf* bufptr = file.rdbuf();
bufptr->open("file.txt", std::ios::out|std::ios::app);
const char text[]="This goes into the file";
bufptr->sputn(text, sizeof(text)-1);
bufptr->close(); 
```

In this example, I open or create a file named <samp class="listingcharacter">file.txt</samp> and directly associate the file content with the file buffer to perform direct operations on it. In the example, I use the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">sputn()</samp> to write the <samp class="listingcharacter">text</samp> text into the buffer and simultaneously into the file.

### 27.8.3    “stringbuf”

<samp class="listingcharacter">stringbuf</samp> contains all the methods from the <samp class="listingcharacter">streambuf</samp> base class. It also contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">str()</samp> method with the same meaning as in the class <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp>, but here in connection with a string stream buffer.

## 27.9    “filesystem”

The <samp class="listingcharacter"><filesystem></samp> header deals less with the contents of files and more with files as a whole and their relationship to each other. Since C++17, it has been part of the standard; previously, it was extensively tested in Boost.Filesystem.

All components of the header are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::filesystem</samp> namespace. The most important components are as follows:

*   Class <samp class="listingcharacter">path</samp>
    Represents the name of a file or directory. A <samp class="listingcharacter">path</samp> can be easily converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> or, starting from C++20, into a <samp class="listingcharacter">u8string</samp>. With <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp>, you add a path component; with <samp class="listingcharacter">concat</samp>, you modify the last path component.

*   Class <samp class="listingcharacter">directory_entry</samp>
    Contains metadata about a file or directory.

*   Classes <samp class="listingcharacter">directory_iterator</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">recursive_directory_iterator</samp>
    Allow iterating over all elements of a directory.

*   Helper functions
    Many free functions to facilitate working with permissions, creating directories, copying or deleting entire files, and so on.

In [Listing 27.30](#27_009.html_l27.30), you can see an example of how to concatenate paths and obtain some basic information about files.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jddKxj7fW
#include <filesystem>   // std::filesystem
#include <iostream>
namespace fs = std::filesystem; using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
    // Path components
    fs::path root {"/"};
    fs::path dir {"var/www/"};
    fs::path index {"index.html"};
    // concatenate
    fs::path p = root / dir / index;     // operator/
    // output
    cout << "Name: " << p << endl;       // "/var/www/index.html"
    // decompose
    cout << "Parent: " << p.parent_path() << endl;   // "/var/www"
    cout << "Name: " << p.filename() << endl;        // "index.html"
    cout << "Extension: " << p.extension() << endl;  // ".html"
    // Information
    cout << std::boolalpha;
    cout << "Exists? " << fs::exists(p) << endl;
    cout << "Regular file? " << fs::is_regular_file(p) << endl;
} 
```

**Listing 27.30**     How to concatenate paths.

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">operator/</samp> to concatenate paths is clever and looks good. With <samp class="listingcharacter">p /=…</samp>, you could directly append an element to <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp>. Both correspond to <samp class="listingcharacter">append</samp>.

When you use <samp class="listingcharacter">concat</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>, you extend the last path component, adding without <samp class="listingcharacter">"/"</samp>.

### Windows, Unix, and Embedded

On some extremely lightweight platforms, <samp class="listingcharacter"><filesystem></samp> will not be available to you. However, the authors of this part of the standard library have managed to unify both the Windows and Unix worlds.

This part of the library is also somewhat heavier and likely not implemented as “header-only.” I read a note that the <samp class="listingcharacter">-lstdc++fs</samp> option when linking with GCC and <samp class="listingcharacter">‐lc++fs</samp> with Clang must be specified. However, this was no longer the case for me.

To give you an idea of the capabilities of <samp class="listingcharacter">filesystem</samp>, I will provide an excerpt from the long list of features:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">copy_file</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">rename</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">remove</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">remove_all</samp>
    Simple copying or renaming of a file as well as removing a single file or recursively all files in a directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">current_path</samp> Returns the current directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">exists</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">equivalent</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">exists</samp> checks if a file exists; <samp class="listingcharacter">equivalent</samp> checks if two different <samp class="listingcharacter">path</samp> instances refer to the same file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">file_size</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">is_empty</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">is_regular_file</samp>
    Provide various information about a file.

## 27.10    Formatting

Since C++20, there is a new way to format data. In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><format></samp> header, the following elements are the most important:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> Formats any number of arguments into a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> according to a provided format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format_to</samp> Formats into a buffer or iterator.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format_to_n</samp> Formats into a buffer up to a specified length.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format_size</samp> Determines the length of a formatted output so you can allocate enough space for a buffer.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">vformat</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">vformat_to</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">make_format_args</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">format_to</samp>, but the format string does not need to be known at compile time. The elements to be formatted must then be wrapped with <samp class="listingcharacter">make_format_args</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">format_error</samp> The exception that can be thrown during formatting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">formattable</samp>  A concept for types that you can format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">formatter</samp> These template classes perform the actual formatting and are your entry point into formatting custom types.

### 27.10.1    Simple Formatting

The return of the <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> function is a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. The first parameter is always the format of type <samp class="listingcharacter">format_string</samp>. This must be known at compile time.

#### I'll Keep It Short

The return value can also be a <samp class="listingcharacter">wstring</samp>, and the format can be a <samp class="listingcharacter">wformat_string</samp> as well. And optionally, you can specify a <samp class="listingcharacter">locale</samp> before the format. I will not go into further detail in this section.

Most of what is said in this section can be applied to <samp class="listingcharacter">format_to</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">format_to_n</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">vformat</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">vformat_to</samp>.

A format string contains curly bracket pairs <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> as placeholders where the arguments should be inserted. The rest of the format string is taken unchanged. An index can be placed inside the brackets. This index refers to the additional arguments to <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp> and indicates which argument should be inserted at this position. Optionally, format attributes that affect the representation of the argument can follow the index, separated by a colon <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp>.

It depends on the <samp class="listingcharacter">formatter</samp> class how exactly the attributes are evaluated. The standard formatters are based on Python's format specification and can also be transferred to the classic <samp class="listingcharacter">printf</samp> syntax:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/hTj94enjK
#include <format>
#include <chrono>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std; using namespace std::literals;
void pr(string_view s) { cout << s << endl; }
double pi = 3.14159265359;

int main() {
  pr(format("Hello, {}!", "Reader"));              // simple C-string
  pr(format("Hello, {}!", "Author"s));             // simple string
  pr(format("You are {} years old.", 30));         // integers
  pr(format("That makes {:.2f} euros.", 19.9933)); // 2 decimal places
  pr(format("Scientific: {:e}", -44.876)); // results in "-4.487600e+01"
  pr(format("Binary of {} is {:b}.", 42, 42));     // binary without base
  pr(format("Hex of {} is {:#x}.", 73, 73));       // hexadecimal with base
  pr(format("Zero-padded: {:03}", 7));     // results in "007"
  pr(format("|{0:<10}|{1:^10}|{2:>10}|", "le", "mi", "ri"));
  // Alignment and index
  pr(format("{} {:.9}!", "Boa", "Constrictor")); // without index, truncate string
  using namespace std::chrono;                   // neat time specifications:
  pr(format("{}, {}", 2023y/11/5, minutes{20})); // Output: 2023-11-05, 20min
} 
```

In the last example, you see that you can also format your own types. Here the <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> header brings in its own <samp class="listingcharacter">formatter</samp>.

By the way, did you notice the new C++20 notation for date literals in <samp class="listingcharacter">2023y/11/5</samp>?

In general, the standard formatting attributes are structured as follows; these are the possible elements in a compact form:

fill align sign <samp class="listingcharacter"># 0</samp> width <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp>precision <samp class="listingcharacter">L</samp> type

All elements are optional, but the order must be maintained. The elements are partially dependent on each other and only make sense in certain combinations and for certain types. There are combinations that are frequently seen, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">.2f</samp> for a floating-point number with two decimal places.

The individual elements mean the following:

*   fill Specifies the character to be used for filling. The default is the space character. Requires align.

*   align Can be <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> (left), <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> (right), or <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> (centered). The default is left.

*   sign <samp class="listingcharacter">–</samp> includes the sign only for negative numbers (default), <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> always includes the sign, and space means that a minus sign is used for negative numbers and a space for positive numbers.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> Enables alternative formats, such as prefixes for integers or points for floating-point numbers.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> Pads numbers with zeros.

*   width Specifies the minimum width that the result should have. The default is zero.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp>precision Decimal places for floating-point numbers or how many characters of the string argument should be used.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">L</samp> Enables <samp class="listingcharacter">locale</samp>-dependent formatting for numbers and Booleans.

*   type Switches the output to a specific type: <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> for integers, <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> for floating-point numbers, and so on.

### 27.10.2    Formatting Custom Types

To use instances of your own class as an argument for <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>, you need to specialize the class template <samp class="listingcharacter">std::formatter<></samp> for your class. This class must then provide two methods with the correct signature:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Parse</samp> Evaluates format attributes and returns an iterator to the first character after the parsed format attributes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Format</samp> Writes the formatted output of the argument to the output and returns the iterator to the end of the output.

The class also must have a default constructor and must be copyable as well as assignable.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/sdWsnTonG
#include <format>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
struct Elf {
  std::string name;
  int birth_year;
  std::string era;
  std::string folk;
};
template<> struct std::formatter<Elf> {
  std::formatter<std::string> sub_fmt;
  constexpr auto parse(std::format_parse_context& pctx) {
    return sub_fmt.parse(pctx); // returns iterator to '}'
  }
  auto format(const Elf& elf, std::format_context& fctx) const {
    std::string s = std::format("{}/{} ({} {})",
        elf.name, elf.folk, elf.birth_year, elf.era);
    return sub_fmt.format(s, fctx); // delegate formatting
  }
};
int main() {
  std::vector<Elf> elves{
    {"Feanor", 1169, "First Age", "Noldor"},
    {"Galadriel", 1362, "EZ", "Noldor"},
    {"Legolas", 87, "DZ", "Sindar"},
    {"Elrond", 532, "EZ", "Half-elf"},
    {"Elwe", 1050, "EZ", "Sindar"},
  };
  for (const auto& e : elves) {
    std::cout << std::format("Elf: {:>20}", e) << std::endl;
  }
} 
```

**Listing 27.31**     A formatter can delegate parsing and formatting.

Here I have delegated both the parsing of format attributes and the formatting of the output to the standard formatting for <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">sub_fmt</samp>. Therefore, I need to somehow generate a string in <samp class="listingcharacter">string s</samp> that contains the output. I make this easy for myself here by building a string with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::format</samp> and then passing it to <samp class="listingcharacter">sub_fmt</samp>.

The output looks like this for Feanor:

```
Elf: Feanor/Nordor (1169 EZ) 
```

If you need more sophisticated formatting, you have to parse the format attributes yourself. When parsing, assume that you have an iterator at <samp class="listingcharacter">pctx.begin()</samp> pointing to the first character after the bracket <samp class="listingcharacter">{</samp> or after the colon <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp>, which marks the beginning of the format attributes. You then need to parse the attributes and return the iterator to the bracket <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp>.

In <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>, the output occurs after <samp class="listingcharacter">fctx.out()</samp>, and you return an iterator to the end of the output.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/WqjK31Gn6
// 'Elf' as before…
template<> struct std::formatter<Elf> {
  std::string attribs;                  // Sequence of '%n', '%g', '%e', '%v', and others
  constexpr auto parse(std::format_parse_context& pctx) {
    auto it = std::ranges::find(pctx.begin(), pctx.end(), '}'); // search for '}'
    attribs = std::string(pctx.begin(), it);                    // save everything
    return it;                                                  // points to '}'
  }
  auto format(const Elf& elf, std::format_context& fctx) const {
    auto out = fctx.out();                                      // into here
    for(auto n=0u; n<attribs.size()-1; ++n) {
      if(attribs[n] == '%') {             // instruction to output a member
        switch(attribs[++n]) {
          case 'n': out = std::format_to(out, "{}", elf.name); break;
          case 'g': out = std::format_to(out, "{}", elf.birth_year); break;
          case 'e': out = std::format_to(out, "{}", elf.era); break;
          case 'v': out = std::format_to(out, "{}", elf.folk); break;
          case '%': out = std::format_to(out, "%"); break;     // %% becomes %
        }
      } else {
        out = std::format_to(out, "{}", attribs[n]);           // everything else
      }
    }
    return out;                                                // points to the end
  }
};
int main() {
  Elf e{"Feanor", 1169, "EZ", "Nordor"};
  std::cout << std::format("{:Elf %n}", e) << std::endl;
  // Output: Elf Feanor
  std::cout << std::format("Elf {:%n, %v, born %g in the age %e}\n", e);
  // Output: Elf Feanor, Nordor, born 1169 in the age EZ
} 
```

**Listing 27.32**     A formatter can parse and output itself.

Here I parse the format string up to the <samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp> and store everything in <samp class="listingcharacter">attribs</samp>. When outputting in <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>, I iterate over <samp class="listingcharacter">attribs</samp> and interpret a percent sign <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> as an instruction to output a member of <samp class="listingcharacter">Elf</samp>. Everything else is simply output.

The idea of using the percent sign as an instruction is not new and is also used, for example, for types from <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>.

If you want to report an error in parsing or output, throw a <samp class="listingcharacter">std::format_error</samp> exception.

# 28    Standard Library: Extras

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>
    Anonymous structures that can be easily created on the spot—for example, for returning multiple values.

*   Regular expression
    Formal description of a pattern for text search.

*   Random number generator
    A mechanism that generates random values.

*   Random distribution
    Defines the probabilities via which a random number generator produces values.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>
    Type-safe data types for point in time and duration.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> A type-safe fraction—that is, a number represented by an integer numerator and an equally integer denominator.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">system_error</samp> Tools for portable error handling with error codes and exceptions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><typeinfo></samp> Runtime type information.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp> The type <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> is found in this header along with many predefined functor classes like <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">plus</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">logical_and</samp>.

In this chapter, you will find more classes and functions of the standard library.

## 28.1    “pair” and “tuple”

A <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> is something similar to an anonymous <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp>. Neither the <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> itself nor its elements have names. You address the elements by their position. <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> is older than <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> and encapsulates exactly two elements. These have the names <samp class="listingcharacter">first</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">second</samp>.

You will often find both in the standard library because they are so useful. It is possible to bundle multiple elements of different types together without much syntactic overhead.

### 28.1.1    Returning Multiple Values

Using a structure or class, you can also pack multiple pieces of data together and thus return multiple values from a function. In C++, however, there are special tools like <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> to directly return multiple values of different types from a function using the <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statement.

The use of <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> is extremely simple. Primarily, you use <samp class="listingcharacter">make_pair</samp> to create.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/4YM9d99xG
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <utility> // pair
using std::pair; using std::cout; using std::cin; using std::string;
std::vector<string> months { "Jan", "Feb", "Mar" };
std::vector temps { 8, 12, 11 };
std::pair<string, int> monthWithTemp(size_t m) {
    auto month = months.at(m);
    auto temperature = temps.at(m);
    return std::make_pair(month, temperature);
}
int main() {
    std::pair data = monthWithTemp(1);
    cout << "Month : " << data.first << std::endl; // Output: Month : Feb
    cout << "Temperature : " << data.second << std::endl;
    // Output: Temperature : 12
} 
```

**Listing 28.1**     How to return two values simultaneously using “pair”.

When declaring the <samp class="listingcharacter">monthWithTemp</samp> function, you can already tell from the return value that this function returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. That's basically all you need to do. You just need to enter the two types (separated by a comma) between the angle brackets that should be returned. In <samp class="listingcharacter">monthWithTemp(1)</samp>, I call the function and also assign the return value to a <samp class="listingcharacter">pair<string,int></samp>. The return is constructed from the two specified data using the <samp class="listingcharacter">make_pair()</samp> function and made into a <samp class="listingcharacter">pair<string,int></samp>.

You can now access the individual values of <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter">first</samp> (for the first value) and <samp class="listingcharacter">second</samp> (for the second value), as you can see in the example.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp>, you are limited to exactly two elements. It is older than <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>, which is the generalization for any number of elements. You use it similarly.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5z4s6WMxG
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm> // min, max
#include <tuple>
using std::tuple; using std::make_tuple; using std::get; using std::cout;
using std::string;
tuple<int,int,int> arrange(int a, int b, int c) {
  using std::min; using std::max;
  auto x = min(a,min(b,c));
  auto y = max(min(a,b), min(max(a,b),c));
  auto z = max(a,max(b,c));
  return make_tuple(x, y, z);
}
auto president(int year) {
  using namespace std::literals;
  if(year >= 2021)
    return std::make_tuple("Joseph"s, "Biden"s, "Democratic"s, 1942);
  if(year >= 2017)
    return std::make_tuple("Donald"s, "Trump"s, "Republican"s, 1946);
  if(year >= 2009)
    return std::make_tuple("Barack"s, "Obama"s, "Democratic"s, 1961);
  // Add more presidents as needed...
  return std::make_tuple(""s, ""s, ""s, 0); // Default case
}
int main() {
  tuple<int,int,int> zs = arrange(23, 42, 7);
  cout << get<0>(zs) <<' '<< get<1>(zs) <<' '<< get<2>(zs) <<'\n';
  // Output: 7 23 42
  auto ps = president(2015);
  cout << get<1>(ps) << '\n'; // Output: Obama
} 
```

**Listing 28.2**     With “tuple”, you can return any number of elements.

You combine multiple values of different types into a tuple using <samp class="listingcharacter">make_tuple</samp>. You can, as with <samp class="listingcharacter">arrange</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">zs</samp>, feel free to write out the <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> type. However, I recommend working with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, as shown with <samp class="listingcharacter">president</samp>and <samp class="listingcharacter">ps</samp>. Here it is actually a <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple<string, string,string,int></samp>, but you can save yourself the typing with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>.

Instead of accessing the elements with <samp class="listingcharacter">first</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">second</samp>, you now use <samp class="listingcharacter">get<0></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">get<1></samp>. For further elements, logically use larger numbers. Note that you can only specify fixed values (<samp class="listingcharacter">constexpr</samp>) as an index here. This does not work with variables.

You can even pass a type instead of a number, the type that you want.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TE1EcEYPv
// … as before …
int main() {
  tuple ps = president(2015);
  cout << get<int>(ps) << '\n';     // Output: 1940
  cout << get<string>(ps) << '\n';  // not unique
} 
```

**Listing 28.3**     “get” works with a type as an index.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> appears only once in <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple<string, string, string, int></samp>, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">get<int></samp> to access the corresponding element. <samp class="listingcharacter">get<string></samp> does not work because that would not be unique.

#### [Übung]  “array” as “tuple”

The real <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> container (see [Chapter 24](#24_001.html_h24), [Section 24.6.4](#24_006.html_h24.6.4)) for a fixed number of elements of the same type also offers the possibility to access its elements with <samp class="listingcharacter">get<…></samp>. You can almost use an <samp class="listingcharacter">array<int,3></samp> like a <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple<int,int,int></samp>.

If accessing elements in this way is too cumbersome for you, then bind the return value of a function to variables with <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zG7zYGf3K
// … as before …
int main() {
  using std::tie; using std::ignore;
  string lastName {};
  int birthYear {};
  tie(ignore, lastName, ignore, birthYear) = president(2015);
  cout << lastName << ' ' << birthYear << '\n'; // Output: Obama 1961
} 
```

**Listing 28.4**     Decomposing tuples with “tie” and “ignore<samp class="listingcharacter">”.</samp>

When you use <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp> on the left side of an assignment as shown here, you can directly assign the individual parts of <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> returns to previously declared variables. If you are only interested in parts of the return, then use <samp class="listingcharacter">ignore</samp> at the positions you are not interested in.

#### Structured Binding with “auto”

With C++17, it has become even easier to directly assign the returns of <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp> to variables. This feature is called structured binding. This makes it possible to declare variables simultaneously:

```
auto [a, lastname, c, birthyear] = president(2015); 
```

Here, four variables are automatically declared with the correct types and initialized with the corresponding parts of the returned tuple. For this, the expression on the right side needs a “tuple-like interface”; that is, it must support <samp class="listingcharacter">get<></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_size<></samp>, which is the case for <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp>.

A C-array or a <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> can also be on the right side.

<samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> has overloaded operators for comparisons, particularly <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, which are necessary for algorithms like <samp class="listingcharacter">sort</samp> and the standard containers. If the first elements of a tuple are equal,then the second elements are compared, and so on. This is called lexicographical order, because it works like sorting words in a dictionary.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/sG4E66YhW
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm> // ranges::sort
using std::tuple; using std::get; using std::cout; using std::string;
int main() {
    std::vector<tuple<string,string,int>> armstrongs =
      { {"Armstrong", "Louis", 1901}  // Initialize using initializer list
      , {"Armstrong", "Lance", 1971}
      , {"Armstrong", "Neil", 1930} };
    std::ranges::sort(armstrongs);    // Lance < Louis < Neil
    for(const auto& a : armstrongs) {
      cout << get<0>(a) << ", " << get<1>(a) << ", " << get<2>(a) << "\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 28.5**     Tuples implement lexicographical order.

First, you can see that it is easy to initialize a tuple when the type is given. This is the case here with <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<tuple<string,string,int>></samp>. Therefore, it is sufficient to initialize each individual element with an initializer list of two <samp class="listingcharacter">const char[]</samp>s and an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>.

When <samp class="listingcharacter">sort</samp> is performed, the <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>s are compared with each other. The first <samp class="listingcharacter">"Armstrong"</samp> elements are always the same, and the comparison is not yet conclusive. Therefore, the second element is considered—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">"Lance"</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">"Louis"</samp>.

Just as you can sort a <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<tuple<…>></samp>, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> as a key for ordered associative containers like <samp class="listingcharacter">map<tuple<…>,…></samp>.

The only thing needed to compare tuples is the comparability of the individual elements. This means that you can compare (and thus sort) <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple<string,int,Ball></samp> exactly when you have implemented comparisons for <samp class="listingcharacter">Ball</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/9qhMo6zbb
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <map>
#include <unordered_set>
using std::tuple; using std::get; using std::cout; using std::string;

int main() {
    std::map<tuple<int,string>,double> m { {{12,"x"},3.14} };
    cout << m[{12,"x"}] << "\n"; // Output: 3.14
    std::unordered_set<tuple<int,string>> s { {12,"x"} }; // no std::hash
} 
```

**Listing 28.6**     Tuples as keys.

In an unordered associative container like <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered_set</samp>, you cannot use <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> without further precautions, as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::hash(tuple<…>)</samp> does not exist. However, this can be retrofitted if necessary.

The fact that <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> supports comparisons can also be used to simplify your own code. If you have your own data structure with multiple elements for which you want to implement a lexicographical order, you can rely on <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp> function helps you here. It breaks down any <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> into its individual parts, which you can then associate with your own variables. The result is very compact code for lexicographical comparisons.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/vdT7TTjWK
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <map>
#include <unordered_set>
using std::tuple; using std::tie; using std::cout; using std::string;
struct Point {
    int x,y,z;
    bool operator<(const Point &b) {
        return tie(x,y,z) < tie(b.x, b.y, b.z);
    }
};
int main() {
    Point a{ 11, 22, 33 };
    Point b{ 11, 33, 0 };
    cout << std::boolalpha << (a < b) << "\n"; // Output: true
} 
```

**Listing 28.7**     Forming tuples in-place using tie.

It is not difficult to implement a lexicographical order yourself. However, this is a tedious task into which errors often creep. When you use <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp>, the code is compact, clear, and correct.

Remember that you should not use <samp class="listingcharacter">make_tuple</samp> here as it would create copies of your data. <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp> works with references, so your data elements are compared without an additional copy.

The superlative of <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_as_tuple</samp>, which you need when writing a function template that should assemble a tuple from multiple arguments while preserving rvalue references. This is a very advanced topic, which you will notice the first time you use it. You should not use <samp class="listingcharacter">forward_as_tuple</samp> until you have worked with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::forward</samp> at least once.

The last way to create a <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp> is by using <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_cat</samp>. You give <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_cat</samp> a list of tuples and receive a single large tuple as a return, with all elements concatenated.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/eq1dqWbe9
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
using std::tuple; using std::cout; using std::string;

int main() {
    tuple<int,string> a { 12, "gnorf" };
    tuple b { 666 };
    tuple<double,double,string> c { 77.77, 33.33, "frong" };
    tuple<int,string,int,double,double,string> r = std::tuple_cat( a, b, c );
    cout << std::get<2>(r) << "\n"; // Output: 666
} 
```

**Listing 28.8**     Combining several small tuples into one large tuple.

Just as well—probably better—you could have written <samp class="listingcharacter">auto r = …</samp> and let the compiler determine the correct type. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>, you can also give <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_cat</samp> a <samp class="listingcharacter">pair</samp> as an argument. As in most cases, the types are compatible.

#### Beware of “tuple” with References

You are not allowed to fill a standard container with references. There is a good reason for this: A <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<T&></samp> would internally make assignments to references that do not do what you want.

However, <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple<T&></samp> is allowed in principle because the standard library needs it to implement <samp class="listingcharacter">tie</samp>. I recommend that you do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple<T&></samp> yourself—and especially not to store references to data, which is treading on thin ice.

And the compiler will not stop you from using <samp class="listingcharacter">vector<tuple<T&>></samp>, but here the ice you are treading on has already melted.

There are still a handful of useful tools for <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>. For example, you can determine the size of a tuple with <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_size<tuple<…>>::value</samp>. If you ever “forget” the types of the elements, you can always get back to the individual types with <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_element <I,tuple<…>>::type</samp>.

For concrete <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>, this is less interesting, but if you allow tuples as template parameters, then these type traits are useful helpers. Templates were discussed in detail in [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Psdz9s9Gc
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
using namespace std;
template<typename Tuple>
auto back(Tuple &&tuple) {
    using Noref = typename remove_reference<Tuple>::type; // in case of Tuple&
    constexpr auto sz = tuple_size<Noref>::value;
    return get<sz-1>(forward<Tuple>(tuple));
}
int main() {
    tuple<string,int,string> enterprise = make_tuple("NCC", 1701, "D");
    cout << back(enterprise) << "\n"; // Output: D
} 
```

**Listing 28.9**     Useful tuple type traits.

With <samp class="listingcharacter">back</samp>, you always get the last element of any tuple. Some other things are needed, but <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_size</samp> is the core:

*   As always, you use <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp> to access a tuple element. <samp class="listingcharacter">sz-1</samp> is always the last element.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> automatically deduces the return type of the function. Without <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>, this would be difficult but not impossible.

*   You need <samp class="listingcharacter">remove_reference</samp> because <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple_size</samp> cannot handle references to <samp class="listingcharacter">tuple</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> in the parameter and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward</samp> ensure that this template works for values, references, and temp-values.

## 28.2    Regular Expressions

C++ now natively supports regular expressions. With them, you can search for patterns in strings and extract parts of them.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/T1YMoM5as
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
#include <regex>
using std::regex; using std::sregex_iterator; using std::string;
const regex rgxMobile(R"(01[567]\d{6,10})");     // Mobile phone 0151-0179
bool isMobilephone(const string& text) {
  return std::regex_match(text, rgxMobile);      // Does the text match completely?
}
bool containsMobilephone(const string &text) {
  return std::regex_search(text, rgxMobile);     // somewhere in the text?
}
void listMobilephones(const string &text) {
  sregex_iterator begin{ text.cbegin(), text.cend(), rgxMobile };
  sregex_iterator end;
  for(auto it = begin; it != end; ++it)
    std::cout << it->str() << " ";               // Matched text
} // "xyz01709999 abc 0161887766 uvw" -> "0161887766" 
```

**Listing 28.10**     Matching, searching, and enumerating with regular expressions.

While <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_match</samp> checks if a text entirely matches a pattern, <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_search</samp> tests whether a pattern occurs anywhere within a larger text.

With various iterator classes like <samp class="listingcharacter">sregex_iterator</samp>, you can iterate over all matches of a pattern in a string.

German mobile phone numbers always start with 01, followed by one of the digits 5, 6, or 7\. And they have a total length between 9 and 13 digits. The regular expression <samp class="listingcharacter">R"(01[567]\d{6,10})"</samp> catches them. We will discuss the pattern used for searching with <samp class="listingcharacter">rgxMobile</samp> in more detail later in [Table 28.1](#28_002.html_t28.1).

### 28.2.1    Matching and Searching

While <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_match</samp> always checks if the entire text matches the pattern, <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_search</samp> also finds matches contained anywhere in the text.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/E9hcWGMW4
#include <regex>
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
using std::regex; using std::regex_match; using std::regex_search;
int main() {
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;
    regex pattern {"ello"};
    std::string text = "Hello world";
    auto b1 = regex_match (text.cbegin(), text.cend(), pattern); // does’t match
    std::cout << b1 << "\n"; // Output: false
    auto b2 = regex_search(text.cbegin(), text.cend(), pattern); // found
    std::cout << b2 << "\n"; // Output: true
} 
```

**Listing 28.11**     Search and match.

### 28.2.2    The Result and Parts of It

You can optionally pass a parameter to the search functions, in which the exact details of the result are stored. This is useful if you are interested in the start and end position of the match or even the covered subexpressions.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Yzefv59en
#include <regex>
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
using std::regex; using std::regex_search; using std::cmatch;
int main() {
    cmatch res;                               // for detailed results
    std::string text = "<h2>Result and parts of it</h2>";
    regex pattern{"<h(.)>([^<]+)"};           // Search pattern with groups
    regex_search(text.c_str(), res, pattern); // Details to res
    std::cout << res[1] << ". "               // ()-Group 1: H-Level
         << res[2] << std::endl;              // ()-Group 2: H-Text
} 
```

**Listing 28.12**     Accessing the match details.

This will print the following output:

<samp class="listingcharacter">2\. Result and parts of it</samp>

The <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp> is the heading level from <samp class="listingcharacter"><h2></samp>, and the rest is the text between the angle brackets.

### 28.2.3    Found Replacement

It is just as easy to get a new string back in which the found pattern has been replaced with new text.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/rErP43G89
#include <regex>
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
using std::string;
int main() {
    string text = "Title;Album;Artist";
    std::regex pattern{";"};
    string new_str = std::regex_replace(text, pattern, string{","});
    std::cout << new_str << "\n"; // Output: Title,Album,Artist
} 
```

**Listing 28.13**     Replace matches with new text.

In the new <samp class="listingcharacter">new_str</samp> string, all occurrences of the <samp class="listingcharacter">";"</samp> pattern were replaced with <samp class="listingcharacter">","</samp>. If you only want to replace the first match, pass <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_replace</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_constants:: format_first_only</samp> as an additional parameter.

### 28.2.4    Rich in Variants

We have already seen that the text to be searched can be passed in different ways. The functions are indeed very flexible for various needs due to numerous overloads.

For example, there are variants of <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_search</samp> that could be informally summarized as follows:

*   Text to be searched, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>, or a pair of iterators

*   Optional <samp class="listingcharacter">match_results</samp>, like <samp class="listingcharacter">cmatch</samp>

*   The pattern to be searched as regex

*   Optional flags, which default to <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_constants::match_default</samp> if omitted

The same applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_match</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_replace</samp> as well.

The standard library's regular expressions are not limited to character strings of <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. Especially <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t</samp> and its string variant <samp class="listingcharacter">wstring</samp> are supported. In the background general templates are working, the central one being <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_traits</samp>. This is where the functions for interpreting regular expressions and text are grouped together. Normally you do not need to do anything here, but there is nothing wrong with interpreting something other than <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> for a regular expression. For example, the standard definitions do not extend to new Unicode string variants <samp class="listingcharacter">u16string</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">u32string</samp>. Conceptually, however, there is nothing to prevent you from processing these strings; it may just require a bit of manual work when extending the templates.

I have stored the details of the search results in [Listing 28.12](#28_002.html_l28.12) in an instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">cmatch</samp>. But this is actually just a <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef</samp> for a template of <samp class="listingcharacter">match_results</samp> for searching in a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. For the other search types, there are other predefined <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef</samp>s:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">smatch</samp> for searching in <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">cmatch</samp> for searching in <samp class="listingcharacter">const char*</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">wsmatch</samp> for searching in <samp class="listingcharacter">wstring</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">wcmatch</samp> for searching in <samp class="listingcharacter">const wchar_t*</samp>

### 28.2.5    Iterators

You saw in [Listing 28.10](#28_002.html_l28.10) that besides searching, matching, and replacing, you can also iterate successively over all matches. This is done with the <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_iterator</samp> template class. We have already seen its work on <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">sregex_iterator</samp> specialization. For <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">wstring</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">wchar_t*</samp>, there are <samp class="listingcharacter">typedef</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ws</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">wc</samp> instead of the prefix <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>.

Internally, <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_iterator</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_search</samp> function for searching and is thus merely an adapter class for the iterators it provides. Therefore, they only point to corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">match_result</samp> instances.

If you want to enumerate all matches in a string, it is recommended to use the iterator variants over a loop with <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_match</samp>. There are cases where you might otherwise produce an infinite loop; <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_iterator</samp> prevents this. Therefore, especially with regular expressions that could match the “empty string,” such as <samp class="listingcharacter">"(abc)*"</samp>, it is better to use the iterator variant.

### 28.2.6    Matches

Matches can do more than just output the found string with <samp class="listingcharacter">str()</samp>, as shown in [Listing 28.10](#28_002.html_l28.10).

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">position()</samp> to find out exactly where the match occurs in the text. The text before and after the match is provided by the call <samp class="listingcharacter">prefix().str()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">suffix().str()</samp>. Subexpressions, as you have already seen in [Listing 28.12](#28_002.html_l28.12), can be obtained using <samp class="listingcharacter">operator[]</samp>.

### 28.2.7    Options

Regular expressions exist in the programming world in many different variants. If you do not specify otherwise, C++ supports the ECMAScript syntax—which is also known from JavaScript and is fundamentally related to Perl regular expression syntax. Anyone familiar with either should quickly find their way around in C++ as well. Other variants can be optionally supported by the implementation and are then selected via the constructor call:

```
regex rgx(R"...", regex_constants::Syntax); 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">Syntax</samp> is a bitmask to select some different syntax variants. The standard specifies at least <samp class="listingcharacter">ECMAScript</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">basic</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">extended</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">awk</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">grep</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">egrep</samp> as options. Implementations are free to offer more.

The bitmask can slightly modify the syntax with some modifiers:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">icase</samp>
    Ignore case sensitivity.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">nosubs</samp>
    Do not store subexpressions in the match result.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">optimize</samp>
    Prefer match speed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">collate</samp>
    Consider the locale settings for expressions like <samp class="listingcharacter">[a-z]</samp>.

### 28.2.8    Speed

With the <samp class="listingcharacter">optimize</samp> option, note that the algorithm preprocesses the regular expression. This can take longer in some cases and consume a lot of memory. However, the result is faster when executing the search. In principle, how often the regular expression should be applied is a trade-off:

*   If the expression is only passed to functions like <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_search</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_match</samp> once or twice, the effort of <samp class="listingcharacter">optimize</samp> is not worth it.

*   If you apply search and replace functions with a regular expression a dozen times or more, you can indeed save time overall.

In general, you don't need to worry about it. For an average expression, the difference is minimal. The case might occur with long, complex expressions that have many ambiguities and overlaps with themselves. An ambiguity would be, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">(abc|abd)</samp>, because <samp class="listingcharacter">ab</samp> is matched by multiple subexpressions. A simple self-overlap occurs in <samp class="listingcharacter">ababa</samp>: with <samp class="listingcharacter">abab</samp>, a new possible match with <samp class="listingcharacter">ab</samp> also starts simultaneously. Nevertheless, such cases are usually completely uncritical, and the algorithm can handle them very well, whether optimized or not. For gigantic, unmanageable, and unspecific expressions, optimization might take longer and require a lot of memory—but because it is then executed faster, the effort can still be worthwhile with multiple applications.[[ 72 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_01)

### 28.2.9    Standard Syntax, Slightly Shortened

Because the default is the ECMAScript regular expression syntax, I provide a brief summary of the most important elements of the syntax in [Table 28.1](#28_002.html_t28.1).

With <samp class="listingcharacter">[</samp>class<samp class="listingcharacter">]</samp>, you can describe a character from a group. You can enumerate characters like <samp class="listingcharacter">[abcd]</samp>, define ranges <samp class="listingcharacter">[A-Za-z]</samp>, invert <samp class="listingcharacter">[^>]</samp> (everything except <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>), and also use class names like <samp class="listingcharacter">[[:alpha:]]</samp>. Which class names are supported exactly is determined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">regex_traits</samp> used. But at least <samp class="listingcharacter">alnum</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">alpha</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">blank</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cntrl</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">digit</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">graph</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lower</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">print</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">punct</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">space</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">upper</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">xdigit</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> exist. They correspond to the C function names, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">isalnum()</samp>.

| Pattern | Meaning | Pattern | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ab</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> followed by <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a{n,m}</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> times <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a&#124;b</samp> | Alternative | <samp class="listingcharacter">( )</samp> | Grouping |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> | Any character | <samp class="listingcharacter">^ $</samp> | Start and end of string |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a?</samp> | 0 or 1 time <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[</samp>class<samp class="listingcharacter">]</samp> | Character from class |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a*</samp> | 0 or more times | <samp class="listingcharacter">\d \w \s</samp> | Class shortcuts |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a+</samp> | 1 or more times | <samp class="listingcharacter">\b</samp> | Word boundary |

**Table 28.1**     A very brief overview of ECMAScript regex syntax.

You can also combine and negate enumerations and class names—for example:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">[[:alpha:]]</samp> matches any letter.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">[abc[:digit:]]</samp> matches the letters <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> and any digit.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">[^[:space:]]</samp> matches any character that is not whitespace.

There are abbreviations for some class names. For example, you can write <samp class="listingcharacter">\d</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">[[:digit:]]</samp>. You can see abbreviations in detail in [Table 28.2](#28_002.html_t28.2). The <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">\w</samp> stands for word, meaning letters that can appear in a word.

| Abbreviation | Stands For | Abbreviation | Stands For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\d</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[[:digit:]]</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">\D</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[^[:digit:]]</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\s</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[[:space:]]</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">\S</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[^[:space:]]</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">\w</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[_[:alnum:]]</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">\W</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">[^_[:alnum:]]</samp> |

**Table 28.2**     Abbreviations for character classes.

To support international texts, there are specially designated group names. There are collation groups (collations) like <samp class="listingcharacter">[[.span-ll.]]</samp>. This allows <samp class="listingcharacter">ll</samp> to be matched as a single character in Spanish. With equivalence groups like <samp class="listingcharacter">[[=e=]]</samp>, an <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp> and all its accented variants, è, é, and ê, can be matched in French.

### 28.2.10    Notes on Regular Expressions in C++

#### Differences in Algorithm

For most applications, the subtleties of regular expression searching are probably irrelevant. Will a short string be found first, or the one further up? Those who are more used to Perl or POSIX expressions might be confused, so we want to point out the small difference here.

Comparing the results of a search according to the POSIX standard and the ECMAScript standard yields the results shown in [Table 28.3](#28_002.html_t28.3).

| Search Pattern | Text | POSIX | ECMAScript |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a&#124;ab</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">"xaby"</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">"ab"</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">"a"</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">.*(a&#124;xayy)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">"zzxayyzz"</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">"zzxayy"</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">"zzxa"</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">([:alnum:])</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">" abc def xyz "</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">m[1] == "abc"</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">m[1] == "z"</samp> |

**Table 28.3**     Differences between POSIX and ECMAScript in regular expressions.

The results may therefore differ slightly:

*   ECMAScript
    Prefers shorter matches if they are the first to return a match.

*   POSIX
    If in doubt, returns a longer hit that starts further left.

With the advanced search options available in Perl, neither flavor can compete. Compared to POSIX, the ECMAScript variant offers the advantage that it often allows writing a more intuitive search pattern. Who hasn't tried to find an opening element in an HTML text with a regex that matches the closing element, such as <samp class="listingcharacter"><font>…</font></samp>?

The attempt to achieve this with the <samp class="listingcharacter"><font[^>]*>.*</font></samp> pattern fails in both cases because <samp class="listingcharacter">.*</samp> consumes as much text as possible. Not only would the matching elements be found, but everything up to the last <samp class="listingcharacter"></font></samp> element in the text—including additional <samp class="listingcharacter"><font></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"></font></samp>.

In ECMAScript syntax, compared to POSIX (for example), you can make an otherwise “greedy” part of the expression nongreedy by appending a <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp>. Thus, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><font[^>]*>.*?</font></samp> pattern accomplishes the task. In case of doubt, <samp class="listingcharacter">.*</samp> will now consume text that is as short as possible.

#### Readable Regular Expressions

I use a lot of regular expressions in my daily life, and you would probably be amazed at how often and for what. They are powerful tools, but they also have their pitfalls. In my experience, you should always outsource a search, match, or replace algorithm into an easily testable function and then feed it with a meaningful set of test cases in the unit test. More than usual, you can overlook one thing or another with regular expressions.

So fine, you have written your function, and it contains a great regular expression. And you have tests—wow! But in three weeks, the trickiest pitfall will catch up with you: you no longer understand the expression. You want to extend or correct it, but no matter what you change, the algorithm just breaks.

Yes, regular expressions are easy to write once you get the hang of them. But reading and understanding them again often becomes difficult. They are not a prime example of meeting the guideline that code should be self-documenting and require few to no comments.

But there is a solution—there are several, in fact. I advise you to write your regular expressions to be readable from the start.

Assume you have numerous messages like this:

```
score 400 for 2 nights at Minas Tirith Airport 
```

Here, the texts and numbers can change. You are supposed to extract the numbers <samp class="listingcharacter">400</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp> as well as the hotel name, Minas Tirith Airport, after <samp class="listingcharacter">at</samp>. The regular expression can look like this:

```
const string pattern = R"(^score\s+(\d+)\s+for\s+(\d+)\s+nights?\s+at\s+(.*))";
```

In the program, it looks like the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/dG5vE3heM
#include <regex>
#include <string>
#include <iostream>
using std::regex; using std::regex_search; using std::cmatch;
const regex pattern{R"(^score\s+(\d+)\s+for\s+(\d+)\s+nights?\s+at\s+(.*))"};
void extract(const std::string &text) {
    cmatch res;
    regex_search(text.c_str(), res, pattern);
    std::cout << res[1] << "," << res[2] << "," << res[3] << "\n";
}

int main() {
    extract("score 400 for 2 nights at Minas Tirith Airport");
    extract("score 84 for 1 night at Prancing Pony");
} 
```

**Listing 28.14**     Hard to maintain regular expression.

This is still barely readable. To improve readability, as always, there are at least three options:

*   Restructure

*   Use descriptive names

*   Comment

Combining the first two approaches, you could perhaps break down the large regex into several smaller ones, give the parts names, and then combine them.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TK6n4dG37
const string scoreKeyword = R"(^score\s+)";
const string numberOfPoints = R"((\d+))";
const string forKeyword = R"(\s+for\s+)";
const string numberOfNights = R"((\d+))";
const string nightsAtKeyword = R"(\s+nights?\s+at\s+)";
const string hotelName = R"((.*))";
const regex pattern{ scoreKeyword + numberOfPoints +
    forKeyword + numberOfNights + nightsAtKeyword + hotelName };
} 
```

**Listing 28.15**     Name parts and then combine them.

Perhaps this is more maintainable. At least this approach is recommended if parts of the expression might be used elsewhere in the program.

The third approach to commenting also works, except that C++ comments within the expression—within the string—do not work.

Here you can use the feature that C++ directly concatenates adjacent string literals if only whitespaces remain after removing comments. In this way, you can then comment parts of the expression in an almost “embedded” way.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/MszTjE3dv
const regex pattern{R"(^score)"
    R"(\s+)"
    R"((\d+))"          // points
    R"(\s+)"
    R"(for)"
    R"(\s+)"
    R"((\d+))"          // number of nights
    R"(\s+)"
    R"(night)"
    R"(s?)"             // optional: plural
    R"(\s+)"
    R"(at)"
    R"(\s+)"
    R"((.*))"           // hotel name
    R"()"}; 
```

**Listing 28.16**     Commenting within the expression.

All raw string fragments <samp class="listingcharacter">R"(…)"</samp> are directly adjacent, ignoring whitespaces and comments. The C++ preprocessor combines these into a single string literal.

## 28.3    Randomness

True random numbers are a difficult thing for computers. But in some applications, you need good random numbers. And the good old <samp class="listingcharacter">rand()</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><cstdlib></samp> no longer suffices—or <samp class="listingcharacter"><stdlib.h></samp>, as the header is called in the C11 standard.[[ 73 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_02) Even in the standard document, you can read about <samp class="listingcharacter">rand()</samp>: “There are no guarantees as to the quality of the random sequence produced and some implementations are known to produce sequences with distressingly non-random low-order bits. Applications with particular requirements should use a generator that is known to be sufficient for their needs.” Or, in short: If you value randomness, do not use <samp class="listingcharacter">rand()</samp>! Instead, use <samp class="listingcharacter"><random></samp>, because according to Bjarne Stroustrup, it is “what every random number library wants to be when it grows up.”[[ 74 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_03)

In C++, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><random></samp> header provides everything you need for random number generation. For 99% of all applications, the provided functionalities should suffice. You may build upon the classes and add your own extensions if necessary. However, let me also mention that <samp class="listingcharacter"><random></samp> does not cater to the 1% of applications that deal with cryptography. For these applications, you will need third-party libraries, and you can use <samp class="listingcharacter"><random></samp> as an inspiration.

If you just want to simulate a die with many sides, it is not really complicated. But if you are a physicist or mathematician and know that you need a random number with a student distribution at a certain performance, then you need to dig deeper, but you will still find what you need in <samp class="listingcharacter"><random></samp>.

This part of the library offers something for every user level:

*   Occasional users
    A preconfigured generator and two uniform distributions

*   Intermediate and advanced users
    Nine more generators, 18 more distributions, a true random number generator, and a helper class for seed values

*   Experts
    Six configurable adapters for combining generators and a function template for writing custom distributions

### 28.3.1    Rolling a Die

For average users who want to get a uniformly distributed random number, the next example looks simple.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ocP83a7ac
#include <random>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
void rollDice() {
  std::default_random_engine engine{};         // Normal quality randomness
  std::vector<size_t> counts{0,0,0,0,0,0};
  std::uniform_int_distribution<int> d6{0, 5}; // uniformly distributed integers
  for(auto i=1200*1000; i>0; --i)
    ++counts[d6(engine)];
  for(auto c : counts) std::cout<<" "<<c;
  std::cout << '\n';
}
int main() {
    rollDice();
} 
```

**Listing 28.17**     This is how you get a uniformly distributed random number between two bounds.

The output is the number of times each number was rolled. If all numbers were rolled equally often, you would see six times <samp class="listingcharacter">200000</samp>. But because it is rolled, it is instead this:

```
199664 200248 199727 200143 200373 199845 
```

As you can see, generating random numbers now consists of two things:

*   Engine
    The “engine” is responsible for generating the (possibly pseudo)random bits. Different generators produce random numbers with different qualities and at different speeds.

*   Distribution
    The distribution is responsible for mapping the bit representation to the actual numbers to be generated. These can be uniformly distributed, within a certain range, clustered at specific points, and so on.

If you combine these two things, you get the desired random number generator. A distribution like <samp class="listingcharacter">d6</samp> defines the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp> call operator. If you pass an engine as an argument to it, you get a random number of the desired distribution with the desired quality, as per the preceding example:

```
auto number = d6(engine); 
```

And <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> is now something between <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> (inclusive) with equal probability. If you don't like having to always carry and specify the engine here, simply combine both into a function object—for example, with a lambda:

```
auto d = [&]() { return d6(engine); };
std::cout << d() << '\n'; 
```

And when I run [Listing 28.17](#28_003.html_l28.17) again, I get the same output. And again and again—but that's a very unlikely coincidence, isn't it? It would be indeed, but all engines (except one, which we will get to shortly) are pseudorandom number generators: initialized with the same seed, they always produce the same bit sequence—which looks random under certain considerations and is sufficient for many (most?) applications. The reason I always got the exact same sequence of pseudorandom numbers here is that I always chose the same seed for the engine—namely, the default value. You can pass a different seed as a constructor argument:

```
std::default_random_engine engine{42};
std::default_random_engine engine{886699};
std::default_random_engine engine{time(0)}; // from <ctime> 
```

Each seed value provides a different pseudo-random sequence. If you start with a variable value—like here with <samp class="listingcharacter">time(0)</samp>, the current time—you will always get a different sequence. This is sufficient for standard cases. If you need more, there is the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::seed_seq</samp> helper class.

However, it may be that you get a different sequence of pseudorandom numbers on your machine than I do. Even though the generators are all well-defined by the standard, the <samp class="listingcharacter">default_random_engine</samp> is mapped to one of the generators by your specific implementation; which one is decided by the manufacturer. If you need true reproducibility, set both the generator and the seed value.[[ 75 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_04)

### 28.3.2    True Randomness

True random numbers are provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">random_device</samp> generator. This does not derive randomness from a seed and a mathematical formula but from various true randomness–producing components of your computer, such as mouse movements or hard disk head movements. However, this generator has a few significant disadvantages:

*   It is slow. Especially on server systems (without a mouse and the like), it is sometimes very slow.

*   Results are not reproducible, for example, for debugging; thus, the advantage can turn into a disadvantage.

*   The C++ implementation does not have to offer this engine; it is optional.

You can check with the <samp class="listingcharacter">enthropy()</samp> function of <samp class="listingcharacter">random_device</samp> whether <samp class="listingcharacter">random_device</samp> can really generate random numbers. If you see <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0</samp>, then some other—deterministic—engine is used.

### 28.3.3    Other Generators

An engine implements <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp>, which returns a random raw bit sequence. You can't do much with it for real experiments yet. Only when combined with a distribution does it become a random number in the correct range.

The distribution—like <samp class="listingcharacter">uniform_int_distribution<int> d6{0,5}</samp>—also overloads the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp>. If you pass the <samp class="listingcharacter">engine</samp> as a parameter to it, the bit sequence becomes an appropriate random number—for <samp class="listingcharacter">d6</samp> in the range between <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">5</samp> (inclusive)—with each <samp class="listingcharacter">engine</samp>.

Engines differ in the quality of the bit sequence they return. This quality is mathematically calculable and extremely important in some scenarios. Our deterministic computers have difficulties with true randomness. Therefore, the algorithms only generate seeming randomness, so-called pseudorandom numbers.

As a rule of thumb, the sequence of random numbers gets better the more time-consuming the generation of the bits is. I have written a program here that first allows you to measure the speed of the individual engines and second shows all the engines that might be present on current systems.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/e67356bMq
#include <random>
#include <chrono>  // system_clock
#include <format>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;
using namespace chrono;
const size_t LOOPS = 10*1000*1000;

template<typename ENGINE>
void measure(const string &title, ENGINE &engine) {
  const auto start = steady_clock::now();
  /* work hard */
  unsigned long long checksum = 0;
  size_t loops = LOOPS;
  while(loops-- > 0)
    checksum += engine();
  const auto now = steady_clock::now();
  nanoseconds dur_ns = now - start;
  cout << std::format("  {}: {:5} ns/loop  {:12} ns\n",
      title, dur_ns.count() / LOOPS, dur_ns.count());
}

int main() {
  { default_random_engine e{}; measure("       default", e ); }
  { random_device e{};         measure("        device", e ); }
  { minstd_rand0 e{};          measure("  minstd_rand0", e ); }
  { minstd_rand e{};           measure("  minstd_rand ", e ); }
  { mt19937 e{};               measure("    mt19937   ", e ); }
  { mt19937_64 e{};            measure("    mt19937_64", e ); }
  { ranlux24_base e{};         measure(" ranlux24_base", e ); }
  { ranlux48_base e{};         measure(" ranlux48_base", e ); }
  { ranlux24 e{};              measure(" ranlux24     ", e ); }
  { ranlux48 e{};              measure(" ranlux48     ", e ); }
  { knuth_b e{};               measure("       knuth_b", e ); }
  {
    using wide_t = unsigned long long ;
    independent_bits_engine<ranlux48, sizeof(wide_t)*8, wide_t> e{};
    measure("indep<ranlux> ", e );
  }
  {
    using wide_t = unsigned long long;
    independent_bits_engine<
          default_random_engine,
          sizeof(wide_t)*8, wide_t>
      e {};
    measure("indep<default>", e );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 28.18**     Speeds of the random number generators.

The results always vary on different systems, of course. Consider the following excerpt:

```
default:          12 ns/loop      126342116 ns
device:           41 ns/loop      417456044 ns
minstd_rand0:     12 ns/loop      122354003 ns
indep<ranlux>:  1086 ns/loop    10865420582 ns 
```

As you can see, the <samp class="listingcharacter">device</samp> here (!) is not that slow, and if you use <samp class="listingcharacter">indep<ranlux></samp>, you should have a reason for it.

### 28.3.4    Distributions

Random numbers can be generated with various characteristics or distributions—from a simple six-sided die to floating-point values.
