With a six-sided die, each of the numbers 1 to 6 should appear roughly equally often. But other random experiments behave differently. If you throw 10 coins (together) and count how often heads appears, then the possible outcomes 0 to 10 are binomially distributed. If you repeat this experiment several times in a row, you will see 0 heads less often than 5 heads. For such experiments, you do not need to generate the numbers 0 or 1 for heads or tails 10 times from the computer, but you can directly generate a number between 0 and 10 with the appropriate probability using <samp class="listingcharacter">binomial_distribution</samp>.

You have already seen in [Listing 28.17](#28_003.html_l28.17) what a uniform distribution looks like for a single die. Let's choose a binomial distribution in [Listing 28.19](#28_003.html_l28.19) to simulate tossing 10 coins.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/rv5fWP5Ya
#include <random>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    static const size_t size = 10;

    default_random_engine e{};              // Random number generator
    vector<size_t> counts(size+1);
    binomial_distribution<int> coins{size}; // tosses 10 coins, 0 to 10 heads
    for(auto i=120*1000; i>0; --i)
        ++counts[coins(e)];                 // Tossing coins
    for(auto c : counts) cout<<" "<<c;
    cout << '\n';
    // Example output:
    // 109 1159 5344 14043 24806 29505 24544 13973 5252 1150 115
} 
```

**Listing 28.19**     A binomial distribution.

As you can see, <samp class="listingcharacter">109</samp> is much less likely to get 0 heads than <samp class="listingcharacter">29505</samp> is to get 6 heads—a binomial distribution.

Suppose you wanted a uniform distribution, but this time not of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values, but instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. You need a different distribution function—namely, <samp class="listingcharacter">uniform_real_distribution<double></samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/94McsP7PG
#include <random>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::default_random_engine e{};
    std::uniform_real_distribution<double> unif{3,7}; // in the half-open interval [3,7)
    double u = unif(e);                         // Generate random number
    std::cout << u << '\n';                     // Example output: 3.52615
} 
```

**Listing 28.20**     A “double” random number.

#### Different Roll Every Time

If you already provide the range to the constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">uniform_int_distribution<int></samp> where the random numbers should be generated, do you always need to create a new distribution if the boundaries change each time?

No, fortunately not. Each distribution has a <samp class="listingcharacter">param_type</samp> with the same constructor arguments as the distribution. You can pass such a <samp class="listingcharacter">param_type</samp> instance to the generating call of <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp> and thus change the conditions for generation from call to call.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xz64qK3e5
#include <random>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::default_random_engine e{};
    using Dstr = std::uniform_int_distribution<int>;
    Dstr card{};                                          // generate distribution
    for(int n=32; n>=1; --n)
      std::cout <<" "<< card(e, Dstr::param_type{1,n} );  // parameters only here
    std::cout << '\n';
    // output for example:
    // 1 5 23 14 15 6 2 17 17 22 9 11 17 1 1 10 11 1 6 1 6 8 6 9 7 4 1 4 2 3 2 1
} 
```

**Listing 28.21**     Change generation parameters for each random number individually.

Here I simulate that the deck of cards gets one card smaller with each draw. The card number in the ever-decreasing deck is printed.

#### Distributions over Distributions

The exact formulas of all distributions and what their parameterizations mean are, of course, mentioned in the standard. To the mathematically inclined, the names will probably mean more. For those, the parameterizations of the distribution functions are probably of more interest. In [Table 28.4](#28_003.html_t28.4), real stands for a real number type such as <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. An int stands for an integer type, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, but of course others like <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp> are also possible.

| Distribution | Distribution Parameters |
| --- | --- |
| Uniform Distributions |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">uniform_int_distribution</samp> | Int a = 0, Int b = max() |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">uniform_real_distribution</samp> | Real a = 0.0, Real b = 1.0 |
| Bernoulli Family |

## 28.4    Mathematical

### 28.4.1    Fraction and Time: “<ratio>” and “<chrono>”

To work with time, you need the <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> header. Everything in it is in its own namespace, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono</samp> introduces central time units for seconds and milliseconds, but also hours and days. All of this is heavily based on compile-time fractions that come from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><ratio></samp> header. Why? Because, for example, one second is the same as 1/86,400 day—and the compiler automatically converts things from <samp class="listingcharacter"><ratio></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> for you. <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> uses <samp class="listingcharacter"><ratio></samp> as a foundation, and you could say it represents an example usage.

<samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> contains types and functions for the following aspects:

*   Time spans, the difference between points in time

*   Points in time for relative comparison to obtain time spans

*   Clocks with different reference times such as the computer's system time or GPS

*   Calendars for date calculation and representation

*   Time zones for converting clocks and calendars between different locations around the world

#### Motivation

Imagine you saw the following line in the code:

```
sleep(10);   // what unit is meant? 
```

What does it tell you? It waits. How long? Ten milliseconds? Ten seconds? Experience suggests that one of the two is likely; less likely is 10 nanoseconds or 10 minutes. But according to the rule that source code should be self-explanatory and ideally without comments, it is possible with <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> to write the following:

```
sleep(10s); 
```

This is clear and not ambiguous. The <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> is a suffix defined by <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""</samp> for the literal <samp class="listingcharacter">10</samp>, as you could also define it yourself (see [Chapter 23](#23_001.html_h23), [Section 23.7](#23_007.html_h23.7)), except that your suffixes must start with an underscore <samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp>. The standard library does not have this restriction, and thus <samp class="listingcharacter">10s</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> generates the following code:

```
sleep(std::chrono::seconds{10}); 
```

This in turn stands for the following:

```
sleep(std::chrono::duration<unsigned long,std::ratio<1>>{10}); 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">std::ratio<1></samp> stands for the seconds unit. If you want to specify 10 minutes, you don't need to calculate it yourself but can instead make one of the following calls:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/173nr4xxd
sleep(10min);
sleep(std::chrono::minutes{10});
sleep(std::chrono::duration<unsigned long,std::ratio<60>>{10}); 
```

There is another great side effect of this strong type system. When you define the <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> function, you naturally specify that the parameter should be a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>—for example:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/5snr1hq9b
#include <chrono>
void sleep(std::chrono::seconds s) { // takes seconds as duration
    /* ... */
}
/* ... */
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;  // make literals available
    sleep(10min);   // wait for 10 minutes, i.e., 600 seconds
    sleep(10ms);    // 10 milliseconds? Cannot be represented with seconds.
} 
```

When you define <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> to expect seconds as a parameter, users can still provide <samp class="listingcharacter">10min</samp> as a parameter, and <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> will automatically perform the conversion.

And <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> also prevents someone from trying to specify <samp class="listingcharacter">10ms</samp> as a time span. If you define <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> to take seconds as a parameter, there must be a reason for that. <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> will not be able to work in the millisecond range. So by choosing the parameter type for <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp>, you are also making a statement about the granularity with which your <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> operates—and you do so without extra comments or documentation.

And what if you find that you need to refine your granularity to nanoseconds? Then you do not need to go through the source code and modify all <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> calls, nor do you need to introduce a <samp class="listingcharacter">sleepNanoseconds</samp> function. You only change the <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep</samp> function:

```
void sleep(std::chrono::nanoseconds ns) { // takes nanoseconds as duration
    /* ... */
} 
```

And <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> automatically handles the conversion at all calling sites at compile time.

#### “chrono::seconds”

<samp class="listingcharacter">chrono::duration</samp> stands for duration, for a time span. This can be something like three seconds, three minutes, three hours, and so on.

The basis of <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> is the seconds in the form of <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::seconds</samp>. At runtime, an instance of this type is no different from an <samp class="listingcharacter">int64_t</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long long</samp>; both occupy eight bytes. So you can (trivially) move, copy, and construct it, and it costs the computer almost no time.

At its core, <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> is a very simple type, and you can roughly think of it like this:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/h8vsjxsME
#include <cinttypes> // int64_t
namespace std { namespace chrono {
class seconds {
    int64_t sec_;
public:
    seconds() = default;
    // … etc …
};
} } 
```

That means you can initialize <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> like this, for example:

```
std::chrono::seconds s1;    // uninitialized value
std::chrono::seconds s2{};  // zero initialized 
```

What you cannot do is this:

```
std::chrono::seconds s = 3; // Error: not implicitly from int 
```

This is very important, because just as important as what you can do with <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> is what you cannot do with it. For example, if this initialization were allowed, you would be able to write <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep(3)</samp> again, and you would have automatic conversion of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">nanoseconds</samp>?).

Instead, you need to write this:

```
std::chrono::seconds s{3}; 
```

This way, you protect yourself from errors.

You can output time spans like these to a stream. <samp class="listingcharacter">cout << s</samp>, for example, outputs <samp class="listingcharacter">3s</samp>. This is possible since C++20. Before that, you would use <samp class="listingcharacter">count()</samp> to get the enclosed value:

```
std::cout << s.count() << "s\n"; 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">chrono::duration</samp> as a parameter or variable looks like the following listing in practice.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/47j8h9e7v
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
void sleep(std::chrono::seconds dur) {
    std::cout << dur.count() << "s\n";
    /* ... */
}
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    sleep(3);          // Error: no implicit conversion from int
    sleep(seconds{4}); // okay
    sleep(5s);         // okay
    seconds x{6};
    sleep(x);          // okay
    auto y = 10s;
    y += 20s;          // Incrementing with seconds
    sleep(y);          // now 30s
    y = y - 6s;        // Subtraction of seconds
    sleep(y);          // and now only 24s
    y /= 2;            // Division by a scalar
    sleep(y);          // 12s
    sleep(y + 7);      // Error: seconds+int is not allowed
} 
```

**Listing 28.22**     With “seconds”, you can perform calculations.

As you can see, you can perform reasonable calculations with <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp>. Various arithmetic operators are overloaded. Can you perform addition of seconds? Yes. Division by a scalar? Yes. Addition of a scalar? No. This is because with <samp class="listingcharacter">y+7</samp> you again do not know whether seven seconds or seven years is meant, and <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> protects you from this ambiguity.

In addition to arithmetic operations, you can also perform comparisons.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/8c1r5xrs5
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
using std::chrono::operator""s;  // only make literal suffix available
constexpr auto limit = 10s;
void action(std::chrono::seconds dur) {
    if(dur <= limit) {           // compare
       std::cout << dur.count() << "s\n";
    } else {
       std::cout << "too long!\n";
    }
}
int main() {
    action(4s);   // Output: 4s
    action(20s);  // Output: too long!
} 
```

**Listing 28.23**     You can compare “seconds”.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp>, a variety of meaningful arithmetic and comparison operators are defined, and many nonmeaningful ones are intentionally not defined.

In [Table 28.5](#28_004.html_t28.5), I have listed the methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> for you.

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">count()</samp> | Access to the enclosed value |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">min()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, largest possible negative representable duration |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">max()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, largest possible representable duration |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">zero()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, zero duration |

**Table 28.5**     Methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp>.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> internally uses <samp class="listingcharacter">int64_t</samp>, you can cover a range of nearly 600 billion years between <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds::min()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds::max()</samp>.[[ 76 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_05)

#### Other Time Spans: “std::chrono::duration”

However, you not only have <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> as a time unit available, but also other time units as mentioned at the beginning. The standard specifies at least those in [Table 28.6](#28_004.html_t28.6). The implementation may offer more. The types from <samp class="listingcharacter">days</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">years</samp> were newly added in C++20, but they do not have suffixes. The <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> suffixes define a <samp class="listingcharacter">day</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp> of a calendar, not the <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">days</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">years</samp>.

| Type | Seconds | Suffix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">years</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<31556952,1></samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">months</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<2629746,1></samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">weeks</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<604800,1></samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">days</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<86400,1></samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">hours</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<3600,1></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">h</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">minutes</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<60,1></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">min</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">milliseconds</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ms</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">microseconds</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000000></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">us</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nanoseconds</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000000000></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ns</samp> |

**Table 28.6**     Various “duration” types of the standard library.

By using <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> as the basis of these time units, <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> allows the automatic conversion of all these time units into each other.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/qrs63vdz1
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;             // Allow suffixes
    seconds mySecs = 121s;                   // seconds{121}
    std::cout << mySecs.count() << "s\n";    // Output: 121s
    milliseconds myMillis = mySecs;          // automatically converted
    std::cout << myMillis.count() << "ms\n"; // Output: 121000ms
    nanoseconds myNanos = mySecs;
    std::cout << myNanos.count() << "ns\n";  // Output: 121000000000ns
    minutes myMinutesErr = mySecs;           // Error: Conversion with loss
    minutes myMinutes = duration_cast<minutes>(mySecs); // explicit works
    std::cout<<myMinutes.count()<<"min\n";   // Output: 2min
} 
```

**Listing 28.24**     Automatic conversion between time units.

As you can see, you then get the converted size in <samp class="listingcharacter">count()</samp>. So long as the conversion can take place without loss, the transformation works automatically. It would also work implicitly for parameters and returns, as you have already seen in the introductory example with <samp class="listingcharacter">sleep(…)</samp>.

It is different when information would be lost during the conversion. This would be the case, for example, if you converted <samp class="listingcharacter">mySecs</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">minutes</samp>. Then, 121 seconds would become 2 minutes, and the remaining 1 second would be lost. Here, the compiler complains if you want to do it implicitly.

If you know what you're doing, you can force exactly this conversion with <samp class="listingcharacter">duration_cast<…></samp>. The result is a rounding toward zero (decimal places are simply truncated). You get other rounding approaches with the <samp class="listingcharacter">floor</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">round</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">ceil</samp> functions.

To be clear, <samp class="listingcharacter">duration_cast<></samp> is not built-in like <samp class="listingcharacter">static_cast<></samp> and its kin, but is a function template that is fully named <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::duration_cast<></samp> and is part of <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>.

All this works because <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> knows the relationships between different time units and knows whether and how to convert them into each other.

##### Do Not Convert Yourself

When you start working with <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>, let the library handle the conversions. Do not convert yourself, like in the following listing.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Y3dnsMYcs
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    milliseconds myMs = 4'000ms;
    std::cout << myMs.count()/1000 << "s\n";  // here loss threatens
    std::cout << myMs.count()*1000 << "us\n"; // here loss threatens
    std::cout << duration_cast<seconds>(myMs).count() << "s\n"; // explicit
    std::cout << microseconds(myMs).count() << "us\n"; // like implicit
} 
```

**Listing 28.25**     Do not make your own calculations using “count()”.

It is much less error-prone to let <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> do the work in one place. The performance is also not worse than if you programmed it yourself by hand.

If the compiler tells you somewhere that it cannot convert something, believe it. Do not bypass its warning by using <samp class="listingcharacter">count()</samp> and your own calculation. The probability is high that you have made a logical error somewhere.

You can also mix conversions and arithmetic. An expression can contain different units. So long as no information is lost during the conversions, it works seamlessly.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/vTx4cdqzq
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
void showDuration(std::chrono::milliseconds dur) {
    std::cout << dur.count() << "ms\n";
}
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    auto x = 2s;
    auto y = 3ms;
    showDuration(x + y); // Output: 2003ms
    showDuration(x - y); // Output: 1997ms
} 
```

**Listing 28.26**     You can mix units.

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> is automatically converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">milliseconds</samp> before <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> is performed.

#### Custom “duration” Types

If you need other time units (Femtoseconds? Ten-day spans?) or if the 64 bits of <samp class="listingcharacter">second</samp> consume too much memory, you can easily create a new type that works seamlessly with the others.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/xMz4s8K8K
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std::chrono; using std::cout;
using seconds32 = duration<int32_t>;                // other representation
using ten_day = duration<int,std::ratio<86400*10>>; // other time unit
using fseconds = duration<double>;                  // Floating point representation
int main() {
  seconds32 s{5};
  cout << milliseconds(s).count() << "ms\n";
  ten_day z{1};
  hours h = z;                  // Conversion free
  cout << "1 ten_day has "<<h.count()<<" hours\n";                // …240…
  fseconds fs{23.75};
  cout << fs.count() << "s\n"; // Floating point output
  auto printDur = [](fseconds f) { cout << f.count() << "s\n"; }; // Function
  printDur(45ms + 63us);       // Conversion to fseconds
  // Output: 0.045063s
} 
```

**Listing 28.27**     Create new time units or more efficient representations.

Conversions between the <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds32</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">week</samp> types and to the normal time types work easily.

You will receive special treatment if you choose a floating-point representation for your own time type, in which case <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> assumes that no precision is lost during conversions. The expression <samp class="listingcharacter">45ms + 63us</samp> is implicitly converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">microseconds</samp> for the calculation. The <samp class="listingcharacter">printDur</samp> function takes <samp class="listingcharacter">fseconds</samp> as parameter. The compiler allows the conversion of <samp class="listingcharacter">microseconds</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">fseconds</samp> and performs the conversion correctly. This would not work with the integer-based <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> because the compiler would protect against loss of precision. If you use a float type, the compiler allows the conversion. An explicit conversion with <samp class="listingcharacter">duration_cast<></samp> then is not necessary.

#### Calendars, Clocks, and Time Zones

For C++20, the <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> header has been extensively expanded. While the C++11 version only included durations, time points, and a few clocks, it now includes calendars, leap seconds, time zones, and additional clocks as well as formatting and parsing.

To work with calendars in a type-safe manner, you now have access to the calendar types shown in [Table 28.7](#28_004.html_t28.7).

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">day</samp> | Day of a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">month</samp> | Month of a year |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp> | Year of the Gregorian calendar |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">weekday</samp> | Weekday in the Gregorian calendar |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">weekday_indexed</samp> | The n-th weekday of a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">weekday_last</samp> | Last weekday of a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">month_day</samp> | Specific day in a specific month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">month_day_last</samp> | Last day in a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">month_weekday</samp> | The n-th weekday in a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">month_weekday_last</samp> | Last weekday in a month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month</samp> | Specific month in a year |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_day</samp> | Specific day, month, and year |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_day_last</samp> | Last day in a specific month and year |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_weekday</samp> | The n-th weekday in a month and year |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_weekday_last</samp> | Last weekday in a month and year |

**Table 28.7**     The complete list of calendar types in <samp class="listingcharacter">chrono::</samp> from C++20.

##### But What Is a Calendar?

A calendar is a collection of dates, each of which has a specific name. In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> sense, <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_date</samp> is the canonical calendar. A calendar that can be converted to and from <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_date</samp> can be converted to any other calendar.

The standard currently supports only the Gregorian calendar and <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_days</samp>. However, other calendars can be easily added. You might need an ISO week-numbering calendar, the Julian calendar, or the Islamic calendar, for example. In the C++ standard, the Gregorian calendar is referred to as the civil calendar as it is the most widely used calendar.

You will find some type aliases, suffixes, and constants that refer to the civil calendar. The constant <samp class="listingcharacter">November</samp> is part of the civil calendar, although of course there is also a November in other calendars.

The class for the civil calendar is <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_day</samp>, with the components <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">month</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">day</samp>. Note that <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp> here does not denote a duration, but rather the “name” of a year in the calendar sense. However, you can subtract two <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp> instances from each other to get a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>.

It is important that an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is not implicitly converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp>. This prevents careless mistakes. A <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp> literal is marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp>, so <samp class="listingcharacter">2024y</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/zMqjqMeav
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std::chrono;
int main() {
    year y{2021};
    std::cout << y << "\n";
    month m{October};
    auto result = m + months{3};   // 'months', not 'month': 3 months later
    std::cout << result << "\n";   // overflowed to January
    weekday wd{Thursday};
    auto result = wd + days{4};    // 'days', not 'day': 4 days later
    std::cout << result << "\n";   // overflowed to Monday
    weekday sun1{0};               // 0 is Sunday
    weekday sun2{7};               // 7 is also Sunday
    std::cout << sun1 << "\t" << sun2 << "\n";
    weekday_indexed wdi{wd, 4};    // unspecified 4th Thursday
    std::cout << wdi << "\n";      // Output: Thu[4] — as given by chrono
                                   // unspecified values
} 
```

And when you put the pieces together, you get this:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6z48xvvvM
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std::chrono;
int main() {
  year this_year{2021};
  year last_year{2020};
  year_month_day ymd{this_year, October, day{28}};
  std::cout << ymd << "\n";
  month_weekday mwd{November, Thursday[4]};  // in an unspecified year
  std::cout << mwd << "\n";                  // Output: Nov/Thu[4]
  month_day_last mdlast{February};           // last day of an unspecified February
  year_month_day_last leap{last_year, mdlast};         // Add year
  year_month_day_last noleap{this_year, mdlast};       // Add year
  std::cout << leap << "\t" << leap.day() << "\n";     // Output: 2020-02-29 29
  std::cout << noleap << "\t" << noleap.day() << "\n"; // Output: 2021-02-28 28
} 
```

You can create a date using the <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_day</samp> constructor. To prevent dangerous mix-up errors, do not simply pass three integers to the constructor. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_day{10, 11, 12}</samp> should not work: What is the day, what is the month, and what is the year? Instead, you create instances of the types <samp class="listingcharacter">year</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">month</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">day</samp>, which you then pass to the constructor:

```
year_month_day ymd{year{2024}, month{11}, day{14}}; 
```

It looks nicer with the predefined suffixes like <samp class="listingcharacter">""y</samp>, constants like <samp class="listingcharacter">November</samp>, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> operator, which combines the individual elements into a date:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/4s69W7qd3
auto a_date = 2024y/11/14d;
auto b_date = 2024y/11/14;
auto c_date = 14d/11/2024;
auto d_date = November/14/2024; 
```

The following orders are possible: <samp class="listingcharacter">month/day/year</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">day/month/year</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">year/month/day</samp>. One of the first two elements must be a calendar type—so, for example, not <samp class="listingcharacter">14/10/2024y</samp>, because <samp class="listingcharacter">14/10</samp> would be recognized as integer division. The <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> operator cleverly creates “incomplete” types as intermediate values until you reach the complete date.

You can also generate the last day of a month:

```
auto ymd = last/February/2024;  // last day in February 2024: 2024-02-29 
```

Isn't that useful? This also makes the somewhat strange-looking “last” and “unspecified” types from [Table 28.7](#28_004.html_t28.7) make sense. These are generated as intermediate results when you create a date with the <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> operator. However, they are also useful in further operations, as you will see, because you can even perform calculations with these intermediate results.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Md38b9zvf
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <format>
using namespace std::chrono;
int main() {
  auto ymd = last/February/2024;   // last day in February 2024: 2024-02-29
  std::cout << ymd << "\n";        // the output with << is simple
  std::cout << std::format("{:%Y-%m-%d}\n", ymd);  // format is more flexible
  std::cout << std::format("{:%e. %B %y}\n", ymd); // much more flexible!
} 
```

**Listing 28.28**     Output of date and time with <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>.

The stream outputs <samp class="listingcharacter">2024/Feb/last</samp>—which is correct, but not helpful. With <samp class="listingcharacter">format</samp>, you can output both <samp class="listingcharacter">2024-02-29</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">29\. February 24</samp> , and so on.

To parse strings into a data type from <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>, since C++20 there are <samp class="listingcharacter">chrono::from_stream</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">chrono::parse</samp>.

##### [Übung]  Invalid Dates and Error Handling

The calendars from <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> leave it up to you how to handle invalid dates. For example, you can create November 31, which is an invalid date. It is neither automatically clamped to November 30 nor rolled over into December, nor is an exception thrown. It is up to you how to handle the invalid intermediate result:

```
auto ymd = 31d/October/2024;
ymd += months{1}; 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">ymd</samp> is now <samp class="listingcharacter">2024y/November/31d</samp>. If you want this to automatically be limited to November 30, then use <samp class="listingcharacter">last</samp>:

```
if (!ymd.ok())
    ymd = ymd.year()/ymd.month()/last; 
```

If you want to round into December, convert to <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_days</samp>. The data type ensures the wraparound at the month's boundary:

```
if (!ymd.ok())
    ymd = sys_days{ymd}; 
```

Here you can see how to use <samp class="listingcharacter">last</samp> and the classes to handle invalid dates.

So you can generate a specific day of a month or the last day of a month. But what about, for example, the second Tuesday of a month—the day you always expect Windows updates? Use the <samp class="listingcharacter">[]</samp> notation for that.[[ 77 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_06)

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/19vf9jfTM
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std::chrono;
int main() {
    for (int mo = 1; mo <= 12; ++mo) {
        year_month_weekday patch_tues{mo/Tuesday[2]/2024y};
        year_month_day ymd{sys_days{patch_tues}};
        std::cout << ymd.month() << " " << ymd.day() << "\n";
    }
} 
```

**Listing 28.29**     Always the second Tuesday of a month.

Note how <samp class="listingcharacter">Tuesday[2]</samp> refers to the second Tuesday of the month. First, we create a <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_weekday</samp> object, then we convert it to the universal <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_days</samp> calendar, and finally to a <samp class="listingcharacter">year_month_day</samp> calendar for output.

##### Time Zones

Since C++20, the standard library can also handle time zones. This is a very complex topic that we can only touch on here. The most important types involved are as follows:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">time_zone</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">zoned_time</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">tzdb</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">tzdb_list</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">time_zone_link</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ambiguous_local_time</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">nonexistent_local_time</samp>

For a time zone and a time within it, there are the <samp class="listingcharacter">time_zone</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">zoned_time</samp> data types:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">time_zone</samp> Represents the time zone of a specific geographic region. It consists of the name, the UTC offset, any daylight saving time rules, and so on—for example, Europe/Berlin or America/New York.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">zoned_time</samp> Combines <samp class="listingcharacter">time_zone</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> to represent a point in time in a specific time zone. Provides <samp class="listingcharacter">local_time</samp> or a time zone–less <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp>.

To convert, use the constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">zoned_time</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">local_time</samp>:

```
auto autumn = local_days{2d/June/2024} + 16h + 33min;
std::cout << zoned_time{"Europe/Berlin", autumn} << '\n'; 
```

Conversions to and from <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">local_time</samp> are usually straightforward. However, there are some tricky edge cases that always cause trouble. And what is to blame? Daylight saving time.

There are local times that do not exist at all, and some that exist twice. In Europe/Berlin, for example, the time 02:01:00 on March 31, 2024, does not exist. Instead, on October 27, 2024, you have the opportunity to interpret the time 02:01 as daylight saving time and thus as 00:01 UTC, or as standard time and thus as 01:01 UTC.

The C++ standard allows you to handle these cases. When you convert <samp class="listingcharacter">local_time</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp>, two types of exceptions can be thrown:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">nonexistent_local_time</samp> The local time does not exist.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ambiguous_local_time</samp> The local time exists twice. You can decide with <samp class="listingcharacter">choose::earliest</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">choose::latest</samp> which one you mean.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ezn568nof
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std::chrono;
int main() {
  auto spring = local_days{31d/March/2024} + 2h + 1min;
  try {
      auto zt = zoned_time{"Europe/Berlin", spring};
  } catch (const nonexistent_local_time& e) {
      std::cout << e.what() << '\n'; // Exception thrown: does not exist
  }
  auto autumn = local_days{27d/October/2024} + 2h + 1min;
  try {
      auto zt = zoned_time{"Europe/Berlin", autumn};
  } catch (const ambiguous_local_time& e) {
     std::cout << e.what() << '\n'; // Exception thrown: already exists
  }
  std::cout << zoned_time{"Europe/Berlin", autumn, choose::earliest} << '\n';
  // Output: 2024-10-27 02:01:00 CEST
  std::cout << zoned_time{"Europe/Berlin", autumn, choose::latest} << '\n';
  // Output: 2024-10-27 02:01:00 CET
} 
```

**Listing 28.30**     Conversion to a time with time zone and the exceptions.

The last two conversions went smoothly, while the first two threw an exception. Their outputs describe the errors quite thoroughly:

```
2024-03-31 02:01:00 is in a gap between
2024-03-31 02:00:00 CET and
2024-03-31 03:00:00 CEST which are both equivalent to
2024-03-31 01:00:00 UTC
2024-10-27 02:01:00 is ambiguous.  It could be
2024-10-27 02:01:00 CEST == 2024-10-27 00:01:00 UTC or
2024-10-27 02:01:00 CET == 2024-10-27 01:01:00 UTC 
```

If you are dealing with multiple time zones, the time zone database comes into play:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">tzdb</samp> This type stores the data of the time zone database. You get it with the <samp class="listingcharacter">get_tzdb()</samp> function. There are the <samp class="listingcharacter">zones</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">version</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">links</samp> vectors as well as the <samp class="listingcharacter">version</samp> field. With the <samp class="listingcharacter">current_zone()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">locate_zone(string_view tz_name)</samp> methods, you get a <samp class="listingcharacter">const time_zone*</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">tzdb_list</samp> You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">get_tzdb_list()</samp> method to get a list of all time zones, and multiple versions may also be stored.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">time_zone_link</samp> This represents an alternative designation of a time zone.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/YTKK3vT7s
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges> // views::transform, views::filter
#include <algorithm> // ranges::for_each
using namespace std; namespace c = std::chrono;
namespace v = std::views; namespace r = std::ranges;
int main() {
  auto show_name = [](const string_view name) { cout << name << ' '; };
  const auto& db = c::get_tzdb();
  auto names = db.zones
   | v::transform([](const c::time_zone& z) {return z.name();})
   | v::filter([](const string_view name) {
       return name.starts_with("Europe/Be");});
  r::for_each(names, show_name);
  cout << " <- Europe/Be*\n"; // Output: Europe/Belgrade Europe/Berlin
  r::for_each(
   db.links
   | v::filter([](const c::time_zone_link& l){
       return l.target()=="Europe/Berlin";})
   | v::transform([](const c::time_zone_link& l)->string_view {
       return l.name();})
   , show_name);
  cout << " <- Links to Europe/Berlin\n"; // Output: Arctic/Longyearbyen …
} 
```

**Listing 28.31**     The time zone database.

###### Standards and Implementations

The standard library defines that the IANA time zone database should be used as the basis for implementations. However, this is not always easy because the database is not available on every system, and furthermore, it is difficult to keep it up to date. Linux systems usually have the database installed (check in <samp class="listingcharacter">/usr/share/zoneinfo</samp>), but Windows systems do not. However, the Microsoft C++ compiler comes with the ICU library, which contains a similar database. The differences are small but present.

#### Compile-Time Fractions: “ratio”

In [Table 28.6](#28_004.html_t28.6), you saw that the second template parameter of <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp>. Indeed, this <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> handles all the conversion that is so useful in <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>. And what is useful for time units can also be helpful elsewhere.

<samp class="listingcharacter">std::ratio</samp> is a fraction that is evaluated at compile-time. <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000></samp> is the compile-time equivalent of ![inline image](bilder/formula-28_01.png). You can perform calculations with different <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> instances. The compiler even performs simplifications. This means that if you multiply <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1000,1></samp> by <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000></samp>, the result is not <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1000,1000></samp> but <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1></samp>. This is important so that the compiler knows exactly when types are identical and when it needs to convert. If it is a “unit fraction,” then you can omit the second template parameter because its default is one. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<88></samp> is the same as <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<88,1></samp>.

##### “ratios” Are Not Values, but Types!

To emphasize once again: the <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,2> a{}</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,3> b{}</samp> variables have different types. For example, if you write a <samp class="listingcharacter">void f(ratio <1,2> v)</samp> function, you cannot call it with <samp class="listingcharacter">f(ratio<1,3>{})</samp>. It makes little sense to create variables of <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp>, as <samp class="listingcharacter">a+b</samp> does not support <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> either. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">duration<ratio<…>></samp> type, for example. There it serves to ensure that when you add <samp class="listingcharacter">second a</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">minute b</samp>, you get an automatic conversion.

So that you don't always have to write <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000></samp> and the like, the standard library predefines the commonly occurring fractions shown in [Table 28.8](#28_004.html_t28.8). The ones with question marks ? are available if <samp class="listingcharacter">intmax_t</samp> can represent them. <samp class="listingcharacter">quecto</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ronto</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ronna</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">quetta</samp> are part of the standard only from C++26 onward.

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<>::num</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<>::den</samp> to determine the numerator and denominator respectively of any fraction.

You can also easily add your own fractions. And from then on, you don't need to worry about conversions anymore. Similar to how <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> demonstrates, you get operators and conversions delivered to you for free:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/ThM8q1zEP
#include <iostream>
#include <ratio>
using std::cout; using std::endl;
int main() {
  using oneThird = std::ratio<1,3>;
  using twoFourths = std::ratio<2,4>;
  cout << oneThird::num << "/" << oneThird::den << endl;     // Output: 1/3
  cout << twoFourths::num << "/" << twoFourths::den << endl; // Output: 1/2
  using sum = std::ratio_add<oneThird,twoFourth>;            // add
  cout << sum::num << "/" << sum::den;                       // Output: 5/6
} 
```

| Typedef | Ratio | Value | Typedef | Ratio | Value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">quecto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[30]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–30) ? | <samp class="listingcharacter">deca</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10,1></samp> | 10¹ |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ronto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[27]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–27) ? | <samp class="listingcharacter">hecto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<100,1></samp> | 10² |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">yocto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[24]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–24) ? | <samp class="listingcharacter">kilo</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1000,1></samp> | 10³ |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">zepto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[21]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–21) ? | <samp class="listingcharacter">mega</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1000000,1></samp> | 10⁶ |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">atto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[18]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–18) | <samp class="listingcharacter">giga</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1000000000,1></samp> | 10⁹ |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">femto</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[15]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–15) | <samp class="listingcharacter">tera</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[12]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00,1></samp> | 10^(12) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">pico</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10…</samp>[12]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00></samp> | 10^(–12) | <samp class="listingcharacter">peta</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[15]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00,1></samp> | 10^(15) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">nano</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000000000></samp> | 10^(–9) | <samp class="listingcharacter">exa</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[18]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00.1></samp> | 10^(18) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">micro</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000000></samp> | 10^(–6) | <samp class="listingcharacter">zetta</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[21]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00.1></samp> | 10^(21) ? |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">milli</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,1000></samp> | 10^(–3) | <samp class="listingcharacter">yotta</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[24]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00.1></samp> | 10^(24) ? |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">centi</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,100></samp> | 10^(–2) | <samp class="listingcharacter">ronna</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[27]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00.1></samp> | 10^(27) ? |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">deci</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,10></samp> | 10^(–1) | <samp class="listingcharacter">quetta</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<10…</samp>[30]<samp class="listingcharacter">…00.1></samp> | 10^(30) ? |

**Table 28.8**     All predefined “ratio” typedefs. The subscripted digits between “…”s indicate the total number of zeros in the omissions.

Even at the definition stage, the compiler simplifies <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<2,4></samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<1,2></samp>. When adding ![inline image](bilder/formula-28_02.png) and ![inline image](bilder/formula-28_03.png), the fractions must first be expanded to sixths to obtain ![inline image](bilder/formula-28_04.png)—that is, <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<5,6></samp>.

Besides <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_add</samp>, there are more options for arithmetic computation and comparison at compile time, which I have listed in [Table 28.9](#28_004.html_t28.9).

| Operator | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_add</samp> | Add |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_subtract</samp> | Subtract |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_multiply</samp> | Multiply |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_divide</samp> | Divide |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_equal</samp> | Comparison for equality |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_not_equal</samp> | Comparison for inequality |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_less</samp> | Comparison for less than |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_less_equal</samp> | Comparison for less than or equal to |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_greater</samp> | Comparison for greater |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio_greater_equal</samp> | Comparison for greater or equal |

**Table 28.9**     Arithmetic and comparisons for “ratio” at compile time.

Otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> contains the best examples of a meaningful use of <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp>.

For example, it would have been possible in [Listing 28.27](#28_004.html_l28.27) instead of

```
using ten_days = std::chrono::duration<int,std::ratio<86400*10>> 
```

to write the following:

```
using ten_days = std::chrono::duration<int,
        std::ratio_multiply<std::ratio<10>,                    // 10 * …
            std::ratio_multiply<std::ratio<24>,hours::period>  // … 24 hours
        >
      >; 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">10*24*hours</samp> results in a ten-day span. Each <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> type has <samp class="listingcharacter">period</samp> defined as <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>. It’s defined as a <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio</samp> of what you requested with the template. For example for <samp class="listingcharacter">hours</samp> the definition <samp class="listingcharacter">hours::period</samp> will be <samp class="listingcharacter">ratio<3600></samp>. That sounds more complicated than it looks in code (slightly simplified):

```
template<typename Rep, typename Period>
class duration {
    using rep = Rep;
    using period = Period;
    // …
};
using hours = duration<int,ratio<3600>>; 
```

#### Time Points: “time_point”

While <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> represents some relative duration, <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> is absolute. For <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> is a firmly connected pair of a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> and a reference point.

For example, the reference point could be January 1, 2000, and the duration 6,518 days; then the pair of these two values would name the time point as November 5, 2017.

Specifically in C++, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">10000s</samp> is 10,000 seconds, while

```
time_point<system_clock, seconds> tp{10000s}; 
```

is 10,000 seconds after 1/1/1970, which is 1970-01-01 02:46:40 UTC (that January 1, 1970, is the start of <samp class="listingcharacter">system_clock</samp> is not a must, so be careful here).

Since C++20, there are aliases for <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point<system_clock, seconds></samp> such as <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time<seconds></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_seconds</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_days</samp> alias has also been added.

However, <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> work well together. You can take the difference between two time points and get a duration—as in C++:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/q1znGWb85
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    time_point<system_clock, seconds> t1{10000s};
    time_point<system_clock, seconds> t2{50000s};
    auto dur = t2 - t1;
    std::cout << duration_cast<hours>(dur).count() << "h"; // Output: 11h
} 
```

The compiler does not allow you to add two time points, as that would not make sense. However, you can add <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> and so on.

Every <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> is bound to a time unit—in this example, <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp>. As with <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>, the compiler allows implicit conversions to more precise <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> types but prevents those to less precise ones. With a <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point_cast</samp>, you can always force a conversion.

To convert a <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>, use the <samp class="listingcharacter">time_since_epoch()</samp> method.

#### Clocks

A clock is a triplet of

*   a duration in the form of a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> type,

*   a point in time in the form of a <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> type, and

*   a function to get the current time.

Here is a somewhat simplified representation of any clock:

```
struct some_clock {
    using duration = microseconds;             // Granularity of the clock
    using time_point = time_point<some_clock>; // Return type of now()
    static time_point now() noexcept;          // get current time
}; 
```

I have omitted the <samp class="listingcharacter">rep</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">period</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">is_steady</samp> members for better clarity. <samp class="listingcharacter">microseconds</samp> is mentioned only as an example; each clock defines its own granularity here. The central function is <samp class="listingcharacter">now()</samp>, which I will explain to you in more detail shortly.

The likelihood that you will need to define new clocks yourself is very low. The standard library comes with a few clocks (up to C++20, only <samp class="listingcharacter">system_clock</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">steady_clock</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">high_resolution_clock</samp>), which you will use depending on the application:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::system_clock</samp> Use this clock if you need a reference to a calendar. With this clock, you can get the current time or date. It provides <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp> and handles leap seconds as we do in everyday life. When you format the seconds, you expect the usual <samp class="listingcharacter">"00"</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">"59"</samp>. This clock can store values from midnight, January 1, 1970 (UTC). However, this is only guaranteed from C++20 onward; before that, the starting point was not defined.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::steady_clock</samp> This is more of a stopwatch. Time measurements within your program are possible with this. It has no relation to a time of day or a calendar.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::high_resolution_clock</samp> This is usually just an alias for one of the other two clocks, depending on which system the clock is more finely granulated for time measurement. Implementations can provide a particularly accurate clock here.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::file_clock</samp> This is the same clock as <samp class="listingcharacter">std::file_system::file_time_type::clock</samp> and is returned by functions like <samp class="listingcharacter">file_system::last_write_time()</samp>. The starting point of the clock is unspecified. However, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">clock_cast</samp> to convert to <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp>, which has a specified starting point.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::utc_clock</samp> Delivers <samp class="listingcharacter">utc_time</samp>, which is like <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp> but accounts for leap seconds. When you calculate differences across the boundaries of leap seconds, they are accounted for with <samp class="listingcharacter">utc_time</samp>. When you format <samp class="listingcharacter">utc_time</samp>, account for a second <samp class="listingcharacter">"60"</samp>, not just <samp class="listingcharacter">"00"</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">"59"</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::gps_clock</samp> The <samp class="listingcharacter">gps_clock</samp> delivers <samp class="listingcharacter">gps_time</samp> and starts on June 1, 1980\. It does not account for leap seconds. It can be, but does not have to be, very accurate. It is currently 18 seconds ahead of <samp class="listingcharacter">sys_time</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">utc_time</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::tai_clock</samp> International Atomic Time (abbreviated to TAI from its French name) is a very accurate time that does not account for leap seconds. It starts on January 1, 1958\. When you format <samp class="listingcharacter">tai_time</samp>, it is always 19 seconds ahead of <samp class="listingcharacter">gps_time</samp>.

##### [Übung]  Local Pseudo Clock

The <samp class="listingcharacter">local_t</samp> clock is a clock for intermediate calculations when you have a time point to which you want to add a time zone later. This clock does not have a <samp class="listingcharacter">now()</samp> method.

If you want the current time of a clock, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">steady_clock</samp>, you can get it as follows:

```
steady_clock::time_point tp = steady_clock::now(); 
```

Or directly with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp>:

```
auto tp = steady_clock::now(); 
```

In general, when working with <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>, you can very often use <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> and thus do not have to remember all return types.

You use this, for example, to measure the time of a function call.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/3MGbYn4d5
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
long fib(long n) { return n<2L ? 1L : fib(n-1L)+fib(n-2L); }
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    auto t0 = steady_clock::now();  // On your marks, get set …
    auto res = fib(17);             // … go!
    auto t1 = steady_clock::now();  // Stop!
    std::cout << "Result: " << res << "\n"; // Output: Result: 2584
    std::cout << "Time: " << nanoseconds{t1-t0}.count() << "ns\n";
    // Output: Time: 50727ns (e.g.)
} 
```

**Listing 28.32**     Simple timing of a function call.

Simply measure the time before and after the call with <samp class="listingcharacter">now()</samp> and get a <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point</samp> each time. Between these two, you calculate the difference with <samp class="listingcharacter">t1-t0</samp> and get a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>. For the output, you then convert this <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> into a time unit appropriate for the measurement—here, <samp class="listingcharacter">nanoseconds{…}</samp>. And you're done.

##### [Übung]  Converting Times and Leap Seconds

Since C++20, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">clock_cast<></samp> to convert values between different <samp class="listingcharacter">time_point<></samp> types. The starting points of the clocks and the leap seconds are taken into account.

For this, there is the <samp class="listingcharacter">clock_time_conversions<></samp> trait. Clocks that support <samp class="listingcharacter">to_utc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">from_utc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">to_sys</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">from_sys</samp> can then be converted using <samp class="listingcharacter">clock_cast<></samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/bsqP75Kr8
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
using namespace std::chrono;
int main() {
    tai_time tai_now = tai_clock::now();
    std::cout << tai_now << "\n";  // Output: 2023-10-19 01:13:06.2810034
    utc_time utc_now = clock_cast<utc_clock>(tai_now);
    std::cout << utc_now << "\n";  // Output: 2023-10-19 01:12:29.2810034
} 
```

**Listing 28.33**     Converting time points with “clock_cast”.

At the inception of these clocks, they were already 10 seconds apart. The additional 27 leap seconds since then lead to a discrepancy of 37 seconds, which will continue to change. The <samp class="listingcharacter">clock_cast</samp> function takes this into account.

The leap seconds are determined by an international committee and synchronize Earth's rotation with atomic time. They are usually added or removed on June 30 or December 31\. Since establishment in 1972, there have been a total of 27 inserted leap seconds, the last one on December 31, 2016\. There has not been a skipped second so far, but it could happen.

If you want a coarser time unit that you cannot implicitly convert due to loss of precision, then you have two already explained options:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/rz38hc1cx
auto res = fib(45);
// …
std::cout << "Time: " << duration_cast<seconds>(t1-t0).count() << "s\n";
// Output: Time: 7s (e.g.)
std::cout << "Time: " << duration<double>{t1-t0}.count() << "s\n";
// Output: Time: 7.35303s (e.g.)
} 
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">duration_cast<></samp>, you can accept loss of precision in the output. If you convert to a floating-point <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp>, the compiler allows the loss of precision—which with floating-point numbers is not actually a loss.

If you don't need a stopwatch but a wall clock, then use <samp class="listingcharacter">system_clock</samp>. The point in time it describes results from the elapsed duration since the epoch. Epoch is the implicit start of this clock. You get the duration since the epoch with <samp class="listingcharacter">time_since_epoch()</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/1xbhhTdEv
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    auto tp = time_point_cast<seconds>(system_clock::now());
    auto d = tp.time_since_epoch();
    std::cout << d.count() << "s\n";
    std::cout << duration<double,std::ratio<86400>>{d}.count() << "days\n";
} 
```

On all systems known to me, the epoch corresponds to 1970-01-01 00:00:00.[[ 78 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_07) <samp class="listingcharacter">time_since_epoch()</samp> returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">duration</samp> here, usually based on seconds, which you can manipulate as usual.

The output is currently as follows for me:

```
1488837296s
17231.9days 
```

### 28.4.2    Predefined Suffixes for User-Defined Literals

In the standard library, three types of user-defined literals are defined—user-defined in the sense that they are defined using <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""</samp>. This means that you can write literals of the respective type directly in the source code using the defined suffixes.

#### Custom User-Defined Literals

Remember that you are only allowed to write custom user-defined literals that begin with an underscore <samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp>. All others are reserved for the present and future of the standard library.

I have already mentioned the literals during the discussion of the respective types. However, I want to list them all together here and mention the commonalities.

The predefined user-defined literal suffixes are in [Table 28.10](#28_004.html_t28.10). Each header defines its literals in its own <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace</samp>. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">std::literals</samp> is an <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><string></samp> defines <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace std::literals::string_literals</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><complex></samp> defines <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace std::literals::complex_literals</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> defines <samp class="listingcharacter">inline namespace std::literals::chrono_literals</samp>

Because the literals are in their own namespaces, you can fetch them separately. But because they are <samp class="listingcharacter">inline</samp> namespaces, you can fetch them all with a single <samp class="listingcharacter">using</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std</samp> makes the suffixes for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">complex</samp> available along with other identifiers of the standard library if you have included the respective headers. <samp class="listingcharacter">chrono</samp> is in its own namespace.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std::chrono</samp> makes the suffixes from <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> available along with other identifiers when you have included <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std::literals</samp> also makes all suffixes available, but other identifiers must still be addressed with <samp class="listingcharacter">std::</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using namespace std::literals::chrono_literals</samp> makes only the literals defined in <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> available.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">using std::literals::string_literals::operator""s</samp> makes only the suffix <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> available for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, but not the other suffixes, especially not <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">second</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>. This also works for all other <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""</samp>s.

| Suffix | Type | Header |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter"><string></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""sv</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::string_view</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter"><string_view></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""i</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::complex<double></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter"><complex></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""if</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::complex<float></samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""il</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::complex<long double></samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""h</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::hours</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""min</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::minutes</samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::seconds</samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""ms</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::milliseconds</samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""us</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::microseconds</samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""ns</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::nanoseconds</samp> |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""d</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::day</samp> (since C++20) |  |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">""y</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">std::chrono::year</samp> (since C++20) |  |

**Table 28.10**     The predefined literals in the standard library for <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""</samp> suffixes.

What you use depends on the situation. In particular, <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><string></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp> can be cleanly separated this way if needed.

You can find plenty of examples, such as in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Listing 4.17](#04_002.html_l4.17) for <samp class="listingcharacter"><string></samp>, [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Listing 4.39](#04_005.html_l4.39) for <samp class="listingcharacter"><complex></samp>, and [Listing 28.24](#28_004.html_l28.24) for <samp class="listingcharacter"><chrono></samp>. Here is a summary with several different literals:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/o359TThMj
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <chrono>
#include <complex>

using std::cout;

int main() {
    { using namespace std;
      cout << "string"s << "\n";           // string
      cout << (1.2+3.4i) << "\n";          // complex
      }
    { using namespace std::chrono;
      cout << (35ms).count() << "ms\n";    // chrono
      }
    { using namespace std::literals;
      cout << (41s).count() << "ms\n";     // chrono seconds
      cout << "text"s << "\n";             // string
    }
    { using namespace std::chrono;
      cout << (4h).count() << "h\n";       // chrono hours
    }
    { using namespace std::literals::chrono_literals;
      cout << (16min).count() << "min\n";  // chrono minutes
    }
    { using std::literals::string_literals::operator""s;
      cout << "letters"s << "\n";          // string
    }
} 
```

Note that although <samp class="listingcharacter">""s</samp> exists for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp>, you can use both simultaneously because the overloads for <samp class="listingcharacter">operator""</samp> do not conflict. Text literals like <samp class="listingcharacter">"text"s</samp> become <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, and numeric literals like <samp class="listingcharacter">41s</samp> become <samp class="listingcharacter">seconds</samp>.

#### [Übung]  The GCC and “complex” Suffixes

For GCC, the <samp class="listingcharacter">""i</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">""if</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">""il</samp> suffixes for complex literals currently only work as expected if you specify <samp class="listingcharacter">-fno-ext-numeric-literals</samp> during compilation. Definitions from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><complex.h></samp> C header along with long-existing GCC extensions otherwise confuse the compiler.

## 28.5    System Error Handling with “system_error”

Errors caused by the operating system or a similarly low level and reaching the program are typically returned to the caller as a numeric value. On a POSIX system, the “Permission denied” error is reported, for example, with the error code <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> (constant <samp class="listingcharacter">EPERM</samp>).

To write portable code, you need to translate these codes into general—portable—representations. In doing so, you must deal with many possible systems. And just to be able to do that, you also need to be able to access the system-specific codes again. On the one hand, you want a portable translation; on the other hand, you want system-specific low-level access.

The <samp class="listingcharacter"><system_error></samp> header tries to bridge this gap. It contains lightweight <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> objects that contain system-specific <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> error codes on the one hand, but on the other hand refer to more abstract and portable <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> objects.

These error objects can also be used without the exception class, which developers who work without exceptions in their environment will appreciate. If you use exceptions, you can trigger an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> along with a text message as a <samp class="listingcharacter">system_exception</samp>.

Extensibility is addressed by the fact that these two fields are each associated with an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp>. Here, users can add their own error groups or recognize those defined by the system.

### 28.5.1    Overview

The <samp class="listingcharacter"><system_error></samp> header primarily defines the following components:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">class error_code</samp>
    Represents a (system-)specific error value that can be returned by an operation, such as a system function call.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">class error_condition</samp>
    A generic error condition against which one checks in their portable code.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">class error_category</samp>
    Classification of errors into groups/families, also an abstract base class for translation into readable text.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">class system_error</samp>
    Is an exception class that contains an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> when an error is propagated by exception.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">enum class errc</samp>
    Is an enumeration of general-purpose values derived from the POSIX standard of type <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_code_enum<></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_condition_enum<></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">make_error_code</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">make_error_condition</samp> Implement mechanisms to convert <samp class="listingcharacter">enum class</samp> values into <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> values.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">generic_category()</samp> Returns an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp> instance that can interpret <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp>-based codes and conditions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">system_category()</samp> Returns an instance to interpret errors from the operating system.

### 28.5.2    Principles

Although <samp class="listingcharacter">system_error</samp> defines its own exception class, throwing an exception is not always the right way to handle an error. Sometimes, the additional return value of a function simply provides information that you want to incorporate into your program's control flow. A broken connection to a network server might be propagated as an exception, but if you are trying multiple servers during connection setup, you should not necessarily implement this in a loop with exceptions. And do not forget that in some areas, exceptions are entirely undesirable: In real-time systems, the requirements for deterministic timing behavior are so high that implementers sometimes avoid exceptions altogether. And in embedded systems, the additional memory consumption that some exception implementations bring cannot be neglected. Therefore, C++ pragmatically supports both types of error handling—return values with error codes as well as exceptions—and bridges the two worlds.

In case of an error, the <samp class="listingcharacter">errno</samp> variable often stores more detailed information about the nature of the error. Many functions from <samp class="listingcharacter"><stdio></samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter"><math></samp> store an error code here in case of failure. On POSIX-compliant platforms, many system functions provide details in <samp class="listingcharacter">errno</samp> when a function call fails. On Windows, <samp class="listingcharacter">GetLastError</samp> is often used additionally or instead. And the more libraries you use, the more sources from which error codes can be determined are added. C++ takes into account the possibility that error codes from different sources need to be evaluated and supports the extension of these by libraries. When that happens, the interface of existing functions must not change.

When users and third-party providers are given the means to extend the error code system, both the low-level error codes (which may vary from system to system) need to be mapped somewhere, and users need to be offered a portable interpretation. For example, someone implementing an HTTP server wants to pass on the error codes defined in the RFC standard in a way that everyone can understand, but must rely on operating system-specific error codes to do so. We will demonstrate this with an example in the next section. Originally, it was intended that libraries (the standard library, but also those from third-party providers) would only offer users the already interpreted error codes. However, the original information is also important for problem analysis, and therefore it must somehow be present in bug reports or logging. Therefore, error code handling must offer both: low-level error codes and interpreted/portable values.

### 28.5.3    “error_code” and “error_condition”

The <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> classes look almost identical, but they have different roles. <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> transports system-dependent errors, while <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> is used for a more portable classification.

So it depends on what you want to achieve. Consider the following example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/1xnY8vd8Y
#include <system_error> // error_code
#include <string>
void create_dir(const std::string& pathname, std::error_code& ec);
void run() {
  std::error_code ec;
  create_dir("/some/path", ec);
  if(!ec) {  // Success …
  } else {   // Failure …
  }
} 
```

**Listing 28.34**     Very simple example of how to check the success of an operation.

Here we are only interested in success or failure, which is why <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> can be easily converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter">if(!ec)</samp>.
