This behavior is derived from checking the return value of a function to see if an error occurred—unfortunately, this varies with each function, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">FILE *f=fopen("f.txt", "r"); if(f==NULL)…</samp>.

You can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> to get more information in case of an error: Do you lack permission, does the filename already exist, is the pathname too long, does the parent directory not exist? And so on. In any case, <samp class="listingcharacter">ec</samp> contains a system-specific value for this—similar to the <samp class="listingcharacter">errno</samp> variable in traditional code (but only in case of an error).

Suppose you were more interested in whether a file or directory with the name already exists. Then you could determine this with <samp class="listingcharacter">if(ec.value() == EEXIST)</samp>—but that would be the wrong way! It would work on a POSIX platform, but on Windows, you would have to compare <samp class="listingcharacter">if(ec.value() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS)</samp>.

As a rule of thumb: If you call <samp class="listingcharacter">value()</samp>, you are probably doing something wrong.

But how do you instead test the system-specific error code (<samp class="listingcharacter">EEXIST</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS</samp>) against the “already exists” event? This is done using the <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>.

You can directly compare the returned <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code ec</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> with instances of <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>. In this case, the comparison is not for exact identity but for equivalence—meaning that it “means the same.”

Therefore, in C++, you must compare the <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code ec</samp> with an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> object that represents “already exists“—namely, <samp class="listingcharacter">errc::file_exists</samp>. For the moment, consider <samp class="listingcharacter">errc::file_exists</samp> (and all other elements of the <samp class="listingcharacter">enum class errc</samp>) as placeholders for a constant of type <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>. The exact mechanism will become clear as we proceed.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/TPWc5nexq
#include <system_error> // error_code, errc
#include <string>
void create_dir(const std::string& pathname, std::error_code& ec);
void run() {
  std::error_code ec;
  create_dir("/some/path", ec);
  if(ec == std::errc::file_exists) {   // specifically …
  } else if(!ec) {                     // Success …
  } else {                             // Failure …
  }
} 
```

**Listing 28.35**     Comparison of “error_code” with “error_condition”.

To enable the comparison, the <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp> free functions are overloaded.

```
bool operator==
 (const error_code&      lhs, const error_code&      rhs) noexcept;
…(const error_code&      lhs, const error_condition& rhs) noexcept;
…(const error_condition& lhs, const error_code&      rhs) noexcept;
…(const error_condition& lhs, const error_condition& rhs) noexcept; 
```

**Listing 28.36**     Overloads of “operator==()” (abbreviated).

These indirectly ensure that both <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code EEXIST</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS</samp> can be compared as equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition errc::file_exists</samp>.

The implementation is responsible for mapping system-specific <samp class="listingcharacter">error_codes</samp> to general <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> error categories.

#### Enumerators as Constants for Classes

The enum class <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp> is defined as in the following listing.

```
enum class errc {
  address_family_not_supported,
  address_in_use,
  // ...
  value_too_large,
  wrong_protocol_type,
}; 
```

**Listing 28.37**     Definition of “enum class errc<samp class="listingcharacter">”.</samp>

It seems that an implicit conversion of the <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp> element to an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> instance occurs when we then apply the comparison <samp class="listingcharacter">ec == errc::file_exists</samp>. Almost, but not quite: for the entire system to be extensible, the <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">ec</samp> must somehow be taken into account. Because there are overlaps in error values, <samp class="listingcharacter">66</samp> can mean one thing in file operations but something entirely different in memory operations. This is resolved through the <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp> mechanism. In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp> here represents a set of constants for <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>. But the library also supports the reverse way—that is, comparing an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> element representing an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> with an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> instance.

Therefore, two steps are necessary for the equivalence check:

1.  Decide whether <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp> represents an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> for specific error codes or generic error conditions.

2.  Associate the value with an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp>.

For step 1, the <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_code_enum</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_condition_enum</samp> type traits are used. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_code_enum<E>::value</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_condition_enum<E>::value</samp> yield the value <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. The standard library now specializes <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_condition_enum</samp> and thus defines <samp class="listingcharacter">is_error_condition_enum<errc>::value == true</samp>.

```
template <>
struct is_error_condition_enum<errc> : true_type {}; 
```

**Listing 28.38**     Specialization of “is_error_condition_enum” for “errc”.

The implicit conversion can then take place through the templatization of the constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>—that is, through <samp class="listingcharacter">template <class E> error_condition(E e)</samp>.[[ 79 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_08) When we then write <samp class="listingcharacter">ec == errc::file_exists</samp>, the compiler chooses the <samp class="listingcharacter">bool operator==(const error_code& a, const error_condition& b)</samp> overload, because the constructor provides a way to convert the <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> into an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>. This makes it easy for us to test a given <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp> against a specific <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>—even if it is only represented by an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> element.

#### Paths to the Error Category

Now follows step 2\. The appropriate <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp> was created by the conversion with a constructor. The free function <samp class="listingcharacter">make_error_condition()</samp> is called in it. This is also overloaded with <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp>:

```
error_condition make_error_condition(errc c) noexcept {
  return error_condition(
      static_cast<int>(e),
      generic_category());
}
error_condition make_error_condition(io_errc c) noexcept /*...*/
error_condition make_error_condition(future_errc c) noexcept /*...*/ 
```

**Listing 28.39**     Among the overloads of “make_error_condition” is also one with “errc”.

The other two are <samp class="listingcharacter">io_errc</samp> (see <samp class="listingcharacter">ios_base::failure</samp>) and <samp class="listingcharacter">future_errc</samp> (see <samp class="listingcharacter">future_error</samp>).

Here the connection with the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp> is established. <samp class="listingcharacter">generic_category()</samp> returns a reference to such an instance and could, for example, be implemented as a singleton.

For end users, the <samp class="listingcharacter">make_error_code()</samp> function family can also be interesting—for example, if you are writing portable code and need to use system-specific error codes.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/n4v78WWod
#include <system_error>
#include <string>

void create_dir(const std::string& pathname, std::error_code& ec) {
#if defined(_WIN32)
  // Windows implementation, with Windows error codes
#elif defined(linux)
  // Linux implementation, with Linux error codes
#else
  // general 'generic' case
  ec = std::make_error_code(std::errc::not_supported);
#endif
} 
```

**Listing 28.40**     Generating system-specific error codes in a portable program.

### 28.5.4    Error Categories

There are two main error categories:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">generic_category</samp> POSIX-compatible error messages, either used on such a system or on other systems by functions that emulate POSIX functionality, like <samp class="listingcharacter">fopen</samp> on Windows.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">system_category</samp> Room for extensions beyond POSIX or on other systems for a custom range. For example, on Windows, this includes the <samp class="listingcharacter">GetLastError()</samp> errors.

### 28.5.5    Custom Error Codes

If you do not want to misuse the standard library error codes in your project, it is recommended to proceed as follows:

*   Define an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> with your own error codes.

*   Then use <samp class="listingcharacter">make_error_code</samp> in your library with these error codes as parameters.

*   Create an overload of <samp class="listingcharacter">make_error_category</samp> for your error code <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> and map your error codes to portable <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp> elements there.

*   Specialize the template <samp class="listingcharacter">std::is_error_condition_enum<></samp> with the content <samp class="listingcharacter">true_type</samp> so that the standard library knows that you support <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp>.

The last step, mapping to <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>, is optional if you do not need the coarse granularity in the consuming code:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/11Tdr6aG1
#include <system_error>
#include <iostream>
using std::error_code; using std::system_category;
namespace mylib {
    // custom error codes
    enum class errc { LOAD_ERR = 1, UNLOAD_ERR = 2, OTHER_ERR = 3 };
    error_code make_error_code(errc ec) {
        switch(ec) {
        case errc::LOAD_ERR: return error_code((int)ec, system_category());
        case errc::UNLOAD_ERR: return error_code((int)ec, system_category());
        case errc::OTHER_ERR: return error_code((int)ec, system_category());
        }
    }
    error_code run(int arg) {
        if(arg == 667) {
            return make_error_code(errc::OTHER_ERR);
        }
        return error_code{}; // all good.
    }
}
int main() {
    std::error_code ec = mylib::run(667);
    if(!ec) {
        std::cout << "Great, it works!\n";
    } else if (ec == mylib::make_error_code(mylib::errc::OTHER_ERR)) {
        std::cout << "Another error\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "Nothing happening here\n" << ec;
    }
} 
```

Similarly, proceed to support the portable <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp> as well.

### 28.5.6    “system_error” Exception

Library functions that prefer to propagate their errors as exceptions use the large aggregate exception class <samp class="listingcharacter">system_error</samp> from the header of the same name. This class again transports

*   an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_code</samp>, consisting of an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> detail and an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_category</samp>; and

*   an error message.

This single exception can then be caught and examined in more detail. This is the alternative to many exception classes in a more or less arbitrary hierarchy—which may also differ on different systems and implementations.

For example, library code might look like this, attempting to join a thread:

```
int osSpecificCode = pthread_detach(thread, 0);
if (osSpecificCode != 0)
  throw system_error(
      error_code(osSpecificCode, system_category()),
      "thread::detach failed"); 
```

You would handle this in user code like this:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/a8zP84j1x
#include <thread>
#include <iostream>
#include <system_error>
int main() {
    try {
        std::thread().detach(); // this will fail
    } catch(std::system_error& e) {
        std::cout
            << "system_error with code:" << e.code()
            << " message:" << e.what()
            << '\n';
    }
} 
```

For me, this outputs the following:

```
system_error with code:generic:22 message:Invalid argument 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter">code</samp> contains the <samp class="listingcharacter">osSpecificCode</samp>.

In the standard library, there are already many places where a <samp class="listingcharacter">system_error</samp> can be thrown. You can handle them like this:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/cjh93oPcr
#include <iostream>
#include <system_error> // std::make_error_condition, std::ios_errc
int main () {
  // switch to exceptions:
  std::cin.exceptions (std::ios::failbit|std::ios::badbit);
  try {
    std::cin.rdbuf(nullptr);        // triggers an exception
  } catch (std::ios::failure& e) {  // derived from system_error
    std::cerr << "Error: ";
    if (e.code() == std::make_error_condition(std::io_errc::stream)) {
      std::cerr << "stream\n";
    } else {
      std::cerr << "other\n";
    }
  }
} 
```

So you catch the exception in a <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp> block. By comparing it with an <samp class="listingcharacter">error_condition</samp>, you can then check portable error conditions more precisely.

## 28.6    Runtime Type Information: “<typeinfo>” and “<typeindex>”

The <samp class="listingcharacter"><typeinfo></samp> header actually contains only a few things:

*   Operator <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid()</samp>
    A function-like operator for determining a unique identification

*   Class <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp>
    The return type of <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid()</samp>

*   Exceptions <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_cast</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_typeid</samp>
    The exceptions that occur in the context of dynamic types

This is a little bit of a lie: <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid()</samp> is similar to <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof()</samp> in that it is not a function but an operator, and <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid</samp> is even a keyword. However, you must include the <samp class="listingcharacter"><typeinfo></samp> header before using <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid()</samp>; otherwise it is an error. Therefore, you can think of <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid()</samp> as a function defined in the header.

With this “function,” you can get information about a type that you specify as a parameter, which you can use for comparison purposes or, to a limited extent, for debugging.

The type can either be directly the name of a type or an expression. In the latter case, <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid()</samp> returns information about the type of the expression. However, the expression cannot include calculations like <samp class="listingcharacter">a+b*c</samp> or even method or function calls.

But what information does <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid</samp> return? Well, mainly a <samp class="listingcharacter">const&</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp> instance; let's call it <samp class="listingcharacter">ti</samp>. The following things can be done with <samp class="listingcharacter">ti</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">size_t ti.hash_code()</samp>
    Returns a hash value, for example, to quickly test for inequality.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">const char* ti.name()</samp>
    Returns a textual representation of the type. However, this does not have a standardized format, nor must it be different for all types in a program, nor is it guaranteed that this text will always be the same for a given type. So, it is not very reliable, although informative, and is therefore mainly used for diagnostics.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">type_index(ti)</samp> This important function from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><typeindex></samp> header is the way to check the equality of two types based on their <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp> references.

More important than what works is perhaps what does not work: You cannot create or copy a <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp>, and you should not compare them with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>. It is not guaranteed that two calls <samp class="listingcharacter">ti1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ti2</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid(A)</samp> will return the same <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp>—in fact, even <samp class="listingcharacter">ti1 == ti2</samp> is not guaranteed, although <samp class="listingcharacter">operator==</samp> is overloaded for <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp>.

If you want to find out whether <samp class="listingcharacter">ti1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ti2</samp> represent the same type, do it like this: <samp class="listingcharacter">type_index(ti1) == type_index(ti2)</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">type_index</samp> can also be used as a key for <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> and similar, which is not possible with <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info</samp>. This allows you to build a mechanism with reliable type names, for example.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/d1G9ez4KW
#include <iostream>
#include <typeinfo>
#include <typeindex>
#include <map>
#include <string>
struct Base {
    virtual ~Base() {}
};
struct Derived_One : public Base {};
struct Derived_Two : public Base {};
int main() {
  using std::string; using std::cout; using std::type_index;
  std::map<std::type_index, string> names {
      { type_index(typeid(int)), "int" },
      { type_index(typeid(double)), "double" },
      { type_index(typeid(Base)), "Base" },
      { type_index(typeid(Derived_One)), "Derived_One" },
      { type_index(typeid(Derived_Two)), "Derived_Two" },
      { type_index(typeid(string)), "string" },
      { type_index(typeid(string::const_iterator)), "string" },
  };
  names[type_index(typeid(names))] = "names-map";
  int integer;
  double floating;
  Base base{};
  Base *one = new Derived_One{};
  Base *two = new Derived_Two{};
  // typeid.name() is implementation- and runtime-dependent:
  cout << typeid(integer).name() << '\n';   // On my system: i
  cout << typeid(floating).name() << '\n';  // On my system: d
  cout << typeid(base).name() << '\n';      // On my system: 4Base
  cout << typeid(*one).name() << '\n';      // On my system: 11Derived_One
  cout << typeid(*two).name() << '\n';      // On my system: 11Derived_Two
  cout << typeid(string).name() << '\n';    // For me: Ss
  cout << typeid(string{"World"}.begin()).name() << '\n';
      // For me: N9__gnu_cxx17__normal_iteratorIPcSsEE
  cout << typeid(names).name() << '\n';
      // For me: St3mapISt10type_indexSsSt4lessIS0_ESaISt4pairIKS0_SsEEE
  cout << typeid(666/0).name() << '\n'; // Expression not executed! For me: i
  // type_index makes type_infos comparable:
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(integer))] << '\n';  // Output: int
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(floating))] << '\n'; // Output: double
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(base))] << '\n';     // Output: Base
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(*one))] << '\n';     // Output: Derived_One
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(*two))] << '\n';     // Output: Derived_Two
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(string))] << '\n';   // Output: string
  cout << names[type_index(typeid(names))] << '\n';    // Output: names-map
} 
```

**Listing 28.41**     Use “typeindex” for reliable type information.

The pure call of <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid(…).name()</samp> provides a name, but not a reliable one. For me, it returns <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> simply as <samp class="listingcharacter">"i"</samp>. And for an iterator or a template like <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp>, the output is only limitedly informative.

You counteract this by applying <samp class="listingcharacter">type_index(…)</samp> to the result of <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid</samp>—that is, to the <samp class="listingcharacter">const type_info&</samp>. As you can see in the <samp class="listingcharacter">names</samp> example, you can also populate a <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> with more readable names this way.

Note that you can use both plain types like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">string::const_iterator</samp> as a parameter for <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid</samp>, as well as an expression like <samp class="listingcharacter">integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*one</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">string{"World"}.begin()</samp>. The expression is not executed; only its type is considered. <samp class="listingcharacter">typeinfo(666/0)</samp> would otherwise cause the program to crash.

Finally, compare the results of <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid(*one)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid(*two)</samp>. These are polymorphic objects, as both are statically of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Base</samp>. Dynamically—at runtime—the objects actually have the <samp class="listingcharacter">Derived_One</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Derived_Two</samp> types. With <samp class="listingcharacter">typeinfo</samp>, you can obtain dynamic type information. Note that this is a slightly different use of the <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid</samp> operator, where it is again necessary for the compiler to execute the expression. Because <samp class="listingcharacter">Base</samp> contains a virtual method, the compiler recognizes that you need dynamic type information and must therefore execute the expression.

My approach of writing all desired types beforehand into a <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> like <samp class="listingcharacter">names</samp> is not always feasible in practice. You might not know in advance what types you will encounter. Then you have only two options:

*   You have to make do with <samp class="listingcharacter">type_info::name()</samp>, even if it is not portable.

*   You use <samp class="listingcharacter">demangled_name</samp> from Boost.

The Boost library provides <samp class="listingcharacter">boost::core::demangled_name(…)</samp>, which returns well-readable type information. Use not <samp class="listingcharacter">typeid</samp> but the <samp class="listingcharacter">BOOST_CORE_TYPEID</samp> macro to get the argument for the function. Although Boost cannot guarantee 100% that this name is readable or stable, the library is so well maintained that it is effectively so.

The outputs for templates will never be pretty, but at least they are readable.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/n54566cqT
#include <iostream>
#include <typeinfo>
#include <string>
#include <map>
#include <boost/core/typeinfo.hpp>
int main() {
  using std::string; using std::cout;
  std::map<int, string> names;
  int i;
  double f;
  // demangled_name
  using boost::core::demangled_name;
  cout<<demangled_name(BOOST_CORE_TYPEID(i))<<'\n';      // Output: int
  cout<<demangled_name(BOOST_CORE_TYPEID(f))<<'\n';      // Output: double
  cout<<demangled_name(BOOST_CORE_TYPEID(string))<<'\n'; // Output: std::string
  cout<<demangled_name(BOOST_CORE_TYPEID(string{}.begin()))<<'\n';
  // Output: __gnu_cxx::__normal_iterator<char*, std::string>
  cout<<demangled_name(BOOST_CORE_TYPEID(namen))<<'\n';
  // Output: std::map<int, std::string, std::less<int>,
  //                                                         std::allocator<std::pair<int const, std::string> > >
  cout<<demangled_name(BOOST_CORE_TYPEID(666/0))<<'\n';  // Output: int
} 
```

**Listing 28.42**     Boost's “demangled_name” is extremely useful for outputting type names.

## 28.7    Helper Classes around Functors: “<functional>”

Even more than <samp class="listingcharacter"><numeric></samp>, the functions in <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp> are there to complement other parts of the standard library. You will rarely include <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp> alone. And if you want to solve a “simple” task with <samp class="listingcharacter"><algorithm></samp> or a container, it's worth taking a look at <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp>, where there might already be a solution for it.

If you want to sum up all elements of a container, for example, use <samp class="listingcharacter">accumulate</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><numeric></samp>. But if you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, you can

*   either write a lambda <samp class="listingcharacter">[](auto a, auto b) { return a*b; }</samp>;

*   or use <samp class="listingcharacter">multiplies</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp>, which does exactly that.

And so it is with many things from <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp>.

I categorize the things offered in <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp> (more or less arbitrarily) into the following areas:

*   Function factories
    <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> is the central point for everything callable in C++. <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp> creates a new function object with one less argument from a function object and an argument. <samp class="listingcharacter">mem_fn</samp> creates a function object from a method. There are several auxiliary constructs in this context.

*   Concrete function objects
    For arithmetic (like <samp class="listingcharacter">multiplies</samp>), comparisons (like <samp class="listingcharacter">equal_to</samp>), logical (<samp class="listingcharacter">logical_and</samp>, etc.), and bitwise (<samp class="listingcharacter">bit_and</samp>, etc.) operations, which you can use instead of a simple lambda.

*   Specialized hash functions
    The <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp> function objects needed for the unordered containers are defined here for the built-in types. So, for example, you will find the template specialization <samp class="listingcharacter">hash<int></samp> and all its relatives. That should be self-explanatory, so I will not go into further detail here.

### 28.7.1    Function Objects

In [Chapter 25](#25_001.html_h25), [Listing 25.15](#25_007.html_l25.15), there’s an example of <samp class="listingcharacter">multiplies</samp> together with <samp class="listingcharacter">accumulate</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><numeric></samp>. The other defined function objects can be found in [Table 28.11](#28_007.html_t28.11) to [Table 28.14](#28_007.html_t28.14).

| Functor | Behavior | Functor | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">plus</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a + b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">divides</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a / b</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">minus</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a - b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">modulus</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a % b</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">multiplies</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a * b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">negate</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">-a</samp> |

**Table 28.11**     Function objects of arithmetic operators.

| Functor | Behavior | Functor | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">equal_to</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a == b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a < b</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">not_equal_to</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a != b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">greater_equal</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a >= b</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">greater</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a > b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">less_equal</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a <= b</samp> |

**Table 28.12**     Function objects for comparison operators.

| Functor | Behavior | Functor | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">logical_and</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a && b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">logical_not</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">!b</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">logical_or</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a &#124;&#124; b</samp> |  |  |

**Table 28.13**     Function objects for logical operators.

| Functor | Behavior | Functor | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">bit_and</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a & b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">bit_xor</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ b</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">bit_or</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a &#124; b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">bit_not</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">~b</samp> |

**Table 28.14**     Function objects for bitwise operators.

You can use the function objects to equip containers and algorithms with your own functionality.

For example, in the definition of <samp class="listingcharacter">std::set</samp>, you will see that <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp> is used here for a comparison operation:

```
namespace std {
  template<class Key, class Compare=less<Key>, class Allocator=allocator<Key>>
    class set;
    // ... 
```

So instead of overloading <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp> for your own data type, you can also specialize the <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp> template for your data type, similar to what you would do for <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp> in the context of <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered_set</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Y3GsPd97d
#include <set>
#include <string>
struct Dragon {
    std::string name_;
};
namespace std {
    template<> struct less<Dragon> { // Template specialization
        bool operator()(const Dragon &lhs, const Dragon &rhs) const {
            return lhs.name_ < rhs.name_;
} }; }
int main() {
  std::set<Dragon> dragons {
    Dragon{"Smaug"},    Dragon{"Glaurung"},
    Dragon{"Ancalagon"},Dragon{"Scatha"}};
} 
```

So if for any reason it is not possible or desired to overload <samp class="listingcharacter">operator<</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">Dragon</samp>, and you also do not want to specify the template parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">Compare</samp>, you can achieve the same with a specialization of <samp class="listingcharacter">less</samp>.

In [Listing 28.43](#28_007.html_l28.43), you see a version of the calculator from [Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8), [Listing 8.18](#08_010.html_l8.18) that uses <samp class="listingcharacter"><functional></samp> from start to finish. Instead of a large <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement, this time all possible characters are stored as keys in <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp>s. Depending on how the stack should be manipulated, the operations end up in one of four <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp>s:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">binOps</samp> Remove two elements from the stack, apply the function to them, and store the result back on the stack. Addition is an example of this.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">unOps</samp> Remove one element from the stack, apply the function to it, and store the result back on the stack. This calculator does not have such an operation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">zeroOps</samp> Execute a zero-argument function and store the result on the stack. The digits do exactly this.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">stackOps</samp> Instead of manipulating the stack before and after, the calculator leaves the entire stack to these functions—for example, to clear or print it.

Of course, not everything can be represented with predefined functors, which is why you will see lambdas in use where necessary—and with <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp>, even a lambda that returns a lambda. It’s often said that this makes “lambdas as first-class citizens”, which means that they are in most ways values like variables of built-in types or classes and thus can be created, passed as parameters, and even put into containers.

This type of calculator is not generally “better” than using the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement. However, when it comes to extensibility, this option is the more skillful choice.

There are a few things I would definitely improve “in the real world”:

*   Instead of using <samp class="listingcharacter">std::cout</samp> as a global variable, the operators should be parameterized on <samp class="listingcharacter">ostream&</samp>.

*   The various <samp class="listingcharacter">find</samp> calls should only be executed when necessary.

*   Processing individual digits is illustrative but impractical. Sequences of digits should be whole numbers, with the space as the delimiter.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/jxvhded75
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <functional>
std::map<char,std::function<int(int,int)>> binOps { // binary operators
    {'+', std::plus<int>{} },
    {'-', std::minus<int>{} },
    {'*', std::multiplies<int>{} },
    {'/', std::divides<int>{} },
    {'%', std::modulus<int>{} },
    };
std::map<char,std::function<int(int)>> unOps { };    // unary operators
auto val = [](auto n) { return [n](){ return n; };}; // returns a lambda
std::map<char,std::function<int()>> zeroOps {        // nullary operators
  {'0', val(0)}, {'1', val(1)}, {'2', val(2)}, {'3', val(3)}, {'4', val(4)},
  {'5', val(5)}, {'6', val(6)}, {'7', val(7)}, {'8', val(8)}, {'9', val(9)},
  };
std::map<char,std::function<void(std::vector<int>&)>> stackOps {
  { ' ', [](auto &stack) { } },           // no operation
  { 'c', [](auto &stack) { stack.clear(); } }, // Clear the entire stack
  { ':', [](auto &stack) {                // swap the top two elements
            auto top = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            auto second = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            stack.push_back(top);
            stack.push_back(second);
  } },
  { '=', [](auto &stack) {                // print the entire stack
            for(int elem : stack) { std::cout << elem; }
            std::cout << "\n";
  } },
};
void calculator(std::string input) {
  std::vector<int> stack {};
  for(char c : input) {
    int top, second;
    if(auto it = unOps.find(c); it != unOps.end()) {
      // if unary operator …
      auto func = it->second;
      top = stack.back(); stack.pop_back(); // … get top element
      stack.push_back(func(top));           // … apply func, push result onto stack
    } else if(auto it = binOps.find(c); it != binOps.end()) {
      // if binary operator …
      auto func = it->second;
      top = stack.back(); stack.pop_back(); // … get the top 2 elements
      second = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
      stack.push_back(func(second, top)); // … apply func, push result onto stack
    } else if(auto it = zeroOps.find(c); it !=zeroOps.end()) {
      // if nullary operator …
      auto func = it->second;
      stack.push_back(func());               // ... result of func on stack
    } else if(auto it = stackOps.find(c); it != stackOps.end()) {
      // if stack operator
      auto func = it->second;
      func(stack);                           // ... apply func to stack
    } else {
      std::cout << "\n'" << c << "' I don't understand.\n";
    }
  } /* for c */
}
int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
    if(argc > 1) {
        calculator(argv[1]);
    } else {
        // 3+4*5+6 with multiplication before addition results in 29
        calculator("345*+6+=");
    }
    calculator("93-=");                      // 9 - 3 = Output: 6
    calculator("82/=");                      // 8 / 2 = Output: 4
    calculator("92%=");                      // 9 % 2 = Output: 1
} 
```

**Listing 28.43**     This calculator maps keys to functors.

### 28.7.2    Function Generators

You have seen <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> used extensively in [Listing 28.43](#28_007.html_l28.43). It is simply the type of all callable objects in C++—almost. In fact, <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> is just something that can implicitly convert to a C function pointer and has various initialization options. It thus acts as a bridge between all callable objects and C function pointers. You have already read quite a bit about this in [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7).

Otherwise, there are a handful of helper functions in the vicinity of <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp>, such as binding parameters.

#### Predefining Parameters with “bind”

If you have a function with two parameters and the first one is already fixed, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp> to make it a function with one parameter:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/e6xT638ch
#include <functional> // subtract, minus, bind
#include <iostream>
using std::cout;
int subtract(int a, int b) { return a - b; }
int main() {
    using namespace std::placeholders;
    cout << subtract(9, 3) << '\n'  ;  // Output: 6
    auto minus3 = std::bind(subtract, _1, 3);
    cout << minus3(9) << '\n';         // Output: 6
    auto from9 = std::bind(subtract, 9, _1);
    cout << from9(3) << '\n';          // Output: 6
    auto againMinus3 = std::bind(std::minus<int>{}, _1, 3);
    cout << againMinus3(9) << '\n';    // Output: 6
} 
```

Here, the strange <samp class="listingcharacter">_1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">_2</samp>, and so on placeholders are important. They are defined in <samp class="listingcharacter">namespace std::placeholders</samp> and are intended to gather the arguments for the function. You insert such a placeholder where you do not yet know the value of the argument now because it will only be determined later at the call. If you create a function with one argument like <samp class="listingcharacter">minus3</samp>, you need to specify <samp class="listingcharacter">_1</samp>. A function with two parameters needs <samp class="listingcharacter">_1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">_2</samp>.

If you create a function that does not require any parameters, then no placeholder is needed. A typical example is random generators, as in the <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp> variant in [Listing 28.44](#28_007.html_l28.44).

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/j7sa9rexh
#include <random>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <functional>
void rollDice() {
  std::default_random_engine engine{};
  std::vector<size_t> counts{0,0,0,0,0,0};
  std::uniform_int_distribution<int> d6{0, 5}; // uniformly distributed integers
  auto d = std::bind(d6, engine);              // d() = d6(engine)
  for(auto i=1200*1000; i>0; --i) ++counts[d()];
  for(auto c : counts) std::cout<<" "<<c;
  std::cout << '\n';
}
int main() {
    rollDice();
} 
```

**Listing 28.44**     With “bind”, you can also set all parameters of a function.

##### Lambda, “bind”, “bind_front”, and “bind_back”

Starting from C++20, there is the <samp class="listingcharacter">bind_front</samp> function and from C++23 also <samp class="listingcharacter">bind_back</samp>. These make writing some generic functions even easier.

The syntax of <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">bind_back</samp> is somewhat confusing for some. A lambda is often easier to read:

```
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }          // given this function
auto add_to_9_lambda = [](auto x) { return add(9, x); };  // as a lambda
auto add_to_9_bind = bind(add, 9, _1);                    // with bind
cout << add_to_9_lambda(3) << '\n';                       // Output: 12
cout << add_to_9_bind(3) << '\n';                         // Output: 12

auto add_to_3_bind_back = bind_back(add, _1, 3);        // with bind_back
auto add_to_3_lambda = [](auto x) { return add(x, 3); };  // as a lambda
cout << add_to_3_lambda(9) << '\n';                       // Output: 12
cout << add_to_3_bind_back(9) << '\n';                    // Output: 12 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">add_to_9_lambda</samp> function does the same thing as <samp class="listingcharacter">add_to_9_bind</samp>. They bind a fixed value to the first parameter of the <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> function. What remains is a function with one parameter, which you can then call later in the program, as is done here with <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp>.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">add_to_3_bind_back</samp> function does the same thing as <samp class="listingcharacter">add_to_3_lambda</samp>. But they bind to the second parameter of the <samp class="listingcharacter">add</samp> function.

In generic programming, lambdas have difficulties with <samp class="listingcharacter">noexcept</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">forward</samp>. For these cases, you can resort to <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">bind_front</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">bind_back</samp>.

#### Member Access with “mem_fn”

With <samp class="listingcharacter">mem_fn</samp>, you turn a method or a data member into a function. You then no longer use the following syntax:

```
instance.method(arg);
instance.data; 
```

Instead, you write this:

```
method(instance, arg);
data(instance); 
```

The following listing shows a more detailed example in which the <samp class="listingcharacter">numbers</samp> class instance is made a parameter of the generated function object.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/GMjcjrvaT
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
struct Numbers {
    int theNumber() {
        return 42;
    }
    int more(int n) {
        return n + data;
    }
    int data = 7;
};
int main() {
    auto func = std::mem_fn(&Numbers::theNumber);
    auto func2 = std::mem_fn(&Numbers::more);
    auto access = std::mem_fn(&Numbers::data);
    Numbers numbers;
    std::cout << func(numbers) << '\n';        // Output: 42
    std::cout << func2(numbers, 66) << '\n';   // Output: 73
    std::cout << access(numbers) << '\n';      // Output: 7
} 
```

**Listing 28.45**     This is how you turn class members into free functions.

Most of the time, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">mem_fn</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp>, but the magic of turning a data member into a function cannot be done directly by <samp class="listingcharacter">bind</samp>. And the same applies here: lambdas are possibly more expressive and easier to read.

## 28.8    “optional” for a Single Value or No Value

In C++, <samp class="listingcharacter">optional<T></samp> has a slightly different meaning than in Java. There, the “generic” <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T></samp> is part of the streaming API and thus represents a “container of size one or zero.” It is recommended not to use it as a parameter for optional values there.

This is different in C++: First, it is not a container that works with algorithms. Second, <samp class="listingcharacter">optional<T></samp> is specifically designed to indicate, as a parameter and return value or in containers, that a value may or may not be present.

The documentation states the intended use: “It is recommended to use <samp class="listingcharacter">optional<T></samp> in situations where there is exactly one clear reason not to have a value of type <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp>, and where the absence of the value seems as natural as assuming a regular value.” Less formally and shorter, but also less precise: Where you are tempted to use a <samp class="listingcharacter">nullptr</samp> to indicate the absence of a value, you should use <samp class="listingcharacter">optional<T></samp>.

The uses of an <samp class="listingcharacter">optional<T> opt</samp> are as follows:

*   You create it via constructor, either empty or with a regular value, the special value <samp class="listingcharacter">nullopt</samp>, or you use <samp class="listingcharacter">make_optional</samp>.

*   You use the implicit conversion to a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> to check if a value is present, so <samp class="listingcharacter">if(opt)</samp>, or you use <samp class="listingcharacter">has_value()</samp>.

*   You access the value via <samp class="listingcharacter">value()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">value_or(fallback)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*opt</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">opt-></samp>.

*   Replace the old value via assignment, <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp>, or delete it with <samp class="listingcharacter">reset()</samp>.

*   Compare with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, and so on. It is possible to compare with the empty value.

*   Chain from C++23 with <samp class="listingcharacter">transform</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">and_then</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">or_else</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter">optional</samp> is not well-suited for storing <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp>s and pointers. For a three-valued Boolean type, it is better to use <samp class="listingcharacter">boost::tribool</samp>, and pointers already have a nonvalue with <samp class="listingcharacter">nullptr</samp>.

## 28.9    “variant” for One of Several Types

With this template, you can model something similar to a <samp class="listingcharacter">union</samp>, but in a safer form.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">union</samp> has the problem in safe programming that constructors or destructors of the contained objects are not reliably called.

A <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp> can take the value of one of several types. Setting a value of one type changes the state of <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp>, so attempting to read another type from it then fails. Thus, its usage is safe.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/baY7Tz91f
#include <variant>
using std::get;
int main() {
    std::variant<int, float> v{};
    v = 12;                   // State changes to int
    auto i = get<int>(v);     // retrieves the int
    std::cout << i << '\n';   // Output: 12
    v = 3.456f;               // State changes to float
    std::cout << get<float>(v) << '\n';  // Output: 3.456
    get<double>(v);           // Error
    get<3>(v);                // Error
    std::variant<int, float> w{};
    w = get<float>(v);        // Access by type
    w = get<1>(v);            // Access is also possible via index
    w = v;                    // entire assignment is also possible
    try {
        get<int>(w);          // triggers exception
    } catch (std::bad_variant_access&) { /* ... */ }
} 
```

**Listing 28.46**     Basic functionalities of “variant”.

Here I declare <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> as a <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp> that can contain either a value of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or one of type <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>. Then I assign <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp> an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, which I then read and output with <samp class="listingcharacter">get<int></samp>. This is followed by another assignment with a value, but this time a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>. I also read and output this one. <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> has thus contained first an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and then a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> in succession.

You cannot request a type with <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp> that <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp> does not know. <samp class="listingcharacter">get<double></samp> does not compile.

At runtime, you will get an error if you query a valid type that <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp> does not currently contain. You will receive the <samp class="listingcharacter">bad_variant_access</samp> exception.

Without an exception, you check the state with <samp class="listingcharacter">holds_alternative<int>(w)</samp>. Here you get a <samp class="listingcharacter">bool</samp> indicating whether <samp class="listingcharacter">w</samp> currently holds an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or not.

If you want to react to the content of <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp>, you can query which one is current with <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp>. However, it is more elegant to use <samp class="listingcharacter">visit</samp>, to which you pass a visitor that can handle the different types.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/G4z8Y5E6P
#include <variant>
#include <iostream>
using std::cout;
struct TypeGreeting {
  void operator()(int) const { cout << "Hello int"; }
  void operator()(float) const { cout << "Hello float"; }
};
int main() {
    std::variant<int, float> var{};
    var = 12;                                   // State int
    std::visit([](auto a) { cout << a; }, var); // generic lambda
    cout << std::endl;
    var = 3.456f;                               // State float
    std::visit(TypeGreeting{}, var);            // Functor with overloads
    cout << std::endl;
} 
```

**Listing 28.47**     Inspecting a “variant” using a visitor.

In the first <samp class="listingcharacter">visit</samp>, the lambda is generic and accepts any parameter that can be output to a stream.

The second use of <samp class="listingcharacter">visit</samp> takes a functor as a parameter, which has specific overloads for both possible types. The <samp class="listingcharacter">operator()</samp> methods for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> could contain entirely different implementations.

## 28.10    “any” Holds Any Type

If you are dissatisfied with having to specify the possible types when declaring <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp>, then perhaps <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> is for you. You can store a value of any type in it. And you can only retrieve that type. If you try with a different type, you will get an exception. However, you can assign <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> a new value and also a new type:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/1eco9Wcr3
#include <any>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
int main() {
    std::any a = 5;
    std::cout << std::any_cast<int>(a) << '\n';
    a = 3.456;
    std::cout << std::any_cast<double>(a) << '\n';
    using namespace std::literals;
    std::vector<std::any> data { 4, 8.976, "Geronimo"s };
    std::cout << std::any_cast<double>( data[1] ) << '\n';
    std::cout << data[1].type().name()  << '\n';
} 
```

You see how I first assign an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and then a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. Instead of using <samp class="listingcharacter">get</samp>, you retrieve the value here with <samp class="listingcharacter">any_cast</samp>, which is a slightly different mechanism. However, if you ask for the wrong type, you will get an exception.

You can also pack <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> into containers. The three <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> elements in <samp class="listingcharacter">data</samp> have different types after initialization. For information, you can also access the currently stored type with <samp class="listingcharacter">type()</samp>. However, this is more for debugging and is not portable information.

Note the following points:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> is not a template class.

*   You create <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> via constructor with or without value or <samp class="listingcharacter">make_any</samp>.

*   You check if an <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> is empty with <samp class="listingcharacter">has_value()</samp>.

*   You change the value with an assignment, <samp class="listingcharacter">emplace</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">reset</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">swap</samp>.

*   You retrieve the value type-safely with <samp class="listingcharacter">any_cast<T></samp>.

*   There is no exception-free check to see if an <samp class="listingcharacter">any</samp> currently contains a specific type. If you need that, consider <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp>.

## 28.11    Special Mathematical Functions

The mathematicians and physicists among you will be pleased that the standard library already includes some (really) very special mathematical functions, so you don't need to use a third-party library. Most of the functions operate on <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp>. Sometimes there are multiple name variants; I only mention one. The functions are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter"><cmath></samp> header.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">laguerre</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">assoc_laguerre</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">legendre</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">assoc_legendre</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">hermite</samp>
    Calculates (associated) Laguerre polynomials, (associated) Legendre polynomials (spherical functions), and Hermite polynomials.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">beta</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">expint</samp>
    Calculates the Euler beta function and the exponential integral function.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">comp_ellint_1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">comp_ellint_2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">comp_ellint_3</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ellint_1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ellint_2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ellint_3</samp>
    Calculates the complete or incomplete elliptic integral of the first, second, and third kind.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">cyl_bessel_i</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cyl_bessel_j</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cyl_bessel_k</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sph_bessel</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sph_legendre</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sph_neumann</samp>
    Regular, nonregular, and irregularly modified cylindrical Bessel functions as well as the spherical Bessel function, Legendre function, and Neumann function.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">cyl_neumann</samp> Cylindrical Neumann function, also called the Bessel function of the second kind.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">riemann_zeta</samp> Calculates the Riemann-ζ function, which you might need in connection with prime numbers.

### [Übung]  C++20: Mathematical Constants

Starting with C++20, you have access to the most interesting mathematical constants. In the <samp class="listingcharacter"><numbers></samp> header, the following <samp class="listingcharacter">inline constexpr double</samp> are defined in the <samp class="listingcharacter">std::numbers</samp> namespace: <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">log2e</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">log10e</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">pi</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">inv_pi</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">inv_sqrtpi</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ln2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ln10</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt3</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">inv_sqrt3</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">egamma</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">phi</samp>.

If you want the <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long double</samp> value of one of these constants, append the <samp class="listingcharacter">_v</samp> suffix to the name for a template—for example:

<samp class="listingcharacter">pi_v<long double></samp>

## 28.12    Fast Conversion with “<charconv>”

There are many ways to convert a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp>) into a number. With C++17, there is another option: <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><charconv></samp> header. The main focus of <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> is on performance, as it becomes increasingly important with the growing number of XML and JSON applications.

<samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> comes with the conversion function <samp class="listingcharacter">to_chars</samp> for converting numbers to strings.

<samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> shows its strengths when you have a <samp class="listingcharacter">char*</samp>, already know that you need to parse a number, and have nothing to do with locales (different decimal and thousand separators) and encodings (UTF-16, etc.).

The existing ways to convert a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or the like include the following:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">sscanf</samp>
    From C; flexible, related to <samp class="listingcharacter">printf</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">atol, atoi, atoll, atof</samp>
    From C; no way to determine the end or success of parsing.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">strtol, strtof, strtod, strtold, strtoll, strtoull</samp>
    Good candidate; error checking is okay, but lacks overflow and underflow checking.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp>
    C++; flexible, but slow, also lacks overflow and underflow checking.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">stol, stoi, stoll, stoull, stof, stod, stold</samp>
    C++11; lacks flexible start position, error handling via exception.

And since C++17 in the assortment:

```
from_chars_result
  from_chars(const char* first, const char* last, T& value, int base = 10); 
```

The type <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> can be any integer or floating-point type. The result is read into the <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> output parameter. Thus, the variable must be declared beforehand.

The return is a <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">const char* ptr</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp> elements. <samp class="listingcharacter">ptr</samp> indicates how much was read and <samp class="listingcharacter">errc</samp> shows any potential error. It’s nice that C++17 also allows structured binding:

```
auto [pbis, errc] = std::from_chars(pbegin, pend, value); 
```

However, <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> does not handle leading whitespaces. These must be skipped beforehand:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/115nE7xsc
#include <charconv>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

std::vector<size_t> num_to_vec(const std::string& nums) {
    std::vector<size_t> result {};
    // without trailing spaces
    const auto end = nums.data() + nums.find_last_not_of( ' ' ) + 1;
    const char* st = nullptr;  // loop pointer
    auto last = nums.data();   // last untranslated character
    size_t n;                  // converted number
    do {
        for(st = last; (st<end)&&(*st==' ' ); ++st); // skip ' '
        if (last = std::from_chars(st, end, n).ptr; last != st)
            result.push_back(n);                     // store number
    } while (last != st);
    return result;
}

void errorDemo(const char* buf, size_t sz) {
    int n;
    auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(buf, buf+sz, n);
    if (ec != std::errc{}) {
       const auto error = std::make_error_code(ec);
       std::cout << error.message() << '\n';
    }
}

int main() {
    auto result = num_to_vec("12 33 43");
    for(auto r : result) std::cout << r << " ";
    std::cout << '\n';
    // Output: 12 33 43
    errorDemo("XYZ", 4);
    // Output: Invalid argument
    errorDemo("123123123123123", 16);
    // Output: Numerical result out of range
} 
```

First, we find the end of the string and ignore any whitespace there. In the loop, we also ignore all whitespace, as <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> would not do that. The result ends up in <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>. In <samp class="listingcharacter">errorDemo</samp>, a conversion error is also handled. In <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp>, we have the position where the conversion stopped.

Experiments show that <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> can be very fast. Depending on requirements and tests, this naturally varies, but one source states: if <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> takes one unit of time, <samp class="listingcharacter">strtoul</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">atoi</samp> take about two, <samp class="listingcharacter">stoul</samp> about four, and <samp class="listingcharacter">stringstream</samp> about six units of time. <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp> was particularly fast in cases only the first number needed to be extracted from a string.[[ 80 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_09) Other experiments are even more in favor of <samp class="listingcharacter">from_chars</samp>.[[ 81 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn28_10)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">to_chars</samp> function works very similarly. It also returns a pointer and error code in a <samp class="listingcharacter">struct</samp> and writes the result to an output parameter:

```
to_chars_result to_chars(char* first, char* last, T value, int base = 10); 
```

Here, structured binding helps again:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/dcqenEd31
#include <iostream>
#include <charconv>
#include <string_view>
#include <array>
int main() {
    std::array<char, 10> str {};
    if(auto [p, ec] = std::to_chars(str.data(), str.data() + str.size(), 42);
       ec == std::errc{} )
        std::cout << std::string_view(str.data(), p - str.data()) << "\n";
} 
```

The result ends up in <samp class="listingcharacter">str</samp>. For this, <samp class="listingcharacter">to_chars</samp> needs the beginning and the end of the range into which it can write.

# 29    Threads: Programming with Concurrency

## [Übung]  Chapter Telegram

*   Thread
    A “strand” of program execution that can run concurrently with other threads.

*   Semaphores
    Mechanism to limit concurrent access to a shared resource. A semaphore exists per shared resource or group of resources.

*   Mutex
    Semaphores that allow access to exactly one thread.

*   Lock
    Group of classes that define the range in which access should be protected using a mutex. A lock exists per thread and resource.

*   Critical section
    Program piece protected from concurrent execution using lock and mutex.

*   Data race
    Condition where multiple threads unpredictably modify data.

*   Deadlock
    Condition when two threads holding locks on mutexes block each other, and neither can proceed.

*   Promise and future
    Model of a communication channel between threads. A promise is the commitment to deliver a result via a future when requested.

*   Memory order
    This specifies the temporal relationship in which read and write operations in different threads on an object must occur.

This chapter introduces you to the parts of the standard library that deal with multithreading. In doing so, I will also explain a few principles around this type of concurrent programming so that you know how to use the classes and functions correctly.

So far, we have considered a program as a sequence of instruction to be executed sequentially. With branches and functions, the computer can jump back and forth, but it has always executed one instruction after another. For some time now, computers have had multiple processing units and thus the ability to work on different parts of a program simultaneously. Your program can work in parallel. These parallel execution threads are called threads.

All running threads share the program's memory. All threads can see all the memory of all other threads—that is, all variables and values. And unfortunately, not only do they see, but they can also write to them if they want. The trick is to do this in an orderly manner so that the data remains consistent.

## Other Forms of Parallelism

There are other forms of parallelism—all that you can imagine. For example, there can be a thread that works on multiple data simultaneously—effectively working on the same memory with the same instructions (SIMD from graphics cards). It is also parallel when a single CPU instruction multiplies eight pairs of numbers simultaneously (MMX, SSE, and AVX). You can also achieve parallelism by running a program distributed across one or more computers and having them communicate with each other (processes, sockets, MPI, and others).

All these forms are not yet covered in the C++ standard and therefore are not part of this book. I limit myself to the execution of a program with one memory with multiple threads.

With C++17, the possibility for SIMD for many algorithms has been added. It is listed under <samp class="listingcharacter">parallel_unsequenced_policy</samp>. You then specify the additional <samp class="listingcharacter">par_unseq</samp> parameter. If you are interested, check what your compiler already supports and what it can do with it.

## 29.1    C++ Threading Basics

You have already started threads, even if you didn't realize it, because in every C++ program, at least the main thread exists. For you, this means that upon entering <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, you are in your first thread, which the system has started for you. When you leave <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, the main thread terminates after some mandatory cleanup.

You achieve multithreading when you start additional threads. Each thread has an entry and exit point, just like <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> for the main thread. Anything callable can define this entry and exit, such as a function, a functor, a lambda, a bound method, a <samp class="listingcharacter">function<></samp> instance—simply anything that can implicitly convert to a function pointer.

In C++, a thread is an instance of type <samp class="listingcharacter">std:thread</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter"><thread></samp> header. With this instance, you can interact a bit, such as waiting for its termination, called joining. If you don't join, but the thread is still running, <samp class="listingcharacter">terminate()</samp> is called, thus ending your program. Alternatively, you can also “detach” the thread by calling <samp class="listingcharacter">detach()</samp>. Then your thread would continue running, but the program is terminated. This is usually not what you want. Therefore, you should always wait for the termination before ending the program.

Hence, since C++20, there is the joining thread with the <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> class. These threads attempt to terminate themselves in the destructor and then wait. Normally, you will use <samp class="listingcharacter">jthreads</samp>. Everything said in this chapter essentially applies to both <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>. If you need to use <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>—for example, because C++20 is not available and <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> is not part of your version of the standard library—then you must not forget to <samp class="listingcharacter">join()</samp> the <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp>. I point out further differences between <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp>. If you still don't want to do without <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>, you can use the library at [https://github.com/josuttis/jthread](https://github.com/josuttis/jthread) by Nico Josuttis, the original author of the <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> class. It is compatible with C++17.

But before you can wait for the termination of a thread, you must of course first start a new <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>.

### 29.1.1    Starting Pure Threads

For this, you need a function object (I will use this term from now on to represent anything that can be started by a thread) and an existing thread that starts the new one. The latter is easy—you have <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/qnadYPWh1
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
using std::cout; using std::endl;

long fib(long n) { return n<=1 ? n : fib(n-1)+fib(n-2); }
void task1() { auto r = fib(40); cout << "fib(40)=" << r << endl; }
void task2() { auto r = fib(41); cout << "fib(41)=" << r << endl; }
void task3() { auto r = fib(42); cout << "fib(42)=" << r << endl; }

struct BackgroundTask {
    void operator()() const {
        task1();
        task2();
        task3();
    }
};

int main() {
    BackgroundTask backgroundTask{}; // Initialization, does not compute anything yet
    std::jthread myThread{ backgroundTask }; // Computation starts
} 
```

**Listing 29.1**     How to start a thread.

You start a thread by creating a <samp class="listingcharacter">std::jthread</samp> object. As a constructor argument, you then pass something callable, here an instance of the <samp class="listingcharacter">BackgroundTask</samp> functor.

Note that the callable object is always copied for the new thread. Therefore, the callable object must be sensibly copyable. If you use <samp class="listingcharacter">backgroundTask</samp> for multiple <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> instances, they do not share the same instance.[[ 82 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn29_01)

It is quite common to create the callable object directly in the constructor call of <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>:

```
std::jthread myThread{ BackgroundTask{} }; // temp-value as constructor argument 
```

Be careful not to write <samp class="listingcharacter">BackgroundTask()</samp> here, as that does not create a temp-value but declares a function. You can completely avoid this problem by writing simple tasks as lambda expressions when you initialize the <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/nPGY47r4K
std::jthread myThread{ [] {
    task1();
    task2();
    task3();
} }; 
```

This means that <samp class="listingcharacter">myThread</samp> starts a new thread that runs in parallel. In that thread, the <samp class="listingcharacter">task1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">task2</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">task3</samp> functions are then executed sequentially.

### 29.1.2    Terminating a Thread Prematurely

It is often the case that you do not want a thread to run until it finishes on its own. For example, perhaps the Cancel button was clicked while the thread is reading a huge file from the disk. It would be undesirable if the thread then continued to read the file to the end, even though the data is no longer needed.

The solution for this is <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_token</samp>, which is already built into <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>. In <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp>, this does not exist yet, so you have to implement it yourself.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_token</samp> is an object that you get from <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> and then use as a communication channel into the thread. In the thread, you should occasionally check whether the outer thread requests premature termination.

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/6cqd7Tsae
struct BackgroundTask {
    void operator()(std::stop_token st) const { // Token for communication
        task1();
        if(st.stop_requested()) return;
        task2();
        if(st.stop_requested()) return;
        task3();
    }
};
int main() {
    BackgroundTask backgroundTask{};
    std::jthread myThread{ backgroundTask };
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100)); // wait 100ms
    myThread.request_stop(); // request the thread to stop
} 
```

**Listing 29.2**     With “stop_token”, the outside world communicates into the thread.

Instead of outputting the result of all three tasks, only the result of the first task is output here.

When a <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> is created, the class always also creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_source</samp>. From this <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_source</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_token</samp> is passed into the called function as a parameter if the method has a parameter of this type. If not, then not. So it is, so to speak, an optional parameter of your actual thread function.

In this case, the thread function received it as <samp class="listingcharacter">st</samp>. In between, we periodically check with <samp class="listingcharacter">st.stop_requested()</samp> to see if someone wants the thread to terminate itself. If that is the case, we stop the work and clean up properly. And that is important! In C++, you cannot simply terminate a thread from the outside using standard means. That would break the RAII concept, because, for example, destructors would no longer be called.

From the outside, you get the <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_source</samp> object with <samp class="listingcharacter">get_stop_source()</samp> and then call <samp class="listingcharacter">request_stop()</samp>. Or you use the shortcut to directly call <samp class="listingcharacter">request_stop()</samp> on the <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp>, as in this example.

It is really convenient with <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> that it can flexibly handle thread functions that have a <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_token</samp> as a parameter, but also those that do not. However, you should note that without such a parameter, you cannot check if the thread should be terminated.

For simplicity, I have mostly omitted <samp class="listingcharacter">stop_token</samp> in this chapter. But you should always include it when writing a thread that runs for more than a few milliseconds.

### 29.1.3    Waiting for a Thread

Normally, you don't want to terminate a thread prematurely but wait until it finishes. Once you have started a thread, you need to do one of the following:

*   Wait until the thread finishes
    You do this by joining the thread. This happens automatically with <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> in the destructor.

*   Let the thread run independently
    You need to detach from the newly started thread.

If you haven't decided before the starting thread ends and use <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp>, your entire program will terminate. Specifically, this means that if the new thread is still running but the destructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> is called, it will invoke <samp class="listingcharacter">std::terminate()</samp>—and thus abruptly end your program:

*   Wait
    <samp class="listingcharacter">myThread.join()</samp>

*   Detach
    <samp class="listingcharacter">myThread.detach()</samp>

So let's use <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">jthread</samp> and make the waiting explicit:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/Tzs93MzfK
std::thread myThread{ [] {  // pure thread
    task1();
    task2();
    task3();
} };
myThread.join();   // waits for the thread to finish 
```

Once again: If the scope of the <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> variable is exited and the thread is still running and you have not detached it with <samp class="listingcharacter">detach()</samp>, your program will basically crash. The call to <samp class="listingcharacter">join()</samp> waits for the thread to finish.

In this simple case, <samp class="listingcharacter">join()</samp> is the only correct solution. Because if the main program terminates otherwise, detached threads will also be terminated. So if you use <samp class="listingcharacter">detach()</samp> here, you will not see any output because <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> will exit shortly after, before the calculations were finished. In another function, however, you can certainly use <samp class="listingcharacter">detach()</samp>, as there are likely many more calculations taking place.

### 29.1.4    Consider Exceptions in the Starting Thread

Note that you also need to consider exceptions: <samp class="listingcharacter">myThread</samp> will also be removed if an exception is thrown somewhere in the calling thread causing your <samp class="listingcharacter">thread</samp> variable to go out of scope. If the started thread is not yet finished, your entire program will be terminated. Thus, an exception that you handle one level too far outside may have significant consequences:

```
// https://godbolt.org/z/E49on6zn3
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <exception>
using std::cout; using std::endl;

long fib(long n) { return n<=1 ? n : fib(n-1)+fib(n-2); }
void task1() { auto r = fib(40); cout << "fib(40)=" << r << endl; }

void main_program() {
    try {
        std::thread th{ &task1 };
        std::vector data{ 0,1,2 };
        data.at(666);                       // triggers out_of_range
        th.join();                          // would wait
    } catch(std::runtime_error &ex) {       // does not match out_of_range
         /*...*/
    }
}

int main() {
  try {
    main_program();
  } catch( ... ) {                          // so far, so good, looks safe
    std::cout << "An error has occurred\n"; // you won't see this
  }
} 
```

In the absence of threads, this would be working code. <samp class="listingcharacter">data.at(666)</samp> does throw an exception, but that's not forbidden. The thrown <samp class="listingcharacter">out_of_range</samp> exception does not match the <samp class="listingcharacter">runtime_error</samp> specified in <samp class="listingcharacter">catch</samp>. So the exception leaves <samp class="listingcharacter">main_program</samp> and is caught in <samp class="listingcharacter">catch(...)</samp>. There—without threads—the output “An error …” would appear.
